### 2.2.9 Known Deviations and Documented Anomalies

The following are documented facts about the repository, not requirements. They are recorded here because they materially affect how the features above behave when consumed, and each was confirmed by direct observation.

| ID | Deviation | Evidence | Affected Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-001 | `package.json` declares `main` as `index.js`, but no `index.js` file exists in the repository | Requiring the package root fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and the message that the `main` entry cannot be found; a full file listing confirms `index.js` is absent | F-004 |
| D-002 | The README title `hao-backprop-test` differs from the npm package name `hello_world` | `README.md` line 1 versus `package.json` line 2 and `package-lock.json` line 2 | F-004, F-006 |
| D-003 | `npm test` fails by design, so any pipeline gating on a passing test suite fails against this repository | `scripts.test` is `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`; measured exit code 1 | F-007 |
| D-004 | No `start` script is declared, yet `npm start` launches the server | The `scripts` map contains only `test`; `npm start` nonetheless printed `> node server.js`, bound the listener, and served a `200`/14-byte response — npm supplies this default because a `server.js` file exists at the package root, so the behavior belongs to the npm CLI rather than to this repository | F-001, F-004 |
| D-005 | No runtime version constraint is expressed, so the supported Node.js range is undeclared | No `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` file exists; verification was performed on Node.js v22.23.1 with npm 11.18.0 | F-001, F-004 |


## 2.3 Feature Relationships

Only relationships that are directly evident in the four repository files are documented here. Because there are no modules, no exports, no dependency injection, and no configuration layer, the relationship graph is shallow: three runtime features share a single file and a single pair of constants, three packaging features share the manifest pair, and one documentary feature constrains all of them.

### 2.3.1 Feature Dependency Map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    HTTPMOD["Node.js core http module<br/>the only import in the repository"]
    NPMCLI["npm CLI<br/>script runner and lockfile reader"]
    GITBASE["Git baseline<br/>single commit 1a0874d"]

    subgraph RuntimeService["Runtime Service - server.js"]
        F001["F-001 HTTP Listener Binding<br/>lines 3-4, 6, 12"]
        F002["F-002 Invariant Fixed Response<br/>lines 6-10"]
        F003["F-003 Startup Announcement<br/>lines 12-14"]
        F001 --> F002
        F001 --> F003
    end

    subgraph Packaging["Packaging and Tooling - manifests"]
        F004["F-004 Package Identity<br/>package.json"]
        F005["F-005 Zero-Dependency Lock<br/>package-lock.json"]
        F007["F-007 Placeholder Test Script<br/>package.json lines 6-8"]
        F004 --> F005
        F004 --> F007
    end

    subgraph Governance["Documentation and Governance"]
        F006["F-006 Purpose and Immutability<br/>README.md"]
    end

    HTTPMOD --> F001
    NPMCLI --> F005
    NPMCLI --> F007
    GITBASE --> F006
    F006 -.->|"constrains change to"| F001
    F006 -.->|"constrains change to"| F004
```

**Dependency edges and their evidence**

| Edge | Type | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| F-001 → F-002 | Hard runtime dependency | The handler registered at `server.js` line 6 executes only for connections the listener accepts |
| F-001 → F-003 | Hard runtime dependency | The announcement is emitted from the `server.listen` callback (`server.js` lines 12–14), so it fires only after a successful bind |
| F-004 → F-005 | Data-consistency dependency | The lockfile root entry duplicates the manifest's `name`, `version`, and `license`; `npm ci` fails on divergence |
| F-004 → F-007 | Containment dependency | `scripts.test` is declared inside `package.json` and is reachable only through the manifest |
| F-006 → all features | Governance constraint (advisory) | The "Do not touch!" directive in `README.md` line 2, elevated to a functional requirement by section 1.1.2 |

**Relationships that do not exist.** The runtime features (F-001…F-003) and the packaging features (F-004, F-005, F-007) have **no code-level coupling**: `server.js` never reads `package.json`, and neither manifest references `server.js`. The two groups are joined only at the level of consumer workflow — a consumer reads the manifests and then executes the script. The one apparent exception is supplied externally: `npm start` reaches `server.js` through npm's built-in default rather than through any declaration in the repository (deviation D-004 in section 2.2.9).

### 2.3.2 Process Flow and Related Flowcharts

The request-level process flow — client, loopback boundary, handler, and fixed response — is documented in the flowchart in section **1.2.2.2** and is not duplicated here. The complementary view below is the **process lifecycle**, including the two terminal paths that the requirements in section 2.2.2 describe.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Invoke(["node server.js invoked"]) --> LoadMod["Load Node core http module<br/>server.js line 1"]
    LoadMod --> CreateSrv["Create server and register inline handler<br/>server.js lines 6-10"]
    CreateSrv --> BindDec{"Is 127.0.0.1:3000 available?"}
    BindDec -->|"available"| Announce["Emit startup line to stdout<br/>F-003-RQ-001"]
    BindDec -->|"already bound"| BindFail["Unhandled error event EADDRINUSE<br/>stack trace to stderr, exit code 1<br/>F-001-RQ-004"]
    Announce --> Ready(["Listener ready on loopback only<br/>F-001-RQ-002"])
    Ready -->|"any method, path, or body"| Serve["Set status 200, text/plain,<br/>14-byte body<br/>F-002-RQ-001 through RQ-005"]
    Serve --> Ready
    Ready -->|"SIGTERM or SIGINT"| Halt(["Immediate termination<br/>no connection drain, port released"])
```

| Flow Stage | Features Exercised | Terminal Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Module load and server creation | F-001 | None; synchronous and unconditional |
| Bind decision | F-001, F-003 | Success announces readiness; conflict exits with code 1 |
| Steady-state request service | F-002 | Loops indefinitely; no request can alter state |
| Termination | F-001 | Immediate on signal; no handler, no drain, no exit log |

### 2.3.3 Integration Points

| Integration Point | Direction | Features | Contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| TCP socket on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | F-001, F-002 | Any HTTP request receives `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes |
| Process standard output | Outbound, host-local | F-003 | Exactly one readiness line, then silence |
| Process standard error | Outbound, host-local | F-001 | Used only by Node's default unhandled-error path on bind failure |
| `package.json` / `package-lock.json` manifest pair | Consumed by tooling | F-004, F-005, F-007 | npm conventions: identity, no-op install, `test` script exiting 1 |
| Git repository and history | Consumed by tooling | F-006 | Single-commit baseline evidencing immutability |

There are **no outbound integration points** beyond the local streams above. Section 1.3.2.3 records the verified absence of databases, brokers, caches, third-party APIs, identity providers, object storage, secret managers, and telemetry backends; the single `require` in the repository targets a Node core module, so no client or SDK exists that could initiate an outbound call.

### 2.3.4 Shared Components

| Shared Component | Location | Consuming Features |
|---|---|---|
| `hostname` and `port` constants | `server.js` lines 3–4 | F-001 (bind target) and F-003 (announced URL) |
| `server` object returned by `http.createServer` | `server.js` line 6 | F-001 (owns `listen`), F-002 (owns the handler) |
| `res` response object | Handler parameter, `server.js` lines 6–9 | F-002 exclusively |
| Package identity fields (`name`, `version`, `license`) | `package.json` and `package-lock.json` | F-004 and F-005 — duplicated and required to agree |
| `scripts` map | `package.json` lines 6–8 | F-004 (declares it) and F-007 (is its only entry) |

The constant-sharing relationship is the single most consequential coupling in the system: because `server.js` line 13 interpolates the same two constants that line 12 passes to `listen`, the announced URL cannot drift from the actual bind target. There is no other mechanism in the repository that guarantees agreement between documentation and behavior.

### 2.3.5 Common Services

All shared services are supplied by the runtime environment; the repository implements none of its own — there is no middleware layer, no logging service, no configuration service, and no error-handling service anywhere in the code.

| Common Service | Provider | Features Relying On It |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP transport, request parsing, response serialization | Node.js core `http` module | F-001, F-002 |
| Default response framing headers (`Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`) | Node.js `http` defaults, not repository code | F-002 |
| Default unhandled-`'error'` termination and default signal handling | Node.js runtime | F-001 |
| Standard output and standard error streams | Operating-system process I/O | F-001, F-003 |
| Script running, manifest parsing, lockfile-driven install | npm CLI | F-004, F-005, F-007 |
| History, working-tree state, and provenance | Git | F-006 |

Because these services are external, their defaults are part of the observable contract without being under repository control. Section 1.2.2.3 makes the same point about response headers: a change to Node.js defaults in a future release would change observed behavior with no change to this codebase. Deviations D-004 and D-005 in section 2.2.9 are further instances of the same principle — npm supplies the implicit `start` behavior, and no `engines` constraint pins the runtime whose defaults are being relied upon.


## 2.4 Implementation Considerations

The considerations below are stated per feature and derive from what the implementation does and does not contain. Several categories resolve to "not applicable" for this system; where that is the case it is stated plainly rather than filled with generic guidance, in keeping with the evidence discipline applied throughout this specification.

### 2.4.1 Technical Constraints

| Feature | Technical Constraints |
|---|---|
| F-001 | Bind address and port are `const` literals (`server.js` lines 3–4) and cannot be changed without editing source — zero `process.env` references exist. Exactly one instance can run per host, because a second bind fails fatally. Plain HTTP only; no `https` usage exists anywhere. No `engines` field declares a supported Node.js range (D-005). |
| F-002 | The response is a compiled-in literal, so it cannot be varied by request, configuration, or content negotiation. Only `Content-Type` is under repository control; all other headers are Node defaults. There is no error path — no status other than `200` can be produced by this code. |
| F-003 | The sink is fixed to standard output via `console.log`; there is no log level, format, rotation, or file destination. The message is emitted exactly once per process, so a consumer that misses it has no second readiness signal to observe. |
| F-004 | `main` points to a non-existent `index.js`, so the package cannot be resolved by name (D-001). No `start` script is declared, making the launch path dependent on npm's implicit default (D-004). No `type` field is present, fixing the module system as CommonJS. |
| F-005 | `lockfileVersion: 3` constrains consumers to an npm release that understands that format. The lockfile must remain synchronized with the manifest's identity fields or `npm ci` will reject the install. |
| F-006 | The directive is advisory: nothing inside the repository enforces it, since there are no hooks, no `.github/` directory, and no CI configuration. Verification of immutability depends on external version-control state rather than on any repository mechanism. |
| F-007 | The script depends on a shell providing `echo` and `exit`; it is a placeholder and cannot be extended into a real suite without violating F-006. |

### 2.4.2 Performance Requirements

**No performance requirement is declared anywhere in the repository.** Section 1.2.3.3 records this as a verified absence — there is no metrics library, no instrumentation, no tracing, no latency or throughput target, no error budget, and no timeout, keep-alive, or socket-tuning setting in the code. This specification therefore states no numeric performance target, because none can be sourced from the artifact.

What can be asserted are the invariance properties that were measured, which are the only performance-adjacent guarantees the implementation makes:

| Feature | Measured Property | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| F-001 | Bind occurs synchronously during process start with no retry loop | Readiness is effectively immediate; failure is immediate as well |
| F-002 | 50 sequential requests across distinct paths and 20 concurrent requests yielded a single response signature (`200` / 14 bytes / `text/plain`) | Response cost is constant and independent of request content or concurrency |
| F-002 | Payload is a fixed 14-byte literal with no serialization, template rendering, or I/O | Per-request work is bounded and identical for every request |
| F-003 | Exactly one line of output per process, irrespective of request volume | Logging contributes no per-request overhead |
| F-005 | `npm ci` completes with no network fetch and creates no `node_modules` | Install cost is effectively fixed and offline-capable |

Any latency, throughput, or availability objective for this system must be defined and measured by the consuming tooling. The observed environment for all measurements in this specification was Node.js v22.23.1 with npm 11.18.0; those figures characterize the environment, not a repository requirement.

### 2.4.3 Scalability Considerations

| Feature | Scalability Position |
|---|---|
| F-001 | Single process, single port, single host. No clustering, worker threads, or child processes exist — searches for `cluster` and `worker` return zero matches. Horizontal scaling on one host is impossible because the port is hardcoded and a duplicate bind terminates the process (F-001-RQ-004). |
| F-001 | Loopback binding precludes any load balancer, reverse proxy, or remote client, so scaling beyond the host is not merely unimplemented but structurally excluded (section 1.3.2.4). |
| F-002 | The handler is stateless and mutates nothing, so concurrent request handling is safe within the single Node event loop — confirmed by 20 concurrent requests returning one identical signature. Vertical concurrency is limited only by the event loop, as no blocking or synchronous I/O call exists in the handler. |
| F-003 | Logging does not scale with load because it is emitted once at startup; there is no per-request log volume to manage. |
| F-004, F-005 | Manifest and lockfile scale trivially: the dependency graph has exactly one node, so install time and audit surface do not grow. |
| F-006, F-007 | No scalability dimension applies; both are static artifacts. |

Scaling this system in any dimension would require code changes, which F-006 places outside the sanctioned scope. Scalability is therefore correctly read as a non-goal of the artifact rather than as an unmet requirement.

### 2.4.4 Security Implications

The repository contains no security controls of its own beyond the network-scope restriction, and it also presents an unusually small attack surface. Both facts are stated below with their evidence; no control is claimed that does not exist.

| Feature | Security Implications |
|---|---|
| F-001 | The loopback bind is the system's **only** network control, and it is effective: connections to the host's routable address were refused. There is no TLS, so traffic is plaintext — acceptable only because it never leaves the host. There is no firewall rule, allowlist, or connection limit in the repository. |
| F-001 | Bind failure prints a stack trace to stderr. The disclosed content is limited to the address, port, syscall, and Node internals — no credential or environment data is exposed, because none exists in the process. |
| F-002 | No authentication, authorization, session, cookie, or token handling exists; every caller is anonymous and receives identical output (section 1.3.1.2). Because the request is never read, whole classes of input-driven vulnerability are structurally absent: no body deserialization, no query or header parsing, no injection sink, and no payload-size handling. |
| F-002 | No filesystem access occurs — there are zero `fs` references — so path traversal is inert; the probe `/../etc/passwd` returned the same `200` / 14-byte response as `/`. Responses set no security headers (no CORS, CSP, HSTS, or `X-Content-Type-Options`), which is consistent with the loopback-only, fixed-plaintext-payload design. |
| F-003 | The startup line discloses only the loopback address and port. Because nothing is logged per request, no client address, header, or payload is ever recorded — there is no log-based data-retention exposure. |
| F-004, F-005 | Zero declared and zero locked dependencies eliminate the transitive supply-chain surface entirely; `npm ci` reported zero vulnerabilities across the single audited package. No credential material, `.npmrc`, or registry token exists in the repository. |
| F-006 | Immutability is a governance control, not a technical one. Detection of unauthorized change relies on the single-commit provenance and a clean working tree; nothing prevents modification. |
| F-007 | The test command executes only shell built-ins and reads no input, file, or network resource. |

**Compliance.** No compliance requirement is expressed or implicated anywhere in the repository. Section 1.3.1.2 establishes that the system processes no personal, regulated, or business data — the entire data domain is one static 14-byte greeting plus two configuration literals — so no data-retention, encryption, residency, or privacy obligation arises from the code as written. The only distribution term stated is the MIT license declared in both manifests, and no `LICENSE` file accompanies that declaration.

### 2.4.5 Maintenance Requirements

| Feature | Maintenance Requirements |
|---|---|
| F-001, F-002, F-003 | No routine maintenance is implied: no dependency updates are possible, no configuration drifts, and no state accumulates. The material maintenance risk is external — because no `engines` constraint pins the runtime (D-005), a future Node.js release could alter default framing headers or default error behavior and thereby change observed responses with no change to this code (section 1.2.2.3). |
| F-004, F-005 | The only synchronization obligation in the repository is between `package.json` and `package-lock.json` identity fields; any change to name, version, or license must be applied to both or `npm ci` will fail. |
| F-006 | The immutability directive inverts normal maintenance expectations: the correct maintenance action for this repository is **no action**. Section 1.3.2.5 confirms no roadmap, backlog, `TODO`/`FIXME` marker, changelog, or open branch exists, and records the current content as the intended final state. |
| F-007 | Because `npm test` fails by design (D-003), consuming pipelines — not this repository — must be maintained to tolerate that exit code. |
| All | The known deviations D-001 through D-005 are recorded as documented facts, not defects scheduled for repair. Correcting D-001 or D-002 would require editing files that F-006 forbids changing. |

### 2.4.6 Assumptions and Constraints Register

| ID | Assumption or Constraint | Basis and Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| A-001 | A Node.js runtime supporting CommonJS `require` and the standard `http` API is available | `server.js` line 1 and the absence of a `"type"` field; no version range is declared, so the assumption is unbounded (section 1.3.1.1) |
| A-002 | TCP port `3000` on the loopback interface is free at launch | Hardcoded `port` with no fallback; contention terminates the process with exit code 1 |
| A-003 | Consumers launch the server by naming `server.js`, or rely on npm's implicit default | No `start` script is declared and `main` is unresolvable (D-001, D-004) |
| A-004 | Consuming automation tolerates a `npm test` exit code of 1 and an install that produces no `node_modules` | Measured behavior of F-007 and F-005 |
| A-005 | The npm CLI in use understands `lockfileVersion: 3` | `package-lock.json` line 4 |
| C-001 | Repository content must not be modified | `README.md` line 2; treated as a first-class functional requirement by section 1.1.2 |
| C-002 | The service is unreachable from outside the host | Verified loopback-only binding; off-host exposure is out of scope (section 1.3.2.1) |
| C-003 | Behavior cannot be altered at runtime by configuration | Zero `process.env` references; no config file exists |
| C-004 | Response headers other than `Content-Type` are outside repository control | Node `http` defaults supply `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` (section 1.2.2.3) |
| C-005 | The package cannot be consumed as a library | `server.js` declares no exports and `main` resolves to a missing file (section 1.3.2.4) |

# 3. Technology Stack

## 3.1 Programming Languages

This repository is a **single-language codebase**. Of the four tracked files established in section 1.1, exactly one contains executable program code — `server.js` — and it is written in JavaScript for direct execution by the Node.js runtime. The other three files are declarative or documentary: `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are JSON documents consumed by the npm CLI, and `README.md` is CommonMark prose. `git ls-files` returns exactly four paths, whose extensions are `.js` (one), `.json` (two), and `.md` (one); no other extension exists anywhere in the repository, and there are no subdirectories.

There is no generated, compiled, transpiled, minified, or bundled source. A search for `sourceMappingURL` returns nothing, no `dist/`, `build/`, or `lib/` directory exists, and no `.map` file is tracked. Consequently the file that is committed is byte-for-byte the file that executes, which is what makes the "no installation, build, transpile, or bundling step" requirement recorded in section 1.3.1.1 literally true rather than merely aspirational.

### 3.1.1 Language Inventory by Component

Each component identified in the component table of section 1.2.2.2 maps to exactly one language or format:

| Component | Language / Format | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP transport, server instance, request handler, listener, startup logger, configuration constants | JavaScript (CommonJS) | `server.js` |
| Package identity, script declaration, license declaration (F-004) | JSON | `package.json` |
| Dependency-graph lock (F-005) | JSON, npm `lockfileVersion: 3` schema | `package-lock.json` |
| Purpose statement and immutability directive (F-006) | CommonMark (Markdown) | `README.md` |
| Placeholder test command (F-007) | POSIX shell one-liner embedded in JSON | `package.json` `scripts.test` |

Measured distribution across the repository:

| Language / Format | Files | Lines | Bytes (share of 913) |
|---|---|---|---|
| JavaScript | 1 | 14 | 342 (37.5%) |
| JSON | 2 | 23 | 498 (54.5%) |
| CommonMark | 1 | 2 | 73 (8.0%) |
| **Total** | **4** | **39** | **913 (100%)** |

JSON and CommonMark are data and documentation formats, not programming languages. Restricted to executable program code, **JavaScript accounts for 100% of the repository**. There is no second language tier of any kind: no browser-executed code exists (no `.html` or `.css` file, and `package.json` declares no `browserslist` target), and no native, mobile, or desktop source exists.

### 3.1.2 JavaScript Language Level and Module System

The language level of `server.js` was determined by enumerating every syntactic construct the file actually uses:

| Construct Used | Source Location | Language Level Required |
|---|---|---|
| `const` binding | `server.js` lines 3, 4, 6 | ECMAScript 2015 |
| Arrow function expression | `server.js` lines 6, 12 | ECMAScript 2015 |
| Template literal with two interpolations | `server.js` line 13 | ECMAScript 2015 |
| `require()` of a string-literal specifier | `server.js` line 1 | CommonJS (a Node module convention, not an ECMAScript feature) |

A construct sweep confirmed **zero** occurrences of `let`, `var`, the `function` keyword, `class`, `import`, `export`, `async`, `await`, optional chaining (`?.`), nullish coalescing (`??`), and spread/rest (`...`). ECMAScript 2015 is therefore both the ceiling and the floor of the dialect in use: nothing newer is required, and nothing older would suffice.

```javascript
const http = require('http');
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { /* three statements */ });
```

**Module system.** `package.json` has exactly seven top-level keys — `name`, `version`, `description`, `main`, `scripts`, `author`, `license` — and `"type"` is not among them. Node.js therefore applies its default and loads `server.js` as **CommonJS**, which is consistent with the `require` on line 1 and with the total absence of ESM syntax. The file declares no exports at all (`module.exports` never appears), so it is an executable script rather than a consumable module — the condition registered as constraint C-005 in section 2.4.6 and reflected in the `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` behaviour of deviation D-001, where `main` names a non-existent `index.js`.

Two further properties of the module were verified and matter for reasoning about the runtime:

- **Static module graph.** The repository contains exactly one `require()` call, and its specifier is a string literal (a search for a non-literal argument returns nothing). The module graph is fully determinable without executing anything: one node, zero edges to non-core code.
- **Sloppy mode.** No `"use strict"` directive appears in any file, so `server.js` evaluates under CommonJS sloppy-mode semantics. Nothing in the 14 lines depends on either mode, so this is a documented fact rather than a behavioural dependency.

**Format conventions of the JSON artifacts.** Both manifests parse without error and use four-space indentation. `package-lock.json` ends with a trailing newline; `package.json` does not. These are recorded because constraint C-001 forbids modification, so even whitespace normalisation would constitute a change to the fixture.

### 3.1.3 Runtime Requirements and Version Constraints

The repository expresses **no runtime version constraint whatsoever** — the condition catalogued as deviation D-005. There is no `engines` field in `package.json` (verified programmatically against a list of 27 candidate manifest fields, none of which are present), no `.nvmrc`, and no `.node-version` file. There is likewise no `packageManager` field pinning an npm version and no `os`/`cpu` platform restriction.

| Attribute | Value | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| Declared Node.js version range | *none* | `package.json` — no `engines` field (D-005) |
| Version-manager pin | *none* | no `.nvmrc`, no `.node-version` |
| Declared package-manager pin | *none* | `package.json` — no `packageManager` field |
| Node.js used for every measurement in this specification | 22.23.1 | measured `process.versions.node` |
| V8 engine | 12.4.254.21-node.56 | measured `process.versions.v8` |
| libuv | 1.51.0 | measured `process.versions.uv` |
| OpenSSL | 3.5.7 | measured `process.versions.openssl` |
| Native add-on ABI (`process.versions.modules`) | 127 | measured |
| Release channel self-reported by the binary | Long Term Support line codenamed `Jod` | measured `process.release.lts` |

Every value in the lower half of that table is an **environment observation, not a repository requirement** — the same framing section 2.5.5 uses for its verification-environment entry. Nothing in the four tracked files would change if the fixture were executed on a different Node.js build.

**Effective capability floor.** Derived from the source rather than from a declaration, a runtime is sufficient if it (a) resolves CommonJS `require`, (b) exposes the standard-library `http` module with the classic callback surface used on lines 6–12, and (c) supports ES2015 `const`, arrow functions, and template literals. Because the source uses no syntax newer than ES2015 and no API newer than that callback surface, the language level imposes no meaningful upper bound either. The ABI number above is relevant only to compiled native add-ons, of which there are none — section 3.3 establishes an empty dependency graph.

The one machine-readable Node.js range anywhere in the observed toolchain belongs to the tool rather than to the repository: npm 11.18.0 in the verification environment declares `engines: { "node": "^20.17.0 || >=22.9.0" }` in its own manifest. That bound applies to consumers who drive the repository through npm commands (`npm ci`, `npm test`, `npm start`); consumers who invoke `node server.js` directly are not subject to it.

**Security implication of the missing pin.** Because no supported range is declared, a consumer can run the fixture on a Node.js build that no longer receives security updates with nothing in the repository to signal the problem. The exposure that results is nonetheless narrow and was measured, not assumed: the process reads no request input (F-002-RQ-004), reads no environment variables or files, holds no credentials, and evaluates no dynamic code — sweeps for `eval(`, `new Function`, `child_process`, `execSync`, `spawn`, and `vm.` all return zero matches. The attack surface that a vulnerable runtime could expose is therefore confined to Node's own HTTP parser on a loopback-only socket (F-001-RQ-002).

### 3.1.4 Selection Criteria and Justification

The repository records no decision rationale — `README.md` is two lines and contains no design notes, links, or code examples. The criteria below are therefore reconstructed from the properties the artifact demonstrably has, in keeping with the reverse-derivation approach established in section 2.1.1.1.

| Selection Criterion | How JavaScript on Node.js Satisfies It | Supporting Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Committed source must be the executed artifact | No compile, transpile, link, or bundle step exists between the file and the running process | 1.3.1.1; direct execution of `node server.js` |
| HTTP service without third-party code | Node's standard library ships a complete HTTP server, so the single `require` on line 1 targets a core module | `server.js` line 1; F-005 empty install graph |
| Byte-level output determinism | 14 statements, no state, no branches, no I/O, no request inspection — one response signature under repetition and concurrency | F-002-RQ-005 |
| Legibility to the consuming automation | npm manifest conventions give external tooling a standard way to read identity and invoke scripts, which is the ecosystem-level integration described in section 1.2.1.3 | F-004; `npm pkg get` resolves `hello_world@1.0.0`, MIT |
| Near-zero cognitive load for reviewers | The complete implementation fits in 14 lines using only ES2015 constructs | 1.1.4; 2.2.1.2 uniform Low complexity |
| Fixture stability across hosts | Bind target and payload are in-source literals, so behaviour cannot drift with the deployment environment | F-001-RQ-003; zero `process.env` occurrences |

An additional consequence worth stating plainly: choosing a language whose runtime bundles an HTTP server is what allows the dependency count to be zero. Any framework-based alternative would have introduced a registry dependency and, with it, the resolution, availability, and vulnerability exposure that section 1.1.4 identifies as deliberately eliminated.

### 3.1.5 Constraints, Dependencies, and Languages Deliberately Absent

**Language-level constraints carried by the choice:**

| Constraint | Consequence for Consumers |
|---|---|
| CommonJS-only, no exports | The package cannot be `require`d as a library; it can only be executed (C-005, D-001) |
| No `engines` declaration | The supported runtime range is undeclared and must be decided by the consumer (D-005) |
| ES2015 syntax ceiling | Portability is maximal, but no modern-syntax affordance (ESM, `async`/`await`) is available to extend from without editing the file, which C-001 forbids |
| Single-file script, no module boundaries | There is no seam at which behaviour can be substituted or stubbed; the process is the unit of use |
| Pure ASCII, LF-only source | All four files contain zero non-ASCII bytes and zero carriage returns, so no encoding or line-ending negotiation is involved |

**Languages and dialects explicitly probed for and found absent.** Because a conventional enterprise default stack — Python with Flask on the backend, React with TypeScript on the web, React Native for cross-platform mobile, and Swift, Kotlin, or Objective-C for native targets — might otherwise be assumed for a document of this class, each was tested for directly:

| Candidate Language or Dialect | Status | Evidence of Absence |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript | Absent | No `.ts`/`.tsx` file; no `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json`; no `types`/`typings` manifest field; no `@types` dependency |
| ECMAScript modules (ESM) | Absent | No `"type": "module"`; no `.mjs` file; zero `import`/`export` occurrences |
| JSX / React dialect | Absent | No `.jsx`/`.tsx` file; zero matches for `react` across tracked files |
| Python | Absent | No `.py` file; no `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `Pipfile`; zero matches for `flask`, `django`, `fastapi`, `langchain` |
| Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C | Absent | No corresponding source files and no `Package.swift`, `build.gradle`, `pom.xml`, or Xcode project |
| Go, Rust, Java, Ruby, PHP, C/C++ | Absent | No `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pom.xml`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, or `CMakeLists.txt` |
| Shell | Present only as an embedded one-liner | `scripts.test` in `package.json` is `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`, executed by npm's script runner (F-007); no `.sh` file exists |

The shell fragment is the only non-JavaScript executable expression in the repository. It uses nothing but shell built-ins, touches no file, reads no input, and terminates with exit code 1 by design (F-007-RQ-001, D-003), so it introduces no interpreter dependency beyond a POSIX-style shell providing `echo` and `exit`.


## 3.2 Frameworks and Libraries

**The repository uses no application framework and no third-party library.** This is a measured fact, not an inference: `package.json` declares neither `dependencies` nor `devDependencies` (F-004-RQ-003), `package-lock.json` locks nothing but the root package (F-005-RQ-001), `npm ls --all` reports no dependency key at all, and the repository contains exactly one `require()` call — for the Node.js core module `http` on line 1 of `server.js`.

The entire framework layer is therefore the **Node.js standard library**, and its version is whatever version of Node.js the consumer happens to run, since the repository pins none (D-005). The only version numbers the repository itself declares are its own identity, `hello_world@1.0.0`, and the lockfile schema version, `lockfileVersion: 3`.

### 3.2.1 The Standard Library as the Framework Layer

Seven standard-library call and property sites constitute the complete framework surface of the system. The list below is exhaustive — no other API is touched anywhere in the repository.

| Standard-Library API | Site | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `require('http')` | `server.js` line 1 | The only module import in the repository; resolves a core module, so no resolution path outside the runtime is consulted |
| `http.createServer(handler)` | `server.js` line 6 | Creates the server object and registers the single inline request handler (F-002) |
| `server.listen(port, hostname, callback)` | `server.js` line 12 | Binds the loopback listener and schedules the readiness callback (F-001-RQ-001) |
| `res.statusCode` | `server.js` line 7 | Sets the invariant `200` status (F-002-RQ-001) |
| `res.setHeader(name, value)` | `server.js` line 8 | Sets `Content-Type: text/plain` — the only header set by repository code (F-002-RQ-002) |
| `res.end(payload)` | `server.js` line 9 | Emits the 14-byte payload and completes the response in a single call, with no chunked writes (F-002-RQ-003) |
| `console.log(message)` | `server.js` line 13 | Writes the single startup line to standard output (F-003-RQ-001) |

Two attributions matter for correctness when reading this surface:

- **The `req` object is never used.** It is bound as a handler parameter on line 6 and never dereferenced; searches for `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers`, and `req.on` all return zero matches (F-002-RQ-004). No parsing, routing, or negotiation capability of the `http` module is exercised.
- **Response framing headers come from the runtime, not from this repository.** The `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers observed on the wire are Node.js `http` defaults. This is the attribution established in section 1.2.2.3 and registered as constraint C-004; it must not be read as repository configuration.

The rest of the standard library is unused. Searches confirm zero references to `fs`, `path`, `https`, `net`, `crypto`, `url`, `os`, `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `child_process`, `vm`, `process.env`, and `process.argv`. Consequently the process performs no filesystem I/O, no TLS, no subprocess execution, no clustering, and no environment or argument parsing.

### 3.2.2 Stack Composition

```mermaid

    subgraph RepoLayer["Repository Source - 4 files, 39 lines, 913 bytes"]
        SRV["server.js<br/>14 lines, JavaScript ES2015, CommonJS"]
        PKG["package.json<br/>7 keys, 1 script, 0 dependencies"]
        LOCK["package-lock.json<br/>lockfileVersion 3, root entry only"]
        DOC["README.md<br/>purpose and do-not-modify directive"]
    end

    subgraph StdLibLayer["Node.js Standard Library - the entire framework layer"]

    end

    SRV --> HTTPMOD
    SRV --> CONSOLEMOD
```
