The diagram makes the load-bearing point visible: there is no layer between the repository source and the Node.js standard library. Every arrow leaving `server.js` terminates inside the runtime.

### 3.2.3 Supporting Libraries and the Roles They Would Otherwise Fill

For a conventional HTTP service, the following concerns are normally delegated to libraries. In this repository each is either satisfied by a standard-library primitive or genuinely absent:

| Concern | What Fills It Here | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP server | Node core `http` module | `server.js` line 1, 6, 12 |
| Routing and method dispatch | Nothing — every request receives the same response | F-002-RQ-001; zero `req.url`/`req.method` matches |
| Middleware, body parsing, CORS, compression | Nothing — the request is never read | F-002-RQ-004; section 1.3.2.1 excludes these |
| Response serialisation or templating | Nothing — a string literal is passed to `res.end` | `server.js` line 9 |
| Input validation | Nothing — validation is deliberately not performed | F-002-RQ-004 validation rules |
| Logging | `console.log`, invoked exactly once | F-003-RQ-001, F-003-RQ-003 |
| Configuration management | Two in-source `const` literals | F-001-RQ-003; zero `process.env` matches |
| Authentication and authorisation | Nothing — all callers are anonymous and indistinguishable | F-002-RQ-001 validation rules |
| Test framework and assertion library | Nothing — a shell `echo` and `exit 1` placeholder | F-007; D-003 |
| Type system | Nothing — no TypeScript, no `types`/`typings` field | section 3.1.5 |
| Build, bundling, transpilation | Nothing — no build step exists | section 1.3.1.1 |
| Process management, clustering, restart supervision | Nothing — a single process with no `cluster` usage | section 1.3.2.1 |
| Metrics, tracing, health endpoints | Nothing — no instrumentation of any kind | section 1.2.3.3 |

### 3.2.4 Compatibility Requirements

Because there is no library layer, there is no inter-library compatibility matrix to manage. `package.json` declares no `peerDependencies`, no `optionalDependencies`, and no `overrides`, so no version-resolution conflict can arise, and `npm outdated` returns empty output with exit code 0 — there is nothing that can drift. The compatibility surface reduces to the runtime and toolchain requirements below.

| Requirement | Floor or Value | Why It Binds |
|---|---|---|
| CommonJS module loader | Required | `server.js` line 1 uses `require`; no `"type"` field exists (assumption A-001) |
| ECMAScript 2015 syntax support | Required | `const`, arrow functions, and template literals are used; nothing newer is |
| Standard-library `http` with the classic callback API | Required | `http.createServer`, `server.listen`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end` on lines 6–12 |
| npm able to read `lockfileVersion: 3` | The v3 format is written by npm v9 and above and, per npm's own bundled documentation, is backwards compatible to npm v7 | Assumption A-005 and the manifest-compatibility requirement in section 1.3.1.1; the file carries no legacy top-level `dependencies` block, so an older CLI would find nothing usable |
| POSIX-style shell providing `echo` and `exit` | Required only to invoke `npm test` | F-007-RQ-001 |
| TCP port 3000 free on the loopback interface | Required at bind time | Assumption A-002; contention terminates the process with exit code 1 (F-001-RQ-004) |
| Native compilation toolchain (`node-gyp`, C++ compiler) | **Not** required | Zero dependencies means no native add-on can be built or loaded |
| Network access to a package registry | **Not** required | `npm ci --offline` and `npm install --offline` both complete with exit code 0 |

### 3.2.5 Justification for the Zero-Framework Design

The framework decision is not documented anywhere in the repository, so the justification below is derived from the properties the design actually delivers.

| Property Delivered | Why the Absence of a Framework Produces It |
|---|---|
| Byte-level determinism | With no middleware chain, no content negotiation, and no framework-supplied error pages, the response cannot vary — one signature across 50 sequential, 20 concurrent, and eight method variants (F-002-RQ-005) |
| Zero supply-chain surface | Nothing is downloaded, so no integrity hash, provenance check, or CVE feed applies; `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across a single audited package (F-005-RQ-002) |
| Offline, no-op installation | A framework would make install a network operation; here `npm ci` completes in about 120 ms without creating `node_modules` |
| Committed source equals executed source | No framework build, code generation, or decorator transform sits between the file and the process |
| Complete auditability | The whole implementation is 14 lines with a seven-call standard-library surface, which is why section 2.2.1.2 rates every requirement Low complexity |
| Attribution of failures to the consumer | Because the subject has no framework behaviour of its own to misconfigure, an anomaly observed by consuming tooling isolates to that tooling — the fixture rationale in section 1.1.2 |

The cost of the decision is equally concrete and is documented as excluded scope in section 1.3.2.1 rather than as a defect: there is no routing, no error handling (no `'error'` listener and no `try`/`catch` anywhere), no graceful shutdown, no TLS, no rate limiting, and no security headers. For a fixture whose contract is invariance, those omissions are the point; for any other purpose they are disqualifying, which is why section 1.3.2.4 lists production and CI-gate usage as unsupported.

### 3.2.6 Frameworks Explicitly Probed For and Found Absent

Every marker below was searched for across all tracked files, case-insensitively, and returned **zero matches**:

| Category | Candidates Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js web frameworks | `express`, `fastify`, `koa`, `hapi`, `nest`, `next` | Absent |
| Front-end frameworks | `react`, `vue`, `angular`, `svelte`, `jquery` | Absent |
| CSS frameworks | `tailwind` | Absent |
| Utility and HTTP-client libraries | `lodash`, `axios`, `socket.io` | Absent |
| API layers | `graphql`, `apollo` | Absent |
| Python frameworks | `flask`, `django`, `fastapi` | Absent |
| AI / LLM frameworks | `langchain` | Absent |
| Desktop, mobile, native toolkits | `electron`, `swift`, `kotlin` | Absent |

A conventional default stack for a system of this description would specify Flask on the backend, React with TypeScript and TailwindCSS on the web, React Native for mobile, and Langchain for AI orchestration. **None of those technologies is present in this repository**, and constraint C-001 forbids introducing them. They are recorded here as verified absences so that no reader mistakes an assumed default for an observed dependency.


## 3.3 Open Source Dependencies

**The open-source dependency set is empty.** No third-party package is declared, locked, vendored, or installed. This subsection documents the evidence for that claim, the lockfile that asserts it, the registry configuration that is never exercised, and the security and licensing consequences — which are unusual precisely because the set is empty rather than merely small.

### 3.3.1 Declared Dependency Inventory

`package.json` contains exactly seven top-level keys, none of which carries dependency information. Every dependency-bearing field defined by the npm manifest schema was probed for programmatically and is absent:

| Manifest Field | Declared Entries | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `dependencies` | 0 | Field absent from the manifest (F-004-RQ-003) |
| `devDependencies` | 0 | Field absent |
| `peerDependencies` | 0 | Field absent |
| `optionalDependencies` | 0 | Field absent |
| `bundleDependencies` | 0 | Field absent |
| `overrides` | 0 | Field absent — no resolution can be forced or patched |
| `workspaces` | 0 | Field absent — not a monorepo root |

The corresponding runtime evidence agrees: the repository contains exactly one `require()` call, and it resolves the Node.js core module `http` (section 3.2.1). `npm ls` prints `hello_world@1.0.0` followed by `└── (empty)`, and `npm ls --all --json` emits no `dependencies` key at all. **The dependency graph is one node — the root package itself — with depth 0 and zero edges.**

### 3.3.2 Lockfile Structure and Schema Version

`package-lock.json` is 13 lines and 247 bytes. Its top-level keys are exactly `name`, `version`, `lockfileVersion`, `requires`, and `packages`:

```json
"lockfileVersion": 3,
"requires": true,
"packages": { "": { "name": "hello_world", "version": "1.0.0", "license": "MIT" } }
```

| Lockfile Element | Value | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| `lockfileVersion` | `3` (numeric) | Modern schema; the file carries **no** legacy top-level `dependencies` block, which is the defining characteristic of v3 |
| `requires` | `true` | Standard flag written by npm for lockfiles that track the manifest's requirement set |
| `packages` | Exactly one key, `""` | The root project only; **no third-party package record exists** (F-005-RQ-001) |
| Root record fields | `name`, `version`, `license` | `hello_world`, `1.0.0`, `MIT` — mirroring `package.json` exactly (F-005-RQ-003) |

**Compatibility floor.** According to the `package-lock.json` manual page bundled with the installed npm CLI, `lockfileVersion: 3` is the format used by npm v9 and above and is backwards compatible to npm v7; version 2 was used by npm v7 and v8, and version 1 by npm v5 and v6. Because this file omits the v1-compatibility block entirely, an npm older than v7 would find nothing usable in it. That is exactly the constraint registered as assumption A-005 in section 2.4.6 and listed as a key technical requirement in section 1.3.1.1. Measured behaviour confirms the format is stable in place: npm 11.18.0 read the file for `ls`, `ci`, `install`, and `audit`, and its MD5 digest was **unchanged** afterwards — npm neither rewrote nor migrated it.

**Why an empty lockfile is present at all.** Shipping a lockfile that locks nothing is a deliberate assertion rather than an oversight. `npm ci` refuses to run without a lockfile, so its presence is what lets consuming automation use the strict, reproducible install path and still get a no-op. Section 2.1.7 makes the same point from the feature perspective.

### 3.3.3 Package Registry Configuration

| Attribute | Observed Value | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| Effective registry | `https://registry.npmjs.org/` | npm's built-in default (`npm config get registry`) |
| Repository-level `.npmrc` | Absent | No `.npmrc` at the repository root |
| User- and global-level npm configuration | Absent | No `.npmrc` in the user home directory and none at `/usr/etc/npmrc`, `/etc/npmrc`, or npm's built-in config path |
| Registry authentication | None configured | No `_authToken`; `always-auth` undefined; `npm config list` reports no non-default entries |
| Scoped registries or mirrors | None | No configuration file exists in which to declare one |

The registry is therefore a **latent default that is never contacted**. Both `npm ci --offline` and `npm install --offline` complete with exit code 0, proving that no registry round-trip is required for any supported workflow. Combined with the absence of credentials anywhere in the repository (a sweep for `token`, `secret`, `password`, `credential`, and `api key` returns zero matches), there is no registry authentication surface to protect.

**Alternate package managers.** No `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, or `bun.lockb` exists, and `package.json` declares no `packageManager` field. npm is the only package manager the repository is configured for, and nothing contradicts the single lockfile — consistent with the alternate-lockfile exclusion recorded in section 1.3.2.

### 3.3.4 Measured Install, Audit, and Drift Behaviour

All measurements below were executed against an unmodified copy of the repository under Node.js 22.23.1 and npm 11.18.0, honouring the do-not-modify directive of F-006 by leaving the tracked checkout byte-identical.

| Command | Observed Result | Exit Code |
|---|---|---|
| `npm ls` | `hello_world@1.0.0` then `└── (empty)` | 0 |
| `npm ls --all --json` | No `dependencies` key; dependency count 0 | 0 |
| `npm ci` | "up to date" in roughly 120 ms; **`node_modules` not created** | 0 |
| `npm ci --offline` | Completes without any network access | 0 |
| `npm install --offline` | Completes without any network access | 0 |
| `npm audit` | "found 0 vulnerabilities" across a single audited package | 0 |
| `npm outdated` | Empty output — nothing can drift | 0 |
| `npm run` (script listing) | Only the `test` lifecycle script exists | 0 |

Two results deserve emphasis because they are counter-intuitive for anyone expecting a normal Node.js project. First, a successful `npm ci` leaves **no `node_modules` directory** — there is nothing to place in one, which is the tolerance requirement registered as assumption A-004 in section 2.4.6. Second, the lockfile's digest is identical before and after install, so repeated installs are provably idempotent at the file level.

### 3.3.5 Licensing Posture

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| Declared license | `MIT`, stated in `package.json` line 10 and duplicated in the `package-lock.json` root record |
| License text file | **None.** No `LICENSE`, `LICENCE`, `COPYING`, or `NOTICE` file is tracked — the declaration exists only as a metadata string |
| Inbound third-party license obligations | **None.** With zero installed packages there is no attribution list to maintain, no copyleft exposure, and no license-compatibility analysis to perform |
| Attribution requirements imposed on consumers | Governed solely by the MIT declaration; no `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` artifact is required because no third-party code is redistributed |

The missing license text is a documentation gap rather than a technical one, and it is consistent with the broader absence of governance artifacts noted in section 2.1.8 (no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no `CODEOWNERS`, no `.gitignore`).

### 3.3.6 Supply-Chain Security Implications

An empty dependency graph eliminates most of the supply-chain risk categories that would otherwise apply to a Node.js project. The table records exposure and the basis for each assessment:

| Risk Category | Exposure | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Transitive vulnerabilities | None | `npm audit` audits one package and reports zero vulnerabilities |
| Typosquatting and dependency confusion | None | No package name is ever resolved against a registry |
| Malicious install scripts | None | No dependencies exist to run lifecycle hooks, and `scripts` contains only `test` — there is no `preinstall`, `postinstall`, or `prepare` hook |
| Artifact integrity and provenance | Not applicable | Nothing is downloaded, so no integrity hash or provenance attestation is consulted |
| Registry availability as a single point of failure | Eliminated | Offline install succeeds with exit code 0 |
| Version drift between environments | None | `npm outdated` is empty and the lockfile digest is stable across installs |
| Lockfile tampering | Confined to the root record | The only lockable data is the root identity; a mismatch against `package.json` would cause `npm ci` to fail, which is what makes F-004-RQ-004 verifiable |
| Credential exposure via registry configuration | None | No `.npmrc` and no auth token exist at any configuration level |

**Residual risk lies outside the dependency graph.** The one unmanaged version surface is the runtime itself: because the repository declares no `engines` range (D-005), responsibility for running a patched Node.js build rests entirely with the consumer, and no repository artifact records or warns about it. Section 3.1.3 bounds the resulting exposure with measured negatives; the point here is simply that a zero-dependency posture removes the package supply chain from consideration but does not remove the runtime supply chain.


## 3.4 Third-Party Services

**The system integrates with no third-party service.** It calls no external API, delegates to no identity provider, reports to no monitoring backend, and consumes no cloud service. Every claim in this subsection rests on an exhaustive census of the four tracked files rather than on the absence of an integration document.

### 3.4.1 External APIs and Outbound Integrations

The `http` module is used exclusively in **server mode**. A case-insensitive sweep across all tracked files returned zero matches for every outbound-call and messaging marker probed:

| Category | Markers Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP clients | `fetch(`, `http.request`, `http.get`, `https.request`, `XMLHttpRequest` | Zero matches |
| Raw sockets and name resolution | `net.connect`, `dns` | Zero matches |
| Streaming and RPC | `WebSocket`, `grpc` | Zero matches |
| Message brokers and queues | `amqp`, `kafka`, `mqtt`, `nats`, `sqs`, `sns`, `pubsub` | Zero matches |
| Event delivery | `webhook` | Zero matches |

A complete census of network literals is decisive on this point. Searching every tracked file for URL schemes, dotted-quad addresses, and the `.com`, `.io`, `.net`, and `.org` top-level domains returns **exactly two lines, both in `server.js`**: the loopback bind constant on line 3 and the self-referential URL interpolated into the startup message on line 13. There is no external hostname, domain, endpoint, base URL, API path, or third-party address anywhere in the repository. Because there is also no `process.env` usage and no configuration file, no endpoint can be injected at runtime either (F-001-RQ-003).

The practical consequence is that the process has **no egress path**. There is no channel through which request data could be forwarded, no telemetry beacon, and no update or licence check.

### 3.4.2 Authentication and Identity Services

No authentication or authorisation technology of any kind is present. Markers probed with zero matches include `auth0`, `okta`, `oauth`, `jwt`, `passport`, and `bcrypt`, alongside the credential-material terms `token`, `secret`, `password`, `credential`, and `api key`.

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| Identity provider | None — no federation, no OIDC or SAML flow, no client registration |
| Credential storage | None — no `.env`, no `.npmrc`, no secret of any kind in any tracked file |
| Request-level authentication | None — the request object is never read, so no header, cookie, or bearer token can be evaluated (F-002-RQ-004) |
| Session or state management | None — the handler is stateless and no session store exists |
| Caller identity | All callers are anonymous and indistinguishable, as recorded in the F-002-RQ-001 validation rules |

Auth0 — the identity service a conventional default stack would specify — is **not present and not applicable**. The only access control in the system is network-level: the listener binds `127.0.0.1`, so it is unreachable from any non-loopback interface (F-001-RQ-002, constraint C-002).

### 3.4.3 Monitoring, Logging, and Observability Services

No monitoring, APM, tracing, or log-aggregation client exists. Markers probed with zero matches: `sentry`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `prometheus`, `opentelemetry`, `statsd`, `winston`, `pino`, and `bunyan`.

| Observability Concern | What Exists |
|---|---|
| Application logging | A single `console.log` call on `server.js` line 13, emitted once per process (F-003-RQ-001, F-003-RQ-003) |
| Error reporting | None. No `'error'` listener and no `try`/`catch`; a bind conflict produces Node's default stack trace on standard error and exit code 1 (F-001-RQ-004) |
| Metrics and tracing | None — no instrumentation, no exporter, no sampling configuration (section 1.2.3.3) |
| Health and readiness endpoints | None distinguishable from the default response; the startup log line is the only readiness signal (section 2.1.5) |
| Log shipping and retention | None — the only sink is the process's standard output stream |

Any observability over this system must therefore be supplied entirely by the consuming harness: capturing the process's standard output for readiness, and probing the loopback endpoint externally for liveness. No performance target, SLO, timeout, or rate limit exists in the repository from which a monitoring threshold could be derived — section 2.2.1.3 records that absence explicitly.

### 3.4.4 Cloud Services and Infrastructure Platforms

| Platform Category | Markers or Artifacts Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| AWS | `aws`, `s3`, `sqs`, `sns`, `dynamo` | Zero matches; no SDK, no client, no bucket or table reference |
| Azure and Google Cloud | `azure`, `gcp`, `google` | Zero matches |
| Infrastructure as code | Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi configuration files | None present anywhere in the repository |
| Container platform artifacts | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore` | None present |
| Serverless or PaaS descriptors | `Procfile`, `serverless.yml`, app manifests | None present |

Neither `docker` nor `terraform` is even installed in the environment used to verify this specification, which is consistent with the repository requiring neither. More fundamentally, the loopback-only bind means the service cannot be exposed by any cloud networking construct without editing `server.js` — and constraint C-001 forbids that edit. AWS, the cloud platform a conventional default stack would specify, is **not present and not applicable**.

### 3.4.5 The Integration Surfaces That Do Exist

Rather than third-party services, the system has a small number of primitive integration surfaces. This is the complete set:

| Surface | Direction | Mechanism | Reach |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | Node `http` server created at `server.js` line 6, bound at line 12 | Host-local only; refused on every non-loopback interface |
| Standard output | Outbound | One `console.log` line at `server.js` line 13 | Host-local; captured by whichever process launched the server |
| Standard error | Outbound, failure path only | Node's default unhandled-`'error'` handling on bind conflict | Host-local; produced only when port 3000 is already bound |
| `package.json` and `package-lock.json` | Tooling | Read by the npm CLI for identity, scripts, and install (F-004, F-005) | Local filesystem; no registry contact occurs |
| Git version control and hosting | Ecosystem | Single-commit baseline `1a0874d` on branch `main`, with an HTTPS origin remote on GitHub | External to the running process; not a runtime dependency |

Two clarifications about the ecosystem-level relationships:

- **"Backprop" is a consumer, not a service the system calls.** `README.md` line 2 names it as the integration context for which the fixture exists (F-006-RQ-001), and it is the only external party named anywhere in the repository. The relationship is inbound and one-directional: that tooling exercises the fixture. Section 1.2.1.3 characterises this as an ecosystem-level integration rather than a code-level one, and nothing in `server.js` is aware of it.
- **GitHub hosting is not an application dependency.** The repository has an HTTPS origin remote on GitHub, which is how the artifact is distributed and how the immutability evidence for F-006-RQ-003 is established. The running process never contacts it.

**Security consequence of having no third-party integrations.** There are no external trust relationships to manage, no third-party credentials to rotate or leak, no vendor availability coupled to the fixture's behaviour, and — because there is no egress path at all — no channel through which data could be exfiltrated even if the process were compromised. The sole trust boundary in the entire system is the loopback socket, and it is enforced by the bind address rather than by any service.

### 3.4.6 Default-Stack Services Explicitly Not Applicable

| Conventional Default Service | Role It Would Play | Status in This Repository |
|---|---|---|
| AWS | Cloud platform and managed infrastructure | Absent — no SDK, no IaC, no deployment descriptor |
| Auth0 | Authentication and identity | Absent — no auth of any kind; callers are anonymous |
| Monitoring and APM backends | Metrics, tracing, error reporting | Absent — telemetry is one stdout line |
| Langchain and LLM provider APIs | AI orchestration | Absent — zero matches for any AI or LLM marker |
| Managed database and cache services | Persistence and caching | Absent — see section 3.5 |

Every entry above was probed for directly and found absent. Introducing any of them would require modifying repository content, which constraint C-001 prohibits and which would invalidate the fixture's role as a fixed reference baseline (F-006).


## 3.5 Databases and Storage

**The system has no database, no persistence layer, no cache, and no storage service.** Statelessness is not a design aspiration here — it is a mechanical property of a 14-line program that imports nothing but `http`, declares four immutable bindings, and performs exactly one property write per request.

### 3.5.1 Primary and Secondary Databases

No database technology of any kind appears in the repository. Every marker below was probed case-insensitively across all tracked files with zero matches:

| Category | Markers Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Document stores | `mongo`, `mongoose`, `cassandra`, `dynamo` | Zero matches |
| Relational databases and drivers | `postgres`, `pg`, `mysql`, `sqlite` | Zero matches |
| ORMs and query builders | `prisma`, `sequelize`, `typeorm`, `knex` | Zero matches |
| Search engines | `elastic` | Zero matches |

There is correspondingly no schema, no migration directory, no seed data, and no fixture file — `git ls-files` confirms that only `.js`, `.json`, and `.md` files are tracked, so no data artifact of any kind exists. There is also no connection string to find: the complete network-literal census reported in section 3.4.1 returned exactly two lines, both referring to the loopback listener itself.

**MongoDB** — the database a conventional default stack would specify — is **not present and not applicable**. Neither a primary nor a secondary datastore exists, so questions of replication, sharding, read replicas, and failover do not arise.

### 3.5.2 Data Persistence Strategy

The persistence strategy is that **nothing is persisted**. Each mechanism by which data could be retained was examined:

| Potential Persistence Mechanism | Finding |
|---|---|
| Filesystem I/O | The `fs` module is never imported. Sweeps for `fs.`, `path.`, `readFile`, `writeFile`, `createReadStream`, `createWriteStream`, `mkdir`, `unlink`, and `os.tmpdir` all return zero matches |
| Working directories | No `data/`, `storage/`, `logs/`, `var/`, `tmp/`, `dist/`, or `build/` directory exists in the checkout, and `node_modules` is never created |
| Module-level mutable state | **None.** All four bindings in `server.js` are `const` |
| Per-request state | One property write, `res.statusCode = 200`, on a response object owned by the runtime and discarded when the response completes |
| Request data retention | None. The request object is never dereferenced (F-002-RQ-004) and nothing about a request is logged (F-003-RQ-003) |
| Session or cookie state | None. No `session` or cookie handling exists anywhere |

The mutable-state census is small enough to state exhaustively. `server.js` contains exactly six lines with an `=` character: four `const` initialisations (lines 1, 3, 4, 6), the arrow-function token on line 12, and the single assignment `res.statusCode = 200` on line 7. **Nothing in the program accumulates across requests**, which is the mechanical reason the invariance measured under repetition and concurrency in F-002-RQ-005 holds rather than being merely likely.

**Data domains.** The only datum the system handles is the 14-byte greeting payload compiled into line 9 as a string literal. No personal, regulated, financial, or business data is read, stored, transmitted, or logged — consistent with the data-domain boundary recorded in section 1.3.1.2.

### 3.5.3 Caching

No caching layer exists at any tier.

| Cache Tier | Finding |
|---|---|
| External cache service | No `redis` or `memcache` client; markers return zero matches |
| In-process cache structure | No `Map(`, `Set(`, `WeakMap`, `globalThis`, or `global.` usage; zero matches for `cache` |
| HTTP response cache directives | Repository code sets exactly one header, `Content-Type` (F-002-RQ-002), so no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Vary` directive is emitted; the only other headers on the wire are Node's defaults (C-004) |
| Build or dependency cache | Not applicable — there is no build step and no dependency to cache |

Caching would serve no purpose here: the response payload is a compiled-in literal returned by a single `res.end` call, so there is no computation, query, or I/O whose result could be reused.

### 3.5.4 Object, File, and Blob Storage

| Storage Category | Finding |
|---|---|
| Object storage services | Zero matches for `s3`, `azure`, `gcp`, or any bucket or container reference |
| Static asset serving | No `public/`, `assets/`, or `static/` directory exists; the response body is a literal, not a file read |
| File upload or download handling | None — the request body is never read, and no multipart or stream handling exists |
| Mounted volumes or persistent disks | Not applicable — no container or orchestration artifact exists (section 3.6) |
| Tracked binary assets | None — every tracked file is `.js`, `.json`, or `.md` |

### 3.5.5 The State That Genuinely Exists

For completeness, the following is the full inventory of state associated with a running instance. All of it is ephemeral, and most of it belongs to the runtime rather than to repository code:

| State Element | Scope | Lifetime | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Listening TCP socket on `127.0.0.1:3000` | OS kernel and libuv | Process lifetime; released by the OS on exit | Node.js runtime |
| Accepted connection sockets and keep-alive timers | Runtime | Per connection, governed by Node's default keep-alive behaviour | Node.js runtime (C-004) |
| `http`, `hostname`, `port`, `server` bindings | Module scope | Process lifetime; immutable | `server.js` lines 1, 3, 4, 6 |
| `res.statusCode` write | Single response object | One request | Runtime-owned object, set by `server.js` line 7 |
| The startup log line | External to the process | As long as the capturing consumer retains it | Whichever process captured standard output |

**Data at rest: none.** Nothing is written to any durable medium, so there is no encryption-at-rest requirement, no backup or retention policy to define, and no data-residency consideration. **Data in transit: plaintext HTTP over the loopback interface only.** No TLS exists — the `https` module is never imported and no certificate material is present — but the traffic never leaves the host, since off-host reachability is refused at the socket level (F-001-RQ-002, C-002).

A direct operational consequence is that **restarting the process loses nothing and changes nothing**. There is no state to migrate, warm, drain, or reconcile, which is why section 1.3.2.1 can exclude graceful shutdown without introducing a data-loss risk.

### 3.5.6 Default-Stack Storage Technologies Not Applicable

| Conventional Default Technology | Role It Would Play | Status in This Repository |
|---|---|---|
| MongoDB | Primary database | Absent — no driver, ODM, schema, or connection string |
| Redis or Memcached | Cache and session store | Absent — no client and no in-process cache |
| AWS S3 or equivalent | Object and blob storage | Absent — no SDK, bucket reference, or asset directory |
| Managed relational database | Secondary or reporting store | Absent — no SQL driver or migration tooling |

Each of these was probed for explicitly and found absent. Adding any of them would require modifying repository content, which constraint C-001 prohibits.


## 3.6 Development and Deployment

The development and deployment toolchain is deliberately minimal: there is no build system, no containerisation, no continuous-integration definition, and no code-quality tooling. What remains is a runtime, a package manager whose only job is to read two manifests, and version control. This subsection documents what is required, what is measurably absent, and what any consuming pipeline must therefore tolerate.

### 3.6.1 Development Tooling

**Tools actually required.** Versions shown are those used for every measurement in this specification; only the capability, not the version, is required by the repository (D-005).

| Tool | Version Measured | Role | Necessity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node.js | 22.23.1 | Executes `server.js`; supplies the `http` module and the CommonJS loader | Required for any use of the system |
| npm CLI | 11.18.0 | Reads `package.json` and `package-lock.json`; runs `test`; resolves the implicit `start` | Required only for npm-driven workflows |
| Git | present at `/usr/bin/git` | Obtains the artifact and verifies the single-commit baseline for F-006-RQ-003 | Required to establish the immutability evidence |
| POSIX-style shell | `sh` and `bash` present | Executes the `scripts.test` one-liner | Required only to invoke `npm test` |
| HTTP client | `curl` present | Exercises the endpoint | Not required by the repository; used for verification only |

**Code-quality and developer-experience tooling — verified absent.** Each of the following was probed for as a configuration file in the repository and, where relevant, as an executable in the environment:

| Tooling Category | Configuration Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Linting | `.eslintrc`, `.eslintrc.json`, `.eslintrc.js`, `eslint.config.js` | None present; `eslint` not installed |
| Formatting | `.prettierrc`, `.prettierrc.json`, `.editorconfig` | None present; `prettier` not installed |
| Type checking | `tsconfig.json`, `jsconfig.json`, `types`/`typings` manifest fields | None present; `tsc` not installed |
| Test runner | Jest, Mocha, or any runner configuration; `test/`, `tests/`, `__tests__/`, `spec/` directories | None present; `jest` and `mocha` not installed |
| Pre-commit automation | `.husky/`, active Git hooks | None present; `.git/hooks` holds only the 14 default `.sample` templates — zero active hooks |
| Editor and workspace settings | `.vscode/`, `.idea/`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitignore` | None present |

`npm run` confirms the script surface from the tool's own perspective: the only lifecycle script declared is `test`. There is no `lint`, `format`, `build`, `dev`, `watch`, or `start` script, and no `pre`/`post` hook of any kind.

### 3.6.2 Build System

**There is no build system, and none is required.** The repository is not a project that produces an artifact; the tracked tree *is* the artifact.

| Conventional Build Stage | Status in This Repository |
|---|---|
| Dependency installation | A no-op. `npm ci` exits 0 in roughly 120 ms and creates no `node_modules` (section 3.3.4) |
| Transpilation | Not applicable. `server.js` uses only ES2015 syntax, which the runtime executes directly; no Babel, SWC, or `tsc` configuration exists |
| Bundling | Not applicable. No Webpack, Rollup, Vite, esbuild, or Parcel configuration exists; the module graph is a single node |
| Minification and asset pipeline | Not applicable. No minifier, no CSS or image processing, no `public/` directory |
| Native compilation | Not applicable. With zero dependencies, no `node-gyp` invocation or C++ toolchain is reachable |
| Artifact packaging and publication | None declared. `package.json` has no `files` allowlist, no `publishConfig`, no `repository` field, and no `private` flag; distribution is via the Git repository rather than a registry publish |

This is what makes section 1.3.1.1's "no installation, build, transpile, or bundling step" requirement verifiable rather than rhetorical, and it is why `make`, absent from the verification environment, is not needed.

### 3.6.3 Launch, Readiness, and Termination

All behaviours below were measured directly against an unmodified copy of the repository.

| Invocation | Mechanism | Measured Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `node server.js` | Direct runtime invocation | Binds the listener and prints the startup line; serves `200` with a 14-byte `text/plain` body |
| `npm start` | **npm's built-in default**, not a declared script — npm falls back to `node server.js` because a `server.js` exists at the package root and no `start` script is declared | Printed `> hello_world@1.0.0 start` then `> node server.js`, bound the listener, and served normally (deviation D-004) |
| `npm test` | Runs the `scripts.test` shell one-liner | Prints `Error: no test specified` and exits **1** (deviation D-003, F-007-RQ-001) |
| `require('hello_world')` | Resolves the manifest `main` field | Fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` because `index.js` does not exist (deviation D-001, constraint C-005) |
| `npm ci` / `npm install` | Lockfile-driven and manifest-driven install | Exit 0, offline-capable, no `node_modules` created |

**Readiness.** The single line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` on standard output is the only readiness signal the system emits (F-003-RQ-001). There is no health or readiness endpoint distinguishable from the default response, so automation must either synchronise on that exact string or poll the loopback endpoint.

**Termination.** No `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler exists, so termination is immediate with no connection draining and no shutdown output; the operating system releases the port on exit. Because section 3.5 establishes that nothing is persisted, abrupt termination carries no data-loss risk.

**Instance cardinality.** Exactly one instance can run per host. A second bind attempt on `127.0.0.1:3000` produces an unhandled `'error'` event — `EADDRINUSE`, errno −98, syscall `listen` — a stack trace on standard error, and process exit code 1 (F-001-RQ-004, assumption A-002). Consuming automation must therefore serialise its use of port 3000 rather than relying on any retry or port-fallback behaviour, because neither exists.

**Configuration at deploy time: none.** There is no environment-variable surface (zero `process.env` matches), no CLI-argument handling (zero `process.argv` matches), no configuration file, and no `.env`. The bind target and payload are in-source literals (F-001-RQ-003), which is registered as constraint C-003. Deployment cannot be parameterised without editing the source, and constraint C-001 forbids that edit.

### 3.6.4 Containerisation

No containerisation artifact exists anywhere in the repository: no `Dockerfile`, no `Dockerfile.dev`, no `docker-compose.yml` or `.yaml`, and no `.dockerignore`. There is likewise no Kubernetes manifest, Helm chart, or other orchestration descriptor, and no infrastructure-as-code definition of any kind. Neither `docker` nor `terraform` is installed in the verification environment, consistent with the repository requiring neither.

One consequence is worth stating explicitly for anyone who might wrap the repository externally. Because the listener binds `127.0.0.1` rather than a wildcard address (C-002), an unmodified container built around this repository would expose the service **only within its own network namespace** — a published port mapping would not reach it. Making the fixture reachable from outside a container would require changing the bind address in `server.js`, which constraint C-001 prohibits. Containerisation is recorded as excluded scope in section 1.3.2 rather than as a gap to be filled.

### 3.6.5 Continuous Integration and Delivery

**No CI/CD definition exists.** All of the following paths were tested for and are absent: `.github/` (and therefore any workflow file), `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.travis.yml`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `Makefile`, and `Procfile`. There are no active Git hooks and no `CODEOWNERS` file, so nothing inside the repository enforces the immutability directive of F-006 — enforcement is by convention only, as section 2.1.8 records.

Because there is no pipeline, the relevant engineering content is what a *consuming* pipeline must accommodate. Each item below follows from a measured behaviour:

| Pipeline Stage | Behaviour Against This Repository | Required Accommodation |
|---|---|---|
| Checkout | Single commit `1a0874d` on branch `main`; clean working tree; no tags | Verifying the baseline is a `git status --porcelain` emptiness check (F-006-RQ-003) |
| Install | `npm ci` exits 0 in roughly 120 ms, works offline, creates no `node_modules` | Must not assert that `node_modules` exists (assumption A-004) |
| Build | No build step exists | Must not require a build target or emit-directory |
| Lint / type check | No configuration exists for any tool | Must not require a lint or type-check stage |
| Test | `npm test` exits **1** by design | Must skip the test stage or explicitly tolerate exit 1; section 1.3.2.4 records CI-gate usage as an unsupported use case (D-003) |
| Start / smoke test | `npm start` works only through npm's implicit default | Must not assume a declared `start` script exists (D-004) |
| Audit | `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across one audited package | Safe to run; will never gate |
| Package / publish | No packaging metadata or publish configuration | No release stage is meaningful |

The net effect is that a conventional pipeline template — install, lint, build, test, publish — fails at the test stage against this repository and has nothing to do at three of the other four. GitHub Actions, the CI system a conventional default stack would specify, is **not present**; the repository is hosted on GitHub, but no workflow definition accompanies it.

### 3.6.6 Source-to-Run Path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph AcquireStage["Acquire - Git"]
        CLONE["clone repository<br/>single commit 1a0874d"]
        VERIFY["git status --porcelain<br/>empty output confirms baseline"]
    end

    subgraph InstallStage["Install - npm, optional"]
        CIRUN["npm ci<br/>exit 0 in about 120 ms"]
        NOMOD["no node_modules created<br/>fully offline capable"]
    end

    subgraph BuildStage["Build - none required"]
        NOOP["no transpile, bundle, minify or compile<br/>committed source is the executed source"]
    end

    subgraph RunStage["Run - Node.js"]
        LAUNCH["node server.js<br/>or npm start via npm implicit default D-004"]
        BIND["bind listener on 127.0.0.1 port 3000"]
        READY["stdout readiness line<br/>announces the loopback bind target"]
    end

    subgraph GateStage["Quality gates - absent"]
        TESTCMD["npm test<br/>echo then exit 1 - D-003"]
        NOPIPE["no CI definition<br/>no container, no IaC"]
    end

    CLONE --> VERIFY
    VERIFY --> CIRUN
    CIRUN --> NOMOD
    NOMOD --> NOOP
    NOOP --> LAUNCH
    LAUNCH --> BIND
    BIND --> READY
    NOOP --> TESTCMD
    TESTCMD --> NOPIPE
```

The diagram is deliberately lopsided: the acquire and run stages carry real, measured behaviour, while the install stage is a verified no-op, the build stage is empty, and the quality-gate stage terminates in absences. That shape is an accurate rendering of the toolchain rather than an omission.

### 3.6.7 Deployment Topology and Environment Requirements

| Requirement | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Host operating system | Any on which a Node.js build runs; no `os` or `cpu` restriction is declared | `package.json` — fields absent |
| Runtime | A Node.js build providing CommonJS `require`, the `http` module, and ES2015 syntax | Derived in section 3.1.3; unpinned per D-005 |
| Network | TCP port 3000 free on the loopback interface | Assumption A-002; F-001-RQ-004 |
| Reachability | Loopback only; unreachable from any other interface | F-001-RQ-002; constraint C-002 |
| Instances per host | Exactly one | Duplicate bind terminates the process with exit code 1 |
| Filesystem | Read access to the four tracked files; no write access needed | Section 3.5.2 — no filesystem I/O occurs |
| Credentials and secrets | None required at any stage | Zero credential markers repository-wide; no `.npmrc` |
| Registry or internet access | Not required | `npm ci --offline` exits 0 |

Because there is no configuration surface, no persistence, and no external dependency, the deployment unit is a single short-lived process co-located with whatever exercises it. That topology is the direct consequence of the technology choices documented in sections 3.1 through 3.5, and it is what makes the artifact usable as the fixed reference baseline described in section 1.1.4.
