Protocol-level faults are answered by the runtime on the same socket and never reach the handler: a malformed request line yields `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`, an oversized header block yields `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`, and a stalled request yields `408 Request Timeout`. Process-level faults bypass the socket entirely and surface on standard error plus the exit code. Section 5.4.3 develops this flow in full.

The single most important property of Flow 2 is that **request data is terminal**. Bytes are parsed into objects and then discarded; nothing derived from a request is read, stored, forwarded, logged, or allowed to influence the response. The flow is unidirectional in the informational sense even though it is bidirectional at the transport layer.

#### 5.1.3.2 Integration Patterns and Protocols

| Interaction | Pattern | Protocol and Format |
|---|---|---|
| Client → service | Synchronous request/response, one response per request | HTTP/1.1 over TCP with persistent connections; response body `text/plain` |
| Runtime → handler | In-process callback dispatch (Reactor); no queue, no thread hand-off | JavaScript function invocation with runtime-owned `req`/`res` objects |
| Service → console | Fire-and-forget one-way stream write | UTF-8 plain-text line on file descriptor 1 |
| Operator → process | Asynchronous signal delivery; response is termination plus exit status | POSIX signals; integer exit codes |
| Tooling → artifact | Pull-based read of static declarations | JSON manifests (`lockfileVersion: 3`); Git over HTTPS |

No asynchronous, brokered, streaming, batch, or publish–subscribe pattern is present; there is no message broker, event bus, scheduler, or webhook anywhere in the repository.

#### 5.1.3.3 Data Transformation Points

The system contains exactly **three transformation points**, only one of which is authored by repository code.

| # | Transformation | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raw request bytes → parsed `req` object (request line, headers, body stream) | CMP-01, the runtime parser. The output of this transformation is never consumed |
| 2 | Empty `res` → status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, 14-byte body | CMP-04, repository code — the only application-authored transformation |
| 3 | `res` state → serialised HTTP/1.1 wire response, with `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` added automatically | CMP-01, the runtime serialiser |

A fourth, single-shot transformation occurs at startup: the `hostname` and `port` constants are interpolated into the readiness string (CMP-05). There is no validation, sanitisation, encoding conversion, compression, templating, or content negotiation at any point — no such construct exists in the source.

#### 5.1.3.4 Data Stores and Caches

**The system has no data store and no cache.** This is a verified absence: no database client, driver, ORM, or connection string exists in the dependency-free manifests; the `fs` and `path` modules are never imported; and no session, cookie, or token store is present. Searches for cache constructs return nothing, and no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Vary` header is emitted, so clients are given no caching directives either.

Only four locations hold data of any kind, and none of them is a store in the architectural sense:

- **The compiled-in response literal** — the 14-byte `Hello, World!\n` string, resident in the loaded module and never varying.
- **The configuration literals** — `hostname` and `port`, fixed at author time.
- **Kernel socket buffers and the runtime's connection bookkeeping** — transient, owned by the OS and CMP-01, released when a connection closes.
- **Git history** — the only durable artifact associated with the project, and it is design-time state, not runtime state.

The single reuse mechanism in effect anywhere is transport-level connection reuse via the runtime's keep-alive default, which measurably lowers per-request cost. Because the response body is a compiled-in constant, there is no computation or I/O for a cache to amortise; section 5.3.5 records the decision not to introduce one.

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

Every integration point is **host-local**. The system makes no outbound network call of any kind: the sole `require` in the repository targets a Node core module, so no HTTP client, SDK, driver, or socket-initiating construct exists that could reach off-host. The table pair below enumerates the complete integration surface.

#### 5.1.4.1 Integration Surface and Exchange Patterns

| External System / Actor | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP client on the host loopback | Inbound network interface (primary) | Synchronous request/response; one 14-byte response per request, invariant across method, path, query, and body |
| Process standard output | Outbound local stream | One-way, fire-and-forget; exactly one line emitted at readiness, then silence |
| Process standard error | Outbound local stream | One-way; used only by the runtime's default unhandled-`'error'` path on bind failure |
| Invoking shell or process supervisor | Bidirectional control plane | Signals inbound, exit status outbound; no draining or acknowledgement |
| Node.js runtime | In-process API binding | Synchronous `require` at load time plus callback dispatch thereafter |
| npm CLI | Design-time tooling | Pull-based manifest read; install is a verified no-op that creates no `node_modules` |
| Git / GitHub repository | Design-time artifact source | Clone plus working-tree verification against the single-commit baseline |

#### 5.1.4.2 Protocols, Formats, and Service-Level Expectations

The repository declares **no SLA, SLO, error budget, availability target, latency target, or throughput target anywhere** — there is no monitoring, alerting, or dashboard configuration in any file, and no such commitment appears in `README.md` or the manifests. The right-hand column below therefore records the *verified absence* of a declared service level alongside the measured behaviour that a consumer may rely on as an observation, not as a guarantee.

| External System / Actor | Protocol / Format | Declared SLA and Measured Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP client on the host loopback | HTTP/1.1 over TCP, port 3000; response `text/plain`, 14 bytes | **No SLA declared.** Measured: p50 0.077 ms on a reused connection, 0.117 ms on a new connection; 50/50 concurrent requests succeeded; a single instance is the maximum capacity unit |
| Process standard output | UTF-8 text, exactly `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | **No SLA declared.** Measured: emitted once at bind; stdout still contained one line after roughly 700 requests |
| Process standard error | UTF-8 stack trace with `code`, `errno`, `syscall`, `address`, `port` | **No SLA declared.** Written only on unhandled bind failure |
| Invoking shell or supervisor | POSIX signals; integer exit status | **No SLA declared.** Measured: exit 1 on `EADDRINUSE`, 143 on `SIGTERM`, 130 on `SIGINT`; no drain period |
| Node.js runtime | CommonJS `require` of the core `http` API; ES2015 syntax | **No version pinned** (no `engines`, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version`) — deviation D-005. Verified against Node.js 22.23.1 |
| npm CLI | JSON manifests; `lockfileVersion: 3` | **No SLA declared.** Measured: `npm ci` exits 0 in roughly 120 ms, works offline, creates no `node_modules`; `npm test` exits 1 by design |
| Git / GitHub repository | Git over HTTPS | **No SLA declared.** Baseline is commit `1a0874d` on `main`, no tags, clean working tree |

One clarification is architecturally important. The "backprop integration" named in `README.md` is an integration performed **on** this repository by external tooling using ordinary Git and npm conventions — clone, read manifests, optionally install, execute the script. No code inside the repository participates in it, and no integration endpoint exists for it. The system integrates by *being a well-formed, conventional Node.js package*, not by calling anything.

Also excluded, each confirmed by the absence of any corresponding client or SDK in the dependency-free manifests: relational and NoSQL databases, message brokers and event streams, caches, third-party REST/GraphQL/gRPC APIs, identity providers and single sign-on, payment and notification services, object storage, secret managers, service discovery, API gateways, feature-flag services, and APM or log-aggregation backends.


## 5.2 Component Details

Each component introduced in section 5.1.2 is developed below against five dimensions: purpose and responsibilities, technologies and frameworks, key interfaces and APIs, data persistence requirements, and scaling considerations. Two dimensions have the same answer for every component and are stated once here rather than repeated seven times: **no component has any data persistence requirement** — the running process writes nothing to any database, file, cache, or session store — and **no component is independently deployable or independently scalable**, because all five runtime components execute inside one process that binds one socket.

### 5.2.1 CMP-01 HTTP Transport Runtime

**Purpose and responsibilities.** CMP-01 is the largest component in the architecture by function and the only one not authored in this repository. It accepts TCP connections on the bound socket, parses HTTP/1.1 request messages, materialises the `req`/`res` object pair, dispatches to the registered handler, serialises the resulting response onto the wire, manages connection persistence and reaping, and answers protocol-level faults without involving application code. Every capability the system exhibits that is *not* the three statements in the handler belongs to this component.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Node.js's built-in `http` module, acquired by the repository's sole dependency edge — `require('http')` on `server.js` line 1. No web framework is present: Express, Koa, Fastify, Hapi, and NestJS are all absent, as is any middleware, router, or plugin layer. The component is reached through CommonJS resolution because `package.json` declares no `"type"` field.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Four surfaces are used by repository code, and no others: `http.createServer(handler)`, `server.listen(port, hostname, callback)`, and the `res.statusCode`/`res.setHeader()`/`res.end()` trio on the response object. A live listener census on the constructed server object shows `request = 1` and `connection = 1` — both installed by `createServer` itself — with `error`, `clientError`, `close`, and `upgrade` all at **zero**. The repository therefore contributes exactly one listener to this component and leaves every other event class to the runtime's default disposition.

**Configuration posture — everything is a runtime default.** `server.js` tunes nothing on this component. The values below were read from a server object constructed identically to `server.js` lines 6–10 under Node.js 22.23.1, and they are part of the observable contract *without being under repository control*.

| Setting | Runtime Default | Architectural Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 ms | Produces the observed `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` header and the measured ~5.8 s idle-socket close |
| `headersTimeout` | 60000 ms | Basis of the `408 Request Timeout` path for stalled clients |
| `requestTimeout` | 300000 ms | Upper bound on a single request's lifetime |
| `timeout` | 0 (disabled) | No socket inactivity timeout beyond the two above |
| `maxHeadersCount` | `null` (unbounded) | The `431` response is driven by header *size* limits, not header count |
| `maxRequestsPerSocket` | 0 (unlimited) | A single keep-alive connection may serve unbounded requests |
| `maxConnections` | unset | No connection ceiling; concurrency is bounded only by OS file descriptors and the default 511-entry accept backlog |

**Scaling considerations.** CMP-01 runs on a single event loop in a single thread. `cluster` and `worker_threads` appear zero times in the source, so the component cannot use more than one core even though the verification host exposed 16. Concurrency is achieved by non-blocking multiplexing rather than parallelism, which is well matched to this workload: the handler performs no I/O and no computation, so requests never block one another — 50 concurrent requests all completed successfully in a measured 25 ms. The practical ceiling is single-core event-loop throughput, and because the accept backlog and file-descriptor limit are untouched defaults, overload behaviour is whatever the OS and runtime defaults produce rather than anything this repository specifies.

### 5.2.2 CMP-02 Listener Bootstrap

**Purpose and responsibilities.** CMP-02 is the activation component: `server.listen(port, hostname, callback)` on `server.js` lines 12–14 converts a configured-but-inert server object into a live service by requesting the socket bind, and it gates the readiness announcement behind that bind's success. It is the single point at which the system transitions from "loading" to "available".

**Technologies and frameworks.** The `net`/`http` listen path of the Node.js runtime, invoked with the two-argument-plus-callback form. No backlog argument is supplied, so the runtime's documented default of 511 applies.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Outbound: the OS socket bind for `127.0.0.1:3000`. Inbound: the two constants from CMP-03. Callback: a single arrow function that invokes CMP-05. Notably, the component exposes **no error interface** — because no `'error'` listener is registered on the server, a failed bind has nowhere to go.

**Persistence.** None. The only durable side effect of a successful bind is an entry in the OS socket table, released automatically when the process exits.

**Scaling considerations.** CMP-02 fixes instance cardinality at **exactly one per host**. A second `node server.js` on the same machine was observed to fail with `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, reported by the runtime as an unhandled `'error'` event and terminating the process with exit code 1. There is no retry, no exponential backoff, and no alternate-port fallback — the bind is attempted exactly once. Horizontal scale-out on a single host is therefore architecturally impossible, and any consuming automation must serialise its use of port 3000 rather than rely on resilience that does not exist.

### 5.2.3 CMP-03 Configuration Constants

**Purpose and responsibilities.** Two module-scope `const` declarations — `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and `port = 3000` (`server.js` lines 3–4) — constitute the system's complete configuration surface. They serve two consumers: CMP-02 uses them as the bind target and CMP-05 interpolates them into the readiness line.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Plain ES2015 `const` bindings. No configuration library, schema validator, or layered-override mechanism exists; `process.env` and `process.argv` each appear zero times in the repository, and there is no `.env` file, config directory, or CLI parser.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Lexical scope only. The constants are not exported, not injectable, and not observable at runtime.

**Persistence.** The values are persisted only as source text in the Git baseline.

**Scaling and evolution considerations.** This is the architecture's principal rigidity and it is deliberate (constraint C-003). Deployment cannot be parameterised: changing the bind address or port requires editing `server.js`, which the change freeze in `README.md` prohibits (constraint C-001). The loopback literal in particular has a non-obvious consequence for anyone wrapping the artifact externally — a container built around this repository would expose the listener only inside its own network namespace, so a published port mapping would not reach it. The compensating benefit is the shared-constant guarantee: because line 13 interpolates the same constants line 12 binds, the advertised URL cannot diverge from reality.

### 5.2.4 CMP-04 Invariant Response Handler

**Purpose and responsibilities.** CMP-04 is the whole of the application layer. Registered as the sole `request` listener at `server.js` line 6, it composes one response for every request via three statements: set status `200`, set `Content-Type: text/plain`, and complete with the 14-byte body `Hello, World!\n`.

```javascript
res.statusCode = 200;
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
res.end('Hello, World!\n');
```

**Technologies and frameworks.** An inline anonymous arrow function — no class, no controller, no service layer, no dependency injection. It operates only on the runtime-owned `res` object.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Inbound: invocation by CMP-01 with `(req, res)`. Outbound: three writes to `res`. The defining architectural property is what the handler *does not* use — `req.` appears **zero** times in the file, so the request's method, URL, query string, headers, and body are all structurally unreachable. This was confirmed empirically: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, and `OPTIONS` all returned the identical 200/`text/plain`/14-byte response, as did `/`, `/any/deep/path`, `/x?y=1&z=2`, `/admin`, `/health`, and `/metrics`. `HEAD` returned 200 with a zero-length body because the runtime suppresses bodies for that method. There is consequently **no routing table, no method dispatch, no content negotiation, no input validation, and no authorisation gate** — and `/health` and `/metrics` are not endpoints, merely paths that fall through to the same constant.

**Persistence.** None, and structurally so. The handler mutates exactly one thing anywhere in the system — `res.statusCode`, a property of a per-request object owned by the runtime and discarded after the response. There are zero module-level mutable variables, which is the mechanical reason the invariance property holds under load: there is no accumulator that repeated or concurrent traffic could disturb.

**Scaling considerations.** The handler is O(1) in time and space, performs no I/O, allocates no per-request state beyond what the runtime provides, and is trivially re-entrant. It is therefore never the bottleneck; whatever limits throughput lies in CMP-01, the kernel, or the client. Its single `res.end` call also gives the response atomic semantics — no chunked or partial writes exist that could leave a response half-emitted.

### 5.2.5 CMP-05 Readiness Announcer

**Purpose and responsibilities.** A single `console.log` inside the listen callback (`server.js` line 13) emits `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` to standard output. This is the entirety of the system's observability output.

**Technologies and frameworks.** The global `console` object writing to file descriptor 1, with a template literal interpolating CMP-03's constants. No logging framework, log level, structured format, sink, or rotation exists.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** One unidirectional write to the process stdout stream. There is no log ingestion contract beyond "one plain-text line".

**Persistence.** None — the line is transient process output. There is no file sink and no request logging: stdout still contained exactly one line after roughly 700 requests plus every fault probe.

**Scaling and operational considerations.** Because CMP-05 fires from inside the listen callback, it is a **trustworthy readiness signal in both directions**: it appears only after a successful bind, and it never appears for a process that failed to bind. It is also the *only* readiness signal — there is no health endpoint distinguishable from the default response, no metrics endpoint, and no liveness probe — so automation must either match that exact string or poll the loopback endpoint. Log volume does not grow with traffic, which means the output stream can never become an operational bottleneck, but it equally means per-request diagnosis is impossible from logs.

### 5.2.6 CMP-06 Package Identity and Dependency Lock

**Purpose and responsibilities.** The manifest pair declares the artifact's identity and guarantees its supply chain. `package.json` supplies `name`, `version`, `description`, `main`, `scripts`, `author`, and `license`; `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`) contains only the root package record, which is formal proof of a **zero-node dependency graph**.

**Technologies and frameworks.** JSON manifests interpreted by the npm CLI. The two files duplicate `name`, `version`, and `license` and must agree, or `npm ci` fails.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Consumed entirely by tooling; there is no code path from `server.js` to either file. Three interface characteristics matter to consumers, all verified: `main` names `index.js`, which does not exist, so `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (deviation D-001, constraint C-005); no `start` script is declared, so `npm start` works only through npm's built-in fallback to `node server.js` (deviation D-004); and `scripts.test` is `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`, which exits **1** by design (deviation D-003).

**Persistence.** The manifests are the persisted declaration; `npm ci` is a verified no-op that exits 0 in roughly 120 ms, works offline, and creates no `node_modules` directory.

**Scaling considerations.** Not applicable at runtime — the component has no runtime role. Its architectural value is negative-risk: zero dependencies means the system cannot fail for registry-availability, transitive-version-conflict, or transitive-CVE reasons, and `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across one audited package.

### 5.2.7 CMP-07 Governance Artifact

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `README.md` performs the only governance function in the repository. Its two lines name the project `hao-backprop-test`, declare it a "test project for backprop integration", and impose the change freeze "Do not touch!". Architecturally this component is what makes every rigidity documented above intentional rather than accidental.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Markdown, with the single-commit Git history (`1a0874d`, clean working tree) as corroborating evidence of the frozen baseline.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Human-readable text plus the Git baseline that automation can verify with a working-tree emptiness check.

**Persistence.** Version control is the persistence mechanism, and the Git history is the only durable state the project has.

**Scaling and enforcement considerations.** Enforcement is **by convention only**: there are no active Git hooks (the `.git/hooks` directory contains only the default `.sample` templates), no `CODEOWNERS`, and no CI check, so nothing inside the repository mechanically prevents modification. A secondary governance weakness is the naming divergence — the artifact is discoverable as `hao-backprop-test` in the README and as `hello_world` in the manifests.

### 5.2.8 Component Interaction Diagram

The diagram below shows every interaction edge that exists in the system, separating the runtime component graph from the design-time components that have no runtime edges at all.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLIENT["HTTP Client<br/>host loopback only"]
    STDOUT["stdout stream"]
    STDERR["stderr stream<br/>then exit code 1"]

    subgraph ProcessScope["Node.js Process - one event loop"]
        subgraph RuntimeScope["CMP-01 HTTP Transport Runtime - Node core http"]
            ACCEPT["Connection acceptor<br/>default backlog 511"]
            PARSER["HTTP/1.1 parser<br/>materializes req and res"]
            SERIAL["Response serializer<br/>adds Content-Length, Date, Connection"]
            PROTOERR["Protocol fault responder<br/>400, 408, 431 then close"]
            ACCEPT --> PARSER
            PARSER --> PROTOERR
            SERIAL --> ACCEPT
        end
        CONFIGC["CMP-03 Configuration Constants<br/>127.0.0.1 and port 3000"]
        BOOT["CMP-02 Listener Bootstrap<br/>server.listen"]
        HANDLER["CMP-04 Invariant Response Handler<br/>200, text/plain, 14 bytes"]
        ANNOUNCE["CMP-05 Readiness Announcer<br/>console.log"]
        CONFIGC --> BOOT
        CONFIGC --> ANNOUNCE
        BOOT --> ACCEPT
        BOOT --> ANNOUNCE
        PARSER -->|"in-process dispatch"| HANDLER
        HANDLER -->|"statusCode, setHeader, end"| SERIAL
    end

    subgraph DesignScope["Design-Time Components - zero runtime edges"]
        MANIF["CMP-06 Package Identity and Lock"]
        GOV["CMP-07 Governance Artifact"]
    end

    CLIENT -->|"request bytes, any method or path"| ACCEPT
    SERIAL -->|"invariant response bytes"| CLIENT
    PROTOERR -->|"error status with Connection close"| CLIENT
    ANNOUNCE -->|"exactly one readiness line"| STDOUT
    BOOT -.->|"unhandled error event on EADDRINUSE"| STDERR
    MANIF -.->|"read by npm CLI before any process exists"| BOOT
    GOV -.->|"change freeze constrains the literals"| CONFIGC
```

Two features of the graph are worth naming. First, **CMP-04 has exactly one inbound and one outbound edge** — it is a leaf in the interaction graph, which is why it can be reasoned about in isolation. Second, the `PROTOERR` path reaches the client **without passing through CMP-04**, which is the structural reason the application layer can only ever emit `200` while the system as a whole can emit `400`, `408`, and `431`.

### 5.2.9 State Transition Diagrams

Two state machines are presented here at component granularity: the availability state of the deployment unit, and the ownership state of a connection as control passes between CMP-01 and CMP-04. The finer-grained process- and connection-lifecycle machines are documented in section 4.4.5, and the per-request response-object transitions in section 4.3.1.2; the views below are the architectural complements to those, not restatements.

**Service availability states.** This machine has two terminal paths and one absorbing steady state. Its most important property is that `Serving → Serving` mutates nothing, which is what makes the service's behaviour identical on request one and request one million.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ModuleLoading : node server.js invoked
    ModuleLoading --> Configured : http required, CMP-03 constants bound
    Configured --> HandlerRegistered : createServer registers CMP-04
    HandlerRegistered --> Binding : CMP-02 requests 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    Binding --> Serving : bind succeeds, CMP-05 writes the readiness line
    Binding --> Aborted : EADDRINUSE, unhandled error event
    Serving --> Serving : request served, no state mutated
    Serving --> Terminated : SIGTERM exit 143 or SIGINT exit 130, no drain
    Aborted --> [*] : exit code 1, readiness line never printed
    Terminated --> [*] : operating system releases the port
```

**Connection ownership states.** Control over a connection alternates between the two runtime components. Note that the transport component owns every state except the brief interval between dispatch and `res.end`, and that both terminal transitions are runtime-driven.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> TransportOwned : CMP-01 accepts the socket and parses the request
    TransportOwned --> ApplicationOwned : CMP-01 dispatches to CMP-04
    ApplicationOwned --> ApplicationOwned : status then Content-Type written
    ApplicationOwned --> TransportReturned : res.end returns control to CMP-01
    TransportReturned --> IdleKeepAlive : response serialized, connection retained
    IdleKeepAlive --> TransportOwned : next request arrives on the same socket
    IdleKeepAlive --> [*] : keepAliveTimeout of 5000 ms elapses, socket closed
    TransportOwned --> [*] : protocol fault answered by CMP-01, socket closed
```

### 5.2.10 Sequence Diagrams for Key Flows

**Startup and bind, including the failure branch.** This flow executes once per process and determines whether the system exists at all.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as Operator or Supervisor
    participant NODE as Node.js Runtime
    participant SRC as server.js module scope
    participant HTTPM as CMP-01 http module
    participant OS as OS socket layer
    participant OUT as stdout and stderr

    OP->>NODE: node server.js
    NODE->>SRC: evaluate module top to bottom
    SRC->>HTTPM: require http
    SRC->>SRC: bind CMP-03 hostname and port constants
    SRC->>HTTPM: createServer registers CMP-04 as the request listener
    SRC->>HTTPM: CMP-02 calls listen with port, hostname and callback
    HTTPM->>OS: bind 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    alt port available
        OS-->>HTTPM: socket bound
        HTTPM-->>SRC: invoke the listen callback
        SRC->>OUT: CMP-05 writes the single readiness line
        Note over HTTPM,OS: event loop keeps the process alive, service is available
    else port already bound
        OS-->>HTTPM: EADDRINUSE
        HTTPM->>NODE: emit error event with zero listeners registered
        NODE->>OUT: default unhandled error stack trace on stderr
        NODE->>OP: exit code 1, no readiness line ever printed
    end
```

**Steady-state request handling with connection reuse.** This flow executes indefinitely and is the system's only hot path.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CL as HTTP client on loopback
    participant OS as OS socket layer
    participant RT as CMP-01 Transport Runtime
    participant H as CMP-04 Response Handler

    CL->>OS: TCP connect to 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    OS->>RT: connection accepted
    CL->>RT: request line, headers and optional body
    RT->>RT: parse into req and res objects
    RT->>H: dispatch with req and res
    H->>H: set statusCode to 200
    H->>H: set Content-Type to text/plain
    H->>RT: end response with the fixed 14 byte body
    RT->>RT: add Content-Length, Date, Connection and Keep-Alive
    RT->>CL: 200 text/plain, 14 bytes
    Note over RT,H: req is never dereferenced, so the response cannot vary
    CL->>RT: second request on the same connection
    RT->>H: dispatch again
    H->>RT: identical response composed
    RT->>CL: identical 200 response, measured p50 0.077 ms
    RT--xCL: socket closed after 5000 ms idle, a runtime default
```

**Protocol-fault handling, which bypasses the application entirely.** This flow demonstrates the structural separation established in section 5.2.8.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CL as HTTP client on loopback
    participant RT as CMP-01 Transport Runtime
    participant H as CMP-04 Response Handler

    CL->>RT: malformed request line or oversized header block
    RT->>RT: parser rejects the message before dispatch
    RT->>CL: 400 Bad Request or 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
    RT--xCL: Connection close, socket destroyed
    Note over RT,H: CMP-04 is never invoked and produces no output
    CL->>RT: well formed request on a new connection
    RT->>H: dispatch proceeds normally
    H->>RT: invariant response composed
    RT->>CL: 200 text/plain, 14 bytes
```


## 5.3 Technical Decisions

### 5.3.1 Basis and Method

The repository contains **no architecture decision records, no design notes, no `docs/` directory, and no decision log of any kind** — this was verified by a full-tree inspection that found only four tracked files. Every decision documented in this section is therefore **reconstructed from the artifact**: it states the decision the code demonstrably embodies, together with the evidence that establishes it and the tradeoffs that necessarily follow. Nothing here is a rationale quoted from the repository, and nothing here should be read as an author's stated intent beyond the two sentences in `README.md`.

That README supplies the single design premise everything else follows from: the artifact is a "test project for backprop integration" that is not to be modified. A fixture optimises for *being identical every time it is used*, which inverts the usual priority ordering of a web service. Extensibility, configurability, throughput, and operability are all subordinated to determinism, reproducibility, and immutability. Read in that light, the architecture is internally consistent rather than merely sparse.

### 5.3.2 Architecture Style Decisions and Tradeoffs

The chosen style is a single-process, single-module monolith executed as a script (section 5.1.1.1). The table below sets each style dimension against the mainstream alternative and names the tradeoff that was accepted.

| Dimension | Chosen Approach | Tradeoff Accepted |
|---|---|---|
| Framework | Node.js core `http` only — the repository's single dependency edge is `require('http')` | No routing, middleware, validation, or content negotiation is available; every such capability would have to be hand-written |
| Module structure | One file, no exports, no build step | The artifact cannot be imported or unit-tested as a module; verification must be black-box against a live listener |
| Process model | One process, one event loop, no `cluster` or `worker_threads` | Cannot use more than one core; 16 CPUs were available on the verification host and 15 are unusable by design |
| Configuration | Two in-source `const` literals | Deployment cannot be parameterised; changing host or port requires a source edit that the change freeze forbids |
| Deployment unit | The Git working tree itself; no container, orchestration, or IaC artifact exists | No portable, reproducible runtime packaging; the consumer supplies the runtime |
| Error strategy | Runtime defaults only; zero `'error'` listeners and zero signal handlers | A bind conflict terminates the process; there is no graceful shutdown and no in-flight-request draining |

**Why the alternatives were rejected — on the evidence of the fixture premise.** Adopting a framework such as Express, Koa, or Fastify would introduce a dependency graph, and the lockfile's single root record shows that a *zero-node* graph was the objective; a graph of any size reintroduces registry availability, transitive version drift, and transitive CVE exposure as failure modes for an artifact whose value is that it never behaves differently. Decomposing into modules would create an internal API surface to maintain for 14 lines of logic. Adding environment-variable configuration would make behaviour a function of the environment, directly contradicting the invariance property that consumers depend on. Introducing `cluster` would make the response path concurrent across processes without changing the response, adding operational complexity for a workload whose handler is O(1) and performs no I/O.

**Where the style has a genuine cost that the premise does not excuse.** Three consequences are liabilities rather than tradeoffs, because they impair the fixture's own usability: `package.json` names `index.js` as `main` while the implementation lives in `server.js`, so `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (deviation D-001, constraint C-005); no `start` script is declared, so `npm start` succeeds only through npm's built-in fallback rather than any repository declaration (deviation D-004); and no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` pins the runtime whose defaults form part of the observable contract (deviation D-005). The last is the most architecturally significant: `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` are all runtime-supplied, so a future Node.js release could change observed behaviour with no change to this codebase.

### 5.3.3 Communication Pattern Choices

Two communication patterns are in use and both are synchronous.

| Pattern | Where It Is Used | Rationale on the Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous request/response over HTTP/1.1 | The only external interface, on `127.0.0.1:3000` | HTTP is the protocol the fixture exists to exercise; one response per request makes assertions trivially deterministic |
| In-process callback dispatch (Reactor) | Transport runtime to response handler | Zero-cost hand-off — a direct function call with no queue, thread, IPC, or network hop between the two runtime components |
| Fire-and-forget stream write | Readiness announcement to stdout | Non-blocking, unacknowledged, and emitted exactly once; no log transport to configure or fail |
| Signal and exit-code exchange | Operator or supervisor to process | Uses the OS-native control plane rather than an in-band administrative endpoint |

**Patterns explicitly not used.** There is no message broker, event bus, publish–subscribe topic, work queue, scheduler, webhook, streaming, long-polling, Server-Sent Events, or WebSocket upgrade path — the `upgrade` listener count on the server object is zero, so upgrade requests are handled by the runtime default rather than by application code. Nor is there any outbound communication of any kind: with a single dependency edge to a core module, no HTTP client, SDK, or driver exists that could initiate a call.

Two consequences of the synchronous choice deserve naming. Positively, persistent connections make the interaction cheap and measurable — p50 0.077 ms on a reused connection versus 0.117 ms when a connection must be established, a difference attributable entirely to the runtime's keep-alive default rather than to any repository setting. Negatively, request/response over a single event loop means there is no backpressure mechanism, no admission control, and no queue depth to observe; overload is absorbed by the OS accept backlog at its untouched default of 511 entries, and its behaviour beyond that is a platform property rather than a designed one.

### 5.3.4 Data Storage Solution Rationale

**The decision was to have no storage tier at all, and on the evidence it is the correct one.** The system's entire data surface is a 14-byte string literal compiled into the module, plus two configuration literals. There is nothing to store because nothing is produced: no request datum is read, so nothing arrives that could be persisted; no state is accumulated, so nothing exists that could be checkpointed.

| Storage Option | Status | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Relational or NoSQL database | Not present — no client, driver, ORM, model, migration, or connection string exists in the dependency-free manifests | No entity, record, or query exists in the domain |
| Filesystem | Not used — `fs` and `path` are never imported | No read, write, stream, or temp-file operation is performed |
| In-memory store | Not present — zero module-level mutable variables | Persisting state would break the invariance property that the fixture guarantees |
| Session or token store | Not present — no session, cookie, or token handling anywhere | There is no identity concept to associate state with |
| Log persistence | Not present — one stdout line per process, no file sink or rotation | Log volume does not grow with traffic, so there is nothing to retain |

The architectural dividends of this decision are substantial and measurable. Recovery never involves state reconstruction — restarting the process restores the full contract in roughly 23 ms. Abrupt termination carries no data-loss risk, which is why the absence of graceful shutdown is tolerable. And because no data is processed, no data-retention, encryption-at-rest, backup, or privacy-compliance obligation arises from the code as written. The only durable state associated with the project is the Git history itself.

### 5.3.5 Caching Strategy Justification

**The decision was to implement no cache and to emit no cache directives.** Both halves are verified: no cache library, TTL construct, or memoisation exists in the source, and the response carries no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Vary` header — only the single `Content-Type` header the application sets, plus the runtime's framing headers.

Three arguments make caching structurally pointless here rather than merely omitted:

- **Nothing to memoise.** A cache trades memory for avoided computation or I/O. The response body is a compiled-in string literal, so the "computation" being avoided would be reading a constant already resident in the loaded module.
- **Nothing to invalidate.** Cache invalidation is the hard part of any caching strategy, and it presupposes that the underlying value can change. This value cannot: it is source text under a change freeze.
- **Nothing to key on.** Cache keys are derived from request attributes, and no request attribute is read. Every possible key would map to the same entry.

The one reuse mechanism actually in effect is **transport-level connection reuse**, and it is supplied by the runtime's 5000 ms `keepAliveTimeout` default rather than by repository configuration. Its benefit is measurable — the 0.077 ms versus 0.117 ms p50 difference cited above — which makes it the only performance optimisation present in the system, and it is one the repository inherited rather than chose. A deliberate consequence of emitting no cache directives is that clients and any intermediary are given no permission to cache, so every request results in a real round trip; for a fixture whose purpose is to be exercised, that is the desirable behaviour.

### 5.3.6 Security Mechanism Selection

**Exactly one security control is implemented, and it is a network-level one:** the listener binds `127.0.0.1` rather than a wildcard address, confining reachability to same-host processes. This is a verified control rather than a nominal one — requests to `127.0.0.1:3000` were served while connection attempts to the host's routable address `10.76.1.16:3000` and to IPv6 `[::1]:3000` were both refused outright.

An audit of all four tracked files found **zero** occurrences of `eval`, `child_process`, `spawn`, `crypto`, `process.argv`, `session`, `cookie`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `apikey`, `authorization`, `cors`, and `helmet`. The security posture that follows is unusual: most of it derives from absence rather than from mechanism.

| Mechanism | Status | Architectural Rationale or Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Network isolation via loopback bind | **Implemented** — the sole control | Off-host attack surface is nil; a co-located fixture needs no wider exposure (constraint C-002) |
| TLS / HTTPS | Not implemented — `https` and `tls` never imported | Plaintext is defensible *only because* traffic never leaves the loopback interface; the control above is what makes this acceptable |
| Authentication and authorisation | Not implemented — no identity, credential, session, or token construct exists | Every caller is treated identically; there is no role, tenant, or permission concept to enforce |
| Input validation and sanitisation | Not applicable — no request input is read | There is no injection sink: no query, body, header, or path value ever reaches an interpreter, filesystem, or datastore |
| Secret management | Not required — no credential material anywhere, and no `.npmrc` | Nothing to leak, rotate, or inject at deploy time |
| Supply-chain controls | **Structurally satisfied** — zero third-party dependencies, lockfile with only a root record | No transitive CVE surface; `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across one audited package |
| Security response headers | Not emitted — no HSTS, CSP, `X-Frame-Options`, or CORS headers | Nothing is rendered as HTML and no browser-origin trust decision depends on this service |
| Rate limiting and abuse controls | Not implemented | A local client can issue unbounded requests; the runtime's `431` and `408` defaults provide the only header-flood and slow-client protection |

**Residual risks, stated plainly.** Any process on the host can reach the endpoint without authentication; there is no request logging, so local access leaves no audit trail; and there is no rate limiting, so a local client can saturate the single event loop. Each of these is a direct consequence of the fixture premise rather than an oversight, and each is bounded by the loopback control. The decision that carries the most latent risk is the absence of a runtime version pin (D-005), because the security-relevant parser defaults that produce the `400`, `408`, and `431` responses belong to the runtime and are therefore unversioned by this repository.

### 5.3.7 Decision Tree

The following tree traces the design questions in the order the architecture answers them. Solid branches are the paths the code takes; dotted branches are the mainstream alternatives and the reason each was not taken.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START(["Design premise: a fixed-response HTTP fixture<br/>that must behave identically every time"]) --> Q1{"Does the workload require routing,<br/>middleware or content negotiation?"}

    Q1 -->|"No - the response is invariant"| Q2{"Can the transport need be met by<br/>a core runtime module alone?"}
    Q1 -.->|"Yes"| ALT1["Adopt Express, Koa or Fastify<br/>not taken: reintroduces a dependency graph"]

    Q2 -->|"Yes - the http module suffices"| D1["ADR-001 core http only,<br/>zero third-party dependencies"]
    Q2 -.->|"No"| ALT2["Add a framework or a reverse proxy<br/>not taken: registry and version drift risk"]

    D1 --> Q3{"Must behaviour vary by environment<br/>at deploy time?"}
    Q3 -->|"No - determinism is the objective"| D2["ADR-003 configuration as<br/>in-source const literals"]
    Q3 -.->|"Yes"| ALT3["Environment variables or a config file<br/>not taken: makes output environment dependent"]

    D2 --> Q4{"Must clients outside the host<br/>reach the service?"}
    Q4 -->|"No - the consumer is co-located"| D3["ADR-004 bind 127.0.0.1,<br/>network isolation as the only control"]
    Q4 -.->|"Yes"| ALT4["Bind a wildcard address with TLS and auth<br/>not taken: widens the attack surface"]

    D3 --> Q5{"Does any response depend on stored,<br/>computed or request derived state?"}
    Q5 -->|"No - the body is a compiled-in literal"| D4["ADR-006 no persistence tier<br/>and no cache tier"]
    Q5 -.->|"Yes"| ALT5["Add a datastore and a cache<br/>not taken: nothing to store or memoize"]

    D4 --> Q6{"Should faults be handled in<br/>application code?"}
    Q6 -->|"No - stateless restart is cheaper than recovery"| D5["ADR-007 delegate all fault handling<br/>to runtime defaults"]
    Q6 -.->|"Yes"| ALT6["Error listeners, retries, graceful drain<br/>not taken: no state to protect"]

    D5 --> Q7{"Is the artifact expected to evolve?"}
    Q7 -->|"No - README imposes a change freeze"| D6["ADR-008 no build, test<br/>or delivery pipeline"]
    Q7 -.->|"Yes"| ALT7["CI, containers and IaC<br/>not taken: nothing to build or promote"]

    D6 --> RESULT(["Resulting architecture: a 14-line,<br/>single-process, loopback-only HTTP service"])
```

### 5.3.8 Architecture Decision Records

The eight records below formalise the decisions traced above. All are marked **Accepted and frozen**, because the change freeze in `README.md` combined with a single-commit history and a clean working tree means no decision here is open for revision within the sanctioned scope of the project.

| ADR | Decision | Primary Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| ADR-001 | Use the Node.js core `http` module exclusively; adopt no web framework and no third-party package | `server.js` line 1; `package.json` with no dependency fields; lockfile with only a root record |
| ADR-002 | Implement the service as a single executable script with no module surface | One file; zero `module.exports`/`export` occurrences; no classes or named functions |
| ADR-003 | Express all configuration as in-source `const` literals | `server.js` lines 3–4; zero `process.env` and `process.argv` occurrences |
| ADR-004 | Bind the listener to `127.0.0.1` and treat network isolation as the only security control | `server.js` line 3; routable-address and IPv6 connections verified refused |
| ADR-005 | Return an invariant, input-independent response | `server.js` lines 6–10; zero `req.` dereferences; identical response across a full method and path matrix |
| ADR-006 | Provide no persistence tier and no caching tier | No database client, no `fs`/`path` import, no cache construct, no cache-control headers |
| ADR-007 | Delegate all fault handling and lifecycle management to runtime defaults | Zero `try`/`catch`; server `'error'`/`'clientError'` listener counts of 0; zero `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`/`uncaughtException` handlers |
| ADR-008 | Ship no build, test, or delivery pipeline and freeze the artifact | `scripts.test` exits 1; no CI, container, or IaC artifact; single commit `1a0874d`; `README.md` change freeze |

#### 5.3.8.1 ADR-001 — Core Runtime HTTP Stack Only

**Context.** An HTTP endpoint is required that returns one fixed response and must behave identically on every invocation, in every environment, indefinitely.
**Decision.** Depend on nothing but Node.js's built-in `http` module. The repository's only dependency edge is `require('http')`.
**Consequences.** Positive: installation is a verified no-op (`npm ci` exits 0 in roughly 120 ms, works offline, and creates no `node_modules`); there is no registry-availability, version-drift, or transitive-vulnerability failure mode; `npm audit` reports zero findings. Negative: no routing, middleware, validation, negotiation, or compression capability exists, and any future need for one would have to be hand-written against the raw runtime API.

#### 5.3.8.2 ADR-002 — Single-File Executable Script

**Context.** The logic totals three response statements and one bind call.
**Decision.** Place everything in `server.js`, export nothing, and let the listener open as a side effect of module evaluation.
**Consequences.** Positive: the committed source is byte-for-byte the executed source, with no build, transpile, or bundle step to introduce variance. Negative: the package cannot be meaningfully imported, which combines with the unresolvable `main` field to make library-style consumption impossible; and because there is no exported unit, verification can only be black-box against a running listener.

#### 5.3.8.3 ADR-003 — Configuration as In-Source Literals

**Context.** The fixture must present the same address and port to every consumer.
**Decision.** Declare `hostname` and `port` as module-scope `const` literals and read no environment variable, CLI argument, or configuration file.
**Consequences.** Positive: behaviour is fixed at author time, and interpolating the same constants into the readiness line guarantees the advertised URL matches the bind target. Negative: deployment cannot be parameterised (constraint C-003), and because the change freeze forbids editing the literals, the loopback address cannot be widened — which means a container built around this repository would expose the service only within its own network namespace.

#### 5.3.8.4 ADR-004 — Loopback-Only Bind as the Sole Security Control

**Context.** The consumer of the fixture runs on the same host, and the service implements no authentication.
**Decision.** Bind `127.0.0.1` instead of a wildcard address, accepting network-level isolation as the complete security posture.
**Consequences.** Positive: off-host attack surface is nil, verified by refused connections on both the routable IPv4 address and IPv6 loopback; the absence of TLS, authentication, and security headers becomes defensible because no traffic leaves the host. Negative: any local process can reach the endpoint unauthenticated and unlogged, and remote use is architecturally impossible.

#### 5.3.8.5 ADR-005 — Invariant, Input-Independent Response

**Context.** A fixture's assertions are only as stable as its output.
**Decision.** Accept the `req` parameter for signature compatibility but never dereference it; return status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a 14-byte body unconditionally.
**Consequences.** Positive: output cannot vary with client behaviour, which was confirmed across a full method and path matrix and held under 50 concurrent and 500 sequential requests; combined with zero module-level mutable state, there is no accumulator that traffic could disturb. Negative: no content-driven scenario can be exercised, no error status can be produced by the application, and paths that look like operational endpoints — `/health`, `/metrics` — are indistinguishable from any other path.

#### 5.3.8.6 ADR-006 — No Persistence and No Cache

**Context.** The response body is a compiled-in constant and no request datum is read.
**Decision.** Implement no database, filesystem, session, or in-memory store, and no caching layer or cache-control directive.
**Consequences.** Positive: recovery never requires state reconstruction, so a restart restores the complete contract in roughly 23 ms; abrupt termination carries no data-loss risk; and no retention, encryption, backup, or privacy obligation arises. Negative: nothing survives a restart, and there is no record of what traffic the fixture served.

#### 5.3.8.7 ADR-007 — Delegate Fault Handling to Runtime Defaults

**Context.** The system holds no state worth protecting and can be replaced in milliseconds.
**Decision.** Register no `'error'` or `'clientError'` listener, no signal handler, and no `uncaughtException` or `unhandledRejection` hook; let the runtime's defaults define all failure behaviour.
**Consequences.** Positive: failure semantics are simple, uniform, and inherited — protocol faults are answered per specification (`400`, `408`, `431`) without any application involvement, and the fault blast radius is a single socket in every case except bind failure. Negative: a port conflict becomes an unhandled `'error'` event that kills the process with exit code 1 and no retry or fallback; `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` terminate immediately with no draining, dropping in-flight connections; and the fault taxonomy is defined by an unpinned runtime version.

#### 5.3.8.8 ADR-008 — No Build, Test, or Delivery Pipeline; Frozen Artifact

**Context.** `README.md` declares the project a fixture and instructs that it not be modified.
**Decision.** Ship no build system, no automated tests, no CI/CD definition, no container image, and no infrastructure-as-code; retain a deliberately failing placeholder `test` script.
**Consequences.** Positive: there is no pipeline that can drift, break, or alter the artifact, and the single-commit history makes the baseline trivially verifiable with a working-tree emptiness check. Negative: `npm test` exits 1, so any conventional CI gate asserting a passing suite fails against this repository; no mechanism inside the repository enforces the change freeze, since there are no active Git hooks and no `CODEOWNERS`; and nothing in the repository will restart the process if it dies, because no supervisor, restart policy, or process-manager definition exists.


## 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns

In a conventional service, cross-cutting concerns are implemented as an aspect layer — middleware, interceptors, decorators, sidecars. This system has no such layer, and the concerns below are therefore addressed in one of three ways: **implemented directly in the 14 lines** (one concern), **inherited from the Node.js runtime as a default** (most of them), or **verifiably absent** (the remainder). The table orients the detail that follows; the distinction between the second and third categories matters, because inherited behaviour is real and testable while absent behaviour is not.

| Concern | How It Is Addressed | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Monitoring and observability | One startup line to stdout; nothing else | Repository (CMP-05) |
| Logging and tracing | `console.log` at startup only; no request logging, no tracing | Repository (CMP-05) |
| Error handling | No application handling at all; every behaviour is a runtime default | Node.js runtime |
| Authentication and authorisation | Not implemented; loopback bind substitutes at the network layer | Repository (CMP-03) for isolation only |
| Performance and service levels | No requirement, target, or SLA declared anywhere | Undefined by the repository |
| Disaster recovery | No documented procedure; statelessness makes restart the whole strategy | External to the repository |

### 5.4.1 Monitoring and Observability Approach

**The system emits exactly one telemetry signal for its entire lifetime.** `console.log` inside the listen callback (`server.js` line 13) writes `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` to standard output, and standard output was still one line long after roughly 700 requests plus every fault probe. There is no metrics library, no instrumentation, no tracing, no health-check endpoint distinguishable from the default response, no monitoring, alerting, or dashboard configuration in any file.

| Signal | Emitted | Consumable By |
|---|---|---|
| Readiness line on stdout | Once, immediately after a successful bind | The invoking shell, a supervisor capturing stdout, or an automated harness matching the exact string |
| Absence of the readiness line | Implicitly, when the bind fails | The same consumers — a reliable negative health indicator |
| Unhandled-error stack trace on stderr | Only on bind failure | Shell or supervisor |
| Process exit status | On termination: `1`, `143`, or `130` | Shell or supervisor |
| HTTP response itself | Per request | The requesting client only |

Two observability properties follow from the architecture rather than from any monitoring design. First, the readiness signal is **trustworthy in both directions** because it is emitted from inside the listen callback: it appears only after a successful bind, and it never appears for a process that failed to bind. Second, because the fixture returns `200` for *every* path, **liveness cannot be distinguished from correctness by probing** — a `GET /health` returns the same `200`/`text/plain`/14 bytes as any other path, so a probe confirms only that the listener is accepting and responding, which for this system happens to be the whole of its contract.

The practical consequence for an operator is that observability must be supplied from outside. The only viable strategies are to capture stdout and match the readiness string, to poll `127.0.0.1:3000` and assert `200` with a 14-byte body, or to watch the process exit status. No in-process signal beyond those exists to collect.

### 5.4.2 Logging and Tracing Strategy

**The logging strategy is a single unstructured line, and there is no tracing strategy at all.** The relevant facts, all verified:

- **One log statement exists** in the entire repository, and it fires once per process lifetime.
- **No logging framework** is present — no Winston, Pino, Bunyan, or `debug`, consistent with a zero-dependency manifest. There are no log levels, no structured/JSON output, no timestamps beyond what a capturing supervisor might add, no file sink, and no rotation.
- **No request logging.** Nothing is written per request, so there is no access log and no record of what traffic the fixture served.
- **No distributed tracing.** There is no OpenTelemetry or APM integration, no span creation, no trace or correlation ID generation, and no propagation of inbound trace headers — the handler never reads any request header, so `traceparent` or `X-Request-ID` values arriving from a client are structurally unreachable and are silently discarded.

This is architecturally coherent for a single-process, single-hop system: with no downstream call and no internal component boundary crossed over a network, there is no distributed context to correlate. It is nonetheless the system's sharpest operational limitation — **per-request diagnosis from logs is impossible**, and any investigation must be conducted from the client side or by observing the socket. A compensating benefit is that log volume is constant and independent of traffic, so the output stream can never become a bottleneck or a disk-space concern.

### 5.4.3 Error Handling Patterns

**Repository code contains no error handling whatsoever, and this is a measured statement rather than an impression.** `try`, `catch`, `finally`, and `throw` appear zero times; the server object's listener counts are `error = 0`, `clientError = 0`, `close = 0`, and `upgrade = 0`; and the process registers zero handlers for `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `uncaughtException`, and `unhandledRejection`. Every error behaviour the system exhibits is therefore a Node.js default, inherited rather than designed, and documented here as such.

The architectural pattern that results is best described as **fail-fast at the process level, delegate-and-close at the socket level**. Three properties define it:

- **Faults are classified by phase, not by type.** A fault during bind kills the process; a fault during parsing costs one socket; a fault inside the handler is structurally impossible because the handler performs three assignments with no I/O and no parsing.
- **The application layer has no error path.** Because CMP-04 is invoked only after successful parsing and can only emit `200`, every non-`200` status the system produces originates in CMP-01 and reaches the client without CMP-04 ever running.
- **Recovery is external in every case.** There is no retry loop, no exponential backoff, no circuit breaker, no alternate-port fallback, no degraded mode, and no static error page. The bind is attempted exactly once.

#### 5.4.3.1 Fault Disposition Flow

The diagram traces each fault class to the component that disposes of it, the channel that reports it, and its blast radius.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    FAULT(["Fault occurs"]) --> WHEN{"In which phase<br/>does the fault occur?"}

    WHEN -->|"during bind, before serving"| B1["CMP-02 causes the runtime<br/>to emit an error event"]
    B1 --> B2{"Is an error listener<br/>registered on the server?"}
    B2 -->|"No - measured listener count is zero"| B3["Runtime rethrows:<br/>unhandled error event"]
    B2 -.->|"Yes - not this system"| B6["Application could recover<br/>or select another port"]
    B3 --> B4["stderr receives the default stack trace<br/>code EADDRINUSE, errno -98, syscall listen"]
    B4 --> B5(["Exit code 1; readiness line never printed<br/>blast radius: the whole process"])

    WHEN -->|"during request parsing"| P1{"What did the parser reject?"}
    P1 -->|"invalid request line or version"| P2["Runtime replies 400 Bad Request"]
    P1 -->|"header block exceeds the size limit"| P3["Runtime replies 431"]
    P1 -->|"headers incomplete past headersTimeout"| P4["Runtime replies 408"]
    P2 --> PC["Connection close header sent,<br/>socket destroyed"]
    P3 --> PC
    P4 --> PC
    PC --> PE(["CMP-04 is never invoked<br/>blast radius: one socket"])

    WHEN -->|"client aborts mid request"| A1["Runtime destroys the socket silently"]
    A1 --> A2(["No stdout or stderr output;<br/>application is never notified<br/>blast radius: one socket"])

    WHEN -->|"inside the request handler"| H1{"Does CMP-04 have<br/>any failure mode?"}
    H1 -->|"No - three assignments, no I/O, no parsing"| H2(["No application fault path exists;<br/>the handler cannot fail on a dispatched request"])

    WHEN -->|"operator signal"| S1["No SIGTERM or SIGINT<br/>handler is registered"]
    S1 --> S2(["Immediate termination, exit 143 or 130,<br/>no connection drain<br/>blast radius: the whole process"])
```

#### 5.4.3.2 Fault Taxonomy and Reporting Channels

| Fault | Runtime Disposition | Reporting Channel |
|---|---|---|
| Bind conflict (`EADDRINUSE`) | Unhandled `'error'` event; process aborts | stderr stack trace plus exit code 1 |
| Malformed request line or HTTP version | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` | HTTP status line to that client only |
| Oversized header block | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` | HTTP status line to that client only |
| Stalled request headers | `408 Request Timeout` after the 60000 ms `headersTimeout` | HTTP status line to that client only |
| Idle keep-alive connection | Socket closed after the 5000 ms `keepAliveTimeout` | None — silent by design |
| Client reset mid-request | Socket destroyed | None — silent by design |
| `SIGTERM` / `SIGINT` | Immediate termination, no drain, port released | Exit code 143 / 130 |

**Silence is part of the contract.** Client aborts and idle-socket reaping produce no output at all, and the only fault that ever reaches stderr is a bind failure. An operator therefore cannot learn from the system that a client misbehaved; only the client learns that, through its status code.

### 5.4.4 Authentication and Authorisation Framework

**There is no authentication framework and no authorisation framework.** An audit of all four tracked files found zero occurrences of `session`, `cookie`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `apikey`, `authorization`, `cors`, `helmet`, and `crypto`. There is no identity concept, no role, no tenant, no account, no permission model, and no credential material anywhere in the repository.

Access control is enforced at exactly one layer, and it is the network layer:

| Control Layer | Mechanism | Verified Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Network reachability | Listener bound to `127.0.0.1` rather than a wildcard address | Only same-host processes can connect; the routable address `10.76.1.16:3000` and IPv6 `[::1]:3000` were both refused |
| Transport confidentiality | None — `https` and `tls` are never imported | Traffic is plaintext, which is bounded by the control above since it never leaves the host |
| Request authentication | None — no header, token, or credential is read | Every caller is anonymous and indistinguishable |
| Request authorisation | None — the handler cannot branch, because `req` is never dereferenced | Every caller receives identical output; no path or method is privileged |
| Auditing | None — no request logging exists | Access leaves no trace on the server side |

The architectural substitution being made is explicit: **network isolation is used in place of identity**. Its adequacy depends entirely on the trust model of the host, and for a co-located test fixture that model is reasonable. It is also brittle in one specific way — the isolation lives in a single source literal (`server.js` line 3), so the entire security posture is one character-level edit away from being removed, with no compensating control behind it. The change freeze in `README.md` is what protects that literal, and enforcement of the freeze is by convention only, since no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check exists.

### 5.4.5 Performance Characteristics and Service-Level Posture

**The repository declares no performance requirement, no SLA, no SLO, no error budget, and no availability, latency, or throughput target.** This is a verified absence: no monitoring, alerting, or dashboard configuration exists in any file, no such commitment appears in `README.md` or the manifests, and there is no instrumentation from which a target could be tracked. Any performance or availability target for this system would have to be established by the consuming tooling; none can be sourced from this repository.

What *can* be documented is measured behaviour. The figures below are **observations of one environment, not commitments**. They were produced against an unmodified copy of `server.js` under Node.js 22.23.1 on a 16-CPU host, using an in-process Node HTTP client over a single keep-alive connection after a 50-request warm-up.

| Measurement | Observed Value | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Startup to readiness | 26.9 ms | Process spawn until the readiness line appeared on stdout |
| Sequential throughput | ≈12,761 requests/second (2000 requests in 156.7 ms) | One keep-alive connection, one event loop |
| Latency p50 / p99 / max | 0.064 ms / 0.184 ms / 0.414 ms | Same run, 2000 measured requests |
| Concurrent request handling | 50 of 50 succeeded with `200` in 25 ms wall time | 50 parallel clients against the single event loop |
| Connection-reuse benefit | p50 0.077 ms reused versus 0.117 ms per new connection | Reported in section 4.3.1.4 |
| Response payload | 14 bytes, invariant | Measured on the wire |

Three structural characteristics govern these numbers and are more durable than the numbers themselves:

- **Throughput is capped by one core.** The design uses one process and one event loop with no `cluster` or `worker_threads`, so 15 of the 16 available CPUs are unusable. Vertical scaling stops at single-core event-loop capacity.
- **Latency is dominated by transport, not by work.** The handler is O(1), performs no I/O, and allocates nothing beyond the runtime-supplied objects, which is why p99 sits within a factor of three of p50 and why the only measurable optimisation in the system is connection reuse.
- **There is no overload control.** No rate limiting, admission control, queue-depth metric, `maxConnections` cap, or backpressure mechanism exists. Beyond the runtime's untouched 511-entry accept backlog, overload behaviour is a platform property rather than a designed one.

Capacity, correspondingly, is not scalable by any mechanism the repository provides: a single instance is the maximum unit, because a second process on the same host aborts with `EADDRINUSE`.

### 5.4.6 Disaster Recovery Procedures

**No disaster recovery procedure is documented in the repository, and no recovery automation exists in it.** There is no supervisor configuration, no container restart policy, no process-manager definition, no CI/CD or deployment pipeline, and no runbook. Nothing inside the repository will restart the process if it dies.

What the architecture *does* provide is a recovery profile so simple that a procedure is nearly unnecessary. Because ADR-006 eliminates all persistence, **recovery never involves state reconstruction**: restarting the process restores the complete contract, and a restart was measured to reach readiness in 26.9 ms (with section 4.3.2.3 reporting roughly 23 ms for the same operation). The system's resilience characteristic is therefore **fast replacement rather than fault tolerance**.

| Recovery Dimension | Characteristic | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable — no data is ever written, so there is nothing to lose | No database, filesystem, cache, or session store exists |
| Recovery time, mechanically | ~27 ms from process launch to readiness; detection time is external and unbounded | Measured startup-to-ready; no health check or watchdog exists in the repository |
| Recovery action | Re-run `node server.js`; the OS releases port 3000 immediately on exit | Verified rebind after `SIGTERM` |
| Recovery verification | Readiness line on stdout, plus a probe returning `200` with a 14-byte body | The only two observable success signals |
| Artifact recovery | Re-clone the single-commit baseline `1a0874d` and confirm a clean working tree | Git is the only durable state the project has |
| High availability | None possible on one host — a second instance aborts with `EADDRINUSE` | Bind conflict terminates the process with exit code 1 |

Two failure scenarios warrant explicit procedures, and both are external to the repository by necessity:

- **Port conflict at startup.** The process exits 1 with an `EADDRINUSE` trace and no readiness line. Recovery is to stop whatever else holds `127.0.0.1:3000` — or wait for it to exit — and relaunch. There is no retry and no port fallback to rely on, so consuming automation must serialise its use of port 3000.
- **Unexpected process death.** Because no readiness line is re-emitted and no metrics exist, death is detectable only by exit status or by a failing probe. Recovery is to relaunch; because termination carries no data-loss risk, no consistency check or replay is needed afterwards.

The single largest gap between this profile and a production posture is not recovery speed but **detection**: the architecture provides a fast, reliable recovery path and no mechanism whatsoever to notice that recovery is required.


## 5.5 References

### 5.5.1 Repository Files Examined

All four tracked files in the repository were read in full; the inventory below is exhaustive, as confirmed by `git ls-files`.

- `server.js` — the sole runtime artifact (14 lines). Established the architecture style (single-file CommonJS script), the one dependency edge `require('http')` on line 1, the configuration constants `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and `port = 3000` on lines 3–4, the invariant response handler on lines 6–10, and the listener bootstrap plus readiness announcement on lines 12–14. Its absences established the error-handling, observability, security, and configuration posture: zero occurrences of `process.env`, `process.argv`, `try`/`catch`, `.on(`, `process.on`, `uncaughtException`, `unhandledRejection`, `cluster`, `https`, `tls`, `req.`, `module.exports`, `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`, `writeHead`, `fs.`, and `Cache-Control`.
- `package.json` — established package identity (`hello_world@1.0.0`, MIT, author `hxu`), the unresolvable `main: "index.js"` entry point, the single deliberately failing `test` script, and the absence of `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `engines`, `type`, and `start`.
- `package-lock.json` — established the zero-dependency graph: `lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`, and a `packages` map containing only the root record.
- `README.md` — established the fixture premise ("test project for backprop integration"), the change-freeze directive that fixes the architecture in place, and the naming divergence from the npm package name.

### 5.5.2 Repository Structure Examined

- `/` (repository root) — the only directory in the repository. Contained exactly four files and zero subdirectories. Its contents established the complete component inventory of section 5.1.2 and, through explicit existence checks, the negative evidence underpinning sections 5.3 and 5.4: `src/`, `lib/`, `config/`, `test/`, `tests/`, `spec/`, `__tests__/`, `dist/`, `build/`, `docs/`, `public/`, `node_modules/`, `.github/`, `k8s/`, `helm/`, `terraform/`, `index.js`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore`, `Makefile`, `Procfile`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `serverless.yml`, `vercel.json`, `.env`, `.env.example`, `.npmrc`, `.nvmrc`, `.eslintrc*`, `.prettierrc`, `tsconfig.json`, `babel.config.js`, and `jest.config.js` are all absent.
- Git metadata — established the frozen baseline: a single commit `1a0874d` ("Add files via upload") on branch `main`, no tags, a clean working tree, and no active hooks.

### 5.5.3 Empirical Verification Performed

Architecture claims that could not be settled by reading alone were verified by executing an isolated copy of `server.js` under Node.js 22.23.1 / npm 11.18.0. The repository files were never modified.

- **Startup and readiness** — confirmed the single stdout line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and an empty stderr; measured 26.9 ms from process spawn to readiness.
- **Response invariance** — a method matrix (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) and a path matrix (`/`, `/any/deep/path`, `/x?y=1&z=2`, `/admin`, `/health`, `/metrics`, `/favicon.ico`) all returned identical `200`/`text/plain`/14-byte responses, establishing the absence of routing, method dispatch, and authorisation gates.
- **Wire headers** — captured `Content-Type` as the only application-authored header, with `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, and `Content-Length: 14` supplied by the runtime; confirmed no cache or security headers.
- **Network boundary** — connections to `10.76.1.16:3000` (the host's routable address) and `[::1]:3000` were refused while `127.0.0.1:3000` succeeded, establishing the loopback bind as a verified control.
- **Protocol fault handling** — a malformed request line and a bad HTTP version each produced `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; a ~20 KB header block produced `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`.
- **Concurrency, reuse, and throughput** — 50 parallel requests all returned `200` in 25 ms; two requests were served over one keep-alive connection; 2000 sequential requests over a single reused connection yielded ≈12,761 requests/second with p50 0.064 ms, p99 0.184 ms, max 0.414 ms.
- **Runtime-default configuration** — read from an identically constructed server object: `keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300000 ms, `timeout` 0, `maxHeadersCount` `null`, `maxRequestsPerSocket` 0, no `maxConnections`; listener counts `request` 1, `connection` 1, and `error`/`clientError`/`close`/`upgrade` all 0; process-level `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`/`uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` handler counts all 0.
- **Failure mode** — a second instance binding `127.0.0.1:3000` produced `Error: listen EADDRINUSE`, reported as an unhandled `'error'` event, terminating with exit code 1.
- **Security construct audit** — a repository-wide search found zero occurrences of `eval`, `child_process`, `spawn`, `crypto`, `process.argv`, `session`, `cookie`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `apikey`, `authorization`, `cors`, and `helmet`, and confirmed that the only `require` in the repository targets a Node core module.

- **1.3 Scope** — supplied the in-scope capability set and the verified out-of-scope inventories relied on throughout sections 5.1.4, 5.3, and 5.4.
