Two of these rows are decisive rather than merely negative. The zero-dependency lockfile means **no data-access library can be in use even transitively**, so absence cannot be hiding in a dependency graph. And the zero-match result for filesystem primitives means the process has no mechanism by which to create durable state even accidentally — a property confirmed at runtime in Section 6.2.2.2.

#### 6.2.1.3 Artifact and History Proof

A data tier can also be evidenced by artifacts rather than code — a dump, a fixture, a schema file, or a deleted file still present in version-control history. All three checks below are negative, which establishes that no data artifact exists now and none ever existed.

| Check Performed | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Tracked-file type census | `git ls-files` with an extension tally | Exactly 4 files: 1 × `.js`, 2 × `.json`, 1 × `.md`. A search for any tracked file that is not `.js`, `.json`, or `.md` returned zero |
| Working-tree artifact probe | Existence test over 32 conventional data paths | None present; the tree contains four files and zero subdirectories |
| Full-history object census | `git log --all --name-status`, `git rev-list --objects --all`, `git fsck --lost-found` | One commit only (`1a0874d`, "Add files via upload"), which **adds** the same four files. No modify or delete record exists anywhere in history, the object database contains no other path, and there are no dangling objects |

#### 6.2.1.4 Governing Decisions and Constraints

The absence of a data tier is traceable to recorded decisions and constraints rather than to incompleteness, and those same constraints prevent a data tier from being introduced within sanctioned scope.

| Identifier | Statement | Consequence for This Section |
|---|---|---|
| ADR-006 (Section 5.3) | No persistence or cache tier | Recovery never involves state reconstruction; no retention, encryption-at-rest, backup, or privacy obligation arises from the code as written |
| C-001 (`README.md` line 2) | Change freeze — "Do not touch!" | Introducing a database, cache, or schema would require modifying repository content, which the freeze prohibits |
| C-003 (`server.js` lines 3–4) | Configuration is compiled in | There is no configuration surface into which a connection string could be supplied; `process.env` appears zero times (F-001-RQ-003) |
| F-002-RQ-003 / F-002-RQ-004 | Fixed 14-byte literal response; request never dereferenced | The response requires no read from any store, and no request datum is available to write to one |

#### 6.2.1.5 Conditions That Would Change This Determination

This assessment is a statement about the repository at commit `1a0874d`, and it is falsifiable. Any one of the following would make a database-design section applicable, and each would be detectable by the same probes used above:

- A dependency entry for a driver, ODM, or cache client in `package.json`, which would also add nodes to the currently root-only `package-lock.json`.
- An import of `fs`, an embedded engine, or any module that opens a durable handle — currently provably absent, since the only `require` in the repository targets core `http`.
- A module-scope `let`, `var`, `Map`, or `Set` used to retain values across requests, which would convert the process from stateless to stateful and invalidate the invariance measured in F-002-RQ-005.
- A tracked schema, migration, seed, or dump artifact, which would change the tracked-extension census away from `.js`/`.json`/`.md`.

None of these can be introduced without editing repository content, which constraint C-001 places outside the sanctioned scope of the project.

#### 6.2.1.6 Structure of the Remainder of This Section

Because the determination is negative, Sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.6 are written as **evidence-based status assessments** rather than design descriptions. Each covers one area this section is expected to address, states what the repository actually provides, and — where a mechanism is absent — records the verified operational consequence of that absence instead of describing a mechanism that does not exist.

| Sub-section | Area Covered | Form of the Content |
|---|---|---|
| 6.2.2 | Data domain, the ephemeral state that genuinely exists, storage and retrieval mechanics, data-flow and entity-relationship diagrams | Exhaustive state inventory with ownership and lifetime, plus measured proof that nothing accumulates |
| 6.2.3 | Schema design: entity relationships, data models, indexing, partitioning, replication, backup architecture | Per-concern not-applicable determination with evidence, an explicit index and constraint register, and the replication topology diagram |
| 6.2.4 | Data management: migrations, versioning, archival, storage and retrieval, caching policies | What Git provides in place of each mechanism, and where no analogue exists at all |
| 6.2.5 | Compliance: retention, backup and fault tolerance, privacy, audit, access control | The obligations that do not arise, the one control that does exist, and the two verified compliance gaps |
| 6.2.6 | Performance: query optimization, caching, connection pooling, read/write splitting, batch processing | Measured figures with explicit non-commitment framing, and correct attribution of the one optimisation in effect |


### 6.2.2 Data Domain and Ephemeral State Model

Although no database exists, the system is not devoid of data — it handles exactly three literal values and creates a small amount of per-request state that the runtime owns. Documenting that state precisely is what makes the determination in Section 6.2.1 verifiable rather than assertive, because it establishes that every datum in the system has a lifetime bounded by a single response or a single process.

#### 6.2.2.1 The Complete Data Domain

The entire data domain of the system is three string or numeric literals compiled into `server.js`. There is no schema because there is no record; there is no record because there is no input — the request object is bound but never dereferenced (F-002-RQ-004), so zero request bytes are parsed, buffered, stored, or logged.

| Datum | Source Location | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| `Hello, World!\n` — the 14-byte response payload | `server.js` line 9, a compiled-in string literal | Non-sensitive static content; no template, file read, or serialization is involved (F-002-RQ-003) |
| `127.0.0.1` — the bind address | `server.js` line 3, an immutable `const` | Non-sensitive configuration; also the system's only access control (Section 6.2.5.5) |
| `3000` — the bind port | `server.js` line 4, an immutable `const` | Non-sensitive configuration |

No personal, regulated, financial, or business data is read, stored, transmitted, or logged anywhere in the system, which is consistent with the data-domain boundary recorded in Section 1.3.1.2 and with the storage findings in Section 3.5.2. The consequence for this section is direct: **there is no data classification tier that would trigger a retention schedule, an encryption-at-rest requirement, or a data-residency consideration.**

#### 6.2.2.2 Ephemeral State Inventory

The inventory below is exhaustive — it is the complete set of state associated with a running instance. Most of it belongs to the Node.js runtime rather than to repository code, and none of it is durable.

| State Element | Scope and Owner | Lifetime | Durable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Listening TCP socket on `127.0.0.1:3000` | OS kernel and libuv; opened by `server.js` line 12 | Process lifetime; released by the OS on exit | No |
| Accepted connection sockets and keep-alive timers | Node.js runtime (`CMP-01`) | One connection; reaped after the runtime's 5000 ms `keepAliveTimeout` default | No |
| `http`, `hostname`, `port`, `server` bindings | Module scope; `server.js` lines 1, 3, 4, 6 — all `const` | Process lifetime; immutable | No — reloaded from source text on every start |
| Request object per request | Runtime-owned | One request; never dereferenced by application code | No |
| `res.statusCode = 200` — the only assignment in the program | Runtime-owned response object; `server.js` line 7 | One response; discarded on completion | No |
| Response header map entry `Content-Type: text/plain` | Runtime-owned response object; `server.js` line 8 | One response | No |
| Startup announcement line on stdout | External to the process once written | As long as the capturing consumer retains it | Only if an external consumer persists the stream |
| Git history at commit `1a0874d` | Version control; the only durable state the project has | Independent of process lifecycle | Yes — but it is design-time artifact state, not application data |

**Measured proof that nothing accumulates.** Static analysis establishes that there is no module-scope mutable binding to accumulate into; execution confirms that the runtime's own bookkeeping is bounded as well.

| Measurement | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Resident-set growth under sustained load | Five cumulative rounds of 5,000 requests over one keep-alive connection, sampling `VmRSS` after each | 48.2 MB at startup, rising to 59.5 MB at 5,000 requests, then 61.6 / 61.6 / 61.7 / 61.9 MB at 10,000 / 15,000 / 20,000 / 25,000 requests — a 268 kB change across the final 20,000 requests. The resident set **plateaus**; the initial rise is heap and JIT warm-up, not accumulating data |
| Durable-handle census | `/proc/<pid>/fd` inspection during and after the load | Open descriptor count constant at 22 throughout; **zero** regular-file descriptors after excluding standard streams, sockets, pipes, and libuv internals. The process never opens a file for reading or writing |
| Emitted-record census | Standard-output line count after 25,000 requests | Exactly one line — the readiness announcement. No per-request record accumulates anywhere (F-003-RQ-003) |
| Filesystem side-effect check | Tree comparison before and after a run, plus a run from an independent scratch working directory | Repository tree unchanged at four files; the scratch directory received no data, log, lock, or socket file |
| Restart equivalence | Terminate, relaunch, and compare the first response and the startup line | Identical response checksum and byte-identical readiness line — nothing is carried across a restart, and nothing is lost by one |

#### 6.2.2.3 Entity-Relationship View of Runtime State

The diagram below is provided because this section is expected to include an entity-relationship view, and it is important to be precise about what it represents. **It is not a database schema.** No entity shown is stored, keyed, indexed, or queryable; there is no primary or foreign key anywhere in the system because there is no record identity to establish. The cardinalities describe *object lifetimes inside one process* — one listener accepts many connections, one connection carries many keep-alive requests, and each request is answered by exactly one response — and every entity carries an explicit `persisted` attribute recording that it is discarded rather than written.

**Diagram 6.2.2-A — Entity-Relationship View of Ephemeral Runtime State (No Persisted Entity Exists)**

```mermaid
erDiagram
    MODULE_CONSTANTS ||--|| LISTENING_SOCKET : "supplies bind target to"
    MODULE_CONSTANTS ||--o{ RESPONSE_OBJECT : "supplies fixed payload to"
    LISTENING_SOCKET ||--o{ CONNECTION_SOCKET : accepts
    CONNECTION_SOCKET ||--o{ REQUEST_OBJECT : carries
    REQUEST_OBJECT ||--|| RESPONSE_OBJECT : "answered by"
    MODULE_CONSTANTS {
        string http_binding "require http - server.js line 1"
        string hostname "127.0.0.1 - immutable const line 3"
        int port "3000 - immutable const line 4"
        string mutability "none - zero let or var declarations"
        string persisted "NO - source text reloaded on every start"
    }
    LISTENING_SOCKET {
        string owner "OS kernel and libuv"
        string lifetime "process lifetime"
        string persisted "NO - released by the OS on exit"
    }
    CONNECTION_SOCKET {
        string keep_alive_timeout "5000 ms - Node runtime default"
        string lifetime "one connection"
        string persisted "NO - destroyed on close or idle reap"
    }
    REQUEST_OBJECT {
        string dereferenced "never - F-002-RQ-004"
        string bytes_retained "zero - not parsed buffered stored or logged"
        string persisted "NO"
    }
    RESPONSE_OBJECT {
        int status_code "200 - the only assignment in the program"
        string content_type "text-plain - only header set by repository code"
        string body "14-byte literal - server.js line 9"
        string persisted "NO - discarded when the response completes"
    }
```

#### 6.2.2.4 Data Flow

The data flow of the system is a single hop with no read from and no write to any store. The response payload is not fetched — it is a string literal already resident in the loaded module, referenced by the one `res.end` call on `server.js` line 9. The inbound direction has no flow at all: request bytes are parsed by the runtime for protocol purposes and then discarded with the socket, never reaching application code.

**Diagram 6.2.2-B — Data Flow Through the Request Path, With the Verified-Absent Persistence Tier**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLIENT["Same-host HTTP client<br/>loopback reachability only"]

    subgraph Runtime["Single Node.js Process - one address space, no data tier"]
        ACCEPT["CMP-01 accept and parse<br/>request bytes never surfaced to the application"]
        HANDLER["CMP-04 invariant handler<br/>one write - res.statusCode = 200"]
        LITERAL["Compiled-in 14-byte literal<br/>server.js line 9 - read-only source text"]
        SERIAL["CMP-01 serializer<br/>adds Content-Length, Date, Connection"]
        ACCEPT -->|"in-process function call, no query, no I/O"| HANDLER
        LITERAL -->|"string reference resident in the loaded module"| HANDLER
        HANDLER --> SERIAL
    end

    subgraph Absent["Persistence and Caching Tier - Verified Absent"]
        WRITE["Write path - INSERT, UPDATE, file write"]
        READ["Read path - SELECT, find, getItem"]
        CACHE["Cache lookup and invalidation"]
        OBJSTORE["Object or blob storage"]
        MIGRATE["Migration or schema-versioning runner"]
        WRITE -.- READ
        READ -.- CACHE
        CACHE -.- OBJSTORE
        OBJSTORE -.- MIGRATE
    end

    DISCARD["Request datum discarded with the socket<br/>zero bytes parsed, buffered, stored or logged"]

    CLIENT -->|"any method, path, query or body"| ACCEPT
    SERIAL -->|"identical 14-byte response every time"| CLIENT
    ACCEPT --> DISCARD
```

#### 6.2.2.5 Storage and Retrieval Mechanics

Mapping each conventional data operation onto what the system actually does makes the scope of the absence concrete.

| Operation Class | Conventional Mechanism | What Actually Happens |
|---|---|---|
| Retrieve | Query a store, deserialise a row or document, map to an object | A reference to a string literal already resident in the loaded module. Constant-time, allocation-free beyond runtime-supplied objects, and incapable of failing — Section 5.2.4 concludes the handler can never be the bottleneck |
| Create or update | `INSERT`/`UPDATE`, file write, or cache `SET` | Nothing. The only write in the program is `res.statusCode = 200` onto a runtime-owned response object |
| Delete or expire | `DELETE`, TTL expiry, tombstoning | Nothing to delete. Per-request objects and sockets are reclaimed by the runtime; the idle keep-alive socket is reaped silently after the 5000 ms runtime default |
| Serialise for transport | ORM serialisation plus response marshalling | The runtime serialises the response and supplies `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive`; repository code sets only `Content-Type` (F-002-RQ-002, C-004) |
| Recover after restart | Reload from the store, replay a log, warm a cache | Re-evaluate `server.js`. Because the payload is source text, the "data" is restored by the module loader itself in roughly 27 ms to readiness (Section 5.4.6) |

The operational dividend is the property recorded in Section 3.5.5: **restarting the process loses nothing and changes nothing.** There is no state to migrate, warm, drain, or reconcile, which is why Section 1.3.2.1 can exclude graceful shutdown without introducing a data-loss risk, and why the recovery point objective in Section 5.4.6 is *not applicable* rather than zero.


### 6.2.3 Schema Design

**No schema exists in this system, in any form and at any layer.** There is no relational schema, no document schema, no key-space design, and no external schema-description artifact: a sweep of all four tracked files returned zero matches for OpenAPI, Swagger, GraphQL SDL, protobuf, Avro, Thrift, JSON Schema, TypeScript declarations, `interface`, `class`, and every validation library probed (`zod`, `joi`, `ajv`, `yup`). The sub-sections below record the status of each schema-design concern this section is expected to cover, together with the verified consequence of its absence.

#### 6.2.3.1 Entity Relationships

There are **no entities and therefore no relationships**. Nothing in the system has an identity, a lifecycle spanning more than one response, or a reference to another record.

| Schema Element | Conventional Definition | Status in This Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Entity or table | A named collection of records with an identifying key | None. No `CREATE TABLE`, model class, collection reference, or record type exists |
| Attribute or column | A typed field on an entity | None. The three literals in the data domain (Section 6.2.2.1) are compiled-in values, not fields of any record |
| Relationship or association | A key-based reference between entities | None. No primary key, foreign key, join, or embedded-document reference exists |
| Cardinality and referential integrity | Rules governing how many records may relate, and enforcement of references | Not applicable. The only cardinalities in the system are the *object lifetimes* shown in Diagram 6.2.2-A, which the runtime manages and which are never written down or enforced by a constraint |

The only relationship structure that genuinely exists is the runtime object graph of Diagram 6.2.2-A — one listener, many connections, many requests, one response per request — and that graph is created and destroyed by the Node.js runtime within a single process lifetime.

#### 6.2.3.2 Data Models and Structures

The system has one data structure, and it is a **response contract rather than a data model**: a fixed status, a fixed header, and a fixed body, none of which is derived from input or from stored state. `server.js` defines no class, no named function, no type, and no export, so there is no model layer to describe.

| Contract Element | Value | Set By |
|---|---|---|
| Status | `200`, for every request regardless of method, path, query, headers, or body (F-002-RQ-001) | `server.js` line 7 — the only assignment in the program |
| Media type | `Content-Type: text/plain`, with no `charset` parameter (F-002-RQ-002) | `server.js` line 8 — the only header set by repository code |
| Body | `Hello, World!\n`, exactly 14 bytes (F-002-RQ-003) | `server.js` line 9, a compiled-in literal emitted by a single `res.end` call |
| Transport metadata | `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive` | Node.js runtime defaults, not repository code (C-004). A full wire census confirmed these five headers and no others |

Because the contract has no variable component, it needs no serialisation format, no versioning envelope, and no validation schema — and, critically for this section, no persisted representation from which to reconstitute it.

#### 6.2.3.3 Indexing Strategy and Index Register

**No index of any kind exists.** An index requires a stored collection and a lookup key; the system has neither. The register below is complete: every index class this section would document is listed, and every one is absent.

| Index Class | Where It Would Apply | Status and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Primary key / clustered index | Row or document identity in a table or collection | None — no store exists; `PRIMARY KEY` returns zero matches |
| Secondary / non-clustered index | Query predicates on non-key attributes | None — no query predicate exists anywhere in the codebase |
| Unique index | Enforcing value uniqueness within a collection | None in a data tier. The only uniqueness enforced anywhere is the kernel's exclusivity on `127.0.0.1:3000` (Section 6.2.3.4) |
| Composite, partial, covering, or full-text index | Multi-column, filtered, or text-search access paths | None — `CREATE INDEX` returns zero matches, and no search engine client exists |
| In-memory lookup structure | A `Map`, `Set`, or routing table used as an access path | None — `new Map`, `new Set`, and `WeakMap` return zero matches, and no routing table exists because `req.url` and `req.method` are never read (F-002-RQ-004) |

Two details make this register unusually easy to verify. First, the handler performs no lookup at all: the response body is a string reference resolved by the module loader, so the access path is constant-time by construction and no index could improve it. Second, the only occurrence of the string `index` anywhere in the repository is `package.json` line 5, `"main": "index.js"` — a field that points at a file which does not exist (deviation D-001) and which has nothing to do with data access.

#### 6.2.3.4 Constraint Register

No database constraint exists, because there is no database. The invariants below are the closest analogues the system has, and they are recorded here because this section is expected to document all constraints. Each is enforced structurally — by lexical scoping, by the absence of a code path, or by the operating system — rather than declaratively by a schema.

| Invariant (Constraint Analogue) | Enforcement Mechanism | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| Bind target is immutable and environment-independent | `const` lexical bindings at `server.js` lines 3–4; `process.env` appears zero times (F-001-RQ-003, C-003) | No `.env`, `.npmrc`, or configuration file exists; no override path was found |
| Status is always `200` | A single unconditional code path — the handler contains three statements and no branch | `200` observed for `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, and the non-standard `PURGE` (F-002-RQ-001) |
| Media type is always `text/plain` | Literal argument to `setHeader` on line 8 | Present with that exact value on every observed response |
| Body is always exactly 14 bytes | Compiled-in literal; no template, file read, or serialization (F-002-RQ-003) | 40 requests across distinct paths, methods, and bodies produced a single distinct body checksum; 25,000 further requests produced no deviation |
| No request-derived datum may enter the system | The `req` parameter is bound but never dereferenced (F-002-RQ-004) | Zero matches for `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers`, and `req.on`; nothing is parsed, buffered, stored, or logged |
| No module-scope mutable state may exist | All four module bindings are `const`; zero `let` and zero `var` declarations | Exactly one assignment in the whole program, onto a runtime-owned response object |
| Uniqueness of the listening endpoint (uniqueness-constraint analogue) | OS kernel port exclusivity — **not** repository code | A second `node server.js` exits with code 1 on `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, raised as an unhandled `'error'` event |

The last row is the only constraint in the system whose violation produces an error, and it is enforced entirely outside the repository. Its failure mode is fail-fast rather than reject-and-continue: there is no retry, no alternate-port fallback, and no readiness line, so consuming automation must serialise its use of port 3000 (Section 5.4.6).

#### 6.2.3.5 Partitioning Approach

**No partitioning of any kind exists, and none has a referent.** Partitioning distributes a dataset across ranges, hashes, or lists to bound the cost of access; there is no dataset here to distribute.

| Partitioning Concept | Status | Reason and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Horizontal partitioning or sharding | Not present | No shard key, no `shard`/`partition` marker, and no data collection to divide |
| Vertical partitioning | Not present | No entity with columns to split |
| Time-based or range partitioning | Not present | Nothing is written, so no time-ordered data accumulates; the storage growth projection is nil (Section 6.1.3.5) |
| Functional partitioning across stores | Not present | One process, one store-free address space; no second deployable unit exists (Section 6.1.1.1) |
| Partition-aware routing | Not present | The handler never inspects the request, so no routing decision — partition-aware or otherwise — is possible |

#### 6.2.3.6 Replication Configuration

**No replication is configured, and no data-tier replication is possible, because there is no data tier.** The distinction worth recording is that the *artifact* is replicated while the *runtime state* is not: Git distributes the source to the `origin` remote and to every clone, which is a design-time mechanism, not a runtime one.

| Replication Element | Status | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Primary / replica topology | Absent | No write node, standby, or read replica exists; `replica`, `replication`, `primary`, `secondary`, `failover`, and `quorum` all return zero matches |
| Log shipping or change stream | Absent | Nothing is written, so no write-ahead log, oplog, or binlog exists to ship |
| Synchronous versus asynchronous mode, and consistency model | Not applicable | With no replicated datum there is no replication lag, no read-your-writes concern, and no conflict resolution to define |
| Multi-instance runtime redundancy | **Impossible on one host** | A second instance aborts with `EADDRINUSE`; and because the loopback literal is compiled in, an off-host replica could not be reached either (F-001-RQ-002, C-002) |
| Source-artifact replication | **Present, design time only** | The single-commit baseline `1a0874d` is replicated to the configured `origin` remote and to every clone; `git status --porcelain` returns no output, confirming the working tree matches that baseline (F-006-RQ-003) |

**Diagram 6.2.3-A — Replication Topology: Verified Reality Against the Reference Replicated Data Tier**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    TRAFFIC["Inbound requests from same-host clients"]

    subgraph Verified["Verified Data Topology - The Entire System"]
        SOCK["TCP listener on 127.0.0.1 port 3000<br/>the only boundary crossed at runtime"]
        PROC["One Node.js process - node server.js<br/>no data tier of any kind"]
        STATE["Ephemeral per-request objects only<br/>resident set plateaus after 25000 requests"]
        SOCK --> PROC
        PROC --> STATE
    end

    subgraph Reference["Reference Replicated Data Tier - No Artifact Exists For Any Element"]
        PRIMARY["Primary write node"]
        WAL["Write-ahead log stream"]
        SYNCREP["Synchronous standby replica"]
        ASYNCREP["Asynchronous read replica"]
        BACKUP["Snapshot and point-in-time-recovery store"]
        PRIMARY -->|"log shipping"| WAL
        WAL --> SYNCREP
        WAL --> ASYNCREP
        PRIMARY -.->|"scheduled dump"| BACKUP
    end

    subgraph Durable["The Only Durable Replicated Artifact"]
        GITLOCAL["Local clone at commit 1a0874d<br/>working tree clean"]
        GITREMOTE["origin remote and every other clone"]
        GITLOCAL -->|"push and fetch - design-time replication"| GITREMOTE
    end

    GATE{"Is there any datum whose loss would<br/>require replication, failover or restore?"}
    VERDICT["Determination - no replication configuration,<br/>no failover target and no backup architecture<br/>exists or is required"]

    TRAFFIC --> SOCK
    STATE --> GATE
    GATE -->|"No - nothing is written to any durable medium"| VERDICT
    GITLOCAL --> VERDICT
```

#### 6.2.3.7 Backup Architecture

**There is no data backup architecture, and none is required: data at rest is nil.** No file, database, cache, or session store is ever written, which is why Section 5.4.6 records the recovery point objective as *not applicable* rather than as a duration. The only thing that can meaningfully be backed up is the source artifact, and that responsibility belongs to version control.

| Backup Dimension | Mechanism | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Application data backup | None — and nothing to back up | Zero regular-file descriptors during a 25,000-request run; no `fs` usage anywhere; no data artifact tracked or ever tracked |
| Snapshot / point-in-time recovery | Absent | No `backup`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `pg_dump`, `mongodump`, or `cron` marker exists in any file |
| Artifact backup and restore | Git: the `origin` remote plus every clone; restore by re-cloning the single-commit baseline `1a0874d` | Git is the only durable state the project has (Section 6.1.4.3) |
| Restore verification | Confirm a clean working tree against the baseline, then confirm the readiness line and a `200`/14-byte probe response | The two observable success signals identified in Section 5.4.6; content integrity is verifiable because provenance is a single commit (F-006-RQ-003) |
| Backup schedule, retention, and encryption of backups | Not applicable | There is no backup set to schedule, retain, or encrypt |


### 6.2.4 Data Management

Data management concerns the lifecycle of stored data — how it is introduced, evolved, retained, retrieved, and cached. With no stored data, four of the five concerns below have no referent, and the fifth (versioning) applies to the *artifact* rather than to data. Each is documented with what the repository actually provides in place of the conventional mechanism.

#### 6.2.4.1 Migration Procedures

**No migration tooling, migration directory, or migration runner exists, and there is no schema or dataset to migrate.** The probe for `migrate`, `migration`, `liquibase`, `flyway`, `alembic`, `umzug`, `db-migrate`, `sqitch`, `seed`, and `fixture` returned zero matches across all four tracked files, and no `migrations/` or `seeds/` directory is present in the tree or anywhere in the repository's single-commit history.

| Migration Concern | Conventional Mechanism | Status in This System |
|---|---|---|
| Forward migration | Versioned DDL or ORM migration applied in sequence | Not applicable — no schema exists to alter |
| Rollback / down migration | Reverse DDL or a restored snapshot | Not applicable — there is no schema state to revert and no snapshot to restore |
| Data backfill or transformation | Batch job rewriting existing records | Not applicable — no record has ever existed (verified across the full Git object database) |
| Zero-downtime change pattern | Expand–contract, dual-write, or shadow-read sequencing | Not applicable, and unnecessary: replacing the process loses nothing, and readiness is re-established in roughly 27 ms (Section 5.4.6) |
| Dependency materialisation before start | Install step producing a runtime tree | Effectively a no-op: `npm ci` exits 0, audits one package, reports zero vulnerabilities, and **creates no `node_modules` directory** (F-005-RQ-002) |

The only state transition the system has between versions is replacement of source text, because the deployment unit is the Git working tree executed in place (Section 6.1.1.3). There is no intermediate schema state that could be left half-migrated, and no compatibility window to manage between a code version and a data version.

#### 6.2.4.2 Versioning Strategy

Versioning exists, but it applies exclusively to the artifact. There is no data version, no schema version, and no wire-format version, because nothing is stored and the response contract carries no version envelope.

| Versioned Artifact | Mechanism | Current Value and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Package identity | Semantic version declared in both manifests, which `npm ci` reconciles and fails on mismatch | `1.0.0`, present at `package.json` line 3 and `package-lock.json` line 3 (F-004-RQ-004, F-005-RQ-003) |
| Source baseline | Git history | A single commit, `1a0874d`, on the `main` branch with no tags; `git status --porcelain` returns no output, so the tree matches the baseline exactly (F-006-RQ-003) |
| Lockfile format | `lockfileVersion` field | `3`, with a `packages` map containing only the root `""` entry — a formal assertion of a zero-node dependency graph (F-005-RQ-001) |
| Schema, data, or API version | — | **None.** No schema exists; the response carries no version header or envelope; and no version prefix could be honoured in a path, because `req.url` is never read (F-002-RQ-004) |
| Runtime version | — | **Not pinned.** No `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` file exists (deviation D-005). Verification was performed on Node.js v22.23.1 |

The last row is the one versioning gap with a data-adjacent consequence. Every behaviour this section attributes to the runtime — the 5000 ms `keepAliveTimeout`, the 511-entry accept backlog, the transport headers listed in Section 6.2.3.2 — is a Node.js default that the repository does not version. A future runtime release could change any of them with no change to repository content.

#### 6.2.4.3 Archival Policies

**No archival policy exists, and nothing accumulates that would require one.** Archival presupposes a growing dataset whose older partitions must be moved to cheaper storage or deleted; the storage growth projection for this system is nil (Section 6.1.3.5).

| Archival Concern | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data archival or cold-storage tiering | Not applicable | Nothing is written to any durable medium; the tree remained at four files across a 25,000-request run |
| TTL, expiry, or tombstoning | Not present | `ttl`, `expire`, `retention`, and `archive` return zero matches in every tracked file |
| Log archival and rotation | Not applicable | Log volume is one line per **process lifetime**, not per request, so the output stream can never become a disk-space concern (Section 5.4.2) |
| Historical artifact retention | Present, by version control only | Git history is the sole archive the project has; it consists of the single commit `1a0874d` |

#### 6.2.4.4 Data Storage and Retrieval Mechanisms

The storage and retrieval mechanics are documented in full in Section 6.2.2.5. The table below records the mechanisms that would normally implement them and their status here, so that the absence is enumerable rather than implied.

| Mechanism | Present | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Database client or connection | No | No driver, ODM, connection string, or `DATABASE_URL`; the network-literal census in Section 3.4.1 returned only the loopback listener |
| Filesystem read or write | No | `fs` is never imported; zero regular-file descriptors were open during a 25,000-request run |
| Module-loader retrieval of the payload | **Yes — this is the entire retrieval mechanism** | The 14-byte body is a string literal resident in the loaded module, emitted by one `res.end` call on `server.js` line 9 |
| Dependency tree on disk | No | `npm ci` completes without creating `node_modules`; nothing is downloaded, so no offline artifact store is consulted |
| In-memory data structure | No | Zero `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `let`, or `var`; the only assignment in the program targets a runtime-owned response object |

#### 6.2.4.5 Caching Policies

**No caching policy exists at any tier**, and the absence is complete rather than partial — including the HTTP layer, where a policy could have been declared without adding a single dependency.

| Cache Tier | Status | Evidence and Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| External cache service | Absent | No `redis`, `memcached`, or equivalent client; the zero-dependency lockfile makes transitive presence impossible |
| In-process cache | Absent | No `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `globalThis`, or `global.` usage, and zero matches for `cache`; there is no module-scope binding in which a cache could live |
| HTTP response cache directives | Absent | A full wire census returned exactly five headers — `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length` — with **no** `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Vary`, `Expires`, or `Age`. Clients and intermediaries are therefore given no permission to cache and no validator to revalidate against |
| CDN or edge cache | Not applicable | The listener is reachable only on the loopback interface (F-001-RQ-002, C-002), so no edge tier can reach an origin to cache |
| Build or dependency cache | Not applicable | There is no build step, and no dependency to cache (Section 3.5.3) |

Two consequences follow, and they point in opposite directions. Negatively, every request is served by re-emitting the literal, and no client is permitted to avoid a round trip. Positively — and more importantly for a fixture whose value is determinism — **there is no cache to invalidate, no stale-read window, and no coherence problem**: the invariance measured in F-002-RQ-005 could not be undermined by a cached copy diverging from the source. Caching would in any case amortise nothing, since the only "cost" it could remove is reading a string literal that is already resident in the loaded module.


### 6.2.5 Compliance Considerations

Data-tier compliance obligations are driven by the data a system holds. This system holds none, so most obligations do not arise at all rather than being satisfied by a control. That is a meaningfully different statement from "the controls are adequate", and the sub-sections below are explicit about which category each concern falls into — and about the two places where the absence of a data tier leaves a genuine gap rather than a non-issue.

#### 6.2.5.1 Data Retention Rules

**No data retention rule exists, and none is required, because no datum is retained.** Retention rules govern how long stored records are kept and when they must be destroyed; the system stores no record at any tier.

| Retention Concern | Applicability | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Retention schedule for stored records | Does not arise | No database, file, cache, or session store exists; zero regular-file descriptors were open during a 25,000-request run |
| Retention of request-derived data | Does not arise | The request object is never dereferenced, so zero request bytes are parsed, buffered, stored, or logged (F-002-RQ-004); no client address, header, or payload is ever recorded (F-003-RQ-003) |
| Log retention and rotation | Does not arise for request data | The only emitted record is a single readiness line per process lifetime; retention of that line belongs to whichever consumer captured standard output |
| Right-to-erasure / deletion-on-request capability | Not applicable | There is no personal datum to erase, and no store from which to delete one |
| Retention of the source artifact | Governed by version control | The single-commit baseline `1a0874d` is retained indefinitely in Git; this is artifact retention, not data retention |

#### 6.2.5.2 Backup and Fault Tolerance Policies

The repository declares no backup policy and no fault-tolerance mechanism of its own. What exists is a recovery profile in which the recovery point objective is *undefined rather than zero* — there is no data whose currency could be lost — combined with fault containment inherited from the Node.js runtime.

| Policy Area | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable — nothing is ever written, so nothing can be lost | Section 5.4.6; corroborated by the zero-regular-file-descriptor census |
| Recovery time, mechanically | Roughly 27 ms from launch to readiness; a restart requires no state reconstruction, cache warming, or reconciliation | Section 5.4.6; restart produced a byte-identical readiness line and an identical first-response checksum |
| Data-tier fault tolerance | No mechanism, and no referent — there is no store to make redundant | Section 6.1.4.3: only Git provides redundancy, and only for source |
| Request-path fault containment | Inherited from the runtime: protocol faults answered with `400`, `431`, or `408` and `Connection: close`, destroying only that socket | Section 5.4.3.2; the application layer has no error path and is never invoked for these faults |
| Backup of the artifact | Git `origin` remote plus every clone; restore by re-cloning the baseline and confirming a clean tree | Section 6.2.3.7 |
| Failure detection | **Gap — externally owned and unbounded.** No health check, watchdog, metric, or heartbeat exists in the repository | Section 5.4.6 identifies detection, not recovery speed, as the largest divergence from a production posture |

#### 6.2.5.3 Privacy Controls

**No privacy control is implemented, and no personal data is processed.** The strongest privacy property of this system is structural rather than procedural: the collection surface does not exist, because the request is never read.

| Privacy Concern | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Personal data collection | None. No personal, regulated, financial, or business datum is read, stored, transmitted, or logged | Section 6.2.2.1 data domain; the data-domain boundary in Section 1.3.1.2 |
| Data minimisation | Absolute by construction — the collection surface is nil, since `req` is bound but never dereferenced | F-002-RQ-004; not reading the body also eliminates deserialization, injection, and payload-size attack surface |
| Encryption at rest | Requirement does not arise — there is no data at rest | Section 3.5.5 |
| Encryption in transit | **None.** `https` and `tls` are never imported and no certificate material exists, so traffic is plaintext | Bounded by the loopback control below: traffic never leaves the host (F-001-RQ-002, C-002) |
| Consent, purpose limitation, subject-access handling | Not applicable — no data subject is involved and no identity is ever established | No `session`, `cookie`, `token`, `secret`, or credential marker exists in any file (Section 5.4.4) |
| Regulatory framework markers | None present. `gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pii`, `consent`, `anonymi`, and `pseudonym` all return zero matches | No compliance framework is claimed by, or applicable to, a static greeting payload |

#### 6.2.5.4 Audit Mechanisms

**There is no data-access audit mechanism, and this is one of the two genuine gaps in this section rather than a non-issue.** Because nothing is logged per request, the server retains no evidence of who connected, when, or what they asked for — Section 5.4.4 states the consequence directly: access leaves no trace on the server side.

| Audit Capability | Status | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Data-access audit trail | Absent, and without referent — there is no store whose reads and writes could be audited | No `audit` marker exists in any file |
| Request or access log | **Absent.** Standard output still contained exactly one line after 25,000 requests | Per-request diagnosis and after-the-fact attribution are impossible from the server side; any investigation must be conducted from the client or by observing the socket (Section 5.4.2) |
| Change audit for the data model | Not applicable to a schema, but present for source | Git provides complete provenance: one commit (`1a0874d`), one branch, no tags, and a clean working tree make any unauthorised content change trivially detectable (F-006-RQ-003) |
| Tamper evidence for the running configuration | Structural | The bind address, port, and payload are compiled-in literals, so the running configuration cannot diverge from the audited source without a source edit |
| Auditable runtime signals | Two only: the readiness line on stdout and the process exit status | Neither varies with load or with client identity, so neither supports access auditing |

#### 6.2.5.5 Access Controls

**Access control is enforced at exactly one layer — the network layer — and it protects a system that has nothing to protect.** There is no identity, role, tenant, account, or permission model anywhere in the repository, and no data-tier authorisation exists because there is no data tier.

| Control Layer | Mechanism | Verified Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Network reachability | The listener binds the literal `127.0.0.1` rather than a wildcard address (`server.js` line 3) | Only same-host processes can connect; the host's routable address `10.76.1.16:3000` and IPv6 `[::1]:3000` were both refused while `127.0.0.1:3000` was served (F-001-RQ-002) |
| Data-tier authorisation | None — no grants, roles, row-level security, or least-privilege database account, because no database account exists | No credential of any kind appears in any tracked file |
| Request authentication and authorisation | None. Every caller is anonymous and indistinguishable; no path or method is privileged | The handler cannot branch, because `req` is never dereferenced (F-002-RQ-004) |
| Secret and credential management | Not applicable — there is no secret to manage and no configuration channel to supply one | Zero matches for `token`, `password`, `secret`, `apikey`, and `authorization`; `process.env` appears zero times (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Artifact and configuration integrity | Filesystem permissions plus the change freeze in `README.md` (C-001) | **Gap — advisory only.** Enforcement is by convention: no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check exists in the repository (Section 5.4.4) |

The architectural substitution being made is explicit and worth restating in a data-design context: **network isolation is used in place of identity, and the absence of data is used in place of data protection.** Both are sound for a co-located test fixture, and both are brittle in the same specific way — the isolation lives in a single source literal, so the entire posture depends on that literal remaining unedited, with no compensating control behind it. Introducing any datastore would remove the "nothing to protect" property immediately, and would require a source change that constraint C-001 prohibits.


### 6.2.6 Performance Optimization

Data-tier performance optimisation has no subject in this system: there is no query to plan, no working set to cache, no pool to size, no replica to read from, and no batch to schedule. Before any figure is quoted, one framing point must be restated from Section 5.4.5: **the repository declares no performance requirement, no SLA, no SLO, no error budget, and no availability, latency, or throughput target.** Every number below is an observation of one environment, not a commitment, and no instrumentation exists in the repository from which such a target could be tracked.

#### 6.2.6.1 Query Optimization Patterns

**No query exists, so no query optimisation pattern applies.** The retrieval path is a reference to a string literal already resident in the loaded module (Section 6.2.2.5), which is constant-time by construction and cannot be improved by an access-path change.

| Optimization Pattern | Applicability | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Query planning, `EXPLAIN` analysis, index selection | Does not arise | No query language, statement, or store exists; the SQL and document-operation probes returned zero matches |
| N+1 elimination, eager loading, projection, pagination | Does not arise | No collection is traversed and no result set is produced |
| Prepared statements and statement caching | Does not arise | No statement is ever prepared or parsed |
| Denormalisation or materialised views | Does not arise | There is no normalised model to denormalise and no view to materialise |
| Constant-time response construction | **Present — structural, not a tuning choice** | The handler performs three assignments with no I/O and no parsing; Section 5.2.4 concludes it can never be the bottleneck |

#### 6.2.6.2 Caching Strategy

There is no caching strategy at any tier; the full tier-by-tier evidence is in Section 6.2.4.5. In data-tier terms the point is narrow and decisive: a cache exists to amortise the cost of a query, a computation, or an I/O operation, and this system performs none of the three. The only cost a cache could remove is reading a literal that the module loader has already resolved.

#### 6.2.6.3 Connection Pooling

A distinction matters here, because a keep-alive connection can be mistaken for a pooled one. **There is no database connection pool, because there is no database connection.** What the system does exhibit is *transport-level connection reuse* on its inbound HTTP listener, and that behaviour is a Node.js runtime default rather than repository configuration — no `keepAlive`, `agent`, `maxConnections`, or socket-tuning setting appears anywhere in the source.

| Pooling Concept | Status | Owner and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Database connection pool (min/max size, acquire timeout, idle eviction) | Absent, without referent | No driver or connection exists; `createPool`, `Pool(`, and `connectionString` return zero matches |
| Inbound HTTP keep-alive reuse | **Present, inherited** | Node runtime default `keepAliveTimeout` of 5000 ms — the source of the observed `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` header (C-004). Measured directly: across two sequential requests, the second reported zero new connections, confirming reuse of the established socket |
| Requests per connection ceiling | Unbounded | `maxRequestsPerSocket` is `0`, so one keep-alive connection may serve unlimited requests (Section 6.1.3.3) |
| Concurrent connection ceiling and queue depth | Not declared by the repository | `maxConnections` is unset; pending connections are bounded only by the runtime's untouched 511-entry accept backlog, and no rate limiting, admission control, or backpressure exists (Section 5.4.5) |
| Outbound connection management | Not applicable | The system makes no outbound call of any kind; its only dependency edge is `require('http')` |

The measured benefit of the inherited reuse is small and transport-bound: Section 5.3.5 reports p50 0.077 ms on a reused connection against 0.117 ms when a connection must be established. It is nonetheless the only performance optimisation in effect anywhere in the system.

#### 6.2.6.4 Read/Write Splitting

**No read/write splitting exists, and neither side of the split has a referent.**

| Splitting Element | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Write path to a primary | Absent | Nothing is written to any store; the only assignment in the program targets a runtime-owned response object |
| Read path to a replica | Absent | No replica exists, and no read operation is performed (Section 6.2.3.6) |
| Routing layer deciding read versus write | Absent | The handler never inspects the request, so it cannot classify an operation; `req.url` and `req.method` return zero matches |
| Replication-lag or read-your-writes handling | Not applicable | With no replicated datum, no consistency window exists to reason about |
| Command/query separation at the application layer | Not present | One unconditional code path serves every request identically (F-002-RQ-001) |

#### 6.2.6.5 Batch Processing Approach

**No batch processing exists.** There is no scheduler, cron entry, queue, worker, job definition, or bulk operation anywhere in the repository, and no data to process in bulk.

| Batch Concern | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduled or periodic job | Absent | `cron` returns zero matches; there is no `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or timer construct in the source |
| Bulk insert, bulk update, or ETL pipeline | Absent, without referent | No store to load into and no dataset to extract or transform |
| Queue or worker pool | Absent | No broker client, and `cluster`, `worker_threads`, and `child_process` appear zero times (Section 6.1.1.2) |
| Batched response writes | Not used — deliberately | A single `res.end` call emits the whole body atomically; no chunked or partial write exists that could leave a response half-emitted |
| Request-level batching by clients | Supported only incidentally | Many requests may be pipelined over one keep-alive connection, but each is answered independently and identically; no aggregation occurs |

#### 6.2.6.6 Measured Behaviour

The figures below were produced against an unmodified working tree. They are recorded so that the "no optimisation is needed" conclusion is grounded rather than asserted, and they carry no commitment of any kind.

| Measurement | Observed Value | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Sustained sequential throughput | 5,000 requests completed in 375.7 ms (≈13,300 requests/second), consistent with the ≈12,761 requests/second reported in Section 5.4.5 | In-process Node HTTP client over a single keep-alive connection, distinct path per request |
| Latency distribution | p50 0.064 ms, p99 0.184 ms, max 0.414 ms | Section 5.4.5, 2,000 measured requests after warm-up |
| Memory behaviour under load | Resident set plateaus: 59.5 MB at 5,000 requests and 61.9 MB at 25,000, a 268 kB change across the final 20,000 requests | `VmRSS` sampled after each of five cumulative 5,000-request rounds |
| Durable I/O under load | Zero regular-file descriptors and zero files written; open descriptor count constant at 22 | `/proc/<pid>/fd` inspection plus tree comparison |
| Startup to readiness | ≈27 ms, with no cache to warm and no state to reconstruct | Section 5.4.6; corroborated by an identical response checksum on the first post-restart request |

| Privacy controls | No personal data processed; minimisation is absolute; no encryption-at-rest requirement | Section 6.2.5.3; data-domain boundary in Section 1.3.1.2 |
| Audit mechanisms | No data-access audit and no access log — a verified gap; Git provides source provenance | Section 6.2.5.4; one stdout line after 25,000 requests |
| Access controls | One network-layer control (loopback bind); no identity, role, or data-tier grant | Section 6.2.5.5; routable and IPv6 addresses refused |
| Query optimization patterns | No query to optimise; constant-time construction is structural | Section 6.2.6.1 |
| Connection pooling | No database pool; inbound keep-alive reuse is a runtime default | Section 6.2.6.3; measured connection reuse |
| Read/write splitting | Neither side has a referent; no routing layer can exist | Section 6.2.6.4 |
| Batch processing approach | No scheduler, queue, worker, or bulk operation | Section 6.2.6.5 |

**Concluding statement.** Database Design is not applicable to this system. The repository defines a 14-line, single-process HTTP listener whose entire data domain is three compiled-in literals, whose only per-request state is one property write on a runtime-owned object, and whose measured behaviour under 25,000 requests shows no durable write and no unbounded memory growth. Every schema, replication, retention, and optimisation mechanism this section would otherwise specify has been verified absent — and in each case the absence traces to ADR-006 rather than to an oversight. Introducing any datastore would require modifying repository content, which constraint C-001, the change freeze declared in `README.md`, places outside the sanctioned scope of the project; it would also forfeit the two properties that make the artifact useful as a fixture: response invariance that no cache or replica can undermine, and a restart that loses nothing.

## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Integration Architecture Applicability Assessment

**Integration Architecture is not applicable for this system in the conventional sense.** The repository contains no integration with any external system or service: it declares no dependency, opens no outbound network connection, publishes to no broker, calls no third-party API, and is fronted by no gateway. What it does have is a single *inbound* protocol surface — one HTTP listener bound to the loopback interface — and that surface is documented in full below, because for a fixture whose entire purpose is to be called by other tooling, the inbound contract *is* the integration architecture.

This determination is not inferred from a missing design document. It is the result of an exhaustive census of the four files that constitute the repository, corroborated by direct runtime measurement of the running process.

#### 6.3.1.1 Adjudication

Four independent tests were applied. Each resolved negative on measured evidence.

| Test | Requirement for "applicable" | Verdict and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Outbound integration | At least one client, SDK, driver or socket that initiates a call to an external system | **Negative.** The repository contains exactly one `require()` — `require('http')` at `server.js` line 1 — used only in server mode. An inode-matched socket census of the running process recorded **zero outbound TCP connections**, both idle and while twenty inbound keep-alive connections were held open. |
| Asynchronous messaging | A broker client, queue, topic, stream consumer or scheduled job | **Negative.** A case-insensitive sweep for sixteen broker technologies, nine job-queue libraries and all cron/scheduler markers returned zero matches. `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` during request handling returned only `["TCPServerWrap","TCPSocketWrap"]` — no timer, worker or child-process handle exists. |
| Mediated API exposure | Gateway, ingress, reverse proxy, service mesh or published contract | **Negative.** An eighty-path existence probe found no gateway, proxy, ingress, serverless or IaC descriptor, and no OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL, protobuf or Postman artifact of any kind. |
| External reachability | The service is addressable by a system beyond the host | **Negative.** `server.js` line 3 hard-codes `hostname = '127.0.0.1'`. A request to the container's routable address on port 3000 is refused while `127.0.0.1:3000` succeeds — the listener is unreachable from any non-loopback interface (constraint C-002). |

Section 3.4 reaches the same conclusion from the technology-selection perspective, stating that the system "integrates with no third-party service", that the `http` module is used "exclusively in **server mode**", and that "the process has **no egress path**". Section 2.3.3 records the same finding at feature level: "There are **no outbound integration points** beyond the local streams."

#### 6.3.1.2 The Integration Surfaces That Do Exist

Five surfaces exist. Only the first three are exercised by the running process; the last two are design-time relationships consumed by tooling.

| Surface | Direction | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| TCP/HTTP listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | Every syntactically valid HTTP request receives `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a 14-byte body — regardless of method, path, headers or payload |
| Process standard output | Outbound, host-local | Exactly one line, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, emitted once per process lifetime; measured still one line after 25,000 requests |
| Process standard error | Outbound, host-local, failure path only | Written only by Node's default unhandled-`'error'` path; observed on port contention with exit code 1 |
| `package.json` and `package-lock.json` | Consumed by tooling, design time | npm identity, a `test` script that exits 1, and a lockfile whose `packages` map contains only the root record |
| Git repository with an `origin` remote | Consumed by tooling, ecosystem | Single-commit baseline `1a0874d` on branch `main`; never contacted by the running process |

The one external party named anywhere in the repository is the consumer identified by `README.md` line 2 — "test project for backprop integration". That relationship is inbound and one-directional: the tooling exercises the fixture, and `server.js` contains nothing that is aware of the tooling's existence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CONSUMER["Host-local HTTP consumer<br/>backprop test tooling or curl"]
    NOEGRESS["Egress capability<br/>measured zero outbound sockets"]

    subgraph Verified["Verified Runtime Integration Surfaces - host local only"]
        LOOPBACK["Inbound TCP listener<br/>127.0.0.1 port 3000<br/>server.js L3-L4 L12"]
        RUNTIME["Node.js core http runtime<br/>parse, dispatch, serialize"]
        HANDLER["Single request listener<br/>200 text-plain 14 bytes<br/>server.js L6-L10"]
        STDOUT["Standard output<br/>one readiness line<br/>server.js L13"]
```
