*Diagram 6.3.1-A — Integration landscape. Solid edges are measured data paths. Dotted edges to the lower subgraph denote relationships that do not exist; no connection is ever opened to any of those tiers.*

#### 6.3.1.3 Why the Absences Are Architecturally Load-Bearing

For most systems, an absent integration control is a gap. Here the absences are the design, and three of them are load-bearing:

- **The loopback literal is the only access control.** Because `server.js` line 3 compiles `127.0.0.1` into the binary path of the program, network isolation substitutes for identity. There is no authentication layer to bypass because there is no reachable network position from which to attempt it.
- **Zero egress makes the fixture non-exfiltrating by construction.** With no HTTP client, no driver and no measured outbound socket, there is no channel through which request data could leave the host even if the process were subverted. Section 3.4.5 draws the same conclusion.
- **An empty dependency graph removes the integration supply chain.** `package-lock.json` locks exactly one package — the root itself — so no transitive broker client, auth SDK or telemetry agent can be present. Section 3.3.1 characterises this as "one node — the root package itself — with depth 0 and zero edges".

#### 6.3.1.4 Scope of the Determination and Structure of This Section

The "not applicable" verdict applies to every integration *tier*: no API gateway, no identity provider, no message broker, no stream platform, no batch pipeline, no third-party service, and no legacy interface. It does **not** apply to the inbound HTTP contract, which is real, measurable and the sole reason the artifact exists.

The remainder of section 6.3 is therefore organised as follows: 6.3.2 documents the inbound API in the terms the prompt requires — protocol, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning and documentation standards — recording each control's measured status. 6.3.3 addresses message processing, where the only genuine event mechanism is the runtime's own event-loop dispatch. 6.3.4 documents external systems and the complete external-dependency inventory. 6.3.5 consolidates the determinations and records the structural constraints any future integration would face.

### 6.3.2 API Design

The system exposes exactly one API: an unauthenticated, unversioned, undocumented HTTP endpoint that answers every request identically. This sub-section specifies that endpoint precisely and records the measured status of each API-design control the prompt enumerates. Every value below was obtained by probing the running process, not by reading a specification — no specification exists.

#### 6.3.2.1 API Architecture

Four layers participate in every call. Only one of them — the application layer — is authored by this repository; the other three are supplied by the operating system and the Node.js runtime, which means their behaviour is part of the observable contract while remaining outside repository control (a principle also recorded in section 2.3.5).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    CLIENTTIER["Client tier<br/>any process on the same host<br/>off-host clients refused"]

    subgraph Transport["Transport layer - kernel and libuv"]
        SOCKET["Loopback socket 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>default accept backlog 511"]
        CONNPOOL["Accepted connections<br/>no maxConnections ceiling"]
        SOCKET --> CONNPOOL
    end

    subgraph Protocol["Protocol layer - Node.js core http, runtime owned"]
        PARSE["Request-line and header parsing<br/>maxHeaderSize 16384"]
        METHODGATE["Method token allow-list<br/>unknown token rejected 400"]
        KEEPALIVE["Keep-alive manager<br/>keepAliveTimeout 5000 ms"]
        PARSE --> METHODGATE
        METHODGATE --> KEEPALIVE
    end

    subgraph Application["Application layer - repository authored"]
        DISPATCH["Single request listener<br/>no router, no middleware chain"]
        INVARIANT["Set status 200<br/>set Content-Type text-plain<br/>end with 14-byte literal"]
        DISPATCH --> INVARIANT
    end

    subgraph Serialize["Serialization layer - runtime owned"]
        FRAMING["Adds Date, Connection,<br/>Keep-Alive, Content-Length"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentControls["API Management Controls Verified Absent"]
        AUTHN["Authentication and credential validation"]
        AUTHZ["Authorization and scope evaluation"]
        RATELIMIT["Rate limiting and quota enforcement"]
        VERSIONING["Version negotiation and deprecation"]
        CONTRACT["Machine-readable API contract"]
    end

    CLIENTTIER --> SOCKET
    CONNPOOL --> PARSE
    KEEPALIVE --> DISPATCH
    INVARIANT --> FRAMING
    FRAMING --> CLIENTTIER
    AUTHN -.->|"no interception point exists"| DISPATCH
    AUTHZ -.-> DISPATCH
    RATELIMIT -.-> DISPATCH
    VERSIONING -.-> DISPATCH
    CONTRACT -.-> DISPATCH
```

*Diagram 6.3.2-A — API architecture. The application layer is 5 lines of code; every control in the lower subgraph is absent, and because there is no middleware chain there is no interception point at which one could be inserted without editing `server.js`.*

#### 6.3.2.2 Protocol Specifications

##### 6.3.2.2.1 Transport and Endpoint

| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP, cleartext; no TLS anywhere in the repository | `server.js` line 1 requires `http`, never `https` |
| Bind address and port | `127.0.0.1:3000`, hard-coded, not overridable | `server.js` lines 3–4; no `process.env` usage exists |
| Reachability | Loopback only; the routable host address refuses connection | Measured — constraint C-002 |
| Advertised protocol | `HTTP/1.1` in every status line | Measured on every response |
| Endpoint count | One implicit endpoint covering the entire URI space | No routing code exists |

A client that attempts HTTPS receives a **cleartext `400 Bad Request`** rather than a TLS alert: the raw ClientHello bytes fail HTTP parsing. Any integrator configured for `https://` will therefore fail at handshake, not at authentication.

##### 6.3.2.2.2 Request-Line and Version Handling

The application never inspects the request line, so everything in this table is enforced by the runtime's parser.

| Request Form | Measured Outcome | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `GET / HTTP/1.1` with `Host` | `200`, `Content-Length: 14` present | Nominal path |
| `GET / HTTP/1.0`, no `Host` | `200`, **`Content-Length` omitted** | Body delimited by connection close; status line still says `HTTP/1.1` |
| `GET /` with no version (HTTP/0.9 form) | `200`, no `Content-Length` | Accepted by the parser |
| `GET / HTTP/1.1` **without** `Host` | `400 Bad Request`, `Connection: close`, chunked empty body | Runtime rejection; handler never runs |
| `GET / HTTP/9.9` | `400 Bad Request`, `Connection: close` | Unsupported version |
| `PRI * HTTP/2.0` (h2 prior-knowledge preface) | `400 Bad Request` | No HTTP/2 support |
| `GET http://example.com/x HTTP/1.1` (absolute form) | `200` with the greeting | Accepted but **not proxied** — the URI is never read |
| `OPTIONS * HTTP/1.1` (asterisk form) | `200` with the greeting body, **no `Allow` header** | Not a conformant `OPTIONS` response |

##### 6.3.2.2.3 Method Handling

| Method Class | Methods Tested | Measured Result |
|---|---|---|
| Standard, body-bearing and safe | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE` | All `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes, byte-identical bodies (same MD5) |
| Head request | `HEAD` | `200` with an empty body; `Content-Length` not emitted |
| Extension method in the parser's allow-list | `PURGE` | `200` / 14 bytes — identical to `GET` |
| Method token outside the allow-list | `FROBNICATE` | **`400 Bad Request`** — rejected by the runtime parser, not by application logic |
| Tunnelling method | `CONNECT` | **Socket destroyed, zero bytes returned** — no `'connect'` listener is registered |

The distinction matters for integrators: a `405 Method Not Allowed` is **unreachable**, because the application performs no method validation at all. The only method-related rejection comes from the parser's token allow-list and surfaces as `400`.

##### 6.3.2.2.4 URI, Content Negotiation and Payload Handling

| Dimension | Probes | Measured Result |
|---|---|---|
| Path and query | `/`, `/v1/orders`, `/api/v2/users?id=7`, `/index.js`, `/../../etc/passwd`, `//double`, deep nested paths | All `200` / 14 bytes / `text/plain` — no routing, no traversal exposure (no filesystem access exists) |
| Content negotiation | `Accept: application/json`, `Accept: application/xml`, `Accept-Language: fr-FR` | Ignored; response is always `text/plain` with no `Vary` header |
| Compression | `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` | Ignored; no `Content-Encoding` is ever emitted |
| Request payload | `Content-Length` body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` body, 1 MiB body | All `200`. The body is consumed by the runtime and discarded; inspected after the handler returned, the request stream showed `readableFlowing=null`, zero `data` listeners and zero bytes buffered |
| `Expect: 100-continue` | `POST` with the expectation header | Runtime emits `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` **automatically** (no `checkContinue` listener is registered), then the ordinary `200` |

##### 6.3.2.2.5 Response Contract

| Element | Value | Set By |
|---|---|---|
| Status | `200` — invariant; no other status is reachable from application code | `server.js` line 7 |
| `Content-Type` | `text/plain`, **no charset parameter** | `server.js` line 8 — the only header set by application code, confirmed programmatically via `res.getHeaderNames()` returning `["content-type"]` |
| Body | `Hello, World!\n` — exactly 14 bytes, a compiled-in literal | `server.js` line 9 |
| `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length` | Runtime-generated framing headers | Node.js `http` defaults (constraint C-004) |
| Headers **not** emitted | `Server`, `ETag`, `Cache-Control`, `Vary`, `Content-Encoding`, any `Access-Control-*`, any `X-RateLimit-*` | Nothing in the repository emits them |

A keep-alive response is 163 bytes on the wire and a `Connection: close` response is 135 bytes, of which the body is 14 bytes in both cases.

##### 6.3.2.2.6 Connection Lifecycle and Runtime-Enforced Limits

Every limit below is a Node.js default read from the live server instance; the repository sets none of them, and because no `engines` range is declared (deviation D-005) these values are unversioned by the repository.

| Property | Live Value | Integration Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 ms — advertised as `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; idle close measured at 6.00 s | Long-lived integrator connections are dropped after five idle seconds and must be re-established |
| `headersTimeout` / `requestTimeout` | 60000 ms / 300000 ms | A slow client is disconnected by the runtime, not by application logic |
| `maxHeaderSize` | 16384 bytes — a ~24 KB header block returned `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` | Integrators propagating large trace or auth headers can be rejected before the handler runs |
| `maxRequestsPerSocket` / `maxConnections` | `0` (unlimited) / `undefined` (no ceiling) | No connection or request ceiling is enforced |
| Pipelining | Two requests in a single TCP segment produced two complete `200` responses | HTTP/1.1 pipelining works, supplied by the runtime |
| Protocol upgrade | `Upgrade: websocket` and `Upgrade: h2c` both received an ordinary `200`; **no `101 Switching Protocols` was ever emitted** | WebSocket and h2c integrations are impossible; the client sees a protocol violation |

#### 6.3.2.3 Key Flow — Successful API Call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Host-local client
    participant K as Kernel loopback socket
    participant R as Node http runtime
    participant H as Request listener server.js L6-L10
    C->>K: TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:3000
    K->>R: connection accepted, connection listener count 1
    C->>R: request line plus headers, any method or path
    Note over R: parse, validate method token,<br/>enforce 16384-byte header limit
    R->>H: emit request event with req and res
    Note over H: req never dereferenced,<br/>readableFlowing stays null
    H->>R: res.statusCode 200
    H->>R: res.setHeader Content-Type text-plain
    H->>R: res.end with 14-byte literal
    Note over R: runtime appends Date, Connection,<br/>Keep-Alive and Content-Length
    R-->>C: HTTP/1.1 200 OK plus 14-byte body
    Note over R,C: connection retained, Keep-Alive timeout 5
    R-->>K: idle socket closed after keep-alive expiry
```

*Diagram 6.3.2-B — The complete lifecycle of the only API operation. The application contributes steps 6, 7 and 8; every other step belongs to the kernel or the runtime.*

#### 6.3.2.4 Authentication Methods

**No authentication mechanism exists.** The request object is bound as a handler parameter and never dereferenced, so no credential can be read, let alone validated. A static sweep for `authorization`, `bearer`, `jwt`, `oauth`, `oidc`, `saml`, `api-key`, `hmac`, `mtls`, `session`, `cookie` and `passport` returned zero matches across all four files.

Runtime probing confirms that credentials are neither required nor rejected. Every request below returned `200`:

| Credential Presented | Measured Response |
|---|---|
| `Authorization: Bearer <JWT-shaped token>` | `200` — token neither parsed nor validated |
| `Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz` | `200` — identical response |
| `Cookie: session=abc123` | `200` — no session lookup occurs |
| `X-API-Key: totally-invalid` | `200` — an invalid key is indistinguishable from a valid one |
| No credential at all | `200` — the baseline is identical |

Consequently **`401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden` are unreachable status codes**. All callers are anonymous and mutually indistinguishable, matching the finding in section 3.4.2. The substitute control is network position: the loopback bind means only same-host processes can reach the endpoint at all. Section 5.4.4 characterises this as network isolation used in place of identity.

Two related integration behaviours were also measured: `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` are ignored (no trust-proxy semantics, so a fronting proxy could not convey client identity even if one existed), and a spoofed `Host: attacker.example` is accepted with a normal `200` (no host allow-list).

#### 6.3.2.5 Authorization Framework

**No authorization framework exists**, and none could operate: authorization requires both a principal and a resource, and the system has neither. There is one implicit resource (the fixed greeting) and no principal at all. A sweep for `role`, `scope`, `permission`, `acl`, `rbac`, `tenant` and `principal` returned zero matches.

| Authorization Concern | Status |
|---|---|
| Policy definition or decision point | None — no policy file, no middleware, no interception point |
| Scope or claim evaluation | None — no token is parsed |
| Resource-level access rules | Not applicable — one undifferentiated resource |
| Multi-tenancy or data isolation | Not applicable — no data and no tenant concept |
| Audit of access decisions | None — after 60 requests each with a distinct `Authorization` header, server stdout still contained exactly one line (the startup banner) |

The audit finding is worth emphasising for integration purposes: **integration traffic leaves no server-side trace.** There is no access log, no request counter and no record of which client called, so integrators cannot reconcile their own call volume against anything the server reports.

#### 6.3.2.6 Rate Limiting Strategy

**No rate limiting, throttling, quota or admission-control mechanism exists.** A sweep for `rate-limit`, `throttl`, `quota`, `token bucket`, `429`, `retry-after` and `x-ratelimit` returned zero matches, and no connection or request ceiling is configured.

Load probes confirm the absence behaviourally:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| 2,000 sequential requests to 2,000 distinct paths | 2,000 × `200` in 114 ms; zero non-`200` responses |
| 200 concurrent requests | 200 × `200` in 117 ms; `429` count = **0** |
| Response headers under load | No `Retry-After` and no `X-RateLimit-*` header ever emitted |

The only bounds an integrator experiences are structural rather than policy-driven: work is serialised through a single event loop in a single process, the accept backlog defaults to 511 entries, and `maxConnections` is unset so there is no explicit ceiling. Section 5.4.5 records that the repository declares no performance requirement, SLA, SLO or error budget from which a limit could be derived; overload behaviour is therefore a property of the platform, not of this system.

#### 6.3.2.7 Versioning Approach

**No API versioning scheme exists in any form.** All conventional mechanisms were probed and none is present:

| Versioning Mechanism | Status |
|---|---|
| URI path versioning | Absent — `/v1/orders` and `/api/v2/users?id=7` return the same response as `/`; no path is ever parsed |
| Header or media-type versioning | Absent — no `Accept-Version`, `X-API-Version` or versioned media type; `Accept` is ignored entirely |
| Query-parameter versioning | Absent — query strings are never read |
| Version advertisement in responses | Absent — no `Server` header, no version header, no version in the body |
| Deprecation signalling | Absent — no `Deprecation`, `Sunset` or `Warning` header |

The only version identifier in the system is the package version `1.0.0`, declared in `package.json` and mirrored in the lockfile root record. It is a *build-time artifact identifier*, not an API version: no runtime response exposes it, so a client cannot discover which build it is talking to. The effective API version contract is therefore the immutability directive in `README.md` — the response cannot change because the source is frozen (constraint C-001) — rather than any negotiated version token.

#### 6.3.2.8 Documentation Standards

**No machine-readable API documentation exists, and no documentation standard is applied.** A sweep for `openapi`, `swagger`, `asyncapi`, `graphql`, `protobuf`, `avro`, `thrift`, `json-schema`, `wsdl`, `raml` and `apiblueprint` returned zero matches, and an existence probe found no OpenAPI/Swagger file, no `.proto`, no GraphQL SDL, no JSON Schema, no Postman or Insomnia collection, no `.well-known/` directory and no `docs/` folder.

| Documentation Artifact | Status |
|---|---|
| Machine-readable contract (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL SDL, IDL) | None |
| Interactive or generated reference (Swagger UI, Redoc) | None |
| Human-readable API description | Effectively none — `README.md` is two lines and describes purpose, not the interface; it contains no endpoint, method, port or example |
| Client collection or example requests | None |
| Schema validation library (`zod`, `joi`, `ajv`, `yup`) | None |
| Response self-description | None — no `Server` header, no discovery endpoint, no `OPTIONS` `Allow` header |

The practical consequence for integrators is that **the running process is the only specification**. The contract must be discovered empirically — which is tractable precisely because it is invariant: one status code, one content type and one 14-byte body for every possible request. This specification section, together with section 2.2's functional requirements, is the closest thing to a published contract that exists.

#### 6.3.2.9 API Design Control Summary

| Control | Status | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol specification | Present but implicit | Cleartext HTTP/1.1 on `127.0.0.1:3000`; all limits are runtime defaults |
| Authentication | Absent | Zero credential markers; `401`/`403` unreachable |
| Authorization | Absent | No principal and no differentiated resource exist |
| Rate limiting | Absent | 2,200 measured requests, zero `429` responses |
| Versioning | Absent | Versioned paths and version headers all ignored |
| Documentation standard | Absent | No contract artifact of any kind; the process is the specification |

### 6.3.3 Message Processing

**Message-oriented integration is not applicable for this system.** There is no broker, no queue, no topic, no stream pipeline and no batch job. The only mechanism that can legitimately be called "message processing" is the Node.js runtime's own event-loop dispatch of a parsed HTTP request to a single in-process listener — a synchronous, one-hop, in-memory hand-off with no intermediary, no durability and no ordering guarantee to make.

This sub-section documents that mechanism precisely, then records the measured status of each message-processing concern the prompt enumerates.

#### 6.3.3.1 Event Processing Patterns

The `http.Server` instance is an `EventEmitter`, so the system is technically event-driven — but the entire event topology consists of two subscriptions, and the repository creates both implicitly by passing callbacks rather than by calling `.on()`. A static sweep confirms this: there are **zero** occurrences of `.on(`, `.once(`, `.emit(`, `addListener`, `subscribe` or `publish` anywhere in the repository.

A listener census taken on the live server instance is decisive:

| Server Event | Listener Count | Owner and Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | 1 | The `createServer` callback at `server.js` lines 6–10 — the sole application-level message handler |
| `listening` | 1 | The `server.listen` callback at `server.js` lines 12–14 — fires once, emits the readiness line |
| `connection` | 1 | Installed internally by the `http` module, not by repository code |
| `error`, `clientError`, `close`, `upgrade`, `connect`, `checkContinue`, `checkExpectation`, `timeout`, `dropRequest` | **0 each** | Every one falls through to the runtime's default disposition |

The pattern is therefore best described as **single-subscriber synchronous dispatch**: one event type carries application meaning, exactly one handler is attached to it, and that handler completes synchronously with no `await`, no callback deferral and no continuation. Because nine other server events have no subscriber, a large part of the system's observable behaviour — including all protocol error handling and all upgrade negotiation — is decided by runtime defaults rather than by code in this repository.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ARRIVE["Inbound bytes on an<br/>accepted loopback socket"]

    subgraph EventLoop["Single Node.js event loop - one process, one thread"]
        READABLE["libuv reports socket readable"]
        PARSER["http parser consumes bytes"]
        EMIT["request event emitted<br/>listener count 1"]
        LISTENER["Invariant response listener<br/>synchronous, no awaits"]
        WRITE["Response bytes queued<br/>to the same socket"]
        READABLE --> PARSER
        PARSER --> EMIT
        EMIT --> LISTENER
        LISTENER --> WRITE
    end

    subgraph Discarded["Inbound Payload Disposition"]
        BODY["Request body bytes<br/>Content-Length or chunked"]
        DRAIN["Consumed by the runtime and discarded<br/>zero bytes buffered, no data listener"]
        BODY --> DRAIN
    end

    subgraph AbsentMessaging["Messaging Infrastructure Verified Absent"]
        PRODUCER["Producer or publisher client"]
        TOPIC["Topic, exchange or queue"]
        CONSUMERGRP["Consumer group or worker pool"]
        DLQ["Retry path or dead-letter queue"]
        SCHEDULER["Scheduler, cron or batch window"]
        PRODUCER --> TOPIC
        TOPIC --> CONSUMERGRP
        CONSUMERGRP --> DLQ
    end

    ARRIVE --> READABLE
    ARRIVE -.-> BODY
    WRITE -->|"14-byte response"| DELIVER["Bytes returned to the calling client"]
    LISTENER -.->|"no publish call exists"| PRODUCER
    LISTENER -.->|"no timer or handle exists"| SCHEDULER
```

*Diagram 6.3.3-A — Message flow. The complete path is five in-process steps on one thread. The lower subgraph is drawn for contrast only: no producer call, no queue and no scheduler exists, and the dotted edges represent relationships that were probed for and found absent.*

#### 6.3.3.2 Message Queue Architecture

**Not applicable — no message queue exists.** Every broker and job-queue technology probed returned zero matches across all four tracked files:

| Category | Technologies Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Brokers and streaming platforms | Kafka, AMQP/RabbitMQ, SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, NATS, MQTT, STOMP, ZeroMQ, ActiveMQ, Pulsar, EventBridge, Service Bus, Kinesis, Celery, Redis | Zero matches |
| In-process job queues | Bull, Bee-Queue, Agenda, Kue, Bree, node-resque, Graphile Worker, pg-boss | Zero matches |
| Queue semantics | acknowledgement, negative acknowledgement, dead-letter, offset, consumer group, idempotency key, deduplication, outbox, saga, CQRS, event sourcing | Zero matches |

Section 3.4.1 reaches the same conclusion, recording zero matches for `amqp`, `kafka`, `mqtt`, `nats`, `sqs`, `sns`, `pubsub` and `webhook`. Because `package-lock.json` locks exactly one package — the root itself — no broker client can be present transitively either.

The **only queue-like structure in the entire system is the kernel's TCP accept backlog**, which defaults to 511 entries and is neither configured nor observed by repository code. It provides no durability, no acknowledgement, no redelivery and no visibility: connections that overflow it are refused by the operating system, and the application never learns that it happened.

#### 6.3.3.3 Stream Processing Design

**Not applicable as a design, though two Node.js streams are structurally present.** Each HTTP request supplies a `Readable` request stream and a `Writable` response stream. The repository uses neither as a stream:

| Stream | Repository Usage | Measured State |
|---|---|---|
| Request (`Readable`) | Never read. `req` is bound as a parameter and never dereferenced | Inspected immediately after the handler returned for a JSON `POST`: `readableFlowing=null`, `data` listeners `0`, `end` listeners `0`, bytes buffered `0`, `complete=false` |
| Response (`Writable`) | Written once, via a single `res.end()` with a literal | `writableEnded=true`, `headersSent=true`, `getHeaderNames()` = `["content-type"]`; zero occurrences of `res.write(` exist in the repository |

Three consequences follow, and all three matter to an integrator:

- **The response is emitted before the request is complete** (`complete=false` at handler exit). The system does not wait for the inbound payload; it answers immediately and lets the runtime drain the remainder.
- **Inbound payloads are consumed and discarded by the runtime.** A 1 MiB `POST` body and a chunked body both produced the ordinary `200`, and no application code ever observed a byte of either.
- **There is no transformation, no backpressure management and no piping.** Zero occurrences of `pipe(`, `pipeline`, `Transform`, `chunk`, `pause(` or `resume(` exist, so no stream-processing topology can be described.

#### 6.3.3.4 Batch Processing Flows

**Not applicable — no batch processing exists.** No scheduler, cron entry, timer, worker pool, child process or bulk-processing routine is present, and this was verified at both the source and runtime levels:

| Batch Concern | Verification | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduler or cron definition | Sweep for `cron`, `schedul`, `setInterval`, `batch`, `bulk`, `etl`, `worker`, `daemon`; existence probe for `cron/`, `jobs/`, `tasks/`, `scheduler/`, `crontab` | Zero matches; no such path exists |
| Live timer or scheduled handle | `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` sampled during request handling | Returned only `["TCPServerWrap","TCPSocketWrap"]` — no `Timeout`, `Immediate`, `FSReqCallback` or `Worker` handle |
| Parallel or background execution | Child-process and thread census of the running server | `0` child processes; 7 threads, all Node/libuv internals with one JavaScript event loop |
| Bulk data ingestion or file drop | Filesystem-primitive sweep (`fs.`, `readFile`, `createReadStream`, `path.`) | Zero matches — the process opens no regular file for data |

The system's unit of work is one HTTP request, processed to completion synchronously. There is no window, no accumulation, no checkpoint and no batch identifier — and because nothing is written anywhere, there would be nothing for a batch job to operate on.

#### 6.3.3.5 Error Handling Strategy

**Every error path in the integration surface is owned by the runtime, not by this repository.** The application contains no `try`/`catch`, no `'error'` listener, no `uncaughtException` or `unhandledRejection` handler, and no signal handler. The listener census in 6.3.3.1 explains why this is consequential: with `clientError`, `error`, `upgrade` and `connect` all at zero subscribers, Node's defaults *are* the error strategy.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    INBOUND["Inbound connection or request received"]
    PARSEOK{"Parses as a supported<br/>HTTP request?"}
    HDRSIZE{"Header block within<br/>16384 bytes?"}
    METHODOK{"Method token in the<br/>runtime allow-list?"}
    HOSTOK{"HTTP/1.1 request<br/>carries a Host header?"}
    TUNNEL{"CONNECT method?"}
    HANDLER["Application listener runs<br/>always returns 200 text-plain 14 bytes"]
    R400["Runtime emits 400 Bad Request<br/>plus Connection close"]
    R431["Runtime emits 431 Request Header<br/>Fields Too Large"]
    DESTROY["Socket destroyed, zero bytes returned<br/>no connect listener registered"]
    BINDFAIL["Bind conflict at startup<br/>unhandled error event, exit code 1"]
    NOAPPERR["No application error path exists<br/>no try-catch, no error listener,<br/>no retry, no dead-letter"]

    INBOUND --> PARSEOK
    PARSEOK -->|"no - malformed line, TLS bytes,<br/>HTTP/2 preface, bogus version"| R400
    PARSEOK -->|"yes"| HDRSIZE
    HDRSIZE -->|"no"| R431
    HDRSIZE -->|"yes"| METHODOK
    METHODOK -->|"no"| R400
    METHODOK -->|"yes"| HOSTOK
    HOSTOK -->|"no"| R400
    HOSTOK -->|"yes"| TUNNEL
    TUNNEL -->|"yes"| DESTROY
    TUNNEL -->|"no"| HANDLER
    HANDLER --> NOAPPERR
    BINDFAIL -.->|"precedes all request handling"| INBOUND
```

*Diagram 6.3.3-B — Inbound fault disposition. Every rejection branch is decided before the application listener is reached; once the listener runs, no failure mode remains that application code could handle.*

##### 6.3.3.5.1 Measured Fault Dispositions

| Fault Condition | Measured Disposition | Handled By |
|---|---|---|
| Malformed request line | `400 Bad Request` + `Connection: close`; handler never invoked | Runtime default `clientError` |
| Method token outside the parser allow-list | `400 Bad Request` | Runtime parser |
| TLS ClientHello sent to the cleartext port | `400 Bad Request` in cleartext | Runtime parser |
| HTTP/2 prior-knowledge preface | `400 Bad Request` | Runtime parser |
| `HTTP/1.1` request without `Host` | `400 Bad Request` + chunked empty body | Runtime |
| Header block exceeding 16384 bytes | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` + close | Runtime |
| `CONNECT` request | Socket destroyed, zero bytes returned | Runtime default (no `connect` listener) |
| `Upgrade: websocket` / `h2c` | Ordinary `200`; no `101` ever emitted | Application listener, upgrade never honoured |
| Idle keep-alive connection | Socket closed; measured at 6.00 s against `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` | Runtime `keepAliveTimeout` |
| Port already bound at startup | Unhandled `'error'` event, stack trace on standard error, **exit code 1** | Runtime default (no `'error'` listener) |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Integrating client
    participant R as Node http runtime
    participant H as Application listener
    Note over C,H: Case 1 - client attempts TLS on the plaintext port
    C->>R: TLS ClientHello bytes
    R-->>C: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request, Connection close
    Note over H: listener never invoked
    Note over C,H: Case 2 - client attempts a WebSocket upgrade
    C->>R: GET with Upgrade websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Key
    R->>H: emit request event, upgrade not honoured
    H->>R: 200 text-plain 14 bytes
    R-->>C: HTTP/1.1 200 OK, no 101 Switching Protocols
    Note over C,H: Case 3 - client attempts a CONNECT tunnel
    C->>R: CONNECT host:443
    R-->>C: socket destroyed, zero bytes
    Note over C,H: Case 4 - client sends Expect 100-continue
    C->>R: POST with Expect 100-continue
    R-->>C: HTTP/1.1 100 Continue emitted automatically
    C->>R: request body bytes
    R->>H: emit request event
    H->>R: 200 text-plain 14 bytes
    R-->>C: HTTP/1.1 200 OK, body never read
```

*Diagram 6.3.3-C — Four measured integration-attempt outcomes that an integrator is most likely to encounter. Cases 1 and 3 never reach application code; cases 2 and 4 reach it but ignore the client's protocol intent.*

##### 6.3.3.5.2 Error-Handling Patterns Verified Absent

| Pattern | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Retry with backoff | Absent | Zero matches for `retry` or `backoff`; a failed bind exits rather than retrying |
| Circuit breaker or bulkhead | Absent | Zero matches; there is no downstream call to protect |
| Dead-letter queue or poison-message handling | Absent | No queue exists, so no message can be parked |
| Compensating transaction or saga | Absent | Nothing is written, so there is nothing to compensate |
| Idempotency keys or deduplication | Not required — every response is identical regardless of repetition | No mutable state exists |
| Error propagation to callers | Absent from application code | The handler can only emit `200`; all error statuses originate in the runtime |
| Graceful shutdown or connection drain | Absent | No `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler; termination is immediate |
| Automatic process restart | Absent from the repository | No supervisor, container restart policy or process-manager definition exists |

The pattern is **fail-fast at the process level and delegate-and-close at the socket level**. For an integrator this has one concrete implication: a failure is never reported *in-band*. Either the response is the same 14-byte `200` as always, or the connection is closed or refused — there is no error payload, no error code and no retry hint to interpret.

### 6.3.4 External Systems

**The system integrates with no external system.** It consumes no third-party API, fronts no legacy interface, sits behind no gateway, and is party to no service contract that it did not itself define implicitly by responding. The external relationships that do exist are of a different kind: one *inbound* consumer, one *design-time* toolchain, and one *distribution* channel. This sub-section documents all of them and enumerates every external dependency in the system.

#### 6.3.4.1 Third-Party Integration Patterns

**No third-party integration pattern is implemented**, because there is no mechanism with which to implement one. The decisive evidence is that the process has no egress capability at all:

| Integration Prerequisite | Verification | Result |
|---|---|---|
| An HTTP or RPC client | Sweep for `axios`, `node-fetch`, `fetch(`, `got`, `superagent`, `undici`, `http.request`, `https.request`, `grpc`, `jsonrpc`, `tRPC` | Zero matches |
| A vendor SDK | Sweep for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Slack, Firebase, Auth0, Okta, Datadog, Sentry, New Relic, Segment, PayPal | Zero matches |
| An endpoint to call | Census of every URL, host and endpoint literal in the repository | Exactly one URL-shaped string exists — the self-referential startup banner at `server.js` line 13 |
| A runtime-injectable endpoint | Sweep for `process.env`, `.env`, config files, `connectionString`, `DSN` | Zero matches; configuration is compiled in (constraint C-003) |
| An actual outbound connection | Inode-matched TCP socket census of the running process | **Zero outbound sockets** — idle, under a 400-request load, and while 20 inbound keep-alive connections were held open |

The socket census is worth stating in full because it is the strongest available evidence: idle, the process owned exactly **1** socket (the listener in `LISTEN` state); holding twenty client connections open, it owned **21** sockets — one listener plus twenty inbound — and **zero** outbound; after the clients disconnected it returned to one. No integration pattern of any kind — synchronous request/reply, webhook callback, polling, publish/subscribe, file exchange or shared database — can be attributed to a process that never opens an outbound connection.

**The one named external party is a consumer, not a provider.** `README.md` line 2 identifies the repository as a "test project for backprop integration". The direction of that relationship is inbound only: the tooling calls the fixture, and nothing in `server.js` references, authenticates against or is even aware of it. Section 3.4.5 records the same characterisation, noting that the relationship is "inbound and one-directional".

#### 6.3.4.2 Legacy System Interfaces

**No legacy system interface exists.** Every conventional legacy integration mechanism was probed for and found absent:

| Legacy Mechanism | Markers Probed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| File transfer and batch exchange | `ftp`, `sftp`, `scp`, `smb`, `nfs`, fixed-width, `csv` | Zero matches; no filesystem primitive of any kind is used |
| Host and mainframe access | `as400`, `mainframe`, `cobol`, terminal emulation | Zero matches |
| Industry message formats | `edi`, `hl7`, `iso8583`, SWIFT MT | Zero matches |
| Database bridges | `jdbc`, `odbc`, any driver or connection string | Zero matches |
| Legacy web services | `soap`, `wsdl`, `xsd`, XML-RPC | Zero matches |

There is also no *predecessor* system: the repository has a single commit (`1a0874d`) that added all four files, so there is no migration path, no strangler façade, no adapter layer and no dual-write period to document. The fixture is not a modernisation of anything.

#### 6.3.4.3 API Gateway Configuration

**No API gateway, reverse proxy, ingress controller or service mesh is configured**, and none is referenced. An existence probe covering nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Envoy, Kong, Apigee, Traefik, Caddy, Istio/Linkerd sidecars, Kubernetes ingress manifests, `serverless.yml`, SAM/CloudFormation templates and Terraform found **no such file anywhere in the repository**, and a source sweep for the same technologies plus `x-forwarded` returned zero matches.

Two findings make this more than a simple absence:

- **A gateway could not front this listener as written.** Because `server.js` line 3 compiles the loopback address into the program, the listener is bound inside whatever network namespace the process runs in. A proxy on another host cannot reach it, and — as section 5.2.3 records — a container built around this repository would expose the listener only inside its own namespace, so even a published port mapping would not reach it. Introducing a gateway would require editing line 3, which the `README.md` change freeze prohibits (constraint C-001).
- **Gateway-conveyed context would be discarded anyway.** `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` were both sent and both ignored, returning the ordinary `200`. There is no trust-proxy setting, no client-IP extraction and no scheme awareness, so even a correctly configured gateway could not pass client identity, TLS termination status or rate-limit decisions into this application.

The practical consequence is that the *only* gateway-equivalent control in the system is the bind address itself: it performs the network-level admission decision that an edge tier would normally own, and it does so by refusing every non-loopback interface.

#### 6.3.4.4 External Service Contracts

No contract is *consumed*, because no external service is called. One contract is *offered*, but it is implicit — it exists only as observed behaviour, since section 6.3.2.8 establishes that no machine-readable contract artifact exists.

| Contract Dimension | Offered Contract (inbound) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Functional guarantee | Every syntactically valid HTTP request receives `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and the 14-byte body `Hello, World!\n` | `server.js` lines 7–9; verified invariant across methods, paths, headers and payloads |
| Addressability | `127.0.0.1:3000` only; every non-loopback interface refuses connection | `server.js` line 3; measured |
| Readiness signal | One standard-output line, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`; no health or readiness endpoint exists | `server.js` line 13 |
| Availability, latency or throughput commitment | **None.** The repository declares no SLA, SLO, error budget or performance target | Verified absence of any such declaration |
| Change and deprecation policy | Immutability by directive: "Do not touch!" (`README.md` line 2), with a single-commit baseline as the evidence of it | Constraint C-001 |
| Support, versioning or notification channel | None — no contact metadata, no repository field, no issue template | `package.json` declares only `name`, `version`, `description`, `main`, `scripts`, `author`, `license` |

Measured figures that appear elsewhere in this specification (throughput of roughly 12,761 requests per second sequentially, p50 latency of 0.064 ms) are **observations of a particular environment, not commitments**; nothing in the repository promises them, and section 5.4.5 records that no performance requirement exists.

#### 6.3.4.5 Complete External Dependency Inventory

This is the exhaustive list of everything outside the repository on which the system depends, in any capacity. There are five entries, and only the first is required at runtime.

| Dependency | Kind | Role and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js core `http` module | Runtime, built-in | The entire integration technology of the system: transport, parsing, dispatch, serialization, connection management and all error defaults. `require('http')` at `server.js` line 1 is the only `require()` in the repository |
| Node.js runtime (unpinned version) | Runtime, platform | Supplies the event loop, the wire framing headers and every timeout/limit default. No `engines` range, `.nvmrc` or `.node-version` is declared (deviation D-005), so the version — and therefore those defaults — is chosen by the consumer. Verification for this specification used Node.js 22.23.1 |
| Operating-system TCP/IP stack and loopback interface | Runtime, platform | Owns the socket, the 511-entry accept backlog and the port-exclusivity check that produces `EADDRINUSE` |
| npm CLI | Design-time tooling | Reads `package.json` and `package-lock.json` for identity, install and the `test` script. Section 3.3.4 records that `npm ci --offline` exits 0 and creates no `node_modules`, so the npm registry is a latent default that is never contacted |
| Git and the `origin` remote | Ecosystem, distribution | Distributes the frozen artifact and evidences immutability via the single-commit baseline `1a0874d` on branch `main`. The running process never contacts it |

**Third-party package dependencies: zero.** `package.json` declares none of `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, `bundleDependencies`, `overrides` or `workspaces`, and `package-lock.json` (lockfileVersion 3) contains exactly one `packages` entry — the root record. Section 3.3.1 describes the resulting graph as "one node — the root package itself — with depth 0 and zero edges".

Two dependency risks that normally dominate integration architecture are therefore eliminated, and one unusual one remains:

- **Eliminated:** third-party service availability coupling (no service is called) and package supply-chain exposure (nothing is installed; `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across one package).
- **Remaining:** the *runtime* supply chain. Because the framing headers, the keep-alive timeout, the 16384-byte header limit and the method allow-list are all Node.js defaults rather than repository settings, a future runtime release could change this system's observable integration contract with no change to its source. Sections 2.3.5 and 3.3.6 record the same exposure.

### 6.3.5 Integration Determination Summary and Extension Constraints

#### 6.3.5.1 Determination Summary

Every topic the Integration Architecture scope requires is listed below with its status and governing evidence. "Present" means an implemented mechanism was found; "Absent" means the mechanism was probed for and verified not to exist; "Not applicable" means the mechanism has no meaning in this system's design.

| Topic | Determination | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol specification | **Present, implicit** | Cleartext HTTP/1.1 on `127.0.0.1:3000`; measured version, method, URI and payload matrices in 6.3.2.2 |
| Authentication methods | **Absent** | Zero credential markers; five credential classes all returned `200`; `401`/`403` unreachable (6.3.2.4) |
| Authorization framework | **Absent / not applicable** | No principal and no differentiated resource exist (6.3.2.5) |
| Rate limiting strategy | **Absent** | 2,200 measured requests produced zero `429` responses; no quota, ceiling or `Retry-After` (6.3.2.6) |
| Versioning approach | **Absent** | Versioned paths, version headers and query versions are all ignored (6.3.2.7) |
| Documentation standards | **Absent** | No OpenAPI/AsyncAPI/GraphQL/IDL/collection artifact of any kind (6.3.2.8) |
| Event processing patterns | **Present, minimal** | Single-subscriber synchronous dispatch; measured listener census with nine events at zero subscribers (6.3.3.1) |
| Message queue architecture | **Not applicable** | 16 brokers and 8 job-queue libraries at zero matches; the only queue-like structure is the kernel accept backlog (6.3.3.2) |
| Stream processing design | **Not applicable** | Both HTTP streams exist structurally but are unused; `readableFlowing=null`, single-shot `res.end()` (6.3.3.3) |
| Batch processing flows | **Not applicable** | No scheduler, timer, worker or child process; active handles are only `TCPServerWrap` and `TCPSocketWrap` (6.3.3.4) |
| Error handling strategy | **Present, runtime-owned** | Ten measured fault dispositions, all decided by Node defaults; no application error path exists (6.3.3.5) |
| Third-party integration patterns | **Absent** | Zero clients, zero SDKs, zero endpoint literals, zero outbound sockets (6.3.4.1) |
| Legacy system interfaces | **Absent** | Five categories of legacy mechanism at zero matches; no predecessor system exists (6.3.4.2) |
| API gateway configuration | **Absent** | No gateway/proxy/ingress/mesh/IaC artifact; the loopback bind also precludes one (6.3.4.3) |
| External service contracts | **One offered, none consumed** | Implicit inbound contract only; no SLA, SLO or performance commitment (6.3.4.4) |
| External dependencies | **Five, one required at runtime** | Core `http` module, Node.js runtime, OS TCP/IP stack, npm CLI, Git origin (6.3.4.5) |

#### 6.3.5.2 Structural Constraints on Any Future Integration

These are not recommendations; they are constraints that follow from the code as it exists. Each would have to be resolved before any integration could be added.

| Constraint | Mechanism | Consequence for Integration Work |
|---|---|---|
| Change freeze | `README.md` line 2 states "Do not touch!"; elevated to constraint C-001 elsewhere in this specification | Every integration below requires editing tracked content, which the directive prohibits — so the constraint is governance, not technique |
| Loopback confinement | `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` compiled into `server.js` line 3 (constraint C-002) | No remote consumer, gateway, load balancer, sidecar or published container port can reach the listener. Exposure requires a source edit, not a configuration change |
| No configuration surface | Zero `process.env` usage, no `.env`, no config file (constraint C-003) | An endpoint, credential or broker address cannot be injected at deploy time; every integration parameter would have to be hard-coded |
| No interception point | One inline handler, no middleware chain, no exports (`server.js` has no `module.exports`) | Authentication, rate limiting, logging or tracing cannot be wrapped around the handler; they would have to be written into it |
| Empty install graph | `package-lock.json` locks only the root record; no `node_modules` is created by `npm ci` | Any client library, broker SDK or auth library would require adding a dependency, re-locking, and accepting a network install — reversing the zero-dependency property |
| Single-instance bind | A second `node server.js` exits with code 1 on `EADDRINUSE` (unhandled `'error'` event) | Horizontally scaling behind a gateway is precluded on one host without both a source change and a supervision strategy |
| Unpinned runtime | No `engines`, `.nvmrc` or `.node-version` (deviation D-005) | The wire contract's framing headers and limits are inherited from whichever Node.js build the consumer runs, so an integration test asserting on them is asserting on the platform |

#### 6.3.5.3 Guidance for Integrating Systems

Derived strictly from measured behaviour, an integrator should expect the following:

- **Address it as plain HTTP on the loopback interface only.** `https://` fails with a cleartext `400`, and any non-loopback address refuses the connection.
- **Do not encode meaning in the request.** Method, path, query string, headers and body are never read; a `POST /v1/orders` with a JSON payload is answered exactly as `GET /` is.
- **Assert on the invariant, not on the framing.** `200`, `text/plain` and the 14 bytes come from `server.js`; `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive` and `Content-Length` come from the runtime and can change with a runtime upgrade.
- **Expect no error semantics.** Failures arrive as a closed or refused connection, or as a runtime-generated `400`/`431` — never as an application error payload.
- **Manage connection lifetime.** Keep-alive connections are closed after five idle seconds (measured at 6.00 s), so long-lived integrator connections must be re-established.
- **Detect readiness from standard output, and liveness by probing.** The single startup line is the only readiness signal; there is no health endpoint, no metrics endpoint and no access log, so the server contributes nothing to reconciliation or diagnosis.
- **Supervise the process externally.** Nothing in the repository restarts it, drains it on `SIGTERM`, or retries a failed bind.

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Security Architecture Applicability Assessment

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The repository contains no authentication framework, no authorization system, and no data-protection mechanism. It tracks exactly four files — `server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, and `README.md` — totalling 39 lines and 913 bytes across zero subdirectories. The single executable file imports one module, declares four immutable `const` bindings, and answers every request with a compiled-in 14-byte literal without ever dereferencing the request object. There is therefore no identity to manage, no credential to validate, no session to maintain, no principal to authorize, no resource to differentiate, and no datum whose confidentiality, integrity, or retention would need to be protected.

That statement requires immediate scoping, because it is easy to misread. It does **not** mean the system exhibits no security-relevant behaviour, and it does not mean the security posture is unexamined. Three security properties are real, measurable, and architecturally load-bearing: the listener is bound to the loopback interface and refuses every other network position; the request is never read, which makes entire vulnerability classes structurally unreachable rather than merely unexploited; and the dependency graph is empty, which removes the transitive supply chain altogether. What is absent is the *framework layer* — the identity providers, token issuers, policy engines, enforcement points, key stores, and audit sinks that this section would normally specify. The standard practices that operate in their place are enumerated in Section 6.4.6.

The remainder of Section 6.4 is therefore written as an evidence-based security assessment rather than a design description. Every claim below was verified either by static census of the four tracked files or by direct measurement against a running copy of the unmodified `server.js`; the checkout itself was left byte-identical throughout, honouring the change freeze recorded as constraint C-001.

#### 6.4.1.1 Determination and Adjudication

Applicability was adjudicated against six independent tests, one for each domain this section is expected to specify. A positive result on any one of them would have made a detailed security architecture applicable. All six resolve negative.

| Applicability Test | Requirement for Applicability | Repository Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Authentication framework | Any mechanism that reads, validates, issues, or challenges a credential | Zero matches across all four files for `authorization`, `bearer`, `jwt`, `oauth`, `oidc`, `saml`, `api-key`, `hmac`, `mtls`, `session`, `cookie`, `password`, `credential`, and `passport`. Fourteen credential-bearing probes returned byte-identical `200` responses; no `WWW-Authenticate` or `Set-Cookie` header was ever emitted | Not present |
| Authorization system | A principal, a differentiated resource, and a decision point between them | Zero matches for `rbac`, `abac`, `role`, `permission`, `privilege`, `scope`, `claim`, `acl`, `policy`, `entitlement`, and `tenant`. `GET /admin/users`, `DELETE /admin/users/1`, and `PUT /internal/config` — all unauthenticated — returned the same 14 bytes as `GET /` | Not present |
| Data protection | Data at rest, data in transit requiring confidentiality, or key material | The entire data domain is three compiled-in literals. `https`, `tls`, `ssl`, `crypto`, `cipher`, and `certificate` return zero matches; the server object is not a `tls.Server`; a file-extension census for `.pem`, `.key`, `.crt`, `.p12`, `.pfx`, `.jks`, and `id_rsa*` found **zero files** | Not present |
| Secret and key management | A secret, key, or configuration channel through which one could be supplied | `process.env` appears zero times; no `.env`, `.npmrc`, `config/`, `secrets/`, `certs/`, or `keys/` path exists. A credential-shaped string scan across the working tree **and every blob in Git history** returned zero hits | Not present |
| Security control layer | A middleware chain, guard, interceptor, or filter at which a control could execute | Zero matches for `middleware`, `guard`, `interceptor`, `decorator`, `helmet`, `csurf`, `cors`, `sanitiz`, `validator`, `joi`, `zod`, and `ajv`. `server.js` declares no exports, so nothing can wrap the handler | Not present |
| Compliance obligation | Personal, regulated, financial, or health data entering, transiting, or leaving the system | `req` is bound but never dereferenced, so zero request bytes are read; no persistence exists; an inode-matched socket census recorded zero outbound connections.
