#### 6.4.1.5 Why the Absences Are Architecturally Load-Bearing

In most systems an absent security control is a gap to be remediated. Here four of the absences are the design, and each has a measurable protective effect that a conventional control layer would not improve upon.

- **The loopback literal is the only access control, and it is the whole perimeter.** Because `server.js` line 3 compiles `127.0.0.1` into the program, network position substitutes for identity. There is no authentication layer to bypass because there is no reachable network position from which to attempt one — a characterisation Section 5.4.4 states as *network isolation used in place of identity*.
- **Not reading the request eliminates the input attack surface rather than defending it.** Zero matches for `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers`, and `req.on` combine with zero injection sinks to make reflected injection, deserialization abuse, path traversal, and payload-size attacks structurally unreachable. Section 2.4.4 records the same conclusion: whole classes of input-driven vulnerability are structurally absent.
- **Zero egress makes the process non-exfiltrating by construction.** With no HTTP client, no driver, and zero measured outbound sockets, there is no channel through which data could leave the host even if the process were subverted.
- **An empty dependency graph removes the transitive supply chain.** `package-lock.json` locks exactly one package — the root itself — so no authentication library, telemetry agent, or transitive vulnerability can be present. `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities, and no install lifecycle script exists that could execute at install time.

Two counterweights must be recorded with equal precision, because they are the section's genuine findings rather than benign absences. First, the entire posture rests on a single unprotected source literal: an edit to `server.js` line 3 would remove the only access control the system has, with no compensating control behind it, and the change freeze that protects that literal is enforced by convention only — no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check exists. Second, no request is ever recorded, so access leaves no server-side trace whatsoever; after-the-fact attribution is impossible.

#### 6.4.1.6 Scope of the Determination and Structure of This Section

The determination applies to every security *framework* tier: no identity provider, no multi-factor mechanism, no session or token infrastructure, no password policy, no role or permission model, no policy decision or enforcement point, no audit pipeline, no cryptographic subsystem, no key-management service, no data-masking layer, and no compliance control programme. It does **not** apply to the four measurable security properties above, nor to the standard practices catalogued in Section 6.4.6, all of which are real and were verified directly.

| Sub-section | Area Covered | Form of the Content |
|---|---|---|
| 6.4.2 | Identity management, multi-factor authentication, session management, token handling, password policies | Per-area status with static and runtime evidence, the authentication flow diagram, and the authentication control matrix |
| 6.4.3 | Role-based access control, permission management, resource authorization, policy enforcement points, audit logging | Per-area status, the authorization flow diagram, the authorization control matrix, and the audit-logging gap analysis |
| 6.4.4 | Encryption standards, key management, data masking, secure communication, compliance controls | Data classification, the transport-security determination, the key-management scope statement, and the compliance requirement tables |
| 6.4.5 | Security zones, trust boundaries, attack surface, threat disposition, process privilege | The security zone diagram, the boundary register, the measured threat-disposition map, and the privilege attribution analysis |
| 6.4.6 | The standard security practices that operate in place of a framework layer | The consolidated control matrix, the residual risk register, and the conditions that would invalidate this determination |
| 6.4.7 | References | Every repository file, folder, specification section, and verification activity cited as evidence |


### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

**There is no authentication framework.** The request object is bound as a handler parameter and never dereferenced, so no credential can be read, let alone validated. This is not an inference from a missing design document: it is a static property of `server.js` (zero matches for `req.headers`, `req.url`, and `req.method`) confirmed behaviourally by fourteen credential-bearing probes that all produced byte-identical responses.

The consequence that matters most to a consumer is a negative capability: **`401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden` are unreachable status codes.** No literal `401` or `403` appears anywhere in the repository, and the handler contains a single unconditional code path with three statements, so no rejection branch can exist to emit one. Section 6.3.2.4 records the same finding from the integration perspective.

What operates in place of authentication is a single network-layer admission decision made by the operating system before any byte reaches the process. Section 6.4.2.1 specifies it precisely, and the sub-sections that follow address each authentication concern this section is expected to cover.

#### 6.4.2.1 The De-Facto Authentication Substitute — Network-Position Admission

The system's only caller-facing control is the bind address literal on `server.js` line 3. It is not authentication, and describing it accurately matters because its guarantees and its limits are both narrow.

| Property | Measured Behaviour | Security Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| What is checked | Whether the inbound TCP connection arrives on `127.0.0.1` | A network-position test performed by the kernel, not an identity assertion |
| Granularity | Binary and host-wide | Every same-host process is admitted; no process, user, or container is distinguished from another |
| Enforcement point | The kernel socket bind, before the Node.js runtime or `server.js` executes | The decision is made outside the application, which is why it cannot be bypassed by any request content |
| Precision of the binding | The single address `127.0.0.1`, not the `127/8` block and not IPv6 | `127.0.0.2:3000` and `[::1]:3000` were both **refused**, as was the host's routable address. `/proc/net/tcp` shows exactly one listener, `0100007F:0BB8`, in state `0A` |
| Failure mode | Connection refused with no bytes exchanged | Rejection is silent from the server's perspective — nothing is logged, and the application never learns that an attempt occurred |

Three limits of this substitute were measured directly and should not be overlooked.

- **It conveys no identity into the application.** `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` were both sent and both ignored, returning the ordinary `200`. There is no trust-proxy semantics, no client-address extraction, and no scheme awareness, so even a correctly configured fronting proxy could not pass a client identity, a TLS-termination status, or an upstream authentication decision into this application.
- **It does not validate the requested authority.** A spoofed `Host: attacker.example` was accepted with a normal `200`; there is no host allow-list, and `OPTIONS *` produced the greeting with no `Allow` header.
- **It is protected by convention alone.** The literal that constitutes the control is one token in an unenforced file. Section 5.4.4 states the exposure precisely: the entire security posture is one character-level edit away from being removed, with no compensating control behind it, and the `README.md` change freeze that protects it has no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI enforcement.

#### 6.4.2.2 Identity Management

**No identity concept exists at any layer.** There is no user, account, service principal, tenant, subject, or machine identity — and no store, directory, or registry in which one could be recorded.

| Identity Capability | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| User or account model | Absent | Zero matches for `identity`, `principal`, `username`, `user-id`, `login`, `signin`, and `logout`; `server.js` defines no class, no named function, and no type |
| Identity provider or directory integration | Absent | Zero matches for `auth0`, `okta`, `keycloak`, `cognito`, `firebase-auth`, `next-auth`, and `passport`; the zero-dependency lockfile makes transitive presence impossible |
| Service or workload identity | Absent | No client certificate, no SPIFFE identity, no `mtls` usage, and no signing key; the certificate and key material census found zero files |
| Caller attribution at runtime | Absent | `req.socket` and `remoteAddress` are never referenced, so the process never determines even the source address of a caller |
| Identity lifecycle — provisioning, deprovisioning, recertification | Not applicable | There is no identity record to create, disable, or review |
| Anonymous access | **The only mode** | All callers are anonymous and mutually indistinguishable; the authenticated, anonymous, and malformed-credential probe responses are byte-identical |

The single identity-adjacent field anywhere in the repository is the `author` value `hxu` in `package.json`. It is package metadata describing provenance, not a runtime principal, and no code reads it.

#### 6.4.2.3 Multi-Factor Authentication

**No multi-factor authentication exists, and the concept has no referent, because there is no first factor.** MFA strengthens an existing primary authentication event; this system performs none.

| MFA Element | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Primary authentication event to strengthen | Absent | No credential of any kind is read or validated |
| One-time-password or authenticator support | Absent | Zero matches for `otp`, `totp`, `hotp`, and any authenticator library |
| Hardware-token or platform authenticator support | Absent | Zero matches for `webauthn`, `fido`, `u2f`, and `passkey`; no `crypto` usage exists with which to verify an assertion |
| Out-of-band channel — SMS, email, push | Absent | The process has zero egress capability; an inode-matched socket census recorded zero outbound connections while twenty inbound connections were held open, so no second-channel challenge could be delivered |
| Step-up or risk-based re-authentication | Absent | The handler has one unconditional code path and cannot branch on any signal |

The out-of-band row is the structurally decisive one: even if a primary factor were introduced, the process as written has no channel through which a second factor could be transmitted or verified.

#### 6.4.2.4 Session Management

**No session management exists, and the system is stateless in the strict sense.** Nothing correlates one request to another, and nothing is retained between them.

| Session Concern | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Session identifier issuance | Absent | **No `Set-Cookie` header is emitted on any response.** A thirteen-header presence check found `set-cookie` absent in every case |
| Session store | Absent | No module-scope mutable binding exists — all four bindings are `const`, with zero `let` and zero `var`; no `Map`, `Set`, or `WeakMap` is used, and no external store is reachable |
| Inbound session recognition | Absent | `Cookie: session=abc123; csrf=xyz` returned the ordinary `200` with no session lookup; the cookie was never parsed |
| Session fixation, rotation, and idle or absolute timeout | Not applicable | There is no session identifier to fix, rotate, or expire |
| Logout and server-side invalidation | Not applicable | There is nothing to invalidate; no state survives a response |
| Cross-site request forgery defence | Not required in the conventional sense | No `csrf` or `xsrf` marker exists, but the precondition for CSRF is also absent: no ambient credential is ever issued, so a forged cross-site request has no authority to borrow, and every request — forged or not — receives the same inert 14-byte response |

**The keep-alive connection is not a session.** The runtime retains an idle TCP connection for its default `keepAliveTimeout` of 5000 ms — advertised as `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` and measured closing at 6.00 s — and `maxRequestsPerSocket` is `0`, so one connection may carry unlimited requests. This is transport-level socket reuse supplied by the Node.js runtime, not application state: no request on a reused connection is treated differently from the first, and nothing about a previous request is remembered. Because the repository configures none of these values and declares no `engines` range (deviation D-005), they are unversioned by this repository.

#### 6.4.2.5 Token Handling

**No token is parsed, validated, issued, refreshed, or revoked.** The measured indistinguishability of valid-looking and invalid tokens is the clearest single demonstration that no credential processing occurs anywhere in the system.

| Token Concern | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound token parsing | Absent | Zero matches for `jwt`, `bearer`, `authorization`, `access-token`, and `refresh-token`; `req.headers` is never dereferenced |
| Signature or integrity verification | Absent, and impossible as written | No `crypto` import, no `createHmac`, no JWKS endpoint, and no key material of any kind exists |
| Claim, audience, issuer, and expiry validation | Absent | No token is decoded, so no claim can be inspected |
| Token issuance or refresh | Absent | The response body is a compiled-in literal; no header other than `Content-Type` is set by repository code |
| Revocation, introspection, or denylisting | Absent | No state exists in which a revocation list could be held, and no outbound call could reach an introspection endpoint |
| Anti-replay protection | Not applicable | Zero matches for `nonce`; because every response is identical and no state changes, replaying a request has no effect that differs from the original |

The measured credential matrix below is the primary evidence. Fourteen probes were issued against the running server; every one returned status `200`, a `Content-Type` of `text/plain`, a 14-byte body, and the same body digest.

| Credential or Request Presented | Measured Response | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| No credential at all — the baseline | `200`, 14 bytes | Anonymous access is the normal mode |
| `Authorization: Bearer` with a JWT-shaped, three-segment token | `200`, byte-identical to baseline | The token is neither decoded nor verified |
| `Authorization: Bearer not-a-real-token` | `200`, byte-identical | A malformed token is indistinguishable from a well-formed one |
| `Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz` | `200`, byte-identical | Basic credentials are never base64-decoded or compared |
| `Authorization:` with an empty value | `200`, byte-identical | A malformed authorization header triggers no rejection path |
| `Cookie: session=abc123; csrf=xyz` | `200`, byte-identical | No session or CSRF token lookup occurs |
| `X-API-Key: totally-invalid` | `200`, byte-identical | An invalid API key is indistinguishable from a valid one |
| `X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9` | `200`, byte-identical | No proxy-conveyed client identity is honoured |
| `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` | `200`, byte-identical | No TLS-termination assertion is honoured |
| `Origin: https://evil.example` | `200`, byte-identical; no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` in the response | No origin check and no CORS negotiation |
| `GET /admin/users` and `GET /api/private` | `200`, byte-identical | No path is privileged |
| Unauthenticated `DELETE /admin/users/1` | `200`, byte-identical | A destructive-looking request is neither authenticated nor refused |
| Unauthenticated `PUT /internal/config` | `200`, byte-identical | No write path exists to protect, and none is guarded |

#### 6.4.2.6 Password Policies

**No password exists anywhere in the system, and therefore no password policy has anything to attach to.** This is a stronger statement than "no policy is documented": there is no field, form, store, comparison, or hashing routine that a policy could govern.

| Policy Dimension | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Password acceptance, storage, or comparison | Absent | Zero matches for `password`, `passwd`, `credential`, and `secret` across all four tracked files |
| Hashing and key derivation | Absent | Zero matches for `bcrypt`, `argon2`, `scrypt`, `pbkdf2`, `salt`, and any `crypto` API |
| Complexity, length, rotation, history, and reuse rules | Not applicable | There is no credential to constrain |
| Lockout, throttling, and brute-force resistance | Not applicable — and structurally moot | There is no authentication attempt to count. Repeated requests carry no authentication semantics; 2,000 sequential and 200 concurrent requests all returned `200` with zero `429` responses |
| Credential material in the repository or its history | **Verified absent** | A credential-shaped string scan across the working tree and **every blob in Git history** returned zero hits for AWS access-key, GitHub token, OpenAI key, Slack token, PEM header, JWT-shaped, and long base64 patterns |

The last row is a positive finding rather than a vacuous one, and Section 6.4.6.2 records it as such: no secret has ever been committed to this repository at any point in its history.

#### 6.4.2.7 Authentication Flow

The diagram traces the measured request path and places the absent authentication pipeline alongside it. Two features are worth reading carefully. The only decision that is genuinely evaluated is the kernel's loopback admission test, which occurs before any application code runs. And the `401` challenge terminal is drawn as unreachable, because no code path in the repository can produce it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ARRIVE(["Inbound TCP connection<br/>on 127.0.0.1 port 3000"])
    ZONE{"Does the connection arrive<br/>on the loopback interface?"}
    REFUSE(["Refused by the kernel - measured on the<br/>routable address and on IPv6 loopback"])
    PARSE["CMP-01 Node http runtime<br/>parses request line and headers"]
    HDRS["Credential-bearing headers arrive intact<br/>Authorization, Cookie, X-API-Key"]
    DISPATCH["CMP-01 emits the request event<br/>request listener count is 1"]
    HANDLER["CMP-04 handler runs - req is bound<br/>but never dereferenced"]
    RESP(["200 OK, text-plain, 14 bytes -<br/>byte-identical across 14 credential probes"])

    subgraph AbsentAuthN["Authentication Pipeline - Verified Absent"]
        EXTRACT{"Extract a credential<br/>from the request?"}
        RESOLVE{"Resolve a principal against<br/>an identity store?"}
        VALIDATE{"Validate the credential<br/>signature or secret?"}
        SESSION{"Look up or issue a<br/>session or token?"}
        CHALLENGE(["Emit 401 with<br/>WWW-Authenticate"])
        EXTRACT -->|"no code reads req.headers"| RESOLVE
        RESOLVE -->|"no identity store exists"| VALIDATE
        VALIDATE -->|"no crypto call and no secret exist"| SESSION
        SESSION -->|"no Set-Cookie is ever emitted"| CHALLENGE
    end

    ARRIVE --> ZONE
    ZONE -->|"no"| REFUSE
    ZONE -->|"yes"| PARSE
    PARSE --> HDRS
    HDRS --> DISPATCH
    DISPATCH --> HANDLER
    HANDLER --> RESP
    HDRS -.->|"credentials are never read -<br/>no interception point exists"| EXTRACT
    CHALLENGE -.->|"unreachable status code"| RESP
```

*Diagram 6.4.2-A — Authentication decision flow. Solid edges are measured. The dotted edge into the lower subgraph marks the point at which a credential would be extracted if any code read the request; the subgraph itself was probed for and found entirely absent.*

#### 6.4.2.8 Authentication Control Matrix

| Control | Implementation Status | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Identity management | Absent — anonymous access only | Zero identity markers; no identity store; caller source address never determined |
| Multi-factor authentication | Absent — no first factor to strengthen | Zero OTP/WebAuthn markers; zero egress for any out-of-band channel |
| Session management | Absent — strictly stateless | No `Set-Cookie` ever emitted; all module bindings are `const`; no session store |
| Token handling | Absent — no parse, verify, issue, or revoke | Fourteen credential probes byte-identical; no `crypto` and no key material |
| Password policy | Not applicable — no password exists | Zero password, hash, salt, and KDF markers; zero secrets in the tree or in history |
| Credential challenge | Unreachable | No `401`/`403` literal and no `WWW-Authenticate` header anywhere in the system |
| Brute-force and rate control | Absent | No rate limiting, quota, or `maxConnections` ceiling; zero `429` across 2,200 measured requests |
| Transport authentication of the server to the client | Absent | Not a `tls.Server`; a TLS ClientHello receives a cleartext `400`, so no server certificate is ever presented |
| Network-position admission | **Present — the only control** | Kernel-enforced loopback bind; routable, IPv6, and `127.0.0.2` addresses all refused |
| Proxy-conveyed identity | Absent, and not honourable | `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` ignored; no trust-proxy setting exists |
| Host authorization | Absent | Spoofed `Host` accepted with `200`; no host allow-list |
| Anti-automation signalling | Absent | No `Retry-After` and no `X-RateLimit-*` header is ever emitted |


### 6.4.3 Authorization System

**There is no authorization system, and none could operate as the code is written.** Authorization is a function of two inputs — a principal and a differentiated resource — and this system has neither. Section 6.4.2 establishes that no principal is ever determined; this sub-section establishes that there is exactly one implicit resource, the fixed greeting, and that the handler contains no conditional branch with which a decision could be expressed.

The system's effective authorization policy is therefore **implicit, unconditional allow**. Every request is permitted, no request is evaluated, and no decision is recorded. The measured evidence and the consequences of each absent capability follow.

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

**No role-based access control exists, and neither of its two preconditions is met.**

| RBAC Element | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Role, group, or scope definition | Absent | Zero matches across all four tracked files for `rbac`, `abac`, `role`, `scope`, `claim`, `entitlement`, `privilege`, and `tenant` |
| Role assignment or membership | Absent | There is no principal to which a role could be assigned, and no store in which an assignment could be recorded |
| Role hierarchy or inheritance | Not applicable | No role exists to inherit from |
| Separation of duties and least privilege | Not expressible in code | The handler has one unconditional path; every caller receives the maximum authority the system can grant, which is a 14-byte greeting |
| Multi-tenancy or data isolation | Not applicable | No tenant concept and no data exist; Section 6.2 establishes the absence of any data tier |
| Administrative role for policy management | Absent | No configuration surface exists — `process.env` appears zero times, and no configuration file is present (constraint C-003) |

The least-privilege row deserves precision rather than a formulaic verdict. Least privilege is normally a property of a granted authority set; here the authority set is a single read-only constant that discloses nothing about the host, the process, or any other caller. The maximum privilege obtainable through the API is therefore inherently minimal, which is a genuine mitigating property — but it is a consequence of the response being a constant, not of any authorization design.

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

**No permission model exists, and there is no surface on which permissions could be administered.**

| Permission Concern | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Permission or capability catalogue | Absent | Zero matches for `permission`, `grant`, `deny`, `acl`, and `can`-prefixed authorization helpers |
| Permission-to-role mapping | Absent | Neither side of the mapping exists |
| Grant and revoke operations | Absent | No mutable state exists in which a grant could be held — all module bindings are `const`, with zero `let` and zero `var` |
| Default-deny posture | **Inverted — the effective default is allow** | The handler cannot refuse; `403` is unreachable, so a deny outcome has no representation |
| Delegation, impersonation, or consent | Not applicable | No principal exists to delegate from or to |
| Policy versioning and change control | Not applicable to a policy; governance only for source | No policy artifact exists. Source change control is the single-commit Git baseline plus the advisory `README.md` freeze (constraint C-001) |

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

**There is exactly one resource and it is undifferentiated.** No path, method, query parameter, or payload identifies a distinct resource, because none of them is read. The probes below were issued against the running server and are the direct evidence for that claim.

| Resource-Authorization Probe | Measured Response | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /` — the nominal path | `200`, `text/plain`, 14 bytes | Baseline |
| `GET /admin/users` | `200`, byte-identical to baseline | A conventionally privileged namespace is not privileged here |
| `GET /api/private` | `200`, byte-identical | No resource is marked private |
| Unauthenticated `DELETE /admin/users/1` | `200`, byte-identical | A destructive method against a privileged path is neither refused nor distinguished. Nothing is deleted, because no state exists |
| Unauthenticated `PUT /internal/config` | `200`, byte-identical | No configuration write path exists to protect; the request is simply ignored |
| `GET /../../../../etc/passwd` and its percent-encoded form | `200`, byte-identical | Path traversal is inert: the path is never parsed and the process opens no regular file — a descriptor census during sustained load found zero regular-file descriptors |
| `GET /.git/config`, `/index.js`, `//double`, deep nested paths | `200`, byte-identical | No static-file handler exists, so no repository content can be served |
| Method sweep — `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `PURGE` | All `200`, one identical body digest | No method is authorized differently from any other |
| `HEAD /` | `200` with a zero-byte body | Runtime-supplied body suppression, not an authorization decision |
| `TRACE /` carrying a marker header | `200` with the ordinary greeting; the marker was **not** echoed and the response is not `message/http` | Cross-Site Tracing is not possible even though `TRACE` is accepted, because the handler answers every dispatched request identically |

Two properties of this table are load-bearing. First, `405 Method Not Allowed` is unreachable for the same reason `401` and `403` are: the application performs no method validation, and the only method-related rejection comes from the runtime parser's token allow-list, which surfaces as `400` for an unknown token such as `FROBNICATE`. Second, the uniform treatment of `/admin` and `/internal` is not a misconfiguration — it is the specified contract, recorded as requirement F-002-RQ-001 (uniform `200`) and F-002-RQ-004 (the request is never dereferenced).

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

**There is no policy enforcement point, and — more consequentially — there is no location at which one could be inserted without editing `server.js`.** This is the structural finding of the sub-section.

| Enforcement Mechanism | Status | Evidence and Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Middleware or interceptor chain | Absent | Zero matches for `middleware`, `interceptor`, `filter`, and `decorator`. The request listener is a single inline anonymous function passed directly to `http.createServer` |
| Route guard or per-path rule table | Absent | No router exists; `req.url` is never read, so no path-scoped rule could be evaluated |
| Wrappable module boundary | **Absent — the decisive constraint** | `server.js` declares no `module.exports`, so the handler cannot be imported, decorated, or wrapped by an external control. Authorization would have to be written *into* lines 6–10 |
| External enforcement tier — gateway, sidecar, service mesh | Absent, and precluded | No gateway or mesh artifact exists, and because the loopback address is compiled in, an external tier could not reach the listener. Section 5.2.3 records that a container built around this repository would expose the listener only inside its own network namespace, so even a published port mapping would not reach it |
| Kernel-level enforcement | **Present — the only enforcement point that exists** | The loopback bind performs the sole admission decision, before any application code executes |
| Policy decision point and policy store | Absent | Zero matches for `policy`, `casbin`, `opa`, and `oso`; no policy file, rule set, or decision cache exists |

The practical reading is that the system has an enforcement point but no decision point. The kernel enforces a single binary admission rule that is encoded in a source literal rather than in a policy; there is no evaluator, no rule set, and no way to express a second rule.

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

**No audit logging exists. This is one of the two genuine security gaps in the system rather than a benign absence**, and it is documented here with both its negative and its positive consequences, because both were measured.

The entire logging surface of the system is one call: `console.log` at `server.js` line 13, inside the listen callback. It fires once per process lifetime and records the address and port the process just bound. It records no request, no caller, no decision, and no outcome.

| Audit Capability | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Per-request access record | **Absent** | Twenty-five requests, each with a distinct bearer token, a distinct session cookie, and a path containing a synthetic identifier, left standard output at exactly one line and standard error empty. Section 6.2.5.4 records the same result at 25,000 requests |
| Caller attribution — source address, port, identity | **Absent** | `req.socket` and `remoteAddress` are never referenced; the process never determines who called |
| Authorization-decision record | **Absent** | No decision is computed, so there is nothing to record |
| Authentication-failure record | Absent | No authentication attempt is recognised, so no failure can be counted or alerted on |
| Structured log format, severity levels, timestamps | Absent | No logging framework is present — zero matches for `winston`, `pino`, `bunyan`, `morgan`, and `log4`. The single line is unstructured and carries no timestamp beyond what a capturing supervisor might add |
| Log integrity, retention, forwarding, or SIEM export | Absent | Zero matches for `syslog`, `siem`, and `audit`; the process writes no file, so no local log artifact exists to protect or ship |
| Tamper evidence for the audited configuration | **Present — structural** | The bind address, port, and payload are compiled-in literals, so the running configuration cannot diverge from the audited source without a source edit |
| Source-change audit trail | **Present — Git only** | One commit (`1a0874d`), one branch, zero tags, and a clean working tree make any unauthorised content change trivially detectable. The commit is unsigned, and no `CODEOWNERS` or branch-protection artifact exists |

##### 6.4.3.5.1 Consequences of the Audit Gap

| Consequence | Direction | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| After-the-fact attribution is impossible | Negative | Nothing records that a request occurred, so a security investigation must be conducted from the client side or by observing the socket |
| Anomaly detection has no input | Negative | The only two observable runtime signals are the readiness line and the process exit status, and neither varies with load or with caller |
| Refused connections are invisible to the server | Negative | A non-loopback connection attempt is refused by the kernel with no bytes exchanged and no notification to the process; reconnaissance against the port leaves no server-side trace |
| No credential or personal datum can leak into a log | **Positive** | Because nothing is written per request, no bearer token, cookie, header, client address, or payload can ever reach a log sink. A search of both streams for the synthetic token and identifier markers after the 25-request probe returned zero hits |
| Log-based data-retention exposure does not arise | **Positive** | Section 2.4.4 records the same conclusion; there is no log artifact whose retention, redaction, or residency would have to be governed |
| Log volume cannot be weaponised | **Positive** | Output is one line per process lifetime rather than per request, so log flooding and disk-exhaustion attacks against the log sink are not available |

The positive rows are not offered as compensation for the negative ones. They record a real property with a real design implication: **redaction, masking, and log-sanitisation controls are unnecessary in this system because the collection surface does not exist**, and any future introduction of request logging would create the need for all three simultaneously.

#### 6.4.3.6 Authorization Flow

The diagram shows the measured path — an implicit, unconditional allow — alongside the three tiers that a conventional authorization system would supply, each probed for and found absent. The `403` terminal inside the decision-point lane is drawn as unreachable for the same reason as the `401` terminal in Diagram 6.4.2-A.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    REQ(["Request dispatched to CMP-04 -<br/>any method, any path, any body"])
    IMPLICIT["Implicit allow - the handler contains<br/>no conditional branch of any kind"]
    WRITE["Three statements execute - set status 200,<br/>set Content-Type, end with the 14-byte literal"]
    OUT(["Identical response - DELETE /admin/users/1<br/>returns exactly what GET / returns"])

    subgraph AbsentPDP["Policy Decision Point - Verified Absent"]
        PRIN{"Who is the principal?"}
        ROLES{"Which roles, scopes or<br/>entitlements are held?"}
        RES{"Which resource and action<br/>are requested?"}
        POLICY{"Evaluate policy -<br/>permit or deny?"}
        DENY(["Emit 403 Forbidden"])
        PRIN -->|"no principal exists"| ROLES
        ROLES -->|"zero role, scope, permission or ACL markers"| RES
        RES -->|"one undifferentiated resource"| POLICY
        POLICY -->|"no policy artifact exists"| DENY
    end

    subgraph AbsentPEP["Policy Enforcement Points - Verified Absent"]
        MW["Middleware or interceptor chain"]
        GUARD["Route guard, decorator or filter"]
        ROUTER["Router applying per-path rules"]
        MW -.- GUARD
        GUARD -.- ROUTER
    end

    subgraph AbsentAudit["Access-Decision Audit - Verified Absent"]
        RECORD["Per-request access record"]
        WHO["Caller identity and source address"]
        TRAIL["Decision outcome and policy version"]
        RECORD -.- WHO
        WHO -.- TRAIL
    end

    REQ --> IMPLICIT
    IMPLICIT --> WRITE
    WRITE --> OUT
    REQ -.->|"server.js declares no module.exports -<br/>nothing can wrap the handler"| MW
    IMPLICIT -.->|"no decision is ever computed"| PRIN
    DENY -.->|"unreachable status code"| OUT
    OUT -.->|"stdout still one line after 25000 requests"| RECORD
```

*Diagram 6.4.3-A — Authorization flow. The measured path is the three solid nodes across the top. Each dotted edge marks a point at which a conventional system would consult a decision point, enforce at an interception point, or emit an audit record; all three tiers were probed for and found absent.*

#### 6.4.3.7 Authorization Control Matrix

| Control | Implementation Status | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Role-based access control | Absent — no role and no principal | Zero RBAC markers; no identity is ever determined |
| Permission management | Absent — no catalogue, grant, or revoke | Zero permission markers; no mutable state to hold a grant |
| Default-deny posture | **Inverted — effective default is allow** | Single unconditional code path; `403` unreachable |
| Resource authorization | Absent — one undifferentiated resource | `/admin`, `/api/private`, `/internal`, and traversal paths all return identical bytes |
| Method authorization | Absent — `405` unreachable | Eight methods returned one identical body digest; unknown tokens are rejected by the runtime as `400` |
| Policy decision point | Absent | No policy artifact, rule set, or evaluator exists |
| Policy enforcement point — application tier | Absent, and not insertable | No middleware chain and no `module.exports`; a control would have to be written into lines 6–10 |
| Policy enforcement point — network tier | **Present — the only enforcement point** | Kernel-enforced loopback bind, evaluated before any application code |
| Policy enforcement point — external tier | Absent, and precluded | No gateway or mesh artifact; the compiled-in loopback address prevents an external tier from reaching the listener |
| Audit logging of access and decisions | **Absent — a genuine gap** | One logging call in the entire system; 25 credential-bearing requests produced no log record |
| Credential and personal-data leakage into logs | **Not possible — a positive control property** | No per-request output exists, so no sensitive value can reach a sink |
| Source-change auditability | Present — Git provenance only | Single unsigned commit, one branch, clean tree; no `CODEOWNERS`, hook, or CI check enforces review |


### 6.4.4 Data Protection

**No data-protection mechanism exists, and for most protection concerns no obligation arises, because the system holds and transmits no protected data.** The distinction between those two statements is the substance of this sub-section: a missing control over sensitive data is a finding, whereas a missing control over a compiled-in greeting is a non-issue. Each concern below is classified explicitly into one category or the other, and the two places where a genuine gap remains are identified as such.

Section 6.2 establishes the data-tier facts this sub-section builds on: there is no database, cache, object store, or file-based artifact; the process never opens a regular file; and nothing accumulates across requests. What follows is the security-architecture treatment — classification, cryptography, key management, masking, transport confidentiality, and compliance.

#### 6.4.4.1 Data Classification

The complete data domain of the system is three values compiled into `server.js`. This is exhaustive: nothing else enters, is derived, is stored, or is emitted.

| Datum | Source and Nature | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| `Hello, World!\n` — the 14-byte response payload | `server.js` line 9, a compiled-in string literal emitted by a single `res.end` call | **Public / non-sensitive.** Static content with no template, file read, or serialization; identical for every caller |
| `127.0.0.1` — the bind address | `server.js` line 3, an immutable `const` | **Public / non-sensitive**, but *security-significant*: it is simultaneously the system's only access control |
| `3000` — the bind port | `server.js` line 4, an immutable `const` | **Public / non-sensitive**; also disclosed in the startup banner on line 13 |

No personal, regulated, financial, health, authentication, or business datum is read, stored, transmitted, or logged anywhere in the system. Three independent measurements establish this rather than assume it: the request object is never dereferenced, so zero request bytes reach application code; a descriptor census under sustained load found zero regular-file descriptors, so nothing is written; and an inode-matched socket census recorded zero outbound connections, so nothing leaves the host. The consequence is that **there is no data classification tier that would trigger an encryption-at-rest requirement, a retention schedule, a residency constraint, or a subject-access obligation.**

#### 6.4.4.2 Encryption Standards

**No cryptography of any kind is used, and no encryption standard is therefore in force.** This is a complete absence rather than a weak configuration: there is no algorithm to assess, no cipher suite to review, and no key length to specify.

| Encryption Concern | Status | Category and Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Cryptographic API usage | Absent | Non-issue. Zero matches for `crypto`, `createHash`, `createHmac`, `createCipheriv`, `randomBytes`, and `webcrypto`; the sole `require` in the repository targets core `http` |
| Symmetric or asymmetric encryption of payloads | Absent | Non-issue — the only payload is a public constant identical for every caller |
| Hashing, salting, or key derivation | Absent | Non-issue. Zero matches for `sha`, `md5`, `bcrypt`, `argon2`, `scrypt`, `pbkdf2`, and `salt`; nothing exists that would require hashing |
| Encryption at rest | **No referent** | Non-issue. There is no data at rest: no database, file, cache, or session store, and zero regular-file descriptors were open during a sustained-load run |
| Encryption in transit | **Absent** | **Genuine gap, bounded.** Traffic is cleartext HTTP/1.1; see Section 6.4.4.5 for the full determination and the bound that limits its impact |
| Signing and integrity verification of the artifact | Absent | **Genuine gap, minor.** The single commit is unsigned; integrity rests on the single-commit Git baseline and a clean working tree rather than on a signature |
| Random-number generation for security purposes | Absent | Non-issue — no nonce, token, session identifier, or salt is ever generated |
| Cryptographic agility and deprecation management | Not applicable | There is no algorithm selection to version or retire |

#### 6.4.4.3 Key Management

**No key material exists in the repository, in its history, or on the filesystem, and there is no channel through which a key could be supplied at runtime.** Key management is therefore not merely unimplemented — it has no subject.

| Key-Management Concern | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Key or certificate material in the working tree | **Verified absent** | A filesystem census for `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.crt`, `*.cer`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore`, `id_rsa*`, `*.gpg`, and `*.asc` returned **zero files**; no `certs/`, `keys/`, `ssl/`, or `tls/` directory exists |
| Key material in version-control history | **Verified absent** | A credential-shaped string scan across **every blob in the object database** returned zero hits, including PEM headers, JWT-shaped strings, and long base64 sequences |
| External key-management service integration | Absent | Zero matches for `kms`, `vault`, `secretsmanager`, `keyvault`, `parameter-store`, `sops`, `keyring`, and `jwks`; the process has zero egress capability with which to reach one |
| Runtime key injection channel | **Absent by construction** | `process.env` appears zero times (requirement F-001-RQ-003); no `.env`, `.npmrc`, `config/`, or `secrets/` path exists. Constraint C-003 records that behaviour cannot be altered at runtime by configuration |
| Key generation, rotation, escrow, and destruction | Not applicable | There is no key whose lifecycle could be managed |
| Registry or package-signing credential | **Verified absent** | No `.npmrc` in the repository or in the invoking user's home directory; the resolved npm `authToken` is empty and the registry default is never contacted |
| Secret-scanning or pre-commit prevention | Absent | No `.github/` directory, no hook, and no scanning configuration exists — so the clean result above is an observed state, not an enforced one |

The last row is the only finding in this sub-section that is a gap rather than a non-issue, and it is a governance gap: the repository is verifiably free of secrets today, but nothing in it would prevent a secret from being committed tomorrow.

#### 6.4.4.4 Data Masking Rules

**No data-masking, redaction, tokenisation, or anonymisation rule exists, and none is required, because the collection surface is nil.** Masking exists to prevent sensitive values from reaching a display, a log, or a downstream consumer; this system reads no value and writes no record.

| Masking Concern | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Masking of request-derived values | Not required | The request is never dereferenced, so no header, cookie, query parameter, or body value is ever held in memory by application code |
| Log redaction | Not required, and not possible to need | Nothing is written per request. After 25 requests carrying distinct bearer tokens and synthetic identifiers, a search of both output streams for those markers returned zero hits |
| Response-payload minimisation | Absolute by construction | The response is a 14-byte public constant; it discloses nothing about the host, the process, other callers, or any stored value |
| Technology and version disclosure in responses | **Not disclosed — a positive finding** | Neither a `Server` nor an `X-Powered-By` header is ever emitted, so the response reveals no framework or runtime fingerprint |
| Error-message and stack-trace disclosure | **Bounded** | The only stderr output in the system is the runtime's default unhandled-`'error'` trace on bind failure, containing the address, port, `errno`, `syscall`, and Node internal frames. No credential or environment value can appear in it because none exists in the process |
| Tokenisation, format-preserving encryption, pseudonymisation | Not applicable | No identifier or personal datum exists to tokenise |

The bind-failure trace is the system's only information-disclosure channel, and its content is fully enumerable: it reveals that `127.0.0.1:3000` was already in use. That fact is already published in the startup banner and in this specification, so the marginal disclosure is nil. Section 2.4.4 reaches the same conclusion.

#### 6.4.4.5 Secure Communication

**All communication is cleartext. The listener is not a TLS server, no certificate exists, and no protocol minimum or cipher policy is configured.** This is the one substantive data-protection gap in the system, and it is bounded — but the bound must be stated as precisely as the gap.

| TLS Verification | Method | Measured Result |
|---|---|---|
| HTTPS request to the endpoint | `curl https://127.0.0.1:3000/` | Returned HTTP code `000` — no response |
| TLS handshake attempt | `openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:3000` | Failed with an SSL record error reporting a **wrong version number**, because the server replied with HTTP text rather than a TLS record |
| Raw ClientHello injection | TLS ClientHello bytes written to the socket | The server replied `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` **in cleartext**, 47 bytes total — the handshake bytes simply failed HTTP parsing |
| Server type check | `server instanceof require('tls').Server` on the live instance | `false` |
| TLS event listeners | Listener census on the live server object | `tlsClientError` = `0` and `secureConnection` = `0`; no TLS event can ever fire |
| Transport-security response header | Header presence check | `strict-transport-security` absent on every response |

The practical consequence for an integrator is that a client configured for `https://` fails at the handshake rather than at authentication, and receives a cleartext `400` instead of a TLS alert.

##### 6.4.4.5.1 What Bounds the Exposure, and What Does Not

| Consideration | Determination | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality of transmitted data | Not at risk in substance | The only bytes transmitted are a public 14-byte constant and runtime framing headers; there is no secret, credential, or personal datum in either direction |
| Network exposure of the cleartext channel | Confined to one host | The listener binds the single address `127.0.0.1`; the host's routable address, IPv6 loopback, and `127.0.0.2` were all refused. Traffic never traverses a network segment |
| Interception risk | Requires a same-host adversary already inside the trust boundary | Loopback traffic does not leave the host. An attacker able to observe it can already read the process memory and the source file that contains the entire payload |
| Server authentication to the client | **Absent** | No certificate is presented, so a client cannot verify it is talking to the intended process. Mitigated only by the fact that the endpoint is a fixed loopback address, and that a competing binder would have caused `EADDRINUSE` |
| Downgrade or stripping attack | Not applicable | There is no secure variant to downgrade from; the endpoint has never advertised TLS |
| Container or namespace change | **This bound is fragile** | The confinement is a property of one source literal. Section 5.2.3 records that a container built around this repository exposes the listener only inside its own network namespace — which preserves the bound — but a single edit to `server.js` line 3 to a wildcard address would place cleartext traffic on a routable interface with no other control behind it |

##### 6.4.4.5.2 Browser and Response Security Headers

No security response header of any kind is emitted. The census below is complete, and the risk assessment is specific to a constant, inert, `text/plain` payload rather than generic.

| Header | Emitted | Assessed Consequence Here |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | No | Minimal — the response contains no script, style, or markup; the body is 14 bytes of plain text |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | No | Not meaningful — there is no HTTPS variant to pin |
| `X-Frame-Options` | No | Minimal — there is no interactive or authenticated content to frame, and no ambient credential to abuse |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | No | Minor — `Content-Type: text/plain` is sent **without a charset parameter**, so a sniffing client is not explicitly prevented from re-interpreting the body. The body is a fixed, script-free constant, so no payload can be smuggled |
| `Referrer-Policy` and `Permissions-Policy` | No | Not applicable — no navigation, no embedded resource, and no browser feature is used |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | No | Fail-safe — a cross-origin `Origin: https://evil.example` request receives a `200` with no CORS grant, so a browser will not expose the response to the calling script |
| `Vary` | No | Not applicable — the response never varies, so no cache key could be poisoned |
| `Server` and `X-Powered-By` | No | **Positive** — zero technology-fingerprint disclosure |

The complete wire census is four headers on a `Connection: close` response — `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Content-Length`, 135 bytes in total — and five on a keep-alive response, which adds `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` for 163 bytes. Only `Content-Type` is set by repository code; the remainder are runtime framing, recorded as constraint C-004.

#### 6.4.4.6 Compliance Controls

**No compliance requirement is expressed or implicated anywhere in the repository.** Zero matches were returned for `gdpr`, `ccpa`, `hipaa`, `pci`, `sox`, `fedramp`, `soc2`, `iso27001`, `nist`, `pii`, `phi`, `consent`, `retention`, and `privacy`, and no attestation, control mapping, data-processing agreement, or audit artifact exists in any form.

The determination below is made strictly on the basis of the data the system actually processes, because that is what triggers each regime. It is not an assertion that the artifact would satisfy any of these regimes in a different context.

| Regulatory Regime | Trigger Condition | Determination for This System |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR / UK GDPR | Processing of personal data of identifiable natural persons | **Not implicated.** No personal datum is collected; the request is never read and no client address is captured, so no processing occurs and no data subject exists |
| CCPA / CPRA | Collection or sale of consumer personal information | **Not implicated.** Nothing is collected, retained, sold, or shared; there is no egress channel through which sharing could occur |
| HIPAA | Creation, receipt, or transmission of protected health information | **Not implicated.** No health datum enters or leaves the system |
| PCI-DSS | Storage, processing, or transmission of cardholder data | **Not implicated.** No payment datum exists; there is no store and no outbound connection |
| SOX | Systems bearing on financial reporting integrity | **Not implicated.** The system produces no financial record and holds no ledger data |
| FedRAMP / NIST SP 800-53 | Federal information system authorisation | **Not implicated and not claimed.** No control-baseline mapping, system security plan, or boundary definition exists |
| SOC 2 | Service-organisation controls over a customer-facing service | **Not implicated and not claimed.** The system is a loopback-only test fixture with no customer, tenant, or service commitment; Section 6.3.4.4 records that no SLA, SLO, or availability commitment exists |
| ISO/IEC 27001 | Certified information security management system | **Not implicated and not claimed.** No policy, risk register, or management-system artifact exists in the repository |

##### 6.4.4.6.1 The One Live Compliance Obligation

The only compliance obligation that genuinely applies to this repository is a licensing one, and it carries a documented gap.

| Obligation | Observed State | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Licence declaration | `MIT` is declared in exactly two places: `package.json` line 10 and the root record of `package-lock.json` line 10 | The intended distribution term is unambiguous and internally consistent between the manifests |
| Licence text | **No `LICENSE` or `LICENSE.md` file exists anywhere in the repository or in its history** | **Gap.** The MIT terms are named but their text — including the copyright and permission notice that MIT requires to accompany copies — is not present in the distribution |
| Copyright attribution | The only attribution field is `"author": "hxu"` in `package.json`; `README.md` names no copyright holder and the commit author is a different identity | **Gap.** No copyright line names a holder or a year, so the notice MIT contemplates cannot be reproduced from repository content |
| Third-party licence obligations | None — the dependency graph is empty | **Satisfied trivially.** `npm ls --all` reports the root package followed by `(empty)`, so no inbound licence obligation, notice file, or SBOM attribution requirement arises |
| Vulnerability-disclosure policy | No `SECURITY.md` and no contact metadata in `package.json` | **Gap, minor.** There is no published channel through which a security issue could be reported, though the change freeze means no fix would be applied in any case |

These are documentation gaps in satisfying a stated intent, recorded here as observations of repository content. They are not legal conclusions.

#### 6.4.4.7 Data Protection Control Matrix

| Control | Implementation Status | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data classification scheme | Present implicitly — all three data elements are public | Complete three-literal domain in `server.js` lines 3, 4, and 9 |
| Encryption at rest | No referent — no data at rest exists | No persistence of any kind; zero regular-file descriptors under load |
| Encryption in transit | **Absent — plaintext only** | Not a `tls.Server`; TLS ClientHello answered with a cleartext `400`; no `Strict-Transport-Security` header |
| Cryptographic algorithm and cipher policy | Absent — no cryptography is used | Zero `crypto` API matches; no cipher, hash, or protocol-minimum setting |
| Key and certificate management | No subject — no key material exists | Zero key/certificate files on the filesystem; zero secret hits across all historical blobs |
| Runtime secret injection | Absent by construction | Zero `process.env` usage; no configuration surface (constraint C-003) |
| Secret-scanning prevention | **Absent — governance gap** | Repository is verifiably clean today, but no hook, CI check, or scanner would prevent a future commit |
| Data masking and redaction | Not required — collection surface is nil | Request never dereferenced; no per-request log record exists |
| Information-disclosure minimisation | **Present** | No `Server` or `X-Powered-By` header; bind-failure trace content fully enumerable and non-sensitive |
| Network confinement of cleartext traffic | **Present — the compensating control** | Single-address loopback bind; routable, IPv6, and `127.0.0.2` addresses all refused |
| Data-in-use isolation | Present — process boundary only | One process, one address space, zero child processes; no shared memory or IPC |
| Exfiltration prevention | **Present — structural** | Zero outbound sockets measured idle, under load, and with twenty inbound connections held open |
| Browser security headers | Absent | Thirteen-header presence check; consequences assessed as minimal for a constant `text/plain` payload |
| Regulatory compliance controls | Not implicated — no regulated data is processed | Regime-by-regime determination in Section 6.4.4.6 |
| Licence compliance | Declared but incompletely satisfied | MIT named in both manifests; no `LICENSE` file and no copyright notice exist |


### 6.4.5 Security Zone Architecture and Trust Boundaries

The system has a single security perimeter and it is the host itself. There is no network zone model in the conventional sense — no public segment, no demilitarised zone, no internal tier, and no management network — because the listener is bound to the loopback interface and no artifact in the repository defines any other zone. What does exist is a small, precisely measurable set of trust boundaries, and documenting them accurately is what makes the applicability determination in Section 6.4.1 verifiable rather than assertive.

Section 6.1.2.1 identifies four boundaries crossed at runtime: the loopback TCP listener, standard output, standard error, and the process/OS control plane. This sub-section treats each as a security boundary, establishes the zone model that contains them, enumerates the reachable attack surface, and records the measured disposition of every threat class that surface admits.

#### 6.4.5.1 Security Zone Model

Three zones exist, nested inside one another; all three are contained within a single host, and none of them is separated from another by a network. The zone identifiers below are introduced by this section for reference within it.

| Zone | Extent | Trust Assumption |
|---|---|---|
| **Zone H** — Host trust domain | The entire operating-system instance on which the process runs | Everything in Zone H is trusted. This is the whole of the system's security model: any process on the host is admitted, and no further distinction is made |
| **Zone L** — Loopback network segment | The `127.0.0.1` interface, on which one socket listens on port 3000 | Membership in Zone L is the sole admission credential. It is granted by co-location, verified by the kernel, and conveys no identity |
| **Zone P** — Process address space | One Node.js process: `CMP-01` runtime, `CMP-03` constants, `CMP-04` handler, `CMP-05` announcer | A single address space with one event loop, zero child processes, and no thread boundary that isolates one request from another |
| **Zone C** — OS control plane | POSIX signals inbound; exit status, standard output, and standard error outbound | Fully trusted and unauthenticated. No signal handler is registered, so any process able to signal this one can terminate it immediately |

The diagram places these zones alongside the five zones a conventional security architecture would define, every one of which was probed for and found absent. Note that the only evaluated decision in the entire model is the kernel's admission test on the left, and that it is evaluated before any code in Zone P executes.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    OFFHOST["Off-host or non-loopback client -<br/>routable address, IPv6 loopback, 127.0.0.2"]
    KERNEL{"Does the connection arrive<br/>on 127.0.0.1 port 3000?"}
    REFUSED(["Connection refused - measured,<br/>zero bytes exchanged"])

    subgraph HostZone["Zone H - Host Trust Domain - the entire security perimeter"]
        subgraph LoopZone["Zone L - Loopback Segment 127.0.0.1"]
            PEER["Any same-host process -<br/>anonymous and indistinguishable"]
            LISTEN["Listener socket 127.0.0.1 port 3000<br/>bound by server.js line 12"]
            PEER -->|"cleartext HTTP/1.1, no TLS"| LISTEN
        end
        subgraph ProcZone["Zone P - Node.js Process Address Space - uid 0 in the test host"]
            RT["CMP-01 http runtime -<br/>parse, dispatch, serialize"]
            APP["CMP-04 handler -<br/>three statements, no I/O"]
            CONST["CMP-03 constants - the bind literals<br/>are the only access control"]
            CONST --> RT
            RT --> APP
        end
        subgraph CtlZone["Zone C - OS Control Plane"]

            SOUT["stdout - one readiness line"]

        end
        LISTEN --> RT
        APP --> SOUT
    end

    subgraph AbsentZones["Security Zones Verified Absent - no artifact defines any of them"]
        DMZ["Public or DMZ network zone"]
        EDGE["Edge tier - WAF, gateway, reverse proxy"]
        IDZ["Identity zone - IdP, token issuer, secret store"]
        DATAZ["Data zone - database, cache, object store"]
        MGMT["Management zone - bastion, log collector, SIEM"]
        DMZ -.- EDGE
        EDGE -.- IDZ
        IDZ -.- DATAZ
        DATAZ -.- MGMT
    end

    OFFHOST --> KERNEL
    KERNEL -->|"no"| REFUSED
    KERNEL -->|"yes"| LISTEN
    SIG -.->|"immediate termination, exit 143 or 130"| RT

    SERR -.->|"no collector exists"| MGMT
```

*Diagram 6.4.5-A — Security zone and trust-boundary model. Solid edges are measured data paths; every dotted edge to the lower subgraph marks a zone relationship that was probed for and found absent. The entire trusted perimeter is the host.*

#### 6.4.5.2 Trust Boundary Register

Four boundaries are crossed at runtime. For each, the register records what crosses it, in which direction, and which control — if any — governs the crossing.

| Boundary | What Crosses, and In Which Direction | Governing Control |
|---|---|---|
| Loopback TCP listener, `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound: arbitrary HTTP/1.1 request bytes from any same-host process. Outbound: the invariant 14-byte response, plus runtime-generated protocol errors | Kernel address binding — the only access control in the system. No authentication, authorization, rate limit, or TLS applies |
| Standard output | Outbound only: exactly one readiness line per process lifetime | None. The stream is inherited from the launching process; no redaction is needed because no sensitive value is ever written |
| Standard error | Outbound only, and only on bind failure: the runtime's default unhandled-`'error'` trace | None. Content is bounded to address, port, `errno`, `syscall`, and Node internal frames |
| Process and OS control plane | Inbound: POSIX signals. Outbound: process exit status | **None — the weakest boundary.** No `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler is registered, so termination is immediate with no connection drain; exit codes `143` and `130` are the only signal of it |

Two boundaries that a conventional architecture would have do not exist here, and their absence is protective rather than deficient. There is no **egress boundary** to control, because an inode-matched socket census recorded zero outbound connections while idle, under load, and while twenty inbound keep-alive connections were held open — the process owned one socket idle and twenty-one with clients attached, none of them outbound. And there is no **persistence boundary**, because a descriptor census under sustained load found zero regular-file descriptors; the process never opens a file for reading or writing.

#### 6.4.5.3 Attack Surface Enumeration and Measured Threat Disposition

The reachable attack surface consists of one inbound socket, reachable only from Zone H, plus the design-time surface of the repository artifact itself. The diagram maps each threat class the surface admits onto its measured disposition.

```mermaid

    subgraph Surface["Reachable Attack Surface - one inbound socket"]

        S2["Credential forgery, replay<br/>or privilege escalation"]
        S3["Injection in path, query,<br/>header or body"]
        S4["Traffic interception<br/>on the loopback path"]
        S5["Connection or event-loop<br/>exhaustion"]
        S6["Source or artifact<br/>tampering"]
    end

    subgraph Disposition["Measured Disposition"]
        D1["Runtime replies 400, 408 or 431<br/>and closes that socket only"]
        D2["No effect - 14 credential probes<br/>returned byte-identical 200"]
        D3["Structurally unreachable - zero sinks<br/>and req is never dereferenced"]
        D4["Plaintext but host-confined -<br/>no TLS anywhere in the repository"]
        D5["Unbounded by the application -<br/>headersTimeout 60000 ms is the only brake"]
        D6["Detectable, not prevented -<br/>single-commit provenance, clean tree"]
    end

    ADV --> S1
    ADV --> S2
    ADV --> S3
    ADV --> S4
    ADV --> S5
```
