```mermaid
    S5 --> D5
    S6 --> D6
```

*Diagram 6.4.5-B — Attack surface mapped to measured disposition. Every disposition on the right was verified against a running instance rather than inferred.*

##### 6.4.5.3.1 Threat Disposition Detail

| Threat Class | Measured Disposition | Owner of the Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| Malformed request line, bogus HTTP version, missing `Host` | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the handler is never invoked | Node.js runtime parser |
| Oversized header block, approximately 24 KB against a 16384-byte `maxHeaderSize` | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`, then close | Node.js runtime |
| Stalled or incomplete header block — slow-header attack | An incomplete header connection remained open past 12 s in direct measurement; the runtime's 60000 ms `headersTimeout` is what eventually terminates it with `408` | Node.js runtime; **no application-level defence exists** |
| Reflected injection — XSS in path or query, template injection, CRLF response splitting | Nothing reflected. The `Hello, World!` body was returned unchanged for all eleven payload classes, and a header census after the CRLF probe found no injected header, so response splitting is impossible | Structural — `req` is never dereferenced |
| Injection into an interpreter — SQL, command, prototype pollution, deserialization | **Structurally unreachable.** Zero injection sinks exist (`eval`, `new Function`, `vm`, `child_process`, `fs`, SQL, `JSON.parse` all at zero matches) *and* the request is never read, so no untrusted byte can reach any interpreter | Structural, at two independent layers |
| Path traversal and local file disclosure | Inert. `/../../../../etc/passwd` and its percent-encoded form returned the standard greeting; the process opens no regular file, so no path can be resolved | Structural — no filesystem primitive is imported |
| Credential forgery, replay, and privilege escalation via the API | No effect. All fourteen credential probes returned byte-identical responses; there is no privilege to escalate to, since every caller already receives the maximum available authority |  Structural — no credential is read and no privilege tier exists |
| Cross-Site Tracing via `TRACE` | Not possible. `TRACE` with a marker header returned the ordinary 135-byte greeting; the marker was not echoed and the response is not `message/http` | Structural — the handler answers every dispatched request identically |
| Cross-origin data theft | Fail-safe. `Origin: https://evil.example` received a `200` with **no** `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so a browser will not expose the response body to the calling script | Absence of a CORS grant |
| Protocol confusion — TLS on the cleartext port, HTTP/2 preface, `CONNECT` tunnelling, WebSocket upgrade | TLS bytes and `PRI * HTTP/2.0` receive a cleartext `400`; `CONNECT` causes the socket to be destroyed with zero bytes returned; `Upgrade: websocket` and `h2c` receive an ordinary `200` and never a `101` | Node.js runtime defaults; no listener is registered for `connect` or `upgrade` |
| Traffic interception | Cleartext, but confined to the loopback path; an adversary positioned to observe it is already inside Zone H and can read both the process memory and the source literal that contains the entire payload | Loopback confinement, per Section 6.4.4.5.1 |
| Reconnaissance against the port | Refused connections are silent on both sides: no bytes are exchanged and the process is never notified. No `Server` or `X-Powered-By` header discloses the technology on a successful request | Kernel refusal plus the absence of fingerprint headers |
| Source or artifact tampering | **Detectable, not prevented.** A single unsigned commit, one branch, zero tags, and a clean working tree make any content change trivially detectable, but no hook, `CODEOWNERS`, branch-protection artifact, or CI check prevents one | Git provenance; governance only |
| Supply-chain compromise via dependencies | Not available. Zero declared and zero locked dependencies, no `node_modules` created by `npm ci`, no install lifecycle script, and `npm audit` reporting zero vulnerabilities | Structural — an empty install graph |
| Data exfiltration following any compromise | No channel exists. Zero outbound sockets and zero child processes were measured; no HTTP client, driver, or SDK is present to open one | Structural — no egress capability |

#### 6.4.5.4 Process Privilege Posture and Correct Attribution

The privilege posture of the running process was measured directly, and the attribution of those measurements requires care: most of them are properties of the **launch context** used for verification, not instructions issued by the repository.

| Measurement on the Live Process | Observed Value | Attribution |
|---|---|---|
| Real, effective, saved, and filesystem UID and GID | `0` for all four; effective user `root`; supplementary group list `0` | **Launch context.** The verification host started the process as `root`; nothing in the repository requests, requires, or drops privilege |
| Permitted and effective capability sets | `000001ffffffffff` — the full set | **Launch context.** No capability bounding, dropping, or `securityContext` exists anywhere in the repository |
| `NoNewPrivs` and `Seccomp` | `0` and `0`, with zero seccomp filters | **Launch context.** No sandbox profile is defined |
| `umask` | `0022` | **Launch context**, and inconsequential: the process never creates a file |
| Open file descriptors | 22, constant; zero of them regular files | **Repository-relevant.** The process opens no file at any point, so file-permission exposure does not arise |
| Child processes | `0` | **Repository-relevant.** `child_process` appears zero times; there is no process-spawning attack path |
| Thread count | 7, all Node/libuv internals with one JavaScript event loop | Runtime property |
| Node.js permission model and policy | `process.permission` and `process.policy` both `undefined` | **Repository-relevant gap.** The runtime's own hardening features are available but unused; no `--experimental-permission` flag or policy manifest exists |
| Bind port privilege requirement | Port 3000 (`0x0BB8`) is in the unprivileged range above 1023 | **Repository-relevant mitigation.** No elevated privilege is *needed* to bind, so running unprivileged is possible without any source change |
| Tracked file permissions | All four files `0644`, owned `root:root`, none executable, no setuid or setgid bit | **Repository-relevant.** No file in the repository grants execute or elevated rights |

The correct architectural statement is therefore this: **the repository contains no privilege management at all.** There is no `Dockerfile` and therefore no `USER` directive, no systemd unit, no process-manager definition, and no launcher script that could specify a service account — a consequence of ADR-008, which records that no build, packaging, or delivery pipeline exists. Whatever privilege the invoking context holds is the privilege the process runs with.

Three structural facts materially contain the consequence. The bind port is unprivileged, so nothing about the design compels elevated execution. The process spawns no children and opens no files, so an elevated identity has almost no surface on which to act. And the handler performs three assignments with no I/O, so there is no code path through which an attacker-supplied value could invoke a privileged operation. The residual exposure is that a compromise of the Node.js runtime itself — the only unpinned input, deviation D-005 — would inherit whatever privilege the launch context supplied, and the repository provides nothing that would constrain it.

#### 6.4.5.5 Availability and Resource-Exhaustion Posture

Availability protection is a security concern and is documented here because the loopback boundary is what bounds it. The repository declares no overload control of any kind.

| Resource Control | Status | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Rate limiting, throttling, or quota | Absent | 2,000 sequential requests to distinct paths and 200 concurrent requests all returned `200`, with **zero** `429` responses and no `Retry-After` or `X-RateLimit-*` header ever emitted |
| Concurrent connection ceiling | Absent — `maxConnections` is `undefined` on the live server | Connection count is bounded only by operating-system file-descriptor limits, not by the application |
| Pending-connection queue | Runtime default only — a 511-entry accept backlog, with no backlog argument supplied to `listen` | Overflow behaviour is a platform property; the application is never notified that a connection was refused |
| Requests per connection | Unlimited — `maxRequestsPerSocket` is `0` | One keep-alive connection may carry unbounded requests |
| Slow-request defence | Absent at the application layer | The runtime's `headersTimeout` of 60000 ms and `requestTimeout` of 300000 ms are the only brakes; an incomplete header connection was still open after 12 s of direct observation |
| Body-size limit | Absent, and moot | A 1 MiB body returned the ordinary `200`; the runtime consumes and discards the payload, and the response is emitted before the request is complete, so no buffer accumulates in application code |
| Multi-core capacity or worker isolation | Absent | One event loop on one core; `cluster` and `worker_threads` appear zero times, so a single local client can saturate the loop |
| Automatic restart after exhaustion | Absent from the repository | Nothing in the repository restarts the process; recovery is external, and detection is externally owned and unbounded |

**Loopback confinement is what makes this posture tolerable.** Every exhaustion vector above requires a same-host attacker, and an adversary already inside Zone H has far more direct means of denying service — including sending a signal, which the process handles with immediate termination because no `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler is registered. The measured mitigating facts are that memory does not grow with traffic (resident set plateaued at roughly 61.9 MB after 25,000 requests, changing 268 kB across the final 20,000) and that log volume is one line per process lifetime rather than per request, so neither memory nor disk can be exhausted through the API.

#### 6.4.5.6 Zone Control Summary

| Zone Boundary | Control Present | Verified Effect |
|---|---|---|
| External network into Zone H | Kernel address binding to `127.0.0.1` | The host's routable address, IPv6 loopback, and `127.0.0.2` were all refused; only `127.0.0.1` and `localhost` were served |
| Zone H into Zone L | None beyond co-location | Every same-host process is admitted anonymously; no process, user, container, or namespace is distinguished |
| Zone L into Zone P | Runtime protocol validation only | Malformed, oversized, and stalled requests are answered with `400`, `431`, or `408` and closed before the application runs |
| Within Zone P | None — one address space | No bulkhead, worker boundary, or per-request isolation exists; no sandbox or permission model is enabled |
| Zone P outbound to any other zone | **None needed — no egress exists** | Zero outbound sockets and zero child processes measured; no data can leave the host |
| Zone C into Zone P | None | Any process able to signal this one terminates it immediately with no connection drain |
| Design-time zone — repository artifact | Git provenance and an advisory change freeze | Tampering is detectable via the single-commit baseline and a clean tree, but no technical control prevents it |


### 6.4.6 Standard Security Practices and Control Matrix

Section 6.4.1 determined that a detailed security architecture is not applicable to this system. The prompt for this section requires that such a determination be accompanied by a statement of the standard security practices followed instead. That statement is given here, and it is deliberately honest about provenance: several of the practices below are genuinely observable properties of the repository, but most of them hold because the repository is 39 lines long and does nothing, not because a control was designed. Both categories are recorded, and each is distinguished.

#### 6.4.6.1 Standard Practices Observably Followed

| Standard Practice | Evidence in the Repository | Deliberate Control or By-Product |
|---|---|---|
| **Least network exposure** — bind to the narrowest interface | `server.js` line 3 binds the exact literal `127.0.0.1`; the routable address, IPv6 loopback, and `127.0.0.2` were all refused in measurement | **Deliberate.** A single literal, but a chosen one, and the only security control in the system |
| **No secrets in source control** | Zero credential-shaped strings across all four tracked files and, critically, zero hits across **every blob in Git history**; the complete string-literal inventory of `server.js` is six values, none sensitive | **By-product**, but verifiably clean. Nothing sensitive exists to leak |
| **No committed key or certificate material** | A file-extension census for `.pem`, `.key`, `.crt`, `.p12`, `.jks`, `.pfx`, and `id_rsa` returned zero files | By-product |
| **Minimal dependency footprint** | Zero declared and zero locked dependencies; `npm ls --all` prints the root package followed by `└── (empty)`; `npm audit` reports **found 0 vulnerabilities** | **Deliberate and strong.** The transitive supply-chain surface is eliminated, not merely reduced |
| **No install-time code execution** | All seven npm lifecycle hooks (`preinstall`, `install`, `postinstall`, `prepare`, `prepublish`, `prepublishOnly`, `prepack`) are absent; the only script is a placeholder `test` | Deliberate consequence of an empty manifest |
| **No registry credential on disk** | No `.npmrc` exists anywhere in the repository or the user profile; the resolved `authToken` is empty | By-product |
| **No technology fingerprint disclosure** | Neither `Server` nor `X-Powered-By` is emitted; the complete response header set is four headers on a closing connection and five on a keep-alive connection | **Runtime-owned**, not repository-owned — Node's `http` module does not add a `Server` header by default. Correct outcome, external cause |
| **No reflection of untrusted input** | Eleven payload classes across path, query, headers, and body were returned with the body unchanged and no injected header; `req` is bound but never dereferenced | **Structural and absolute.** The strongest property in the system |
| **No filesystem or interpreter reach from a request** | `fs`, `child_process`, `vm`, `eval`, `new Function`, and `JSON.parse` all appear zero times | Structural |
| **Immutable, compiled-in configuration** | Zero `process.env` references; the address and port are module-scope constants that are neither exported nor injectable (constraint C-003) | **Deliberate benefit.** The running configuration cannot diverge from the audited source, so there is no environment-variable injection surface and no configuration drift |
| **Deterministic, atomic response construction** | The handler performs three statements — status, one header, one `end()` with a literal — with no conditional branch and no partial-write path | By-product of triviality, but it removes response-splitting and inconsistent-state classes entirely |
| **Version-controlled provenance with a clean baseline** | One commit `1a0874d` on a single branch, zero tags, and `git status --porcelain` empty; any content change is trivially detectable against that baseline | **Deliberate but advisory.** Detection only — see 6.4.6.5 |
| **Stated distribution terms** | `MIT` declared at `package.json` line 10 and at `package-lock.json` line 10 | Deliberate, though incomplete — no `LICENSE` file accompanies the declaration |

#### 6.4.6.2 Standard Practices Not Followed

The distinction that matters is between a control that is missing and a control that has no referent. Only the first column of verdicts below represents a finding.

| Standard Practice | Status | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Transport encryption for all network traffic | **Not followed** | `https`, `tls`, and `crypto` are never imported and the listener is not a `tls.Server`; traffic is cleartext. Contained by loopback confinement, not solved by it — a **genuine gap** whose severity is bounded by the boundary, not by a control |
| Dependency and runtime version pinning | **Partially followed** | Dependencies are pinned trivially by being absent, but no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` exists (deviation D-005). The Node.js runtime is the **only unpinned input to the system** and therefore its entire remaining supply chain |
| Distribution of the license text with the licensed work | **Not followed** | MIT is declared in two manifests; the `LICENSE` file is absent. A documentation gap, not a security one |
| Automated secret scanning or a pre-commit guard | **Not followed** | No hook, no scanner configuration, no CI workflow. The tree and history are verifiably clean today; nothing prevents a future commit from introducing a secret — the **one governance gap with a plausible future cost** |
| Enforced change control on the protected artifact | **Not followed** | `README.md` line 2 states `Do not touch!`, and that freeze is what protects the loopback literal, but no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, branch-protection artifact, or CI check enforces it (constraint C-001). Immutability is a governance control, not a technical one |
| Commit signing and artifact integrity attestation | **Not followed** | The single commit is unsigned; no checksum, signature, or attestation accompanies the tree |
| Request-level audit logging | **Not followed** | Exactly one logging call exists — the startup banner at `server.js` line 13. No request, caller, or outcome is ever recorded; this is the second genuine gap |
| Privilege separation and least-privilege execution | **Not followed** | No `Dockerfile` and therefore no `USER`, no service unit, no launcher, and neither `process.permission` nor a policy manifest is enabled. Materially contained by the unprivileged port, zero children, and zero file opens (Section 6.4.5.4) |
| Graceful shutdown with connection draining | **Not followed** | No `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler; termination is immediate. An availability concern at the control-plane boundary |
| Browser response security headers — CSP, HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options` | **Not followed; low materiality** | None are emitted. The payload is a 14-byte `text/plain` literal with no markup, script, form, or credential, so no header has a risk to mitigate here |
| Input validation and schema enforcement | **No referent** | There is no input to validate: the request is never read. A validation layer would have nothing to act on |
| Authentication, authorization, session, and token controls | **No referent** | Documented in full in Sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3. There is no principal, no protected resource, and no state to bind |
| Encryption at rest, key rotation, and secret management | **No referent** | No data tier, no persisted byte, and no secret exist; a descriptor census under load found zero regular-file descriptors |
| Rate limiting and quota enforcement | **Not followed; contained** | Zero `429` responses across 2,000 sequential and 200 concurrent requests, and `maxConnections` is `undefined`. Every exhaustion vector requires an in-zone attacker (Section 6.4.5.5) |
| Vulnerability management process | **Followed by circumstance** | `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities against an empty graph, so there is nothing to triage — but no scheduled scan, advisory subscription, or patch process exists either |

#### 6.4.6.3 Supply-Chain and Provenance Trust Chain

The one trust chain the system genuinely possesses is the design-time chain from the Git origin to the running process. Because there is no build step, no artifact registry, and no packaging stage — the deployment unit is the Git working tree executed in place, per ADR-008 — the chain is unusually short, which is itself a security property.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    GIT["Git origin remote -<br/>single commit 1a0874d on main"]
    TREE["Local working tree - four files,<br/>git status porcelain empty"]
    FREEZE{"Is the README change freeze<br/>technically enforced?"}
    ADVISORY["Advisory only - no hook,<br/>no CODEOWNERS, no CI check"]
    NPMSTEP["npm ci reads the manifests -<br/>zero packages installed"]
    NODE["Node.js runtime -<br/>version chosen by the consumer"]
    PROC["node server.js -<br/>one process on port 3000"]
    RISK["Residual risk - the runtime is the<br/>only unpinned input, deviation D-005"]

    subgraph AbsentSupply["Supply-Chain Vectors Verified Absent"]
        DEPS["Third-party packages -<br/>zero declared, zero locked"]
        HOOKS["Install lifecycle scripts -<br/>none present"]
        REGCRED["Registry credential -<br/>no .npmrc, empty authToken"]
        KEYS["Committed key or certificate<br/>material - zero files"]
        SECRETS["Secrets in history -<br/>zero hits across all blobs"]
        DEPS -.- HOOKS
        HOOKS -.- REGCRED
        REGCRED -.- KEYS
        KEYS -.- SECRETS
    end

    GIT --> TREE
    TREE --> FREEZE
    FREEZE -->|"no"| ADVISORY
    TREE --> NPMSTEP
    NPMSTEP --> NODE
    NODE --> PROC
    NODE --> RISK
    NPMSTEP -.->|"nothing is fetched or executed"| DEPS
```

*Diagram 6.4.6-A — Supply-chain and provenance trust chain. Two findings are visible in it: the change freeze that protects the only access control is enforced by convention alone, and the Node.js runtime is the single unpinned input to an otherwise fully determined chain.*

#### 6.4.6.4 Consolidated Security Control Matrix

The matrix consolidates every control domain examined in Sections 6.4.2 through 6.4.5. **Status** uses four values: *Present* (a control exists and was verified to act), *Absent — gap* (a control is missing and its absence has a real consequence), *Absent — no referent* (a control is missing but has nothing to protect), and *Runtime default* (behaviour is supplied by Node.js, not by the repository).

| Domain / Control | Status | Verified Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Authentication** — credential verification | Absent — no referent | 14 credential probes returned byte-identical `200`; `401` is an unreachable status code |
| **Authentication** — identity store, MFA, password policy | Absent — no referent | Zero identity, MFA, or credential markers; no principal exists |
| **Authentication** — session and token handling | Absent — no referent | No `Set-Cookie` ever emitted; keep-alive is transport reuse, not session state |
| **Authorization** — RBAC, permissions, resource rules | Absent — no referent | `/admin/users`, `/api/private`, and unauthenticated `DELETE` and `PUT` all returned the identical greeting; `403` and `405` unreachable |
| **Authorization** — policy enforcement point | Absent — structural | One inline handler, no middleware chain, and no `module.exports`, so nothing can wrap the handler |
| **Audit** — access, decision, and admin logging | **Absent — gap** | One logging call total; stdout remained one line after 25,000 requests with distinct tokens and cookies |
| **Data protection** — encryption in transit | **Absent — gap** | Not a `tls.Server`; TLS `ClientHello` receives a cleartext `400` |
| **Data protection** — encryption at rest, key management, rotation | Absent — no referent | Zero regular-file descriptors under load; no secret and no data tier exist |
| **Data protection** — masking and sanitisation | Absent — no referent | Nothing is logged and nothing is echoed; the only disclosure channel is the bind-failure trace |
| **Data protection** — data minimisation | **Present — absolute** | No request attribute is read, retained, or transmitted anywhere |
| **Network** — interface restriction | **Present — the only access control** | Non-loopback and IPv6-loopback connections refused with zero bytes exchanged |
| **Network** — host allow-list, CORS grant, proxy trust | Absent | Spoofed `Host` accepted; no `Access-Control-*` header emitted (fail-safe); `X-Forwarded-*` ignored |
| **Network** — browser security headers | Absent — low materiality | Thirteen security and auth headers checked, all present-count zero |
| **Protocol** — malformed, oversized, and stalled request handling | Runtime default | `400`, `431`, and `408` returned before the handler runs; that socket only is closed |
| **Protocol** — tunnelling and upgrade refusal | Runtime default | `CONNECT` destroys the socket with zero bytes; `Upgrade` receives an ordinary `200`, never `101` |
| **Input handling** — injection sink exposure | **Present — structural, two layers** | Zero sinks exist *and* `req` is never dereferenced; traversal and CRLF-splitting probes inert |
| **Availability** — rate limit, connection ceiling, body limit | Absent — contained | Zero `429` across 2,200 requests; `maxConnections` `undefined`; memory plateaued at ~61.9 MB |
| **Availability** — graceful shutdown, restart, health endpoint | Absent | No signal handler; nothing in the repository restarts the process |
| **Process** — privilege separation, sandbox, capability drop | Absent | No `USER`, unit file, or launcher; `process.permission` and `process.policy` both `undefined` |
| **Supply chain** — dependency surface and install execution | **Present — eliminated** | Zero dependencies, `npm audit` zero vulnerabilities, no lifecycle script, no registry credential |
| **Supply chain** — runtime version pinning | **Absent — gap (D-005)** | No `engines`, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version`; the runtime is the sole unpinned input |
| **Governance** — change control on the protected literal | Absent — advisory only (C-001) | `README.md` line 2 freeze with no hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check |
| **Governance** — commit signing and artifact attestation | Absent | Single unsigned commit; no checksum or signature |
| **Governance** — secret scanning | **Absent — gap** | Tree and full history verifiably clean today; no control prevents future introduction |
| **Compliance** — regulated-data obligations | No referent | Zero compliance keywords; no personal, financial, or health data is processed |
| **Compliance** — license attribution | Partially present | MIT declared in both manifests; `LICENSE` file absent |

#### 6.4.6.5 Residual Risk Register

Six residual risks follow from the evidence. Each is recorded with the measurement that establishes it and the containment that currently applies.

| Risk | Measured Basis | Current Containment |
|---|---|---|
| **R-01 — The entire security posture is one edit away from removal.** Changing the `127.0.0.1` literal to `0.0.0.0` would expose an unauthenticated, unlogged, unencrypted, unthrottled endpoint to the network | The access control lives in a single source literal at `server.js` line 3, with no compensating control behind it | Governance only: the `README.md` change freeze, enforced by convention. **This is the highest-consequence risk in the system** |
| **R-02 — No forensic capability.** A same-host compromise, abuse, or misconfiguration leaves no server-side trace | Stdout remained exactly one line after 25,000 requests; no client address, header, or payload is ever captured | None. Any investigation depends entirely on host-level or external telemetry |
| **R-03 — Cleartext transport.** Request and response bytes are readable on the loopback path | `https` and `tls` never imported; a raw `ClientHello` is answered with a cleartext `400` | Loopback confinement. An observer of that path is already in Zone H and can read the greeting from the source or from process memory |
| **R-04 — Unpinned runtime.** The Node.js version is chosen by whoever launches the process, so a vulnerable or incompatible runtime may be used | No `engines`, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` (D-005); the runtime supplies all protocol parsing, all timeouts, and all fault handling | None in the repository. Because the runtime owns nearly all observable security behaviour, this is the largest technical dependency |
| **R-05 — Undetectable-in-time tampering.** A content change is detectable against the single-commit baseline but nothing prevents or alerts on it | One unsigned commit, no hook, no `CODEOWNERS`, no branch protection, no CI check | Detection after the fact via `git status` and `git diff` |
| **R-06 — Unbounded local resource consumption.** A same-host client can hold connections open and saturate the single event loop | `maxConnections` `undefined`, 511-entry backlog, `maxRequestsPerSocket` `0`, and an incomplete header connection still open after 12 s | The 60000 ms `headersTimeout` as the only brake, plus loopback confinement; memory and log volume do not grow with traffic |

#### 6.4.6.6 Conditions That Would Invalidate This Determination

The determination in Section 6.4.1 is contingent, and it is worth stating precisely what would falsify it. Each row identifies a change, why the determination would no longer hold, and the controls that would become mandatory.

| Change to the System | Why the Determination Fails | Controls That Become Mandatory |
|---|---|---|
| Binding to a non-loopback address, or fronting the process with a proxy that forwards to it | Removes constraint C-002, the only access control. Every absence documented in 6.4.2 through 6.4.5 becomes directly reachable at once | Transport encryption, request authentication, rate limiting, and access logging — all four simultaneously, since none of them can be added incrementally |
| Reading any request attribute — path, query, header, or body | Removes the structural immunity established in 6.4.5.3, where injection is unreachable at two independent layers | Input validation and output encoding, plus a defined trust boundary for every attribute consumed |
| Introducing routing, or more than one response variant | Creates the first protected resource and therefore the first authorization decision | An authorization decision point and a policy enforcement point — neither of which can currently be wrapped around the handler, because no module boundary exists |
| Introducing a user, tenant, or caller concept | Creates a principal, which is the missing precondition for authentication, session management, and audit | Identity management, credential handling, session or token lifecycle, and per-principal access logging |
| Introducing persistence, a cache, or any outbound integration | Creates data at rest and an egress path, dissolving both the "no referent" verdicts in the data-protection matrix and the non-exfiltrating property established in 6.4.5.2 | Encryption at rest, key management and rotation, connection-credential storage, and egress control |
| Declaring any dependency | Reintroduces the transitive supply chain that an empty install graph currently eliminates | Lockfile review, vulnerability scanning in CI, and provenance verification for install-time scripts |
| Handling personal, financial, or health data | Replaces the three-literal data domain with a regulated one, activating regimes that Section 6.4.4.6 records as not implicated | Data classification, lawful-basis and retention controls, subject-rights handling, and the corresponding regime-specific technical safeguards |
| Deploying to any shared or multi-tenant host | Invalidates the Zone H trust assumption that every same-host process is trusted | Process-level authentication or mutual TLS, privilege separation with a dedicated service account, and audit logging |
| Making the module importable, or adding a configuration surface | Removes constraints C-003 and C-005 and creates an injection point for configuration | Configuration validation, secret management, and a guarantee that the audited source and the running configuration cannot diverge |

Until one of these conditions holds, the appropriate security posture for this repository is the one it already has: preserve the loopback literal, keep the dependency graph empty, keep the request unread, and treat the change freeze as the control it actually is.


### 6.4.7 References

Every determination in Section 6.4 rests on the artifacts, cross-references, and verification activities listed below. Because this section documents an architecture defined substantially by what is *absent*, negative evidence — the artifact classes and code markers that were searched for and not found — is recorded with the same specificity as positive evidence.

#### 6.4.7.1 Repository Files Examined

- `server.js` — the entire application and the entire security surface, read in full (14 lines). Established the loopback bind literal `127.0.0.1` at line 3 and port `3000` at line 4 as the system's only access control; the `require('http')` import as proof that neither `https`, `tls`, nor `crypto` is loaded; the three-statement handler at lines 6–10 in which `req` is bound but never dereferenced; the `listen` call at line 12; and the single logging call at line 13 that constitutes the whole of the system's audit capability. Its complete six-value string-literal inventory established that no credential, secret, or sensitive value exists in the source.
- `package.json` — read in full (10 lines). Established zero `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies`, and `optionalDependencies`; the absence of all seven npm lifecycle hooks, with the only script being a placeholder `test` at line 7; the `MIT` license declaration at line 10 as the single live compliance obligation; the `author` field at line 9 as design-time metadata rather than a runtime principal; and the absence of an `engines` field, which is the basis of the unpinned-runtime finding (D-005).
- `package-lock.json` — read in full (13 lines). Established `lockfileVersion 3` with a `packages` map containing only the root entry, corroborating the empty dependency graph, and repeated the `MIT` declaration at line 10.
- `README.md` — read in full (2 lines). Established the change freeze at line 2 (`Do not touch!`) that is the only protection over the loopback literal, and confirmed that no security policy, threat model, deployment instruction, or hardening guidance is documented anywhere.
- `/` (repository root) — enumerated exhaustively. Contained exactly four tracked files, 39 lines and 913 bytes in total, with zero subdirectories; all files mode `0644`, none executable, and none carrying a setuid or setgid bit.
- Git repository metadata — established a single unsigned commit `1a0874d` on a single branch with zero tags and a clean working tree, providing the tamper-detection baseline used throughout Sections 6.4.5 and 6.4.6. The origin remote is the repository `28-july-existing-projects-qa-test-01` owned by `Sandeep01Kumar`; the stored remote URL embeds an access token and is deliberately not reproduced.

#### 6.4.7.2 Artifact Classes Probed and Verified Absent

Forty-six candidate paths were probed across the repository and the surrounding filesystem, and all forty-six were absent. The security-relevant classes, recorded as negative evidence:

- Security documentation and policy — `SECURITY.md`, threat model, and any hardening guide.
- Licensing — a `LICENSE` or `LICENCE` file, despite the MIT declaration in both manifests.
- Configuration and secrets — `.env` and any variant, `config/`, `.npmrc`, and any credential or token file.
- Cryptographic material — a census of `.pem`, `.key`, `.crt`, `.p12`, `.jks`, `.pfx`, and `id_rsa` returned **zero files**.
- Application security layers — `auth/`, `middleware/`, `routes/`, and any interceptor, guard, or filter module.
- Governance and CI — `.github/workflows/`, any Git hook, `CODEOWNERS`, any branch-protection artifact, `.gitignore`, and any linter or scanner configuration.
- Packaging and runtime control — `Dockerfile`, any container or orchestration manifest, any systemd or process-manager unit, any launcher script, `.nvmrc`, and `.node-version`.
- Dependency tree — `node_modules/`, which `npm ci` does not create for this manifest.
- `.blitzyignore` — searched for across the repository and the wider filesystem and confirmed absent, so no path exclusions applied to this investigation.

#### 6.4.7.3 Static Analysis Activities

- **Twelve-group case-insensitive marker census** across all four tracked files, covering authentication (`jwt`, `oauth`, `oidc`, `saml`, `bearer`, `basic`, `api-key`, `hmac`, `mtls`, `passport`, `authenticat*`, `authoriz*`, `www-authenticate`, `401`, `403`, `unauthori*`, `forbidden`), session and token state, identity and credential terms, authorization primitives (`rbac`, `role`, `permission`, `scope`, `acl`, `policy`, `guard`, `middleware`, `tenant`, `principal`), cryptography and TLS, browser security headers, injection sinks, resource controls, and manifest dependency fields. **Every group returned zero matches except a single `console.log` call** at `server.js` line 13.
- **Request-object reference sweep** — `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers`, `req.socket`, `req.on`, `remoteAddress`, and `x-forwarded` all returned zero matches, which is the static half of the two-layer injection immunity finding.
- **Full Git history blob scan** — a credential-shaped and high-entropy string search across every blob in the repository's history returned zero hits, establishing that no secret has ever been committed.
- **String-literal enumeration** of `server.js`, which bounded the system's entire data domain to three values and confirmed no sensitive payload exists.

#### 6.4.7.4 Runtime Verification Activities

All runtime measurements were taken against an isolated copy of the repository in a scratch directory; the repository working tree was never executed in place and was confirmed unmodified before and after every activity.

- **Startup and stream census** — verified the single readiness line on stdout and a zero-byte stderr, and confirmed stdout remained one line after sustained traffic.
- **Fourteen-probe credential matrix** — `Authorization: Bearer`, `Authorization: Basic`, malformed and empty `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `X-API-Key`, session-shaped headers, and a no-credential baseline. All fourteen returned `200 | 14 bytes | identical body digest`, establishing that no request-borne credential alters behaviour.
- **Response header census** — the complete four-header closing-connection set (135 bytes) and five-header keep-alive set (163 bytes) were enumerated, and thirteen security and authentication headers were checked for presence, all returning zero — including `Set-Cookie`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Server`, and `X-Powered-By`.
- **Eleven-class injection probe** — script, SQL, command, template, path-traversal, encoded-traversal, null-byte, and CRLF payloads injected via path, query, headers, and body; nothing was reflected and no header was injected.
- **TLS probe suite** — `curl --insecure` against the port, `openssl s_client`, and a raw `ClientHello`, together with a direct `instanceof tls.Server` check on the live server object, establishing cleartext-only operation.
- **Network exposure probe** — `127.0.0.1` and `localhost` served; the host's routable address, IPv6 loopback `[::1]`, and `127.0.0.2` all refused; corroborated by the kernel socket table showing a single listening entry bound to the loopback address on port 3000.
- **Process privilege census** — real, effective, saved, and filesystem UID and GID; permitted and effective capability sets; `NoNewPrivs`, `Seccomp`, and `umask`; open file descriptors with type classification; child-process and thread counts; and `process.permission` and `process.policy` availability. The privileged values observed are properties of the verification launch context, not of the repository.
- **Runtime timeout and limit census** — `keepAliveTimeout`, `headersTimeout`, `requestTimeout`, `timeout`, `maxHeadersCount`, `maxRequestsPerSocket`, `maxHeaderSize`, and `maxConnections`, which established which availability behaviour is runtime-owned and which ceilings do not exist.
- **Audit-trail probe** — twenty-five requests bearing distinct tokens, cookies, and identifier-shaped paths, after which stdout remained one line, stderr remained empty, and a marker search across both streams returned zero hits.
- **`TRACE` and Cross-Site Tracing probe** — a marker header was not echoed and the response was not `message/http`, establishing that XST is structurally impossible.
- **Resource and load observations** — sequential and concurrent request batches producing zero `429` responses, a stalled-header connection still open after 12 s, a resident-set plateau under sustained load, and a constant file-descriptor count with zero regular files.
- **Egress census** — inode-matched socket enumeration while idle, under load, and with multiple inbound keep-alive connections held open, returning zero outbound connections in every state.
- **Supply-chain audit** — `npm audit` reporting zero vulnerabilities, `npm ls --all` reporting an empty tree, verification that no lifecycle script exists, and confirmation that no registry authentication token is resolvable.

#### 6.4.7.5 Cross-Referenced Specification Sections

- **5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns** — supplied the framework-level determination that no authentication and no authorization framework exists, the characterisation that network isolation is used in place of identity, the fragility analysis of the single-literal control, and the observability findings on which the audit-logging gap in 6.4.3.5 rests.
- **6.1 Core Services Architecture** — supplied the component identifiers used in the diagrams and zone model (`CMP-01` runtime, `CMP-03` constants, `CMP-04` handler, `CMP-05` announcer), the four-boundary inventory that became the trust boundary register, ADR-008 on the absence of any build or delivery pipeline, and the container consequence of a loopback bind.
- **6.2 Database Design** — supplied the confirmation that no data tier exists, the exhaustive three-literal data domain used for the classification in 6.4.4.1, the descriptor and memory measurements proving nothing is persisted, and the privacy, audit, and access-control positions reconciled in 6.4.4.
- **6.3 Integration Architecture** — supplied the credential-probe and protocol-fault results reused in 6.4.2 and 6.4.5, the finding that `401` and `403` are unreachable status codes, the ignored `X-Forwarded-*` and absent host allow-list findings, the rate-limit measurements, the listener census, the egress census, and the structural-constraints table — including the decisive finding that no interception point exists around the handler.

## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Monitoring Architecture Applicability Assessment

**Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The scope of that statement must be precise. It does not mean the system is unobservable — a running instance can be checked in several verified ways, and this section documents each of them. It means that **no monitoring architecture exists in the repository to document**: there is no metrics collection tier, no log aggregation tier, no tracing tier, no alert-evaluation tier, and no dashboard definition in any of the four tracked files, and none can be introduced through configuration or dependency because neither surface exists. The entire telemetry output of the repository's code is one 41-byte line written to standard output once per process lifetime, from `server.js` line 13.

That conclusion is not a shortcut, and the absences it records are architecturally load-bearing rather than incidental. Section 5.4.6 identifies the consequence in one sentence: the architecture provides a fast, reliable recovery path and no mechanism whatsoever to notice that recovery is required. Section 6.5 is the section that must confront that detection gap, so the remainder of it is written as an **evidence-based operational assessment**: for every capability a monitoring section would normally specify, it records what the repository actually provides, what an operator can measure from outside without violating the change freeze, and — where a mechanism is absent — the verified consequence of that absence.

#### 6.5.1.1 Determination and Adjudication

Applicability was adjudicated against four independent tests. A positive result on any one of them would have made a detailed monitoring architecture applicable; all four resolve negative.

| Applicability Test | Architectural Requirement | Repository Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instrumented application | Code that emits measurements — counters, timers, gauges, or structured events | Exactly one emission call site exists (`console.log` at `server.js` line 13). A census of 100+ telemetry tokens across all four files found zero occurrences of `console.error`, `process.stdout`, `perf_hooks`, `process.hrtime`, `Date.now`, `process.memoryUsage`, `process.cpuUsage`, `diagnostics_channel`, or `util.debuglog` | Not present |
| Telemetry pipeline | An agent, exporter, collector, shipper, or backend that receives signals | 66 conventional monitoring artifact paths were probed and **none exists** — no `prometheus.yml`, `alertmanager.yml`, `grafana/`, `otel-collector-config.yaml`, `newrelic.js`, `datadog.yaml`, `.sentryclirc`, `fluent-bit.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `promtail.yaml`, or `vector.toml` | Not present |
| Dedicated health or metrics surface | An endpoint whose response varies with system state | Verified by probe: `/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/readyz`, `/live`, `/livez`, `/status`, `/metrics`, `/debug/vars`, and `/-/healthy` all return the identical `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte greeting, collapsing to a single body signature. `req.url` is never referenced, so no path-specific behaviour is reachable | Not present |
| Declared service level to monitor against | An SLA, SLO, error budget, or threshold that alerting could evaluate | Zero occurrences of `sla`, `slo`, `threshold`, `alert`, `alarm`, `uptime`, `dashboard`, `monitor`, `incident`, `runbook`, `oncall`, `escalat`, or `pager` anywhere in the repository — the vocabulary itself never appears. Section 2.2.1.3 records the absence of performance targets as a verified finding | Not present |

The third row is the one most often misread. The conventional probe paths are not merely unimplemented; they are **served successfully by the invariant handler**, which is a materially worse condition than a 404. A monitoring system pointed at `/health` receives a green result that carries no health information, and a Prometheus scrape of `/metrics` succeeds at the HTTP layer and then fails at parse time.

#### 6.5.1.2 Evidence Base for the Determination

Every artifact class that would evidence a monitoring architecture was searched for explicitly. The result column reports what a full-tree inspection of the four-file, zero-subdirectory repository found.

| Artifact Class Searched | Role in a Monitoring Architecture | Result of Inspection |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics client libraries | Counter, gauge, histogram registration and exposition | Absent — zero matches for `prometheus`, `statsd`, `dogstatsd`, `graphite`, `influx`, `telegraf`, or `metric`; `package.json` declares no `dependencies` or `devDependencies` and `package-lock.json` locks zero packages, so none can be present transitively |
| Logging frameworks | Levels, structure, sinks, rotation | Absent — zero matches for `winston`, `pino`, `bunyan`, `morgan`, `log4js`, `loglevel`, `debug`, `signale`, `roarr`; no `logger.js`, `winston.js`, `pino.config.js`, `logrotate.conf`, or `.logrotate` |
| Distributed tracing SDKs and context | Span creation, propagation, correlation | Absent — zero matches for `otel`, `opentelemetry`, `tracing`, `span`, `baggage`, `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `zipkin`, `jaeger`, `x-request-id`, `correlation`; no `instrumentation.js` or `tracing.js` |
| APM and error-tracking agents | Automatic instrumentation and exception capture | Absent — zero matches for `apm`, `newrelic`, `datadog`, `dd-trace`, `sentry`, `bugsnag`, `rollbar`, `appinsights`, `cloudwatch`, `stackdriver`; no agent config file of any kind |
| Container and orchestration health directives | `HEALTHCHECK`, liveness / readiness / startup probes | Absent — no `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose` file, `.dockerignore`, `k8s/`, `manifests/`, `helm/`, `Chart.yaml`, or `values.yaml`, so no probe definition can exist |
| Process supervision and restart policy | The conventional failure-detection and remediation layer | Absent — no `ecosystem.config.js`, `pm2.json`, `Procfile`, `nodemon.json`, systemd unit, or `supervisord.conf`. Section 6.1 records the consequence: nothing inside the repository restarts the process if it dies |
| CI/CD definitions carrying smoke tests or synthetic checks | Post-deploy verification and scheduled probing | Absent — no `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `.travis.yml`, or `Makefile`. Section 3.6.5 confirms the repository is hosted on GitHub with no workflow definition |
| Purpose-built health, status or metrics scripts | A separate probe target invoked by a monitor | Absent — no `healthcheck.js`, `health.js`, `status.js`, `monitor.js`, `metrics.js`, or `statsd.js`; `package.json` declares exactly one script, `test`, and no `start`, `monitor`, or `healthcheck` entry |
| Configuration surface pointing at a backend | Endpoint, API key, or sampling configuration for a collector | Absent — no `.env`, `.env.example`, `config/`, `config.json`, `config.js`, or `settings.json`; Section 3.6.3 records zero `process.env` and zero `process.argv` references, so no agent could be enabled at deploy time |

Two findings from this table are decisive rather than merely confirmatory. The **zero-dependency lock** means no observability agent can arrive through the dependency graph, and the **absence of any configuration or script surface** means none can be enabled at launch by a manifest change — there is no `start` script into which `NODE_OPTIONS` or a `--require` preload could be inserted. Instrumentation could therefore only be added by editing `server.js` itself, which `README.md` line 2 prohibits (constraint C-001).

#### 6.5.1.3 The Single Instrumentation Call Site

The whole of the repository's monitoring implementation is one statement, and characterising it precisely determines what is and is not possible downstream.

```javascript
// server.js line 13 — inside the server.listen callback
console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
```

| Property | Observed Value | Consequence for Monitoring |
|---|---|---|
| Emission count | Once per process lifetime; stdout remained exactly one line after roughly 1,300 requests and again after 25,000 requests | Log volume is constant and independent of traffic; there is no access log and no per-request record |
| Payload | 41 bytes including the newline, byte-verified; carries no timestamp, no severity level, no PID, no counter, no duration | Nothing in the line is a measurement. Because `Date.now`, `new Date`, and `process.hrtime` are all absent, the process cannot self-timestamp anything — timestamps must be added by whatever captures the stream |
| Position in the lifecycle | Inside the `server.listen` callback, so it fires only after the socket is successfully bound | It is a genuine readiness gate rather than an optimistic message, and its **absence is a reliable negative signal** (Section 5.4.1) |
| Destination | File descriptor 1, unbuffered to whatever the launching context attached | The repository defines no supervisor, so in normal use the line is read by a human in a terminal rather than by a log pipeline |

Two structural facts complete the picture and are what make the determination irreversible without a source change. First, `.on(` appears zero times, so the application subscribes to **no server or process event** — no `error`, `clientError`, `connection`, or `close` listener, and no `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `uncaughtException`, or `unhandledRejection` handler. Failure and termination are therefore silent from the application's point of view. Second, the handler at `server.js` lines 6–10 contains no conditional, no router, and no dereference of `req`, and the module exports nothing — so there is **no interception point** at which probe-specific behaviour, request counting, or log emission could be wrapped around it.

### 6.5.2 Monitoring Infrastructure

No monitoring infrastructure is defined by the repository. Each of the five areas below therefore records the same two things: the verified status of the conventional mechanism, and the basic practice that stands in its place — where a practice is possible at all. Every substitute described here operates entirely from outside the process, because Section 6.5.1.3 establishes that the code offers no interception point and `README.md` line 2 forbids adding one.

#### 6.5.2.1 Metrics Collection

**No metrics are collected by the application, and none can be.** There is no counter, gauge, histogram, or summary anywhere in the source; no exposition endpoint; and no push client. `/metrics` is an ordinary path that returns the 14-byte greeting, so an HTTP scrape of it succeeds at the transport layer and then fails at parse time — a failure mode more misleading than a refused connection.

The practical consequence is that **every metric available for this system is OS-sourced and PID-scoped**. The catalogue below is complete: it is everything measurable about a running instance without editing `server.js`. All values were read externally from `/proc` for a live process on the verification host and are observations, not targets.

| Metric | Source Read Externally | Observed Value or Range |
|---|---|---|
| Resident set size | `VmRSS` in `/proc/<pid>/status` | 48.2 MB at start, 59.5 MB after 5,000 requests, 61.9 MB after 25,000 requests — a 268 kB increase across the final 20,000 requests |
| Virtual reservation | `VmSize` in `/proc/<pid>/status` | 1,014,076 kB — a Node.js address-space reservation, not consumption; misleading if charted as memory use |
| JavaScript heap in use | `javascriptHeap.totalMemory` in an on-demand diagnostic report | 5,873,664 bytes — roughly one tenth of RSS, the rest being runtime and native allocation |
| User and system CPU time | `utime` and `stime` in `/proc/<pid>/stat` at `CLK_TCK` 100 | 13 → 15 user ticks and 3 system ticks to serve roughly 1,300 requests, i.e. about 0.15 s user and 0.03 s system |
| Thread count | `Threads` in `/proc/<pid>/status`; `num_threads` in `/proc/<pid>/stat` | Constant at 7, of which exactly one executes JavaScript |
| Open file descriptors | Entry count in `/proc/<pid>/fd` | Constant at 22 before and after load — no descriptor leak observable |
| Listener presence | Socket in state `0A` with local address `0100007F:0BB8` in `/proc/net/tcp` | Exactly one listening socket, confirming the bind on 127.0.0.1 port 3000 |
| Established connections | Rows in state `01` for the same local address in `/proc/net/tcp` | 0 at idle; the only concurrency indicator available |
| IO bytes and syscalls | `rchar`, `wchar`, `syscr`, `syscw` in `/proc/<pid>/io` | 32,337 / 205 / 41 / 3 — the closest available proxy for traffic volume, though it counts bytes rather than requests |
| Context switches | `voluntary_ctxt_switches` in `/proc/<pid>/status` | 1,399 — rises with event-loop activity and is the nearest thing to a work-rate signal |
| Process age | `ps -o etimes=` for the PID; `starttime` in `/proc/<pid>/stat` | Available; a reset is the only evidence an unlogged restart occurred |
| libuv handle count | `libuv` section of an on-demand diagnostic report | 11 handles |

The limitation of this catalogue is categorical rather than a matter of coverage: **not one of these metrics is application-aware**. No request count, error count, status-code distribution, latency histogram, in-flight-request gauge, or queue depth can be obtained from the process, because nothing in `server.js` records one. Section 6.1.3.2 draws the operational conclusion — an external autoscaler or capacity controller pointed at this system would have no load-varying input to act on.

| Metric Class Conventionally Expected | Obtainable? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Request rate and total request count | No | The handler increments nothing; `/proc/<pid>/io` byte counters are the only proxy and cannot separate requests from connections |
| Error rate and status-code breakdown | No | The application can emit only `200`; the runtime-generated `400`, `408`, and `431` responses bypass the application and are never recorded anywhere |
| Server-side latency histogram | No | `process.hrtime`, `Date.now`, and `perf_hooks` are all absent, so no duration is ever measured in-process |
| Event-loop lag or utilisation | No | No `perf_hooks` monitor and no periodic timer exist; `setInterval` appears zero times |
| Saturation or queue depth | No | Section 5.4.5 records the absence of any queue-depth metric; the runtime's 511-entry accept backlog is untouched and not exposed |

#### 6.5.2.2 Log Aggregation

**There is no log aggregation, and there is almost nothing to aggregate.** The system produces one 41-byte stdout line for its entire lifetime and, in normal operation, zero bytes on stderr. After a 17-path probe matrix, a 200-sample latency loop, a 1,000-request keep-alive batch, and 100 concurrent requests — over 1,300 requests in total — stdout was still exactly one line and stderr still zero bytes. The same invariance was confirmed at 25,000 requests and after 60 requests each carrying a distinct `Authorization` header.

| Log Pipeline Stage | Status | Verified Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Emission | One unstructured line, once per process | No access log exists; Section 5.4.2 states that per-request diagnosis from logs is impossible |
| Structure and levels | Absent — no JSON, no severity, no field schema | Nothing can be filtered, faceted, or parsed; the line is matched as a literal string or not at all |
| Timestamping | Absent in-process — `Date.now`, `new Date`, and `process.hrtime` all appear zero times | Time must be attached by the capturing layer; the process cannot say when anything happened |
| Sink and rotation | Absent — no file sink, no `logrotate` configuration, no write to disk at all | Section 3.6.7 records that no filesystem write access is needed, so a log file cannot be produced without a source change |
| Shipping and indexing | Absent — no Fluent Bit, Fluentd, Filebeat, Vector, or Promtail configuration | Aggregation, retention, and search must be provided by whatever captures fd 1 and fd 2 |
| Redaction and privacy controls | Not required | No client address, header, or payload is ever recorded, so no log-borne data-handling obligation arises |

The basic practice that substitutes for aggregation is **stream capture at the launch site**: redirect fd 1 and fd 2 to a durable destination, attach timestamps at capture time, and treat the readiness string as the sole positive event. Two properties make this cheap and reliable — volume is constant and independent of traffic, so the stream can never become a bottleneck or a disk-space concern; and the readiness line is trustworthy in both directions, so its presence and its absence are both meaningful.

One genuine per-request log channel exists without any code change, and it is the most useful finding in this sub-section. Launching the process with `NODE_DEBUG=http` makes the Node core `http` module trace its own activity to stderr. Three requests produced 17 stderr lines, 15 of which were `HTTP`-prefixed:

```text
HTTP 33675: SERVER new http connection
HTTP 33675: outgoing message end.
```

| Property of `NODE_DEBUG=http` Output | Observed Characteristic |
|---|---|
| Volume | Roughly five stderr lines per request; unlike the application's output, this scales linearly with traffic |
| Structure | Unstructured free text, prefixed with the literal `HTTP` and the PID; not machine-parseable in any standard format |
| Content | Connection acceptance, parser progress, write results, and message completion — transport-level, not application-level |
| Caveat | Node.js itself warns that setting `NODE_DEBUG` to `http` can expose sensitive data; it also requires a relaunch, so it cannot be enabled on an already-running process |

#### 6.5.2.3 Distributed Tracing

**There is no distributed tracing, and the architecture provides no referent for it.** Section 5.4.2 establishes the design rationale: with one process, one hop, and no outbound dependency, there is no distributed context to correlate. The verified facts are stronger than a simple absence of an SDK.

| Tracing Capability | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Span creation and export | Absent | Zero matches for `otel`, `opentelemetry`, `span`, `baggage`, `zipkin`, or `jaeger`; zero dependencies locked |
| Trace-context propagation | Absent | The handler never dereferences `req`, so `traceparent` and `tracestate` are structurally unreachable |
| Correlation identifier generation | Absent | No `x-request-id`, `request-id`, or `correlation` token appears anywhere; the response carries no generated identifier |
| Correlation identifier echo | **Verified absent by measurement** | A request carrying `X-Request-Id: probe-abc-123` and a W3C `traceparent` header produced a response containing zero occurrences of either — inbound context is silently dropped |

The measured echo test matters operationally: because nothing is echoed and nothing is logged, **a client-side observation cannot be joined to a server-side one by any identifier**. The only in-band field that varies between two responses is the `Date` header — two probes 1.2 seconds apart differed in exactly that one line — and it is generated by the Node.js runtime rather than by repository code. The complete response header block is the status line plus four headers: `Content-Type: text/plain` (the only one set by repository code), `Date`, `Connection`, and `Content-Length: 14`.

Two runtime facilities substitute for tracing when a specific instance must be investigated, and neither requires a source change. Both were verified to leave the process running, which is what makes them usable on a live instance:

- **On-demand inspector attach.** Sending `SIGUSR1` to the running PID caused the runtime to print `Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/<uuid>` to stderr and to keep serving. This enables CPU profiling, heap snapshots, and step debugging of the live process.
- **On-demand structured process snapshot.** Launching with `--report-on-signal --report-directory=<dir>` and then sending `SIGUSR2` wrote a JSON diagnostic report and left the process alive. The report contains eleven sections — `header`, `javascriptStack`, `javascriptHeap`, `nativeStack`, `libuv`, `resourceUsage`, `environmentVariables`, `sharedObjects`, `userLimits`, `uvthreadResourceUsage`, and `workers` — with `resourceUsage` exposing `rss`, `userCpuSeconds`, `free_memory`, `total_memory`, `constrained_memory`, and `available_memory`. This is the closest thing to a metrics endpoint the system can offer, and it is obtained with a launch flag rather than a code edit.

#### 6.5.2.4 Alert Management

**No alert management exists at any layer.** The words `alert`, `alarm`, `threshold`, `incident`, `oncall`, `escalat`, and `pager` appear zero times in the repository, and no rule file, notifier configuration, or routing definition is present.

| Alert Management Component | Status | Where the Function Must Live Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Rule definition and evaluation | Absent — no `alerts.yml`, `recording_rules.yml`, or `alertmanager.yml` | Inside the prober itself: the script that issues the probe must compare the result against the expected `200` / 14-byte / `text/plain` signature and decide |
| Signal to evaluate | Effectively absent from the application | The four boundaries of Section 6.5.1.4 — probe result, stdout presence, stderr content, exit status — plus the procfs catalogue of 6.5.2.1 |
| Deduplication, grouping, silencing | Absent | Not available; each probe cycle is independent and stateless, so a persistent fault re-fires on every cycle unless the operator suppresses it manually |
| Notification transport | Absent — no webhook, email, chat, or paging integration | The terminal or harness that ran the probe; Section 6.5.4 documents the resulting routing path in full |
| Automated remediation | Absent — Section 6.1.4.2 records that nothing in the repository restarts the process | A human, or a supervisor the consuming environment supplies |

The structural point is that **alert evaluation cannot be delegated to the monitored system**. In a conventional service a threshold is evaluated against emitted telemetry; here there is no telemetry to evaluate, so the assertion logic and the expected values must both live in the monitor. Section 6.5.5.1 supplies the consolidated threshold matrix that such a monitor would encode.

#### 6.5.2.5 Dashboard Design

**No dashboard definition exists** — there is no `grafana/` directory, no `dashboard.json`, and no saved-board artifact of any kind. What *can* be built is a small operator console assembled entirely from external commands. Every panel below is populated by an observation this specification actually made, and the expected-value column is what a correct instance produced.

| Panel | Populated By | Expected Value |
|---|---|---|
| Liveness | `curl` to any path on 127.0.0.1 port 3000 | `http_code` 200; a `curl` exit status of 7 with `http_code` 000 means nothing is listening |
| Readiness banner | Literal match against captured stdout | Exactly one occurrence of `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, 41 bytes |
| Listener presence | `/proc/net/tcp` scan for `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A` | Exactly one listening socket |
| Response integrity | Status, `Content-Length`, and body checksum from the probe | `200`, `Content-Length: 14`, and a body checksum identical to the frozen signature |
| Header set | Response header block with `Connection: close` | Exactly four headers — `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Content-Length` |
| Probe latency | `curl` `time_total` over repeated probes | p50 0.138 ms and p95 0.237 ms observed with a new connection per request |
| Resident memory | `VmRSS` from `/proc/<pid>/status` | Within the 48–62 MB envelope observed across all runs |
| CPU time | `utime` plus `stime` from `/proc/<pid>/stat` | Monotonic and near-flat at idle; about 0.18 s total for 1,300 requests |
| Descriptors and threads | `/proc/<pid>/fd` count and `Threads` | Constant at 22 and 7 respectively |
| Process age | `ps -o etimes=` | Monotonically increasing; a reset indicates an unlogged restart |
| Last exit status | Shell `wait` or supervisor reaping | `1` bind conflict, `143` SIGTERM, `130` SIGINT, `137` SIGKILL, `140` SIGUSR2 without the report flag |
| Baseline drift | `git status --porcelain` and `git rev-parse HEAD` | Empty output and `1a0874d`; any change invalidates every other panel's expected value |
