Two design principles follow from the evidence and are worth stating because they invert normal dashboard practice. First, **the availability row is the whole dashboard**: Section 6.1.4.5 establishes that availability here is binary, so rows 2 through 4 add integrity and trend context but cannot express partial degradation. Second, **the resource row must be read as a trend, not a threshold**, because the repository declares no memory, CPU, or descriptor limit against which any value could be judged.

#### 6.5.2.6 Zero-Code-Change Diagnostic Channel Matrix

The three channels below are the complete set of deeper diagnostics available on this artifact without violating the change freeze. They are consolidated here because they are the principal practical contribution this section can make to an operator.

| Channel | Activation | Observable Output | Process Survives |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP core tracing | `NODE_DEBUG=http node server.js` — requires a relaunch | About five unstructured, PID-prefixed lines per request on stderr | Yes |
| Live inspector | `kill -USR1 <pid>` on a running process | `Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/<uuid>` on stderr; CPU profiles, heap snapshots, step debugging | **Yes** — verified still serving after attach |
| Structured process snapshot | `node --report-on-signal --report-directory=<dir> server.js`, then `kill -USR2 <pid>` | An eleven-section JSON report file per signal, including `resourceUsage` and `javascriptHeap` | **Yes** — verified still serving after the report was written |

> **Operational hazard, verified by measurement.** If the process was **not** started with `--report-on-signal`, sending `SIGUSR2` **terminates it** with exit code 140 and no shutdown output. An operator must never use `SIGUSR2` as a diagnostic trigger unless that launch flag is known to be in effect. Of the six signals tested, only `SIGUSR1` was non-destructive by default; `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGQUIT`, `SIGUSR2`, and `SIGKILL` all terminated the process with exit codes 143, 130, 129, 131, 140, and 137 respectively — each exactly `128 + signum`, confirming that no handler ran.


### 6.5.3 Observability Patterns

This sub-section documents the observability patterns that are actually available against a running instance. One of the five — health checking — exists in a de-facto form and is genuinely useful once its limits are understood. The other four are absent, and in three of those cases the absence is structural rather than an omission that could be corrected by configuration.

#### 6.5.3.1 Health Checks

**No dedicated health check exists, but a usable de-facto liveness probe does.** The distinction is important and is grounded in measurement. Seventeen paths were probed against a running instance — `/`, `/health`, `/healthz`, `/health/live`, `/health/ready`, `/ready`, `/readyz`, `/live`, `/livez`, `/status`, `/metrics`, `/debug/vars`, `/-/healthy`, `/-/ready`, `/favicon.ico`, `/admin`, and `/nonexistent-path-xyz`. Every one returned `200` with 14 bytes of `text/plain`, and the body checksums across all of them collapsed to a **single distinct signature**.

| Probe Property | Measured Result | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Status code, all 17 paths | `200` | Uniform success is the contract (F-002-RQ-001), not evidence of health logic |
| Body size and checksum | 14 bytes; one signature across all paths | The response is path-independent, so no path carries health semantics |
| Content type | `text/plain`, with no `charset` parameter | The only header set by repository code (`server.js` line 8) |
| Probe latency | 0.000135 s to 0.003439 s per probe; the 3.4 ms figure was the first, cold probe | Warm-up matters when interpreting a single sample |
| Effect on server output | stdout stayed at one line; stderr stayed at 0 bytes | Probing is invisible to the server and leaves no record |

What a `200` from this system **does** prove is narrow but real: the process is running, the socket is bound and accepting, the event loop is turning, and the handler completed a full response. Section 5.4.1 notes that for this fixture those four facts happen to constitute the whole of its contract, which is why the de-facto probe is adequate here in a way it would not be for a real service.

What it **cannot** prove is more extensive, and each item below is a verified structural limit rather than a caveat:

| Claim a Probe Cannot Support | Why Not |
|---|---|
| That `/health` was routed to health logic | `req.url` is never referenced; the handler has no conditional and no router, so path-specific behaviour is unreachable |
| That the system is correct rather than merely alive | Every path returns the same response, so there is **no negative case** to assert against — a 404 is unreachable, and a monitor cannot distinguish correct behaviour from wrong-path behaviour |
| That dependencies are healthy | There are none: the only `require` targets a core module and no outbound client exists |
| That the instance is ready to serve versus merely started | Readiness and liveness are the same event here; the bind either succeeded, in which case both hold, or it failed, in which case the process is gone |
| That degradation is or is not occurring | Section 6.1.4.5 establishes availability as binary; no intermediate state can be expressed by the code |
| That a `/metrics` scrape is meaningful | The path returns the greeting; the scrape succeeds at the HTTP layer and fails at parse time |

Two further findings bear directly on how a probe should be configured. First, **the negative signature is ambiguous**: a `curl` exit status of 7 with `http_code` 000 is produced both when nothing is listening and when the request is sent to a non-loopback interface — the refused connection to the host's routable address recorded in F-001-RQ-002 produces the identical signature to a dead process. A probe must therefore pin its target to `127.0.0.1` for the result to be diagnostic. Second, Section 3.6.4 establishes that an unmodified container built around this repository exposes the listener only inside its own network namespace, so **an orchestrator probe issued from outside that namespace would fail against a perfectly healthy instance**.

The practice that follows is a compound assertion rather than a status-code check. A correct probe asserts all four of: target `127.0.0.1:3000`; `http_code` equal to `200`; `Content-Length` equal to `14`; and a body checksum matching the frozen signature. Section 6.1.4.5 phrases the operational question the same way — *is the readiness line present and does a probe return `200` with 14 bytes?*

#### 6.5.3.2 Performance Metrics

**No performance metric is produced by the system**; every figure below was measured from outside. Two independent instruments were used, and because their results differ by design, the method is stated in every row. These are observations of specific runs on the verification host, **not commitments** — the framing Section 2.2.1.3 requires, since no latency, throughput, or timeout target exists anywhere in the repository.

| Measurement | Observed Value | Instrument and Method |
|---|---|---|
| Per-request latency, new connection each time | min 0.112 ms, p50 0.138 ms, p90 0.197 ms, p95 0.237 ms, p99 0.346 ms, max 0.876 ms, mean 0.154 ms | `curl` `time_total`, n = 200, one fresh TCP connection per request |
| Per-request latency, connection reused | p50 0.064 ms, p99 0.184 ms, max 0.414 ms | In-process Node client over one keep-alive connection after a 50-request warm-up, as reported in Section 5.4.5 |
| Connection-establishment cost | p50 0.077 ms reused versus 0.117 ms per new connection | Section 4.3.1.4; the only measurable optimisation in the system, and it is a runtime keep-alive default |
| Sequential throughput | 1,000 requests in 81 ms, about 12,300 requests/second | `curl` over reused keep-alive connections |
| Sequential throughput, second instrument | 2,000 requests in 156.7 ms, about 12,761 requests/second | In-process client, Section 5.4.5 — corroborating the figure above |
| Concurrency | 100 requests at parallelism 50 completed in 45 ms; distinct status codes `{200}`; non-200 count 0 | Parallel `curl` invocations |
| Concurrency, second instrument | 50 of 50 parallel requests returned `200` in 25 ms wall time | Section 5.4.5 |
| Path-cardinality independence | 2,000 sequential requests to 2,000 distinct paths returned 2,000 × `200` in 114 ms | Section 6.3.2.6 |
| Time to readiness | 29 ms, 29 ms, 34 ms across three launches | Polling for the first byte on stdout from process exec |
| Time to readiness, second instrument | 26.9 ms; about 23 ms for a restart | Sections 5.4.5 and 4.3.2.3 |
| CPU cost of load | 15 user ticks and 3 system ticks at `CLK_TCK` 100 for roughly 1,300 requests | `/proc/<pid>/stat` sampled before and after |
| Memory cost of load | VmRSS +64 kB after roughly 1,300 requests; +268 kB across 20,000 requests | `/proc/<pid>/status` sampled before and after |

The two latency rows differ by roughly a factor of two purely because of connection handling, which is the single most important caveat when reading any performance number for this system: **latency here is dominated by transport rather than by work**, so the measurement instrument affects the result more than the server does. Section 5.4.5 explains the structural reason — the handler is O(1), performs no I/O, and allocates nothing beyond runtime-supplied objects.

For monitoring purposes the practicable performance signals reduce to three, and their limits should be recorded alongside them:

| Available Performance Signal | Where It Comes From | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Probe round-trip time | The monitor's own clock | Measures the monitor, the loopback stack, and the server together; the server's contribution cannot be isolated |
| CPU tick delta | `/proc/<pid>/stat` | Aggregate only; cannot be attributed to individual requests or paths |
| Context-switch delta | `voluntary_ctxt_switches` in `/proc/<pid>/status` | A proxy for event-loop activity, not a request counter |

#### 6.5.3.3 Business Metrics

**No business metric exists, and none has a referent.** This is the shortest finding in the section and the most definitive: the system has no domain. The response is a compiled-in 14-byte greeting; no request datum is read, parsed, stored, or counted; there is no user, account, tenant, transaction, order, or session concept anywhere in the repository; and Section 6.2 establishes that no data is written to any store. A business metric requires a business event to count, and the handler at `server.js` lines 6–10 produces none.

The nearest analogue an operator can track is **fixture availability for its consumers** — that is, whether the artifact was reachable and byte-correct when a consuming integration test needed it. That is an availability measure, recorded by the consumer, not a business metric produced by the system. `README.md` states the artifact's purpose as a test project for backprop integration, so its only value-bearing property is being present and unchanged.

#### 6.5.3.4 SLA Monitoring

**No SLA, SLO, error budget, availability target, latency threshold, or throughput commitment exists in the repository.** This is a verified absence, not an undocumented one: the tokens `sla`, `slo`, `threshold`, and `uptime` appear zero times across all four tracked files; Section 5.4.5 records the same finding from the architecture side; and Section 2.2.1.3 states the governing position — any latency or throughput objective for this system must be established by the consuming tooling, because none can be sourced from this repository.

Consequently there is nothing to monitor an SLA against, and no compliance calculation is defined. If a consumer chooses to impose one externally, the table below records what could and could not be computed from the signals that exist.

| Conventional SLI | Computable From Available Signals | Basis and Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | **Yes, as a probe success ratio** | Successful probes divided by attempted probes. Resolution is limited to the probe interval; the system contributes no uptime counter, and process age from `ps -o etimes=` resets silently on restart |
| Latency objective | **Partially** | Probe round-trip time is measurable, but it includes client and loopback cost and cannot be decomposed; no server-side duration is ever recorded |
| Error rate | **No** | The application can only emit `200`. The runtime-generated `400`, `408`, and `431` responses bypass the application entirely and are recorded nowhere, so a server-side error rate cannot be computed at all |
| Correctness or data-integrity objective | **Yes, trivially** | The full contract is a byte-comparison: `200`, `Content-Length: 14`, and a fixed body checksum |
| Durability or recovery-point objective | Not applicable | Section 5.4.6 records that no data is ever written, so nothing can be lost |
| Time to recover | **Yes, mechanically** | Measured at 29 ms to readiness; but Section 6.1.4.2 records detection time as externally owned and unbounded, so an end-to-end recovery objective is dominated by the probe interval, not by the system |

The honest summary is that **availability and correctness are measurable; error rate is not measurable at all; and latency is measurable only as an end-to-end figure that includes the monitor**. Any SLA written for this artifact should be confined to the first two.

#### 6.5.3.5 Capacity Tracking

**No capacity metric, quota, or limit is declared anywhere in the repository.** Section 6.1.3.3 establishes that every value governing resource consumption is an inherited Node.js runtime default — `maxConnections` unset, the untouched 511-entry accept backlog, `keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300000 ms, `timeout` 0, and `maxRequestsPerSocket` 0 — and that because no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` pins the runtime (deviation D-005), those values are unversioned by this repository.

What can be tracked is resource trend and instance availability. The measured envelope below is what a correct, unmodified instance produced under load, and it is the only baseline against which a future observation can be compared.

| Capacity Dimension | Observed Envelope | Tracking Source |
|---|---|---|
| Resident memory | 48.2 MB at start, 59.5 MB at 5,000 requests, 61.9 MB at 25,000 requests; only +268 kB across the final 20,000 | `VmRSS` in `/proc/<pid>/status` |
| File descriptors | Constant at 22 before and after load — no leak observable across 25,000 requests | `/proc/<pid>/fd` entry count |
| Threads | Constant at 7, one of which runs JavaScript | `Threads` in `/proc/<pid>/status` |
| CPU headroom | About 0.18 s of CPU consumed for 1,300 requests on a 16-CPU host, with 15 cores unusable by design | `/proc/<pid>/stat` and Section 6.1.3.1 |
| Concurrent connections | 0 established at idle; 100 requests at parallelism 50 all succeeded | `/proc/net/tcp` rows in state `01` |
| Instance cardinality | Exactly one per host; a second launch aborts with `EADDRINUSE` and exit code 1 | Verified bind conflict |
| Log and storage growth | Zero — one output line per process lifetime, no filesystem writes at all | Sections 5.4.2 and 6.2 |

Three properties make capacity tracking for this artifact unlike capacity tracking for a service. **The binding resource is not CPU, memory, or bandwidth but exclusive availability of `127.0.0.1:3000`** — Section 6.1.3.5 concludes that capacity here is a scheduling constraint rather than a scaling variable, so the metric that matters most is whether the port is free. **There is no saturation signal to track**: Section 5.4.5 records the absence of rate limiting, admission control, queue-depth metrics, a `maxConnections` cap, and backpressure, so overload behaviour is a platform property, and the only externally visible symptom of saturation would be rising probe latency. And **the trend baseline must be re-established after any runtime upgrade**, because the resource defaults above belong to Node.js rather than to the repository.


### 6.5.4 Incident Response

No incident-response mechanism is defined by the repository — the tokens `incident`, `runbook`, `oncall`, `escalat`, and `pager` appear zero times across all four tracked files, and no supervisor, restart policy, or notification artifact exists. What follows is therefore an account of the response path that genuinely exists, plus four runbooks derived entirely from measured behaviour. Each runbook prescribes only actions that were actually performed and verified during the preparation of this specification.

#### 6.5.4.1 Alert Routing

**There is no alert routing tier. Detection and routing collapse into a single step: whatever issued the probe displays the result, and a human reads it.** Every automated element of a conventional routing path was verified absent.

| Routing Element | Status | What Exists Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Alert rule evaluation | Absent — no rule file or engine | The prober must encode the expected `200` / `Content-Length: 14` / checksum assertion itself |
| Notification transport | Absent — no webhook, chat, email, or paging integration | The terminal or harness output stream |
| Routing by severity or service label | Absent — no severity model and no labels exist | A single undifferentiated channel |
| Deduplication, grouping, silencing | Absent | None; each probe cycle is stateless, so a persistent fault re-fires every cycle |
| Automated remediation trigger | Absent — Section 6.1.4.2 records that nothing in the repository restarts the process | A human executing one of the runbooks in 6.5.4.3 |

Six detectable conditions exist, and they are the complete set derivable from the four signal boundaries. They are named here so that the runbooks and the threshold matrix in 6.5.5.1 can refer to them.

| ID | Condition | Detection Basis |
|---|---|---|
| AL-01 | Service absent — nothing listening on `127.0.0.1:3000` | TCP connect fails; `curl` exit status 7 with `http_code` 000 |
| AL-02 | Malformed or stalled client traffic | Response is `400`, `431`, or `408` — all runtime-generated, with the application never invoked |
| AL-03 | Contract violation — status `200` but the body differs from the frozen 14-byte signature | Body checksum mismatch; implies the frozen source was edited, since the handler has only one code path |
| AL-04 | Bind conflict at launch | Readiness line never appears, exit code 1, and a 20-line `EADDRINUSE` trace on stderr naming errno −98 and syscall `listen` |
| AL-05 | Launch failed silently — no banner and no stderr output | Absence of the 41-byte readiness line within roughly 35 ms of exec, with stderr empty |
| AL-06 | Resource trend outside the observed envelope | `VmRSS` beyond the 48–62 MB range, or `/proc/<pid>/fd` count above 22, or `Threads` above 7 |

**Diagram 6.5.4-A — Alert Flow: Detection Basis, Condition Identification, Human Routing, and Runbook Selection**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LAUNCH(["Process launch - node server.js<br/>foreground, no supervisor defined anywhere"])
    TICK(["Operator-initiated monitoring cycle<br/>no scheduler exists in the repository"])
    SAMPLE(["Operator-initiated procfs sample"])

    TICK --> Q1{"Does a TCP connect to<br/>127.0.0.1 port 3000 succeed?"}

    Q1 -->|"No - curl exit 7, http_code 000"| SEV1["Condition AL-01 - Service absent<br/>the process is not listening"]
    Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"Is the reply 200 with<br/>Content-Length 14 and text-plain?"}

    Q2 -->|"Yes"| OK(["No condition raised<br/>the entire published contract is satisfied"])
    Q2 -->|"No - 400, 408 or 431"| SEV2["Condition AL-02 - Malformed client traffic<br/>runtime-generated, application never invoked"]
    Q2 -->|"No - 200 but body differs"| SEV3["Condition AL-03 - Contract violation<br/>implies the frozen source was edited"]

    subgraph StartupPath["Launch-Time Detection - evaluated once per start"]
        S0{"Did the 41-byte readiness line<br/>appear on stdout within about 35 ms?"}
        S0 -->|"No, and stderr carries an EADDRINUSE trace"| SEV4["Condition AL-04 - Bind conflict<br/>exit code 1, port 3000 already held"]
        S0 -->|"No, and stderr is empty"| SEV5["Condition AL-05 - Launch failed silently<br/>wrong working directory or missing runtime"]
        S0 -->|"Yes"| SREADY["Readiness confirmed<br/>bind and announce share one source"]
    end

    subgraph ResourcePath["Trend Detection - procfs sampling, PID-scoped"]
        R0{"Has VmRSS grown beyond the<br/>48 to 62 MB observed envelope?"}
        R0 -->|"Yes"| SEV6["Condition AL-06 - Memory growth<br/>no baseline exists in the repository"]
        R0 -->|"No"| RSTEADY["Steady state<br/>fd count 22 and Threads 7 held constant"]
    end

    subgraph Routing["Alert Routing - what actually happens"]
        RT1["The condition surfaces in the terminal<br/>or harness that issued the probe"]
        RT2["A human reads it<br/>there is no notifier, no webhook, no queue"]
        RT3{"Is a runbook defined for<br/>this condition?"}
        RT1 --> RT2
        RT2 --> RT3
    end

    subgraph Response["Response Actions - all external to the repository"]
        RB1["RB-01 Relaunch<br/>run node server.js, confirm the banner,<br/>then confirm 200 with 14 bytes"]
        RB2["RB-02 Release port 3000<br/>identify the holder, stop it, then relaunch<br/>no retry or port fallback exists"]
        RB3["RB-03 Restore the baseline<br/>git checkout the tracked files and verify<br/>a clean working tree at 1a0874d"]
        RB4["RB-04 Deep diagnosis<br/>relaunch under NODE_DEBUG=http, or send<br/>SIGUSR1, or use --report-on-signal"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentRouting["Automated Routing and Escalation - verified absent"]
        N1["Alert rule file or evaluation engine"]
        N2["Paging, chat or email integration"]
        N3["On-call schedule and rotation"]
        N4["Ticket creation and incident timeline"]
        N5["Automatic restart policy or supervisor"]
        N1 -.- N2
        N2 -.- N3
        N3 -.- N4
        N4 -.- N5
    end

    SEV1 --> RT1
    SEV2 --> RT1
    SEV3 --> RT1
    SEV4 --> RT1
    SEV5 --> RT1
    SEV6 --> RT1

    RT3 -->|"AL-01 or AL-05"| RB1
    RT3 -->|"AL-04"| RB2
    RT3 -->|"AL-03"| RB3
    RT3 -->|"AL-02 or AL-06"| RB4

    RB1 --> VERIFY["Verification is identical for every runbook<br/>readiness line present AND probe returns 200 with 14 bytes"]
    RB2 --> VERIFY
    RB3 --> VERIFY
    RB4 --> VERIFY
    VERIFY --> CLOSED(["Condition cleared - mechanical recovery about 29 ms<br/>detection latency remains bounded only by probe interval"])

    RT2 -.->|"no automated hand-off exists"| N1
```

The shape of the diagram carries the finding. Detection is cheap and reliable; routing is a person looking at a screen; remediation is fast and uniform; and the entire left-to-right automation that a production posture would supply is confined to the verified-absent lane. Section 5.4.6 identifies the resulting asymmetry precisely — mechanical recovery is measured in tens of milliseconds while **detection latency is bounded only by how often someone chooses to probe**.

#### 6.5.4.2 Escalation Procedures

**No escalation procedure exists, and there is no tier to escalate to.** No on-call schedule, rotation, severity taxonomy, response-time commitment, or contact list appears in the repository, and Section 3.6.5 confirms there is no `CODEOWNERS` file and no active Git hook that would identify an owner or gate a change.

The escalation model that the evidence supports is single-tier and is stated here so that consuming teams do not assume a tier that does not exist:

| Escalation Question | Answer From Repository Evidence |
|---|---|
| Who is notified? | Whoever launched the process and is watching its terminal. No other party is reachable by any mechanism the repository defines |
| What is the severity model? | None exists. Section 6.1.4.5 establishes availability as binary, so every condition is either "the contract holds" or "it does not" — there is no partial-impact tier to assign |
| What is the response-time commitment? | None. Section 2.2.1.3 and Section 5.4.5 both record that no service-level target of any kind exists |
| When does an incident become someone else's? | Only when the resolution requires editing `server.js`, which constraint C-001 (the `README.md` change freeze) places outside sanctioned scope. That is the single genuine escalation boundary the artifact has |
| What identifies the owning team? | Nothing in the repository. `package.json` names the author `hxu`; `README.md` names the consuming context. Neither is a support contact |

The one substantive escalation rule that follows from the evidence is therefore a **scope rule rather than a severity rule**: any condition whose remediation requires a source change must be escalated to whoever owns the change freeze, because no runbook may resolve an incident by modifying the four tracked files.

#### 6.5.4.3 Runbooks

The repository contains no runbook. The four below are derived from behaviour that was directly measured, and each was executed at least once during verification. They share one verification step, because Section 6.1.4.5 establishes that there is only one question to ask about this system.

##### 6.5.4.3.1 RB-01 — Service Absent or Silent Launch Failure

| Step | Action | Expected Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | AL-01 or AL-05 raised | `curl` exit 7 with `http_code` 000, or no readiness line within roughly 35 ms of exec |
| 1 | Confirm nothing is listening | `/proc/net/tcp` contains no `0100007F:0BB8` entry in state `0A` |
| 2 | Confirm the working tree is intact | `git status --porcelain` empty; four tracked files present; `HEAD` is `1a0874d` |
| 3 | Relaunch from the repository root | `node server.js`, or `npm start` which resolves to the same command through npm's implicit default (deviation D-004) |
| 4 | Verify readiness | The 41-byte line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` appears on stdout, typically within 29–34 ms |
| 5 | Verify the contract | A probe to `127.0.0.1:3000` returns `200`, `Content-Length: 14`, and the expected body checksum |

Two cautions apply. `npm start` runs **in the foreground** with stdout and stderr attached to the invoking shell, so the process dies with that shell — there is no supervisor artifact anywhere in the repository to prevent this. And because `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (deviation D-001, the `main: index.js` mismatch), the service must be started by executing `server.js`, never by requiring the package.

##### 6.5.4.3.2 RB-02 — Bind Conflict on Port 3000

| Step | Action | Expected Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | AL-04 raised | Exit code 1, no readiness line, and a 20-line stderr trace containing `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` with `errno: -98` and `syscall: 'listen'` |
| 1 | Identify the holder of the port | The `0100007F:0BB8` listening entry in `/proc/net/tcp` and its owning PID |
| 2 | Stop the holder, or wait for it to exit | `SIGTERM` yields exit 143 with no shutdown output; the OS releases the port immediately on exit |
| 3 | Relaunch | As RB-01 steps 3–5 |

The critical property is that **no retry and no port fallback exist** — Section 6.1.2.6 records that the bind is attempted exactly once. Consuming automation must therefore serialise its use of port 3000 rather than relying on resilience the system does not have. A prior instance that has been signalled but not yet reaped will still hold the port, so step 2 must be confirmed rather than assumed.

##### 6.5.4.3.3 RB-03 — Contract Violation

| Step | Action | Expected Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | AL-03 raised | Status `200` but the body, `Content-Length`, or `Content-Type` differs from the frozen signature |
| 1 | Treat the cause as source drift, not runtime failure | The handler has one code path and no conditional, so a differing response cannot be produced by the unmodified source |
| 2 | Detect the drift | `git status --porcelain` output, `git diff`, and `git rev-parse HEAD` against `1a0874d` |
| 3 | Restore the baseline | Restore the tracked files from the single-commit baseline and re-confirm a clean working tree (F-006-RQ-003) |
| 4 | Relaunch and verify | As RB-01 steps 3–5 |

This runbook exists because the change freeze in `README.md` is **advisory only** — Section 3.6.5 confirms there is no Git hook, `CODEOWNERS` file, or CI check enforcing it. A contract violation is therefore both the symptom of an unauthorised edit and, given the single-commit provenance, trivially attributable.

##### 6.5.4.3.4 RB-04 — Deep Diagnosis Without Modifying the Repository

| Step | Action | Expected Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | AL-02 or AL-06 raised, or any condition that survives RB-01 | A recurring anomaly with no application-side evidence available |
| 1 | Snapshot the live process non-destructively | With `--report-on-signal` in effect, `kill -USR2 <pid>` writes an eleven-section JSON report and the process keeps serving |
| 2 | Attach the inspector if deeper analysis is needed | `kill -USR1 <pid>` prints `Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/<uuid>` and the process keeps serving; CPU profiles and heap snapshots become available |
| 3 | Obtain per-request tracing | Relaunch with `NODE_DEBUG=http` for roughly five unstructured stderr lines per request. This requires a restart and Node warns it can expose sensitive data |
| 4 | Correlate from the client side | Because no correlation identifier is echoed or logged, the client's own records are the only per-request evidence that exists |
| 5 | Verify the instance afterwards | As RB-01 steps 4–5 |

> **Do not send `SIGUSR2` unless the process was launched with `--report-on-signal`.** Without that flag, `SIGUSR2` terminates the process with exit code 140 and no shutdown output. This was verified directly, along with the full default disposition of every signal tested: 143, 130, 129, 131, 140, and 137 for `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGQUIT`, `SIGUSR2`, and `SIGKILL`.

#### 6.5.4.4 Post-Mortem Processes

**No post-mortem process is defined, and — more consequentially — the system preserves almost no evidence for one.** This is the sharpest operational limitation in the whole of Section 6.5, and it follows directly from Section 5.4.2's finding that there is no request logging and therefore no record of what traffic the fixture served.

| Forensic Question | Evidence Available After the Fact |
|---|---|
| Was the service up, and when did it stop? | Only what the monitor recorded. The process emits nothing on termination; stdout stays at one line and stderr at 0 bytes for every signal tested |
| How did it stop? | The exit status, if a shell or supervisor captured it: `1` bind conflict, `143`/`130`/`129`/`131`/`140`/`137` for the signalled cases. Nothing distinguishes an operator `SIGTERM` from an out-of-memory kill except the code itself |
| Why did it fail to start? | The stderr trace, but **only** for a bind conflict. AL-05 — no banner and no stderr — leaves no artifact at all |
| Which requests were affected? | **Nothing.** No access log, no counter, no trace. Client-side records are the only source |
| Who called, and with what? | **Nothing.** No client address, header, or payload is ever recorded; even 60 requests bearing distinct `Authorization` headers left stdout at exactly one line |
| Did the artifact change? | Git: `git status --porcelain`, `git diff`, and the single-commit baseline `1a0874d`. This is the one durable, high-quality evidence source the project has |
| What was the process state at the time? | Only if a diagnostic report was captured while it was alive; nothing is written on death |

The practice this dictates is that **a post-mortem for this system must be reconstructed from the consumer's side and from the monitor's own records**, not from the service. Three consequences should be written into any consuming team's process:

- **Retain the monitor's raw probe log.** It is the only timeline that will exist, and its resolution is the probe interval.
- **Capture fd 1 and fd 2 at launch, with timestamps added at capture time.** The process cannot self-timestamp, since `Date.now`, `new Date`, and `process.hrtime` are all absent, so an uncaptured stream is unrecoverable.
- **Capture the exit status.** It is the only cause-of-death signal, and it is lost the moment the launching shell exits.

Because Section 5.4.6 establishes that no data can be lost — nothing is ever written — a post-mortem for this artifact never needs a data-integrity or replay assessment. The entire scope of any post-mortem is availability, detection latency, and whether the baseline was altered.

#### 6.5.4.5 Improvement Tracking

**No improvement-tracking mechanism exists inside the repository, and the change freeze deliberately makes the artifact non-improvable within sanctioned scope.**

| Tracking Mechanism | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Issue tracker or backlog reference | Absent from the repository | No issue template, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or tracker link in any of the four files; `package.json` declares no `repository` or `bugs` field |
| Change history | **Present** — the single durable record | Git: one commit `1a0874d`, one branch `main`, zero tags. Any future change is trivially visible against it |
| Enforcement of the freeze | Absent | No active Git hook — `.git/hooks` holds only the 14 default `.sample` templates — no `CODEOWNERS`, and no CI check. Section 2.1.8 records enforcement as by convention only |
| Regression detection | **Present but deliberately failing** | `npm test` prints `Error: no test specified` and exits 1 by design (D-003), so the only exit status the repository can produce from a verification command is a failure. Nothing in the repository can confirm a deployment automatically |
| Post-incident action tracking | Absent | No document, checklist, or workflow exists to record a follow-up action |

The improvement loop that the evidence supports is therefore not a change to the artifact but a change to **the monitoring around it**. Every deficiency identified in this section — no metrics, no logs, no tracing, no alerting, no dashboards — is remediable only by editing `server.js`, which constraint C-001 forbids; so the actionable improvements available to a consuming team are exclusively external: shorten the probe interval, capture the streams and the exit status, assert the full response signature rather than the status code alone, verify baseline integrity before each run, and serialise access to port 3000. Section 6.5.5.4 records the conditions under which the applicability determination itself would have to be revisited, which is the only route by which internal improvement could become in scope.


### 6.5.5 Alert Thresholds, Service Levels and Baseline Practice

This sub-section consolidates the section into the three artifacts the prompt requires — a threshold matrix, an explicit service-level determination, and a statement of the basic practices followed in place of a monitoring architecture — and closes with the conditions that would invalidate the determination.

#### 6.5.5.1 Alert Threshold Matrix

**No threshold is configured anywhere in the repository.** The token `threshold` appears zero times, and there is no rule file, limit declaration, or budget against which a value could be judged. The matrix below therefore separates two things that are easy to conflate: the **configured threshold**, which is uniformly absent, and the **evidence-derived expected value**, which this specification measured and which a monitor can legitimately assert against.

| Condition | Detection Basis and Assertion | Configured Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| AL-01 Service absent | TCP connect to `127.0.0.1:3000` fails; `curl` exit 7 with `http_code` 000. Assert on the **first** failure — availability is binary, so there is no partial state to wait out | None in the repository. Recommended external value: 1 consecutive failure, because no retry, fallback, or degraded mode exists |
| AL-02 Malformed or stalled client traffic | Response is `400`, `431`, or `408`. These are runtime-generated and bypass the application; the runtime's own `headersTimeout` of 60000 ms governs the `408` case | None. The three governing timeouts are inherited Node.js defaults, unversioned by the repository per D-005 |
| AL-03 Contract violation | Status `200` but body length ≠ 14, `Content-Type` ≠ `text/plain`, or body checksum ≠ the frozen signature. Assert on the first mismatch | None. The expected values come from F-002-RQ-002 and F-002-RQ-003, not from a configured limit |
| AL-04 Bind conflict | No readiness line, exit code 1, and a stderr trace containing `EADDRINUSE`, `errno: -98`, `syscall: 'listen'` | None. Not tunable — the bind is attempted exactly once |
| AL-05 Silent launch failure | No 41-byte readiness line on stdout within the startup window, and stderr empty | None. Observed readiness times were 29 ms, 29 ms, 34 ms, and 26.9 ms across runs; an external window of roughly 5 s would be generous by two orders of magnitude |
| AL-06 Memory trend excursion | `VmRSS` outside the 48.2–61.9 MB envelope observed across 25,000 requests | None. No memory limit, `--max-old-space-size` flag, or container limit exists |
| AL-07 Descriptor or thread excursion | `/proc/<pid>/fd` count ≠ 22, or `Threads` ≠ 7 | None. Both were measured constant before and after load, so any deviation is itself the signal |
| AL-08 Latency excursion | Probe round-trip time far outside the measured range | None, and this is the weakest condition in the matrix: the figure includes client and loopback cost and cannot be attributed to the server |
| AL-09 Baseline drift | `git status --porcelain` non-empty, or `HEAD` ≠ `1a0874d` | None enforced — Section 3.6.5 confirms no hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check exists. Enforcement is by convention |
| AL-10 Unexplained restart | Process age from `ps -o etimes=` resets without an operator action | None. There is no restart counter and no restart log; the process emits nothing on death |

Three cross-cutting properties of this matrix are worth stating explicitly, because they differ from conventional alerting practice:

- **Most conditions are single-sample, not rate-based.** Availability is binary and the response is invariant, so there is no error-rate curve to average over and no reason to require consecutive failures before firing.
- **Every "expected value" is a measurement, not a commitment.** Section 2.2.1.3 governs: any objective for this system must be established by the consuming tooling, since none can be sourced from the repository.
- **Two conditions detect editing rather than failure.** AL-03 and AL-09 exist because the handler has exactly one code path, so a deviant response is evidence of source drift rather than of runtime malfunction.

#### 6.5.5.2 Service-Level Requirements

**The repository declares no service-level requirement of any kind.** This is a verified absence across four independent checks: the tokens `sla`, `slo`, `threshold`, and `uptime` appear zero times in all four tracked files; no monitoring, alerting, or dashboard configuration exists that could carry an objective; `README.md` and both manifests contain no availability, latency, or throughput commitment; and no instrumentation exists from which compliance could be tracked. Sections 2.2.1.3, 5.4.5, and 6.1.3 record the same finding from the requirements, cross-cutting, and scalability perspectives respectively.

If a consuming team elects to impose a service level externally, the following is the complete set of commitments the available signals can actually support. The reference values are measured observations of the verification host and are **explicitly not commitments**.

| Candidate Commitment | Supportable? | Measured Reference Value |
|---|---|---|
| Availability, as a probe success ratio | Yes | 100% of all probes succeeded across every run in this specification; resolution is limited to the probe interval |
| Response correctness, byte-for-byte | Yes — the strongest available commitment | `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes, one distinct signature across 17 paths, 2,000 distinct paths, 25,000 sequential requests, and 100 concurrent requests |
| Time to readiness after launch | Yes | 29 ms, 29 ms, 34 ms measured here; 26.9 ms in Section 5.4.5; about 23 ms for a restart in Section 4.3.2.3 |
| Mechanical recovery time | Yes | About 29 ms from relaunch to readiness, with no state to rebuild |
| End-to-end recovery time | **No** | Section 6.1.4.2 records detection time as externally owned and unbounded; the total is dominated by the probe interval, not by the system |
| Latency objective | Only end-to-end | p50 0.138 ms and p95 0.237 ms with a new connection per request; p50 0.064 ms and p99 0.184 ms over a reused connection. The server's own contribution cannot be isolated |
| Throughput objective | Only as a host-specific observation | About 12,300–12,761 requests/second over reused connections on a 16-CPU host, with capacity capped at one single-core event loop |
| Error-rate objective | **No** | The application can emit only `200`; runtime-generated `400`, `408`, and `431` responses bypass it and are recorded nowhere |
| Concurrency commitment | Bounded observation only | 100 requests at parallelism 50 all returned `200` in 45 ms; Section 5.4.5 reports 50 of 50 in 25 ms. No `maxConnections` cap or admission control exists |
| Durability or recovery-point objective | Not applicable | No data is ever written, so nothing can be lost |
| High availability | **No** | Impossible on one host — a second instance aborts with `EADDRINUSE` and exit code 1 |

The defensible conclusion is that an externally imposed service level for this artifact should commit to **availability and byte-correctness only**, treat readiness and recovery times as informational, and explicitly disclaim error rate and end-to-end recovery as unmeasurable with the signals that exist.

#### 6.5.5.3 Basic Monitoring Practices Followed Instead

Because a detailed monitoring architecture is not applicable, the practices below constitute the monitoring regime for this system. Each is derived from a verified property of the artifact rather than from convention, and none requires modifying the four tracked files.

| Practice | Concrete Procedure | Verified Property It Relies On |
|---|---|---|
| Readiness gating | Synchronise on the exact 41-byte line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` before sending traffic | The line is emitted from inside the `listen` callback, so it appears only after a successful bind and never appears for a failed one |
| Compound liveness probing | Assert target `127.0.0.1:3000`, `http_code` 200, `Content-Length` 14, and body checksum — not the status code alone | Every path returns the same `200`, so a status-only check cannot detect a contract violation |
| Loopback pinning | Always probe `127.0.0.1`, never a routable address or hostname | A non-loopback target produces the identical `curl` exit 7 / `http_code` 000 signature as a dead process |
| Stream capture with external timestamps | Redirect fd 1 and fd 2 at launch and timestamp at capture time | The process cannot self-timestamp; `Date.now`, `new Date`, and `process.hrtime` are all absent |
| Exit-status capture | Have the launching shell or supervisor record the exit code | It is the only cause-of-death signal; `1`, `143`, `130`, `129`, `131`, `140`, and `137` are the observed values |
| Listener and process-age sampling | Watch for the `0100007F:0BB8` entry in state `0A` and for resets of `ps -o etimes=` | An unlogged restart is otherwise invisible, since nothing is emitted on death or on re-launch beyond the banner |
| Resource trend sampling | Periodically read `VmRSS`, `/proc/<pid>/fd` count, and `Threads` | Measured constant at 22 fds and 7 threads, with RSS bounded at 48.2–61.9 MB across 25,000 requests |
| Port serialisation | Ensure exactly one consumer uses `127.0.0.1:3000` at a time | The bind is attempted once with no retry or fallback; a second instance exits 1 |
| Baseline integrity checking | Confirm `git status --porcelain` is empty and `HEAD` is `1a0874d` before each run | The freeze is advisory only — no hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check enforces it |
| Non-destructive deep diagnosis | Use `--report-on-signal` plus `SIGUSR2`, or `SIGUSR1` inspector attach, or relaunch under `NODE_DEBUG=http` | All three were verified; the first two leave the process running |

Two anti-practices are worth recording, because both are natural mistakes against this particular artifact. **Do not scrape `/metrics`** — it returns the greeting, so the scrape succeeds at the HTTP layer and fails at parse time, producing a misleading collector error rather than a clear absence. And **do not send `SIGUSR2` for diagnostics unless `--report-on-signal` is in effect**, because it terminates the process with exit code 140.

#### 6.5.5.4 Conditions That Would Change This Determination

The determination in 6.5.1 is falsifiable. Any one of the following would make a detailed monitoring architecture applicable and would require this section to be rewritten rather than amended.

| Condition | Why It Would Change the Determination |
|---|---|
| A metrics client, exporter, or exposition endpoint is added to `server.js` | Creates a collection tier and a scrape contract where none exists; a metrics pipeline would then need specification |
| A logging framework or any per-request emission is introduced | Turns log volume from constant into traffic-proportional, creating sink, structure, retention, rotation, and privacy concerns that do not currently arise |
| The handler begins to dereference `req` | Makes path-, method-, and header-specific behaviour reachable, which in turn makes a genuine health endpoint and a real negative test case possible |
| A tracing SDK or correlation-identifier generation is added | Creates propagation and sampling concerns; today inbound `traceparent` and `X-Request-Id` are silently dropped, verified by measurement |
| Any dependency is declared in `package.json` | Instrumentation could then arrive transitively; the current zero-dependency lock is what makes that impossible |
| A `start` script, `.env`, or `process.env` read is introduced | Creates the configuration surface through which an agent, preload hook, or `NODE_OPTIONS` value could be enabled without a source change |
| A container, orchestration, or supervisor artifact is added | Introduces probe definitions, restart policies, and an automated detection tier — the layer whose absence Section 5.4.6 identifies as the largest gap |
| A CI/CD workflow is added | Enables scheduled synthetic checks and post-deploy verification; today `npm test` exits 1 by design and nothing can verify a deployment automatically |
| The bind address changes from `127.0.0.1` to a wildcard | Makes the instance reachable by off-host monitors and by orchestrator probes from outside a network namespace, both currently impossible |
| Any SLA, SLO, or threshold is declared in the repository | Gives alerting something to evaluate and makes compliance measurement meaningful; 6.5.5.2 currently has to construct candidate commitments from measurements |

Each of these requires editing one or more of the four tracked files, which constraint C-001 — the change freeze declared in `README.md` — places outside the sanctioned scope of the project. The determination is therefore stable for as long as the freeze holds.

#### 6.5.5.5 Consolidated Capability Traceability

Every capability this section is expected to cover, with its verified status and governing evidence.

| Capability | Verified Status | Governing Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics collection | Absent in-process. Substituted by a twelve-item OS-sourced, PID-scoped catalogue, none of it application-aware | Zero metric tokens; zero dependencies; `/proc` readings in 6.5.2.1 |
| Log aggregation | Absent. One 41-byte line per process lifetime; no structure, sink, rotation, or shipper | `server.js` line 13; stdout still one line after 25,000 requests; Section 5.4.2 |
| Distributed tracing | Absent, and without a referent. Inbound trace context is silently dropped, verified by echo test | Zero tracing tokens; `req` never dereferenced; zero echo of `X-Request-Id` and `traceparent` |
| Alert management | Absent. Rule evaluation must live in the prober; there is no notifier, deduplication, or silencing | Zero alerting tokens; no rule or notifier artifact among 66 probed paths |
| Dashboard design | No definition exists. A twelve-panel operator console is buildable entirely from external commands | No `grafana/` or `dashboard.json`; Diagram 6.5.2-A |
| Health checks | No dedicated check. A de-facto compound probe is adequate for this fixture's contract but cannot report degradation | 17-path probe matrix collapsing to one body signature; Sections 5.4.1 and 6.1.4.4 |
| Performance metrics | None produced. Measured externally by two instruments with the method disclosed per row | 6.5.3.2 baseline table; Sections 5.4.5 and 4.3.1.4 |
| Business metrics | None, and no referent — the system has no domain and writes no data | `server.js` lines 6–10; Section 6.2 |
| SLA monitoring | No SLA, SLO, or error budget exists. Availability and correctness are measurable; error rate is not | Zero `sla`/`slo`/`uptime` tokens; Sections 2.2.1.3 and 5.4.5 |
| Capacity tracking | No limit or quota declared. Capacity is one instance and is a scheduling constraint on port 3000 | Inherited runtime defaults in Section 6.1.3.3; verified `EADDRINUSE`; 6.5.3.5 envelope |
| Alert routing | Detection and routing collapse into one step — a human reads a terminal | Six-condition register and Diagram 6.5.4-A; no notification transport exists |
| Escalation procedures | No tier, severity model, or response commitment. The one real boundary is the change freeze | No `CODEOWNERS`, no on-call artifact; Section 6.1.4.5 binary availability |
| Runbooks | None in the repository. Four are derived here from measured behaviour, sharing one verification step | RB-01 to RB-04 in 6.5.4.3, each executed during verification |
| Post-mortem processes | Undefined, and the system preserves almost no evidence. Reconstruction must be client-side | Seven-row forensic table in 6.5.4.4; no request record of any kind |
| Improvement tracking | Only Git. The freeze makes internal improvement out of scope; improvements are external to the artifact | Single commit `1a0874d`; 14 `.sample` hooks only; `npm test` exits 1 by design |


### 6.5.6 References

#### 6.5.6.1 Repository Files Examined

- `server.js` - The sole executable artifact and the entire source of the system's telemetry. Established the single instrumentation call site (`console.log` at line 13, inside the `server.listen` callback at line 12), the bind constants that the readiness line interpolates (lines 3–4), and the invariant handler (lines 6–10) whose three statements contain no counter, timer, log call, conditional, or `req` dereference. Also established by exhaustive census the absence of `console.error`, `process.stdout`, `perf_hooks`, `process.hrtime`, `Date.now`, `new Date`, `process.memoryUsage`, `process.cpuUsage`, `process.resourceUsage`, `diagnostics_channel`, `util.debuglog`, `inspector`, `async_hooks`, `setInterval`, `setTimeout`, `.on(`, `process.on`, and every metrics, tracing, APM, logging, and health-vocabulary token searched for.
- `package.json` - Established that no observability agent can arrive through the dependency graph or be enabled at launch: no `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, or `peerDependencies`; no `engines` pin (deviation D-005, which leaves the inherited runtime resource defaults unversioned); and exactly one script, `test`, with no `start`, `monitor`, `healthcheck`, or preload-bearing entry into which `NODE_OPTIONS` could be inserted. The deliberately failing `test` script is why nothing in the repository can verify a deployment automatically.
- `package-lock.json` - `lockfileVersion: 3` with a `packages` map containing only the root key. Formal proof of a zero-node dependency graph and therefore that no metrics client, logging framework, tracing SDK, or APM agent is present even transitively.
- `README.md` - Established the change freeze on line 2 (constraint C-001), which is the reason this section documents zero-code-change diagnostic channels rather than instrumentation additions, and which makes the applicability determination stable. Also the source of the artifact's stated purpose, which is why the only value-bearing property to monitor is being present and unchanged.

- `` (repository root) - Contained exactly four first-order files and zero subdirectories. Established the absence of every monitoring artifact class through a probe of 66 conventional paths, none of which exists: no `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose` file, or `.dockerignore` (so no `HEALTHCHECK` directive can exist); no `k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `manifests/`, `helm/`, `Chart.yaml`, or `values.yaml` (so no liveness, readiness, or startup probe definition can exist); no `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, or `.travis.yml`; no `prometheus.yml`, `alertmanager.yml`, `alerts.yml`, or `recording_rules.yml`; no `grafana/`, `grafana.json`, `dashboard.json`, or `dashboards/`; no `otel-collector-config.yaml`, `opentelemetry.js`, `instrumentation.js`, or `tracing.js`; no `newrelic.js`, `datadog.yaml`, `dd-trace.js`, `.sentryclirc`, or `sentry.js`; no `ecosystem.config.js`, `pm2.json`, `Procfile`, `nodemon.json`, systemd unit, or `supervisord.conf`; no `logrotate.conf`, `logger.js`, `winston.js`, or `pino.config.js`; no `healthcheck.js`, `health.js`, `status.js`, `monitor.js`, or `metrics.js`; no `.env`, `config/`, `config.json`, or `settings.json`; no `fluent-bit.conf`, `fluentd.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `vector.toml`, `promtail.yaml`, or `loki.yaml`; and no `observability/`, `monitoring/`, `telemetry/`, or `.well-known/` directory.

- `4.1 System Workflows` and `4.3 Technical Implementation` - The connection-reuse latency comparison (p50 0.077 ms reused versus 0.117 ms per new connection) and the restart-to-readiness timing of about 23 ms, both used as corroborating instruments in the performance baseline.

#### 6.5.6.4 Verification Activities Performed

All runtime verification was performed against a scratch copy of the four tracked files under Node.js v22.23.1; the repository working tree was never modified, and its unmodified state was re-confirmed afterwards (`git ls-files` = 4, `git status --porcelain` = 0 lines, `HEAD` = `1a0874d`, no probe process remaining, no listener on port 3000).

- **Observability artifact absence probe.** 66 conventional monitoring, health-check, supervision, CI, dashboard, tracing, APM, log-shipping, and configuration paths tested for existence; every one absent.
- **Static telemetry census.** Over 100 tokens searched across all four tracked files, covering emission primitives, metrics and tracing vendors, logging frameworks, health and alerting vocabulary, route and endpoint prerequisites, and process-lifecycle hooks. Confirmed exactly one `console.` occurrence and that the only match for `status` is `res.statusCode` on line 7.
- **Startup and readiness measurement.** Three launches timed by polling for the first byte on stdout: 29 ms, 29 ms, 34 ms; stdout exactly one line of 41 bytes; stderr 0 bytes.
- **Seventeen-path health-probe matrix.** `/`, `/health`, `/healthz`, `/health/live`, `/health/ready`, `/ready`, `/readyz`, `/live`, `/livez`, `/status`, `/metrics`, `/debug/vars`, `/-/healthy`, `/-/ready`, `/favicon.ico`, `/admin`, and `/nonexistent-path-xyz` — all `200` / 14 bytes / `text/plain`, collapsing to a single body signature.
- **Request-telemetry invariance.** After more than 1,300 requests across the probe matrix, a 200-sample latency loop, a 1,000-request keep-alive batch, and 100 concurrent requests, stdout remained exactly one line and stderr remained 0 bytes.
- **Externally measured performance baseline.** `curl` `time_total` over 200 requests with a fresh connection each (min 0.112 ms, p50 0.138 ms, p95 0.237 ms, p99 0.346 ms, max 0.876 ms); 1,000 requests over reused connections in 81 ms; 100 concurrent requests at parallelism 50 in 45 ms with zero non-`200` responses.
- **OS-level metric source enumeration.** `/proc/<pid>/status` (`VmRSS`, `VmSize`, `Threads`, `voluntary_ctxt_switches`), `/proc/<pid>/stat` (`utime`, `stime`, `num_threads`, `starttime`), `/proc/<pid>/fd` count, `/proc/<pid>/io` (`rchar`, `wchar`, `syscr`, `syscw`), `/proc/net/tcp` listener and established-connection rows, and `ps -o etimes=`.
- **Failure-signal verification.** Bind conflict producing exit code 1, no readiness line, and a 20-line `EADDRINUSE` stderr trace with `errno: -98` and `syscall: 'listen'`; full signal disposition census yielding exit codes 143, 130, 129, 131, 140, and 137 for `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGQUIT`, `SIGUSR2`, and `SIGKILL`, each exactly `128 + signum` with no shutdown output; and connection-refused signature (`http_code` 000, `curl` exit 7) with nothing listening.
- **Zero-code-change diagnostic channel verification.** `NODE_DEBUG=http` producing 17 stderr lines for 3 requests; `SIGUSR1` activating the inspector on `127.0.0.1:9229` with the process still serving; and `--report-on-signal` plus `SIGUSR2` writing an eleven-section JSON diagnostic report with the process still serving, including `javascriptHeap.totalMemory` of 5,873,664 bytes and a libuv handle count of 11.
- **Response-side observability checks.** Header-block enumeration confirming the status line plus exactly four headers; a two-probe comparison 1.2 seconds apart differing in exactly one line, the `Date` header; and a correlation-echo test confirming zero occurrences of `X-Request-Id` or `traceparent` in the response.
- **npm-level signal verification.** `npm test` exiting 1 with `Error: no test specified`, and `npm start` resolving to `node server.js` through npm's implicit default and running in the foreground with both streams attached to the invoking shell.
- **Diagram render validation.** All three Mermaid diagrams in this section were rendered to SVG with mermaid-cli 11.16.0 before inclusion, each returning a zero exit status, and were audited for balanced `subgraph`/`end` pairs and for the absence of any edge originating from or terminating on a subgraph identifier.

No external or web sources were required for this section. Every statement is grounded in the repository's four tracked files, in direct measurement of a scratch copy of those files, or in the cross-referenced sections of this specification listed above.


## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Approach

#### 6.6.1.1 Applicability Determination

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system.**

The reason is arithmetic before it is architectural. The system under test is `server.js` — fourteen lines totalling 342 bytes — inside a repository of four tracked files, 39 lines and 913 bytes with zero subdirectories. That file contains one request handler with no conditional, no routing, no `req` dereference and no error path, so it has exactly **one** code path and produces exactly **one** response for every input. Twenty-one method-and-path combinations were exercised against a running instance during the preparation of this section and every one returned the identical signature `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes with an identical body checksum. A system with one equivalence class does not need a test pyramid; it needs a small set of invariance assertions.

Two further facts make the determination structural rather than a matter of effort. First, `README.md` line 2 states that this is a test project for backprop integration and directs that it not be modified — constraint C-001 in section 2.4.6 — so no test file, framework configuration, or dependency may be added to the repository. Second, the repository is itself the fixture: the authoritative test suite that consumes it lives outside it, in the "backprop" integration harness that `README.md` names. Section 6.6 therefore documents the **basic unit-testing approach applicable to this artifact**, which is a small out-of-tree behavioural suite, and records for every conventional testing capability what the repository actually provides.

Applicability was adjudicated against five independent tests. A positive result on any one would have made a comprehensive strategy applicable; all five resolve negative.

| Applicability Test | What a Comprehensive Strategy Requires | Repository Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-trivial behavioural surface | Branches, input partitions, or state transitions worth designing cases around | The handler at `server.js` lines 6–10 never dereferences `req`; a 21-case matrix of 7 methods × 3 paths produced one distinct signature and one body checksum | Not present |
| An existing test suite to document | Test files, a runner configuration, and assertions | Zero test files. A repository-wide search for `*test*` and `*spec*` by filename matched nothing, and `describe(`, `it(`, `test(`, `assert`, and `expect(` all return zero matches | Not present |
| Testable module boundaries | Exports, injection seams, or dependency boundaries that can be substituted | `module.exports` and `exports` both return zero matches; the only `require` targets the Node core `http` module; the listener binds during module evaluation | Not present |
| An automation substrate | A CI definition, coverage tooling, and quality gates to hang tests on | No `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, or `.travis.yml`; no coverage configuration; no linter; `.git/hooks` holds only the default `.sample` templates | Not present |
| A changing codebase to protect | Ongoing development that regression tests would guard | One commit, `1a0874d`, introduced all four files; there are no tags, no branches beyond `main`, and a clean working tree. Section 2.5.5 records that any change simultaneously establishes a new baseline and violates F-006-RQ-003 | Not present |

Because the determination is negative, the remainder of this section is written as an **evidence-based verification assessment**. Each area a testing strategy would normally specify is addressed in the same form: the verified status of the conventional mechanism, followed by the basic practice that stands in its place.

| Sub-section | Areas Covered | Form of the Content |
|---|---|---|
| 6.6.1 | Unit, integration, end-to-end and security testing; test environment and test data | Per-area status with measured evidence, the out-of-tree suite that substitutes for an in-repo suite, and two diagrams |
| 6.6.2 | CI/CD integration, triggers, parallelism, reporting, failure and flake handling | The pipeline behaviour a consumer must accommodate, plus the test execution flow diagram |
| 6.6.3 | Coverage targets, success rate, performance thresholds, quality gates, documentation | The metrics that are measurable, those that are not, and why |
| 6.6.4 | References | Every file, folder, specification section and verification activity relied upon |

#### 6.6.1.2 Evidence Base for the Determination

Every artifact class that would evidence a testing strategy was probed for explicitly. The result column reports what a full-tree inspection of the four-file, zero-subdirectory repository found.

| Artifact Class Searched | Role in a Testing Strategy | Result of Inspection |

| Test runner configuration | Selects the framework, roots, transforms and reporters | Absent — no `jest.config.{js,ts,mjs,cjs,json}`, `vitest.config.{js,ts}`, `.mocharc.{json,yml,js}`, `mocha.opts`, `ava.config.js`, `karma.conf.js`, `tap.config.js`, `jasmine.json`, or `protractor.conf.js` |
