Semantic inspection of the indexed repository corroborates the file-level probes: a search for unit test files, test suites and testing framework configuration returned no results, and a search for folders containing automated tests, CI pipeline definitions or quality-assurance tooling returned no results.

Two findings from this table are decisive rather than merely confirmatory. The **zero-dependency lock** means no test framework can arrive through the dependency graph, and the **absence of any script surface beyond `test`** means none can be introduced without editing `package.json`. Adding any conventional testing tool therefore requires modifying a tracked file, which constraint C-001 forbids — which is precisely why the approach documented below is out-of-tree.

#### 6.6.1.3 The Declared Test Command

The repository declares exactly one lifecycle script, and it is a guaranteed failure.

```json
"test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
```

Invoked twice during verification, `npm test` printed its banner `> hello_world@1.0.0 test`, echoed `Error: no test specified`, and exited with status **1** on both occasions.

| Property | Observed Value | Consequence for Testing |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | The `npm init` placeholder, unmodified | Its presence is evidence that no suite was ever written, not that one is expected |
| Exit status | `1`, deterministically | Any pipeline stage wired to `npm test` fails by design; section 1.3.2.4 records CI-gate usage as an unsupported use case (deviation D-003) |
| Output | One line on stdout; no test names, no counts, no report file | There is nothing for a reporter, a coverage tool, or a results parser to consume |
| Requirement trace | F-007-RQ-001, verified by invocation | The failure is the specified behaviour; a passing `npm test` would itself be a contract violation |

The corollary matters for everything that follows: **the repository cannot verify itself**. The only exit status it can produce from a verification command is a failure, so any real assertion must come from outside the four tracked files.

#### 6.6.1.4 Testability of the System Under Test

Before choosing a technique it is worth stating precisely why the conventional ones do not fit. Each row below is a measured or statically verified property of `server.js`, followed by its testing consequence.

| Property of the Implementation | Verified Evidence | Testing Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| No exported surface | `module.exports` and `exports` both return zero matches; the file declares no class, no named function, and no type | The handler cannot be imported and invoked in isolation. There is no unit smaller than the process |
| Binding is a module-evaluation side effect | `server.listen(port, hostname, ...)` executes at top level, lines 12–14 | `require('./server.js')` inside a test process immediately binds port 3000. Importing the module *is* starting the server |
| Bind target is a compiled-in literal | `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` (line 3) and `port = 3000` (line 4); zero `process.env` and zero `process.argv` matches repository-wide | A harness cannot relocate the listener to an ephemeral port, so port 3000 becomes an exclusive precondition of every run |
| One dependency, and it is a core module | The only `require` in the repository targets `http`, at line 1 | There is no dependency boundary at which a stub or fake could be injected |
| Request input is never read | Zero matches for `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers`, and `req.on` | Input partitioning collapses to a single equivalence class; there is no negative case at the application layer, and a `404` is unreachable |
| No `'error'` listener and no shutdown handler | `.on(` returns zero matches | Faults surface as process-level events — an uncaught `EADDRINUSE` and exit 1 — rather than as assertable application behaviour |
| Entry point in the manifest is unresolvable | `main` is `index.js`; no `index.js` exists | `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (deviation D-001, constraint C-005). Tests must target `server.js` by path |

The technique that follows from these constraints is **black-box process-level testing**: spawn `node server.js` as a child process, assert on its standard output and on HTTP responses over loopback, then terminate it. This is the only approach that respects the change freeze, because the alternative — refactoring `server.js` to export its handler — would modify a tracked file.

#### 6.6.1.5 Unit Testing

**There is no unit test in the repository, and no unit smaller than the whole process exists to test.** What is documented here is the basic approach that a consuming harness can apply without adding a single file to the repository or a single package to the lock file.

##### 6.6.1.5.1 Testing Frameworks and Tools

The framework choice is determined by one constraint: nothing may be installed. Node.js ships a test runner and an assertion library in core, and both were verified to resolve on the runtime used for every measurement in this specification — `require('node:test')` and `require('node:assert')` each returned a function, and `node --test` is available.

| Tool | Role in the Approach | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `node:test` | Test declaration, lifecycle hooks (`before`, `after`), and the runner invoked by `node --test` | Available in core on Node.js 22.23.1; requires no `devDependencies` entry |
| `node:assert` | Strict equality assertions on status, headers, body bytes and the readiness banner | Available in core |
| `node:child_process` | `spawn` of `node server.js`, capture of fd 1 and fd 2, and signal-based teardown | Available in core |
| `node:http` | Issues loopback requests and exposes status and headers to the assertions | Available in core; the same module the system under test uses |
| `curl` | Alternative probe for shell-driven checks; used for the 21-case matrix and the oversized-header probe in this section | Present in the verification environment; not required by the repository |
| `git` | Baseline-integrity assertions against commit `1a0874d` | Required, per section 3.6.1 |

Jest, Mocha, Vitest, AVA and Tap were all considered and are all **rejected for this artifact** — not on merit, but because each requires a `devDependencies` entry and a configuration file, and both changes would modify tracked files in violation of constraint C-001. Section 3.6.1 independently confirms that `jest` and `mocha` are neither configured nor installed.

##### 6.6.1.5.2 Test Organisation Structure

The organising principle is that **the suite lives outside the repository**. The repository is a read-only fixture; the tests are an artifact of the consumer.

| Structural Element | Prescribed Arrangement | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Suite location | A directory outside the repository checkout, alongside the consumer's own code | Adding `test/` to the repository would violate the change freeze and change the tracked file count from four |
| Fixture reference | An absolute or configured path to the repository root, used as the `cwd` of the spawned child | The manifest `main` field cannot be used to resolve the entry point (deviation D-001) |
| File granularity | One suite file is sufficient; the entire contract is six assertions | There is no module decomposition to mirror, because the repository has no modules |
| Grouping | Group by observable channel — startup banner, HTTP response, output invariance, process lifecycle, baseline integrity | These are the four verified signal boundaries plus the git baseline; they are the only axes along which behaviour varies |
| Lifecycle hooks | `before` spawns the server and waits for the banner; `after` terminates it | Section 6.6.1.6 documents why polling for the banner is preferable to a fixed sleep |

##### 6.6.1.5.3 Mocking Strategy

**No mocking is required, and there is nothing that could usefully be mocked.** This is a consequence of the dependency graph, not a stylistic choice.

| Candidate Mock Target | Present in This System? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Third-party libraries | No — `package-lock.json` locks zero packages | Nothing to intercept; `proxyquire`-style module substitution has no target |
| Outbound HTTP or service calls | No — the repository contains no client, and zero matches exist for `https` | `nock` and `msw` have no request to intercept |
| Database or cache clients | No — section 6.2 establishes that nothing is persisted | No in-memory substitute or fake is needed |
| Filesystem and clock | No — zero matches for `fs.`, `Date.now`, and `setTimeout` | No fake timers and no temporary-directory fixtures are needed |
| The Node core `http` module | Yes, but it is the transport itself | Substituting it would replace the behaviour under test rather than isolate it |

The single test double that the approach does use is not a mock at all but a **process boundary**: `child_process.spawn` stands in for whatever normally launches the server, which lets the suite own the process lifecycle and read fd 1 and fd 2 directly.

##### 6.6.1.5.4 Code Coverage Requirements

**No coverage requirement, threshold, or tool is declared anywhere in the repository**, and line coverage of `server.js` is not obtainable with built-in tooling. Both halves of that statement were verified by measurement.

Running the out-of-tree suite under `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` produced a coverage report covering **only the suite file** at 100% line, branch and function coverage; `server.js` did not appear, because it executes in a separate child process. An attempt to profile the child directly with `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` produced **zero** coverage artifacts when the process was terminated by `SIGTERM` and again when terminated by `SIGINT`, while a control run against a cleanly exiting script produced one artifact. The cause is documented elsewhere in this specification: `server.js` registers no `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler, so it never exits cleanly and the V8 profile is never flushed.

Coverage is therefore expressed as **behavioural contract coverage** rather than line coverage, and the target is 100% of the observable contract.

| Coverage Dimension | Target | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Observable contract coverage | 100% — status, content type, body bytes, readiness banner, output invariance, exit status | Six assertions cover every element of the published contract in sections 2.2 and 6.5.3.1 |
| Statement coverage of `server.js` | 100% by construction, verified by inspection rather than instrumentation | Lines 1, 3, 4, 6 and 12–14 execute at startup; lines 7–9 execute on the first request. A single successful GET after a successful launch executes all fourteen lines |
| Branch coverage | Not applicable — the file contains no conditional | Zero `if`, `switch`, `try`, or ternary constructs; one code path only |
| Instrumented line coverage | Not obtainable | Measured: `--experimental-test-coverage` attributes nothing to a child process, and `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` produces no artifact for a signal-terminated process |

##### 6.6.1.5.5 Test Naming Conventions

No naming convention exists in the repository, because no test exists. The convention prescribed for an out-of-tree suite is chosen to make each name a restatement of the assertion, since with one code path a test name is the only documentation of intent.

| Element | Convention | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Suite file | `<fixture-name>.test.js`, discovered by `node --test` | `hello-world-fixture.test.js` |
| Test name | Present-tense behavioural sentence naming the exact expected value | `emits the exact 41-byte readiness banner` |
| Invariance test name | State the invariant and the sweep breadth | `returns 200, text/plain and 14 bytes for every method and path` |
| Negative test name | Name the condition and the runtime-owned outcome | `rejects an oversized header with 431 without invoking the handler` |
| Integrity test name | Name the baseline explicitly | `working tree is clean and HEAD is 1a0874d` |

##### 6.6.1.5.6 Test Data Management

Test data management is almost entirely absent as a concern, because every value the system emits is a literal compiled into the frozen source. The five constants at `server.js` lines 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 constitute the whole of the fixture data, and the expected values in the suite are copies of them. Section 6.6.1.10 documents the resulting data flow and the concerns that do not arise.

##### 6.6.1.5.7 Example Test Pattern

The pattern below is the shape of the entire suite: a lifecycle hook that spawns the fixture and waits for its banner, followed by strict assertions on invariant values.

```javascript
before(async () => { child = spawn(process.execPath, ['server.js'], { cwd: REPO });
  await new Promise(r => child.stdout.once('data', d => { banner = d.toString(); r(); })); });
```

```javascript
test('returns 200, text/plain and 14 bytes for every method and path', async () => {
  const r = await request('/anything?q=1', 'POST');
  assert.strictEqual(r.status, 200); assert.strictEqual(r.body, 'Hello, World!\n'); });
```

This pattern was executed during the preparation of this section against an unmodified copy of the repository. A two-test suite asserting the exact banner and the response invariance across `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE` reported `# pass 2`, `# fail 0` with a total `duration_ms` of roughly 85 ms under the TAP reporter, with **zero packages installed and no repository file modified**.

#### 6.6.1.6 Integration Testing

**There is no service integration to test.** Section 6.3 establishes the integration surface, and the code confirms it: the only `require` targets a core module, no outbound client exists, and zero matches exist for `https`. The one integration boundary in the system is the loopback socket between a client and the process, which makes "integration testing" and "API testing" the same activity here.

##### 6.6.1.6.1 Service Integration Test Approach

| Integration Boundary | Exists? | Test Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Client to HTTP listener over loopback | Yes — the only boundary | Spawn the process, issue requests to `127.0.0.1:3000`, assert the full response signature |
| Process to standard output | Yes | Capture fd 1 and assert the exact 41-byte banner and a line count of exactly one |
| Process to operating system | Yes | Assert the exit status after termination: `143` for `SIGTERM`, `130` for `SIGINT`, `1` for a bind conflict |
| Service-to-service or message broker | No | Nothing to integrate; no client, queue, or broker exists in any tracked file |

##### 6.6.1.6.2 API Testing Strategy

The API is one endpoint that answers every request identically, so the strategy is an **invariance matrix** rather than a per-endpoint contract suite. The matrix executed for this section swept 7 methods — `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS` and the non-standard `PURGE` — across 3 paths (`/`, `/health`, `/deep/path?x=1`), giving 21 cases. Every case returned `200|14|text/plain` with an identical body checksum, and the body length was independently confirmed at 14 bytes.

| Assertion | Expected Value | Source of the Expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Status code | `200` for every method and path, including non-standard methods | `server.js` line 7; F-002-RQ-001 |
| Content type | `text/plain`, with no `charset` parameter | `server.js` line 8; F-002-RQ-002. This is the only header set by repository code |
| Body | Exactly `Hello, World!` plus a newline — 14 bytes, one checksum across all cases | `server.js` line 9; F-002-RQ-003 |
| Runtime-supplied headers | `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, `Content-Length: 14` | Node.js `http` defaults, not repository code — assert loosely or not at all, since deviation D-005 leaves the runtime unpinned |

One trap deserves explicit statement because it will mislead an ordinary API test suite: **`/health` returns `200` with the same 14-byte body as every other path**. Section 6.5.3.1 measured this across 17 conventional probe paths, all of which collapsed to a single body signature. A suite that treats a `200` from `/health` as a health signal is asserting nothing, and a suite that expects `404` from an unknown path will fail against correct behaviour.

##### 6.6.1.6.3 Database Integration Testing

**Not applicable.** Section 6.2 establishes that the system performs no persistence of any kind; the repository contains no database client, no schema, no migration, and no `fs.` usage. There is no test database to provision, no fixture to seed, no transaction to roll back, and no migration to verify.

##### 6.6.1.6.4 External Service Mocking

**Not applicable.** The system makes no outbound call, so there is no external dependency to stub, no contract test to write against a provider, and no service virtualisation to configure. This is the same conclusion 6.6.1.5.3 reaches from the unit-testing side, and it holds for the same reason: `package-lock.json` locks zero packages and the only `require` targets Node core.

##### 6.6.1.6.5 Test Environment Management

The environment is a single host, and the binding constraint is not compute but a socket. Both facts were verified by measurement.

| Environment Requirement | Verified Behaviour | Management Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Port 3000 free on loopback | A second `node server.js` while the first holds the port exits **1** with an uncaught `EADDRINUSE` (errno −98, syscall `listen`) | Suites must acquire port 3000 exclusively and release it before the next run; there is no retry and no port fallback |
| Executor co-located with the fixture | A request to the host's routable address `10.76.1.16:3000` failed to connect while `127.0.0.1:3000` returned `200` | The test runner must share the host or network namespace. Section 3.6.4 notes that an orchestrator probe from outside a container's namespace would fail against a healthy instance |
| No configuration to manage | Zero `process.env` and zero `process.argv` matches repository-wide | There is no test-specific configuration, no `.env.test`, and no environment matrix; every run is identical by construction |
| Readiness synchronisation | The banner appeared 31.1 ms after `spawn` in a timed run; section 6.5 reports 29 ms, 29 ms and 34 ms across three launches | Poll fd 1 for the banner rather than sleeping a fixed interval; its absence is a reliable negative signal |
| Dependency provisioning | `npm ci` reported "up to date, audited 1 package in 137 ms", found 0 vulnerabilities, and created no `node_modules`; wall time 0.186 s | The install stage is optional and must not assert that `node_modules` exists (assumption A-004) |

#### 6.6.1.7 End-to-End Testing

For this system, end-to-end testing is the **only** kind of testing that exists, because the smallest testable unit is the whole process. The scenarios below are the complete set derivable from the four verified signal boundaries; each was executed during the preparation of this section.

##### 6.6.1.7.1 End-to-End Scenarios

| ID | Scenario | Expected Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| E2E-01 | Cold start to readiness | `spawn` of `node server.js` yields the exact 41-byte banner on fd 1 within tens of milliseconds; stderr remains empty |
| E2E-02 | Response invariance sweep | 21 method-and-path cases each return `200`, `text/plain` and the same 14-byte body checksum |
| E2E-03 | Output invariance under traffic | After the sweep, fd 1 still contains exactly one line — proving no per-request logging exists |
| E2E-04 | Bind conflict | A second instance exits `1` with an uncaught `EADDRINUSE` trace and never prints a banner |
| E2E-05 | Oversized-header rejection | A request carrying a roughly 20,000-byte header returns **431** while fd 1 stays at 41 bytes, proving the runtime answered and the handler was never invoked |
| E2E-06 | Loopback confinement | The host's routable address refuses the connection while `127.0.0.1` succeeds |
| E2E-07 | Clean teardown | `SIGTERM` terminates the process with exit `143`, emits no shutdown output, and releases the port immediately |
| E2E-08 | Fixture integrity | `git status --porcelain` is empty, `git ls-files` returns four paths, and `HEAD` is `1a0874d` |
| E2E-09 | Dependency-free install | `npm ci` exits `0`, audits one package, reports zero vulnerabilities, and creates no `node_modules` |
| E2E-10 | Declared test command | `npm test` prints `Error: no test specified` and exits `1`, as F-007-RQ-001 requires |

##### 6.6.1.7.2 UI Automation Approach

**Not applicable — there is no user interface to automate.** The repository contains no HTML, CSS, template, client-side script, static asset, or `public/` directory; the sole response is `text/plain` with a fixed 14-byte body and no markup. A browser pointed at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` would render one line of plain text with no scripting, no styling, no form, and no navigable link. There is consequently no page object to model, no selector to maintain, and no interaction to drive.

##### 6.6.1.7.3 Test Data Setup and Teardown

Setup and teardown reduce to process lifecycle, because there is no state anywhere in the system.

| Phase | Action | Verified Property |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Confirm the baseline, confirm port 3000 is free, `spawn` the process, wait for the banner | The banner appears only after a successful bind, so it is a true readiness gate |
| Between cases | Nothing — no reset, no truncation, no cache eviction | The handler is stateless; 21 cases in sequence produced one signature, and section 6.5 reports the same invariance at 25,000 requests |
| Teardown | Send `SIGTERM`, confirm exit `143`, confirm the port is released | No handler runs, so termination is immediate with no drain and no output |
| Failure teardown | Kill the child even when assertions fail | A leaked child holds port 3000 and will cause the *next* run to fail with `EADDRINUSE` rather than with the real defect |

Because no data is ever written — section 6.5.3.5 records zero log and storage growth — there is no cleanup obligation beyond reaping the process.

##### 6.6.1.7.4 Performance Testing Requirements

**The repository declares no performance requirement, threshold, timeout, or throughput target.** Section 2.2.1.3 governs this: any latency or throughput objective for the system must be established by the consuming tooling, because none can be sourced from the repository. Performance testing therefore has no acceptance criterion to test against, and the values below are **measured baselines for regression comparison only, not commitments**.

| Measurement | Observed Value | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Boot to readiness banner | 31.1 ms | Timed from `spawn` to first byte on fd 1 |
| Loopback request latency | p50 0.20 ms, p95 0.62 ms, p99 1.27 ms, max 6.25 ms | 200 sequential GETs, a new connection per request, timed with `process.hrtime.bigint()` |
| Latency, second instrument | p50 0.138 ms and p95 0.237 ms per new connection; p50 0.064 ms and p99 0.184 ms reused | Section 6.5.3.2, `curl` and an in-process keep-alive client |
| Sequential throughput | About 12,300 to 12,761 requests per second over reused connections | Section 6.5.3.2, two independent instruments |
| Concurrency | 100 requests at parallelism 50 completed in 45 ms with zero non-`200` responses | Section 6.5.3.2 |

Any performance suite must disclose its connection-handling method, because the two latency rows above differ by roughly a factor of two purely on that basis — latency here is dominated by transport rather than by work.

##### 6.6.1.7.5 Cross-Browser Testing Strategy

**Not applicable, for three independent reasons.** The response is `text/plain` with no markup, script, or style, so no rendering-engine difference can manifest. The listener binds `127.0.0.1` only, so no remote browser or hosted browser grid could reach it — section 3.6.4 records that even a container port mapping would not. And the handler never reads a request header, so user-agent negotiation, cookie handling, CORS preflight, and cache-directive behaviour are all structurally unreachable: the zero matches for `cors`, `csrf`, and `helmet` in the security census confirm there is no browser-facing policy to vary.

#### 6.6.1.8 Security Testing

Security testing is included here because the section's scope requires it, and because the answer is unusually clean: the attack surface is small enough to enumerate exhaustively, and most conventional test classes have no target. A security-vocabulary census across all four tracked files returned **zero** matches for every one of `authorization`, `token`, `password`, `secret`, `apiKey`, `api_key`, `credential`, `https`, `tls`, `ssl`, `cert`, `cors`, `helmet`, `csrf`, `sanitize`, `validate`, and `escape`.

| Security Test Class | Applicability and Method | Verified Result |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency and supply-chain scanning | `npm audit` in the repository root | "found 0 vulnerabilities", exit `0`, one package audited. Section 3.6.5 records it as safe to run and incapable of gating |
| Lockfile integrity | Read `package-lock.json` | `lockfileVersion: 3` with only the root entry — no resolved URL and no integrity hash to verify, because no package is locked |
| Static application security testing | Manual review is exhaustive at 14 lines; no SAST tool is configured | No `eval`, `child_process`, `fs`, `crypto`, or `vm` usage in `server.js`; no dynamic code path exists |
| Secret scanning | Token census across all four files | Zero credential markers; section 3.6.7 records that no secret is required at any stage |
| Authentication and authorisation testing | Not applicable — no such code exists | Zero matches for `authorization` and `token`; every caller is anonymous and receives the identical response |
| Transport security testing | Not applicable — no TLS | Zero matches for `https`, `tls`, and `cert`; the listener is plaintext HTTP on loopback |
| Input validation and injection testing | Structurally unreachable at the application layer | `req` is never dereferenced, so no request datum reaches an interpreter, a query, a filesystem path, or a template |
| Fuzzing and malformed-input testing | Exercises the Node runtime, not repository code | A roughly 20,000-byte header produced **431** while fd 1 remained at 41 bytes, proving the handler was never invoked and no application-side record exists |
| Network exposure testing | Probe every interface | The routable address refused the connection while loopback succeeded — the smallest possible network attack surface |
| Denial-of-service resilience testing | No control exists to test | Section 6.5.3.5 records no rate limiting, no admission control, and no `maxConnections` cap; overload behaviour is a platform property |
| Tamper and integrity testing | The most valuable security check available | `git status --porcelain` empty and `HEAD` equal to `1a0874d`; the change freeze is advisory only, with no hook, `CODEOWNERS`, or CI check enforcing it |

The security-testing conclusion is that **integrity testing matters more than vulnerability testing for this artifact**. There is no dependency to patch, no credential to leak, no input to sanitise and no interface to expose; the only realistic security event is an unauthorised edit to one of the four tracked files, and the only test that detects it is a git baseline assertion.

The diagram below is the complete test environment. It shows the out-of-tree executor, the mandatory co-location boundary that the loopback bind imposes, the frozen artifact that must be read without modification, and — kept separate so that inherited capability is not mistaken for provisioned infrastructure — the conventional test infrastructure verified absent.

Resource requirements for a full verification run are correspondingly small, and every figure below was measured.

| Resource | Requirement | Measured Basis |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | One core is sufficient for the fixture and the runner together | The handler is single-threaded; section 6.5.3.5 records about 0.18 s of CPU for 1,300 requests |
| Memory | Well under 256 MB for the pair of processes | Fixture RSS measured at 51,616 kB and 58,644 kB in two runs; section 6.5 reports a 48.2–61.9 MB envelope across 25,000 requests |
| Wall-clock time | Sub-second for the behavioural suite | A two-test out-of-tree suite completed in about 85 ms; `npm ci` adds 0.186 s |
| Network | Loopback only; no egress and no registry access | The routable address refuses connections; `npm ci --offline` exits `0` per section 3.6.7 |
| Storage | Read-only access to 913 bytes across four files; no writable volume | Section 3.6.7 records that no write access is needed and nothing is persisted |
| Exclusive resource | TCP port 3000 on `127.0.0.1`, held for the duration of the run | Assumption A-002; a second bind exits `1` with `EADDRINUSE` |
| Credentials | None at any stage | Zero credential markers repository-wide; no `.npmrc` |

#### 6.6.1.10 Test Data Management and Flow

Test data management for this system inverts the usual arrangement: the **inputs** are supplied entirely by the test and are then discarded unread, while the **expected values** are literals compiled into the frozen source. There is no external fixture file, no factory, and no seeded store — a claim the repository proves by containing no such artifact and no filesystem access at all.

**Diagram 6.6.1-B — Test Data Flow: Discarded Inputs, In-Source Fixture Literals, Emitted Data, and the Assertion Set**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs["Test Inputs - supplied entirely by the test, never read by the system"]
        M["HTTP method<br/>GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, PURGE"]
        P["Request path and query<br/>/, /health, /deep/path?x=1"]
        H["Request headers<br/>including Authorization and traceparent"]
        BODY["Request body<br/>arbitrary payload"]
    end

    DISCARD{"Does the handler dereference req?<br/>zero matches for req.url, req.method, req.headers"}

    subgraph Fixture["Fixture Data - compiled into the frozen source, not externalised"]

        C2["port literal 3000<br/>server.js line 4"]
        C3["status literal 200<br/>server.js line 7"]
        C4["content type literal text/plain<br/>server.js line 8"]
        C5["payload literal Hello, World! plus newline<br/>server.js line 9, 14 bytes"]
    end

    subgraph Emitted["Emitted Data - the complete observable output"]
        R1["Status line 200 OK"]
        R2["Content-Type text/plain, set by repository code"]
        R3["Body of exactly 14 bytes, one checksum for every case"]
        R4["Runtime-supplied headers<br/>Date, Connection, Keep-Alive, Content-Length"]
        R5["One 41-byte readiness line on fd 1"]
    end

    subgraph Assertions["Assertion Set - the entire testable contract"]
        AS1["assert.strictEqual on status, expect 200"]
        AS2["assert.strictEqual on content-type, expect text/plain"]
        AS3["assert.strictEqual on body, expect the 14-byte literal"]
        AS4["assert.strictEqual on the banner string"]
        AS5["assert on stdout line count, expect 1"]
        AS6["assert git status is empty and HEAD is 1a0874d"]
    end

    subgraph NoData["Test Data Concerns That Do Not Arise"]
        N1["No seed script, migration or schema"]
        N2["No factory, builder or faker"]
        N3["No teardown or truncation step"]
        N4["No sensitive or personal data"]
        N5["No environment-specific variant"]
        N1 -.- N2
        N2 -.- N3
        N3 -.- N4
        N4 -.- N5
    end

    M --> DISCARD
    P --> DISCARD
    H --> DISCARD
    BODY --> DISCARD
    DISCARD -->|"no - every input is discarded unread"| C3

    C3 --> R1
    C4 --> R2
    C5 --> R3
    C1 --> R5
    C2 --> R5

    R1 --> AS1
    R2 --> AS2
    R3 --> AS3
    R5 --> AS4
    R5 --> AS5
    R4 -.->|"attributed to the Node runtime, asserted only loosely"| AS2

    AS3 --> VERDICT{"Do all assertions hold?"}
    AS4 --> VERDICT
    AS6 --> VERDICT
    VERDICT -->|"yes"| OK(["Fixture is byte-correct and unmodified"])
    VERDICT -->|"no - body or banner differs"| DRIFT(["Source drift - the handler has one code path,<br/>so a deviant response implies an edit, see RB-03"])
```

Two properties of this flow deserve emphasis. First, **input variety buys nothing**: because the decision node resolves negative for every input, adding methods, paths, headers or bodies increases case count without increasing coverage — the 21-case matrix and section 6.5's 2,000-distinct-path sweep produce the same single signature. Its value is therefore as a *proof of invariance*, not as partition coverage. Second, **a failed assertion has only one plausible cause**. With one code path, a deviant response cannot be produced by the unmodified source, so a body or banner mismatch is evidence of source drift rather than of runtime malfunction — which is why the diagram routes that outcome to the baseline-restoration runbook in section 6.5.4.3.


### 6.6.2 Test Automation

**No test automation exists in the repository.** There is no pipeline definition, no scheduler, no active Git hook, no reporter configuration, and no retry policy — and the only automated command the repository declares, `npm test`, terminates with exit status 1 by design. This sub-section therefore documents two things: the automation behaviour a **consuming** pipeline must accommodate, each item grounded in a measured result, and the automation capabilities available from the Node.js runtime without adding a dependency or editing a tracked file.

#### 6.6.2.1 Test Execution Flow

The diagram below is the complete execution flow of a verification cycle against this artifact. It shows the one in-repository gate that can pass, the declared test command that fails by design, the install stage that is a verified no-op, the out-of-tree behavioural suite that does the real work, and the two fault paths that block a run.

**Diagram 6.6.2-A — Test Execution Flow: Baseline Gate, the Failing Declared Command, the No-Op Install, the Out-of-Tree Suite, and the Blocking Fault Paths**


The shape of the diagram is the finding. The stage that a conventional pipeline treats as authoritative — Stage 2 — always fails, and the stage that actually establishes correctness — Stage 4 — is not defined by the repository at all. A pipeline that wires its gate to Stage 2 rather than Stage 4 will report a failure for a perfectly correct artifact.

#### 6.6.2.2 CI/CD Integration

**No CI/CD definition exists.** Every conventional path was probed and is absent: `.github/` and therefore any workflow file, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `.travis.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `appveyor.yml`, `.drone.yml`, `buildkite.yml`, `Makefile`, and `Procfile`. Section 3.6.5 records the same result and adds the relevant nuance: the repository is hosted on GitHub, but no workflow definition accompanies it.

The engineering content that matters is therefore what a consuming pipeline must do differently. Each row below follows from a measured behaviour.

| Pipeline Stage | Measured Behaviour Against This Repository | Required Accommodation |
|---|---|---|
| Checkout | Single commit `1a0874d` on `main`; clean working tree; no tags | Add a baseline assertion — `git status --porcelain` empty and `HEAD` equal to `1a0874d` — as the first gate (F-006-RQ-003) |
| Install | `npm ci` reports "up to date, audited 1 package in 137 ms" and creates no `node_modules`; wall time 0.186 s | Must not assert that `node_modules` exists (assumption A-004); the stage is optional |
| Build | No build system, no transpile, no bundle | Must not require a build target or an output directory |
| Lint and type check | No configuration for any tool, and none installed | Must not require a lint or type-check stage; there is nothing to configure it against |
| Unit and integration test | `npm test` exits **1** deterministically | Must skip the stage or explicitly tolerate exit 1 (deviation D-003), and run the out-of-tree suite instead to obtain a real verdict |
| Security audit | `npm audit` returns "found 0 vulnerabilities" with exit `0` across one audited package | Safe to run; will never gate, so it should not be relied on as a meaningful control |
| Package and publish | No `files` allowlist, no `publishConfig`, no `repository` field, no `private` flag | No release stage is meaningful; distribution is by Git checkout |

Two pipeline-level constraints deserve calling out because they are easy to violate accidentally. **The runner must be co-located with the fixture** — a hosted runner that spawns the process in one container and probes it from another cannot reach the loopback listener, and section 3.6.4 records that even a published container port mapping would not. And **the pipeline must serialise its use of port 3000**, because concurrent jobs on a shared runner will collide.

#### 6.6.2.3 Automated Test Triggers

**No trigger mechanism exists inside the repository.** There is no workflow with a `push`, `pull_request`, or `schedule` event; `.git/hooks` contains only the default `.sample` templates, so no `pre-commit`, `pre-push`, or `post-receive` hook fires; and there is no `.husky/`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, or `lefthook.yml`. Nothing inside the repository can start a test run, which also means nothing inside it enforces the change freeze — section 3.6.5 records enforcement as by convention only, with no `CODEOWNERS` file either.

Every trigger is therefore owned by the consumer. The three that the evidence supports are:

| Trigger | Rationale Grounded in Evidence | Cadence Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Before each consuming integration run | The fixture's whole value is being present and byte-correct when a consumer needs it; a stale or drifted fixture invalidates the consumer's own result | Run the baseline assertion and a single compound probe; both complete in well under a second |
| On any change to the four tracked files | Section 2.5.5 records that any change simultaneously establishes a new requirement baseline and violates F-006-RQ-003 | Detection is a `git status`/`git rev-parse` comparison, cheap enough to run unconditionally |
| On runtime upgrade | Deviation D-005 leaves the Node.js version unpinned, and the response headers `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Date` and `Content-Length` come from runtime defaults rather than repository code | Re-establish the measured baselines in 6.6.1.7.4 after any interpreter change |

#### 6.6.2.4 Parallel Test Execution

**Parallel execution is structurally impossible on a single host, and this is the sharpest automation constraint the artifact imposes.** The cause is measured, not theoretical: launching a second `node server.js` while the first holds the port produces an uncaught `EADDRINUSE` error (errno −98, syscall `listen`) and exit status 1, because `port = 3000` and `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` are compiled-in literals with no `process.env` override and the bind is attempted exactly once with no retry and no fallback.

The distinction that matters is between the runner and the fixture: the Node.js test runner on the verified toolchain **can** parallelise — `--test-concurrency`, `--test-shard`, and `--test-name-pattern` are all available — but the fixture cannot tolerate it.

| Parallelisation Strategy | Viability | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrent test files in one process tree | **Not viable** — pin the runner with `--test-concurrency=1` | Every worker after the first fails to bind port 3000 |
| Concurrent requests within one test | **Viable** | 100 requests at parallelism 50 all returned `200` in 45 ms with zero non-`200` responses, per section 6.5.3.2 |
| Sharding across separate hosts or network namespaces | **Viable, and the only true parallelisation route** | Each shard gets its own loopback stack and therefore its own port 3000 |
| Multiple fixture instances on one host | **Not viable** | Exactly one instance per host; the second exits 1 |
| Reusing one long-lived fixture across suites | **Viable and recommended** | The handler is stateless and output is traffic-independent, so cross-test interference is impossible |

The practical consequence is that the suite is fast because it is small, not because it is parallel — a two-test suite completed in about 85 ms, so serialisation costs nothing here.

#### 6.6.2.5 Test Reporting Requirements

**The repository produces no test report of any kind.** `npm test` emits one line of prose and no machine-readable artifact, so there is nothing for a results parser, a trend dashboard, or a coverage service to ingest. No reporter configuration exists, and no `coverage/`, `lcov.info`, or JUnit output directory is present.

Reporting capability is nevertheless available from the runtime at zero installation cost. All four built-in reporters below were exercised against the out-of-tree suite during the preparation of this section.

| Reporter | Output Observed | Suitable For |
|---|---|---|
| `spec` | Human-readable tree ending in `duration_ms 82.121596` | Local runs and terminal output |
| `tap` | TAP version 13 with per-test `ok` lines and a summary block ending `duration_ms 89.291548` | Streaming consumption and TAP-aware CI |
| `dot` | Compact progress output | Large suites; of little value for a two-test suite |
| `junit` | JUnit XML terminating in `</testsuites>` | CI results parsing and historical trend storage |

`--test-reporter-destination` is also available, so a report can be written to a file without a wrapper script. The reporting requirements that follow from the artifact's nature are minimal but specific: emit JUnit XML for the CI parser, retain the **exact banner string** and the **body checksum** in the failure output rather than a boolean, and record the Node.js version with every run, because deviation D-005 means the runtime is not pinned by the repository and the runtime supplies four of the five response headers.

#### 6.6.2.6 Failed Test Handling

Failure handling for this artifact is unusual in one respect: **a genuine assertion failure has essentially one cause**, so blanket retries are counterproductive. With a single code path and an invariant response, a deviant body or banner cannot be produced by the unmodified source.

| Failure Mode | Correct Handling | Evidence and Cross-Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `npm test` exits 1 | Expected. Record it and continue; do not treat it as a defect | Deviation D-003; F-007-RQ-001 verified by invocation |
| Bind conflict — no banner, exit 1, `EADDRINUSE` trace | Identify and stop the port holder, then relaunch. Do **not** retry blindly; there is no port fallback | Runbook RB-02 in section 6.5.4.3.2 |
| Banner absent with empty stderr | Treat as a launch failure — usually the wrong working directory or a missing runtime — not as a slow start | Condition AL-05 in section 6.5.5.1; readiness measured at 26.9–34 ms across all runs |
| Status `200` but body, length or content type differs | Treat as source drift: verify `git status --porcelain` and `HEAD`, restore the baseline, then re-run | Runbook RB-03; the handler has one code path |
| A `431` or `408` response | Not an application defect. These are runtime-generated; the handler is never invoked and leaves no record | Measured: a roughly 20,000-byte header returned 431 while fd 1 stayed at 41 bytes |
| Suite aborts leaving the child alive | Kill the child in a failure-safe teardown | A leaked child holds port 3000 and causes the *next* run to fail with `EADDRINUSE` rather than with the real defect |

Two handling rules follow from measured behaviour. **Assert on the first failure rather than after N consecutive failures**, because availability is binary — section 6.1.4.5 establishes there is no degraded state to wait out. And **never resolve a failure by editing the fixture**: section 6.5.4.2 identifies the change freeze as the single genuine escalation boundary the artifact has, so any failure whose remediation requires a source change must be escalated rather than fixed in place.

#### 6.6.2.7 Flaky Test Management

**No flaky test exists, because no test exists** — but the out-of-tree approach has three identifiable flake sources, and all three are properties of the harness rather than of the system under test. The system itself is exceptionally resistant to flakiness: the response is invariant across 21 measured cases here and across 2,000 distinct paths and 25,000 sequential requests in section 6.5, it holds no state between requests, and it emits no traffic-dependent output.

| Flake Source | Mechanism | Mitigation Grounded in Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Port contention | A previous run's child, or a concurrent job, still holds `127.0.0.1:3000`; the new instance exits 1 | Serialise port access; verify the port is free before spawning; guarantee teardown even on assertion failure |
| Fixed-duration readiness waits | A hard-coded sleep races against a startup measured at 26.9–34 ms | Poll fd 1 for the 41-byte banner instead of sleeping; the banner is emitted only after a successful bind, so it is a true gate |
| Cold-start latency in performance assertions | The first probe is materially slower than the steady state — 3.4 ms versus a 0.138 ms p50 in section 6.5.3.1, and a 6.25 ms max against a 0.20 ms p50 in this section's run | Warm up before measuring, report percentiles rather than single samples, and never gate on a latency figure the repository does not declare |

The genuine anti-flake practice here is to **assert only on values the repository actually fixes** — status, content type, body bytes, and the banner string — and to treat runtime-supplied headers and every latency figure as informational, since deviation D-005 leaves the runtime that produces them unversioned.


### 6.6.3 Quality Metrics

**No quality metric, coverage threshold, success-rate requirement, or performance budget is declared anywhere in the repository.** The tokens `coverage`, `nyc`, `c8`, `lint`, and `audit` all return zero matches across the four tracked files, and no configuration file exists that could carry a threshold. This sub-section therefore separates two things that are easy to conflate: the **configured target**, which is uniformly absent, and the **evidence-derived expected value**, which this specification measured and which a consuming harness can legitimately assert against.

#### 6.6.3.1 Code Coverage Targets

The repository sets no coverage target and provides no tool to measure one. Section 6.6.1.5.4 records the measured reason that instrumented line coverage of `server.js` is not obtainable: `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` attributes coverage only to the suite file because the fixture runs in a child process, and `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` produced zero artifacts under both `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` because `server.js` registers no shutdown handler and never exits cleanly — a control run against a cleanly exiting script produced one artifact, confirming the mechanism itself works.

| Coverage Metric | Target | Status and Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Observable contract coverage | **100%** — status, content type, body bytes, readiness banner, output invariance, exit status | Achievable and achieved; six assertions cover the entire published contract |
| Statement coverage of `server.js` | **100%**, established by inspection | All fourteen lines execute from one successful launch plus one successful request; lines 1, 3, 4, 6 and 12–14 at startup, lines 7–9 on the first request |
| Branch coverage | **Not applicable** | The file contains no `if`, `switch`, `try`, or ternary; there is exactly one code path |
| Instrumented line coverage | **Not obtainable** | Measured: child-process execution defeats `--experimental-test-coverage`, and signal termination defeats `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` |
| Coverage of the runtime-owned fault paths | **Partial and bounded** | The `431` path was exercised; `400` and `408` belong to the Node `http` parser and timeout machinery rather than to repository code |

The honest formulation is that **a coverage percentage would be a misleading metric for this artifact**. A single GET request against a running instance already executes every line, so an instrumented figure of 100% would convey almost nothing; the meaningful measure is whether all six contract assertions ran and passed.

#### 6.6.3.2 Test Success Rate Requirements

| Verification Activity | Required Result | Measured Result |
|---|---|---|
| Out-of-tree behavioural suite | 100% pass — there is no acceptable failure, because a failure implies source drift | 2 of 2 passed in about 85 ms with `# fail 0` under the TAP reporter |
| Response invariance matrix | 100% of cases return the identical signature | 21 of 21 returned `200|14|text/plain` with one body checksum |
| Baseline integrity assertion | 100% — clean working tree and `HEAD` equal to `1a0874d` | Verified before, during and after all measurement; `git status --porcelain` empty every time |
| Dependency audit | Zero vulnerabilities | "found 0 vulnerabilities" across one audited package, exit `0` |
| Declared test command | **Expected failure** — exit 1 is the specified behaviour | Exit 1 on both invocations, with `Error: no test specified` (F-007-RQ-001) |

The last row is the carve-out that any success-rate calculation must encode: `npm test` is the one command whose **failure** constitutes a pass, and a passing `npm test` would itself be evidence that a tracked file had been modified.

#### 6.6.3.3 Performance Test Thresholds

**No performance threshold, timeout, rate limit, or throughput target exists in the repository.** Section 2.2.1.3 governs the treatment: any latency or throughput objective must be established by the consuming tooling, because none can be sourced from this repository. Every value below is a measured reference for regression comparison and is **explicitly not a commitment**; the timeout values are inherited Node.js defaults that deviation D-005 leaves unversioned.

| Dimension | Measured Reference Value | Configured Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Boot to readiness | 31.1 ms measured here; 29/29/34 ms and 26.9 ms in section 6.5 | None. An external window of a few seconds would be generous by two orders of magnitude |
| Request latency, new connection | p50 0.20 ms, p95 0.62 ms, p99 1.27 ms, max 6.25 ms over 200 requests | None. Includes client and loopback cost; the server's contribution cannot be isolated |
| Request latency, reused connection | p50 0.064 ms, p99 0.184 ms, per section 6.5.3.2 | None. Roughly half the new-connection figure, so the instrument must always be disclosed |
| Throughput | About 12,300 to 12,761 requests per second over reused connections | None. Capped by one single-threaded event loop; a host-specific observation only |
| Resident memory | 51,616 kB and 58,644 kB in two runs; a 48.2–61.9 MB envelope in section 6.5 | None. No memory limit, `--max-old-space-size` flag, or container limit exists |
| Protocol timeouts | `keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300000 ms | None set by the repository; all are runtime defaults, unversioned per D-005 |

A performance suite that gates on any of these numbers is gating on a property of the verification host, not of the artifact. The defensible use is trend comparison after a runtime upgrade or a suspected regression.

#### 6.6.3.4 Quality Gates

**The repository enforces no quality gate.** No CI check, no active Git hook, no `CODEOWNERS` file, and no branch protection artifact exists, so nothing prevents a change to the four tracked files. The matrix below records every gate a consuming harness can construct, its pass criterion, and whether anything in the repository enforces it.

| Gate | Pass Criterion | Enforced by the Repository? |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline integrity | `git status --porcelain` empty and `HEAD` equal to `1a0874d` | No — the freeze in `README.md` is advisory only; enforcement is by convention |
| File inventory | `git ls-files` returns exactly four paths and no subdirectory | No |
| Dependency-free install | `npm ci` exits `0`, audits one package, creates no `node_modules` | No, but the lockfile makes the outcome deterministic |
| Vulnerability audit | `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities | No — it passes trivially and can never gate |
| Readiness | The exact 41-byte banner appears on fd 1 | No — no health endpoint distinguishable from the default response exists |
| Response contract | `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, body exactly 14 bytes with the expected checksum | No |
| Output invariance | fd 1 still contains exactly one line after the request sweep | No |
| Clean teardown | Exit `143` after `SIGTERM`; port released | No — no shutdown handler and no supervisor exist |
| Static analysis | No lint or type-check configuration exists to satisfy | No — nothing to run, and the tools are not installed |
| Coverage threshold | No threshold can be evaluated | No — instrumented coverage is not obtainable |

The single most valuable gate is the first. Because the handler has one code path, **every other gate's expected value is invalidated the moment the baseline changes** — which is why the execution flow in 6.6.2.1 places the baseline assertion ahead of every other stage.

#### 6.6.3.5 Documentation Requirements

The repository's own test documentation is a two-line `README.md` that states the artifact is a test project for backprop integration and directs that it not be modified. There is no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no `docs/` directory, no test plan, and no inline comment in `server.js`. That is the complete inventory.

Because the fixture cannot document its own verification without being modified, the documentation obligation falls on the consumer.

| Documentation Item | Requirement | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline identifier | Record the commit the suite was written against — `1a0874d` — and the four expected file paths | Section 2.5.5 makes "the working tree matches commit `1a0874d`" the single assertion that defines the baseline |
| Expected values | Record the exact banner string, the 14-byte body, and the body checksum as literals in the suite | These are the only values the repository fixes; everything else is runtime-supplied |
| Runtime version | Record the Node.js version of every run | Deviation D-005 leaves the runtime unpinned, and it supplies four of the five response headers |
| Environment preconditions | Record that port 3000 on `127.0.0.1` must be free and exclusively held, and that the runner must be co-located | Assumption A-002; the routable address refuses connections |
| Known non-defects | Record that `npm test` exits 1, that `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and that `/health` returns the ordinary greeting | Deviations D-003 and D-001; the 17-path probe result in section 6.5.3.1 |
| Measurement method | Record the connection-handling method for every performance figure | New-connection and reused-connection latency differ by roughly a factor of two |

#### 6.6.3.6 Consolidated Test Strategy Matrix

Every testing capability this section is expected to cover, with its verified status and the practice adopted in its place.

| Capability | Verified Status | Practice Adopted |
|---|---|---|
| Unit testing | No test file and no unit smaller than the process; no exports to import | Out-of-tree `node:test` suite spawning `node server.js`; verified 2 of 2 passing in about 85 ms |
| Test organisation | No `test/`, `spec/`, or `__tests__/` directory | Suite lives outside the repository, grouped by observable channel |
| Mocking | No mocking library, and nothing mockable | `child_process.spawn` as the sole process boundary; no test doubles |
| Code coverage | No tool, no threshold; instrumented coverage not obtainable | 100% observable-contract coverage; statement coverage established by inspection |
| Test naming | No convention exists | Behavioural sentences naming the exact expected value |
| Test data | No fixture file, factory, or seed | Five in-source literals at `server.js` lines 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 |
| Integration testing | One boundary only — the loopback socket | 21-case invariance matrix; the `/health` trap documented explicitly |
| API testing | One endpoint answering every request identically | Compound assertion on status, content type and body bytes |
| Database integration | No persistence anywhere | Not applicable |
| External service mocking | No outbound call and zero locked packages | Not applicable |
| Test environment | No container, compose file, or `.env` | Single host, exclusive port 3000, co-located runner |
| End-to-end testing | The only viable granularity | Ten scenarios E2E-01 to E2E-10, all executed |
| UI automation | No markup, asset, or client script | Not applicable |
| Setup and teardown | No state to manage | Spawn, poll for the banner, `SIGTERM`, confirm exit 143 |
| Performance testing | No threshold declared | Measured baselines as non-commitments, with the instrument disclosed |
| Cross-browser testing | Plain text over loopback with no header negotiation | Not applicable |
| Security testing | No auth, TLS, validation, or credential code | Audit passes trivially; integrity testing is the meaningful control |
| CI/CD integration | No pipeline definition of any kind | Documented accommodations for a consuming pipeline |
| Test triggers | No workflow event and no active Git hook | Consumer-owned: pre-run, on-change, on-runtime-upgrade |
| Parallel execution | Impossible on one host — exclusive port bind | Pin runner concurrency to 1; shard across hosts; parallel requests within a test are fine |
| Test reporting | Nothing machine-readable produced | Built-in `junit`, `tap`, `spec` and `dot` reporters, all exercised |
| Failed test handling | No retry, no port fallback | Six-mode handling table; assert on first failure; never edit the fixture |
| Flaky test management | No test, therefore no flake | Three harness-side flake sources mitigated |
| Quality gates | None enforced by the repository | Ten-gate matrix, with baseline integrity first |

#### 6.6.3.7 Conditions That Would Change This Determination

The determination in 6.6.1.1 is falsifiable. Any one of the following would make a detailed testing strategy applicable and would require this section to be rewritten rather than amended.

| Condition | Why It Would Change the Determination |
|---|---|
| `server.js` begins to export its handler or server instance | Creates a genuine unit boundary; the handler could then be invoked in-process without binding a port, and instrumented line coverage would become obtainable |
| The handler begins to dereference `req` | Creates input partitions, reachable negative cases such as a `404`, and therefore a real test-design problem |
| A conditional, error handler, or shutdown handler is added | Creates branches to cover and makes `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` able to flush a profile on clean exit |
| The bind target becomes configurable via `process.env` | Removes the exclusive-port constraint and unlocks parallel and sharded execution |
| Any dependency is declared in `package.json` | Introduces a supply-chain surface worth scanning and a dependency boundary worth mocking |
| A test framework and suite are added to the repository | Replaces the out-of-tree approach with an in-repo one and makes runner configuration, naming and organisation real concerns |
| `scripts.test` is replaced with a real command | Removes deviation D-003 and makes `npm test` usable as a CI gate |
| A CI/CD workflow is added | Creates triggers, reporting, artifact retention and gate enforcement where none exist |
| Persistence or an outbound integration is introduced | Makes database integration testing and external service mocking applicable for the first time |
| Any SLA, SLO, or threshold is declared | Gives performance testing an acceptance criterion instead of a reference baseline |

Each of these requires editing one or more of the four tracked files, which constraint C-001 — the change freeze declared in `README.md` — places outside the sanctioned scope of the project. The determination is therefore stable for as long as the freeze holds.

#### 6.6.4.1 Repository Files Examined

- `server.js` - The entire system under test, 14 lines and 342 bytes. Established the five fixture literals that every assertion compares against: the loopback hostname (line 3), the port (line 4), the status code `200` (line 7), `Content-Type: text/plain` (line 8), and the 14-byte payload (line 9), with the bind and readiness announcement at lines 12–14. Also established, by exhaustive search, every property that determines the testing technique: zero `module.exports` and zero `exports` (no importable unit), zero `process.env` and zero `process.argv` (no configurable port, hence no parallelism), zero `req.url`/`req.method`/`req.headers`/`req.on` (a single input equivalence class and no reachable negative case), zero `.on(` (no `'error'` listener and no shutdown handler, which is why `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` never flushes a profile), and a single `require` targeting the Node core `http` module (no dependency boundary to mock).
- `package.json` - Established the declared test contract: `scripts.test` is the unmodified `npm init` placeholder `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`, which exited 1 on both invocations (F-007-RQ-001, deviation D-003). Also established the absence of `devDependencies` — the reason no test framework, assertion library, mocking library, coverage tool, or browser driver can be present — the absence of any script other than `test`, the absence of an `engines` field (deviation D-005, leaving the runtime under which any suite executes unversioned), and the `main: index.js` mismatch that makes `require('hello_world')` fail with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (deviation D-001) so that suites must target `server.js` by path.
- `package-lock.json` - `lockfileVersion: 3` with a `packages` map containing only the root key. Formal proof of a zero-package install graph, which is simultaneously the reason no testing tool is present transitively, the reason `npm audit` passes trivially, and the reason external service mocking has no target. Verified in use: `npm ci` reported "up to date, audited 1 package in 137 ms" with zero vulnerabilities and created no `node_modules`.
- `README.md` - Two lines. Established that the repository is itself a test fixture for backprop integration and that it must not be modified (constraint C-001) — the constraint that makes the entire approach out-of-tree, rules out adding any test file or dependency, and makes baseline-integrity assertion the most valuable quality gate. Also the reason the authoritative test suite is understood to live outside this repository.
