## 8.2 Cloud Services

**The system does not use cloud services, and this sub-section is therefore recorded as a determination rather than a design.** No cloud provider is selected, no managed service is consumed, no cloud account or credential is referenced, and — critically — the system could not be exposed through any cloud networking construct even if one were provisioned, because the listener binds the loopback address (**C-002**) and the source may not be modified (**C-001**).

### 8.2.1 Cloud Services Applicability Determination

| Applicability test | Result | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does any manifest declare a cloud SDK or provider client? | No | `package.json` declares no `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, or `overrides`; `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion: 3`) locks a single root entry with zero packages |
| Does any provider configuration file exist? | No | Filename audit found no `*cloudformation*`, `cdk.json`, `Pulumi*`, `*.bicep`, `*.tf`, `serverless*`, `app.yaml`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `fly.toml`, `render.yaml`, `Procfile`, or `*task-definition*` |
| Does the code reference any cloud endpoint or region? | No | Content grep across all four tracked files for `aws`, `azure`, `gcp`, `google-cloud`, `s3`, `lambda`, `cloudflare`, `heroku`, `vercel`, `netlify` returned no matches; §3.4 records that the only two network literals in the repository are the loopback bind constant (`server.js` line 3) and the self-referential startup URL (line 13) |
| Could a cloud service reach the process if one were provisioned? | No | A probe from the host's own routable interface to port 3000 was refused (`curl` exit 7, code `000`); §3.4 states the loopback bind means the service "cannot be exposed by any cloud networking construct without editing `server.js`" |
| Does the process make any outbound call a cloud service could serve? | No | §3.4 records zero HTTP-client, socket-connect, DNS, broker, or webhook calls and concludes "the process has no egress path" |

### 8.2.2 Provider Selection and Justification

No provider selection exists, and none is deferred pending a decision — the absence is structural rather than pending.

| Consideration | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Selected provider | None. There is no account identifier, region, project, subscription, tenant, or organisation reference anywhere in the four tracked files |
| Justification for having no provider | The repository's declared purpose is to be a test fixture for a *backprop* integration (`README.md`), consumed by a harness on the same host. A provider adds no capability to a loopback-only, stateless, 14-byte responder |
| Why a provider cannot simply be added later | Any provider integration requires either a new file (an IaC template, a workflow, a container manifest) or an edit to `server.js` to bind a routable address. Both are forbidden by **C-001** and would invalidate **F-006-RQ-003** |
| Lock-in exposure | Zero. With no provider, no managed service, and no dependency, the system has no vendor coupling of any kind (§3.4) |

### 8.2.3 Core Services and Versions

The conventional cloud service catalogue is empty. The table records each category with the specific evidence of its absence, followed by the only two platform services the system actually consumes — both supplied locally by the operating system and language runtime.

| Cloud service category | Status | Evidence of absence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compute (VM, container service, serverless function) | Absent | No instance definition, task definition, or function handler export; the process is started by a human or harness invoking `node server.js` |
| Managed relational or NoSQL database | Absent | §3.5 records no database; no driver, connection string, ORM, or migration file exists |
| Managed cache (Redis, Memcached) | Absent | No cache client and no cache semantics; the response is a literal, recomputed per request |
| Object storage / block storage / file share | Absent | `server.js` performs no `fs` operation and writes nothing to disk |
| Message queue, broker, or event bus | Absent | §3.4 records zero matches for `amqp`, `kafka`, `mqtt`, `nats`, `sqs`, `sns`, `pubsub`, `webhook` |
| Secrets manager / KMS / parameter store | Absent | No credential, key, token, or certificate material exists in the tree (§2.4.4); no `.env` or `.npmrc` at any level |
| Managed identity provider | Absent | §3.4 records "all callers are anonymous and indistinguishable" (**F-002-RQ-001**); `req` is never dereferenced (**F-002-RQ-004**) |
| CDN, DNS, global load balancer, WAF | Absent | No hostname other than the literal `127.0.0.1`; nothing can front a loopback listener |
| Managed monitoring, log, or trace backend | Absent | §6.5 records 66 conventional monitoring artefact paths probed and none present; the only telemetry is one stdout line |

| Platform service actually consumed | Provider | Version basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP transport, request parsing, response serialisation | Node.js core `http` module, required at `server.js` line 1 | Whatever the host runtime provides — `package.json` declares no `engines` field (**D-005**); verified on Node.js v22.23.1 |
| Process standard output (readiness line) and standard error (default failure trace) | Host operating system | Not versioned by the repository |
| Manifest parsing, script running, lockfile install | npm CLI, reading `package.json` and `package-lock.json` | Not pinned by the repository; verified with npm 11.18.0; **A-005** requires an npm release that understands `lockfileVersion: 3` (§3.3 records that format as npm v9+, backwards compatible to npm v7) |

### 8.2.4 High Availability Design

There is no high-availability design, and the architecture forecloses one.

| HA dimension | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redundancy | None. Exactly one instance can run per host | A second `node server.js` raises an unhandled `'error'` event (`EADDRINUSE`, `errno -98`, `syscall 'listen'`) and exits 1 — **F-001-RQ-004**, **A-002** |
| Multi-AZ or multi-region failover | Structurally impossible | Requires a routable endpoint; the bind is loopback-only (**C-002**) |
| Load balancing / health-check-driven traffic shifting | Not applicable | No balancer can reach the listener; additionally, every conventional health path (`/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/metrics`, …) returns the identical `200` / 14-byte body, so §6.5 records that a probe "cannot distinguish liveness from correctness" |
| Automatic restart / supervision | None | No systemd unit, PM2 file, container restart policy, or orchestrator exists; `server.js` registers no `'error'` handler and no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler, so failure and termination are both immediate and silent |
| Horizontal scaling | Structurally excluded | §2.4.3 records no `cluster` or `worker_threads` usage and concludes that scaling would require a source change forbidden by **C-001**/**F-006** |
| Recovery in practice | Operator re-launch | Measured 7 ms local clone; §6.5 records a ~23 ms restart and 26.9–34 ms to readiness — the practical mitigation for a single-instance design at this scale |

### 8.2.5 Consolidated Infrastructure Cost Estimate

Because nothing is provisioned, every cost line is zero for a structural reason rather than through an optimisation choice. This is the consolidated view referenced from 8.1.2.6; the "basis" column states the repository fact that makes the charge impossible, so the table remains valid as evidence rather than as a forecast.

| Cost line | Basis in the repository | Recurring charge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud compute (instances, containers, functions) | No compute definition of any kind; execution is by direct invocation on an existing host | None — no resource is created |
| Managed data services (database, cache, object store) | None referenced; the process never writes to disk or opens an egress socket | None |
| Network egress and inter-zone transfer | All traffic traverses the loopback interface; zero outbound sockets (§3.4) | None |
| Load balancer, CDN, DNS, TLS certificates | No routable endpoint exists to attach them to (**C-002**) | None |
| Secrets, KMS, identity services | No credential or key material exists in the tree | None |
| Observability backends (metrics, logs, traces, APM) | §6.5 records no exporter, agent, or shipping configuration; log volume is one 41-byte line per process lifetime | None |
| Container registry storage and image pulls | No image is built or published (see 8.3) | None |
| CI/CD compute minutes | No workflow definition exists in the repository (see 8.5) | Zero minutes |
| Third-party licences and subscriptions | Zero dependencies; MIT declared as a string in both manifests, with no `LICENSE` file | None |
| Source hosting storage | 913-byte working tree plus a 188 KB git object store in an existing GitHub repository | Negligible; no metered tier engaged |

**Cost optimisation strategy.** The optimisation is already maximal and is a property of the design: zero dependencies (nothing to fetch, cache, scan, or patch), zero build output (nothing to store), zero persistence (nothing to back up), and a ~47 MB idle footprint that fits inside the smallest plausible allocation. The only cost lever an operator retains is *not leaving the process running when it is not in use* — there is no idle-scaling, right-sizing, or reserved-capacity decision to make, because there is no provisioned capacity.

### 8.2.6 Security and Compliance Considerations

Consistent with §2.4.4 and §6.4, the cloud dimension contributes no security controls and no compliance obligations because there is no cloud footprint to secure.

| Consideration | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Cloud IAM, roles, and least-privilege policy | Not applicable — no account, principal, or policy document exists. The only access control in the system is network-level: the listener binds `127.0.0.1` (**F-001-RQ-002**, **C-002**) |
| Encryption at rest and key management | Not applicable — nothing is persisted; no KMS, key, or certificate material exists |
| Encryption in transit | Not implemented and not required off-host; traffic is cleartext HTTP confined to the loopback interface |
| Network isolation controls (VPC, subnets, security groups, NACLs) | Not applicable — the kernel already refuses every non-loopback connection to port 3000, which is a stronger boundary than any perimeter rule could express |
| Supply-chain exposure | Eliminated at the root: the dependency graph is one node with zero edges (§3.3); `npm audit` reports `vulnerabilities: {}` with all severity totals at 0 and `dependencies.total = 0`, so a vulnerability gate can never fire |
| Data exfiltration risk | No egress path exists at all (§3.4), so there is no channel through which data could leave the host even if the process were compromised |
| Regulatory or certification scope | None expressed or implicated (§2.4.4 and 8.1.1.6) |
| Residual risk carried by the cloud-free posture | The unpinned runtime (**D-005**): host-supplied Node.js defaults — including the framing headers of **C-004** and the timeout defaults recorded in §6.5 — are part of the observable contract without being under repository control |

### 8.2.7 Complete External Dependency Inventory

The section prompt requires all external dependencies to be documented. The complete set is four items, none of which is a cloud service and none of which is contacted by the running process at run time.

| External dependency | Nature and direction | Criticality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js runtime (core `http` module) | Host-installed prerequisite; loaded in-process at `server.js` line 1; no network involvement | **Required** — without it nothing runs. Unpinned (**D-005**), so the runtime's defaults are inherited (**C-004**) |
| TCP port 3000 on the loopback interface | Host resource claimed at start-up (`server.js` line 12) | **Required** — assumption **A-002**; if occupied, the process exits 1 with `EADDRINUSE` |
| npm CLI | Optional tooling that reads `package.json` and `package-lock.json`; no registry contact required (`npm ci --offline` exits 0) | **Optional** — needed only to run `npm ci`/`npm test`/`npm start`; **A-005** applies |
| Git and the GitHub `origin` remote | Design-time source of truth only; the running process never contacts it | **Optional at run time, required for distribution** — the checkout carries an ephemeral credential supplied by the environment and stored in no tracked file |
| npm public registry | A latent default that is never contacted; there is no package to fetch and no `.npmrc` anywhere (§3.3) | **Not required** — registry availability is not a runtime or build dependency |


## 8.3 Containerization

**The system is not containerized, and containerization is not merely absent — it would not achieve its usual purpose here.** No container artefact of any kind exists in the repository, and an image built around the repository as-is would produce a service reachable only from inside its own network namespace, because `server.js` binds `127.0.0.1`.

### 8.3.1 Containerization Applicability Determination

| Artefact or marker probed | Result | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.*`, `*.dockerfile`, `Containerfile*` | Absent | Case-insensitive filename audit across the whole tree (excluding `.git`) |
| `.dockerignore` | Absent | Same audit |
| `docker-compose.yml` / `docker-compose.*.yml` / any `*.yml` or `*.yaml` at all | Absent | Same audit — the repository contains **no YAML file whatsoever** |
| Base-image reference, registry host, image tag, or layer directive in tracked content | Absent | Content grep for `image`, `registry`, `tag`, `latest`, `alpine`, `distroless`, `slim`, `buildkit`, `layer` across all four tracked files returned no matches |
| Container runtime available in the verification environment | Absent | `command -v docker` reports nothing on the verification host (an environment observation, not a repository fact) |
| Semantic index corroboration | Empty result set | A semantic file search for deployment/Dockerfile/CI/IaC definitions and a semantic folder search for build-automation, release-pipeline, and orchestration-manifest folders both returned no results |

The repository has four files and no subdirectories, so there is also no directory (`docker/`, `build/`, `deploy/`) in which container tooling could be hiding.

### 8.3.2 The Structural Obstacle — Loopback Bind Versus Container Networking

This is the substantive finding of the sub-section, and §3.6.4 records it as well: an unmodified container built around this repository would expose the listener **only inside its own network namespace**, so a published port mapping would not reach it.

| Step in the reasoning | Grounding |
| --- | --- |
| The listener binds the loopback address, not a wildcard | `server.js` line 3 sets `const hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and line 12 passes it to `server.listen(port, hostname, …)`; there is no `0.0.0.0` anywhere in the tree |
| Loopback-bound sockets are unreachable from outside their network namespace | Independently verified on the host: a request to the host's own routable address on port 3000 was refused (`curl` exit 7, HTTP code `000`), while `127.0.0.1:3000` succeeded |
| Therefore a `-p 3000:3000` style publish would forward to a port with no listener on the container's external interface | Direct consequence of the two facts above; §3.6.4 states the same conclusion |
| The obvious remedy — binding `0.0.0.0` — is forbidden | `README.md` line 2 imposes the content freeze recorded as **C-001**; the loopback confinement is itself recorded as **C-002** and as requirement **F-001-RQ-002** |
| Net effect | Containerization could package the fixture, but could not publish it. Any harness would still have to execute inside the same namespace, which is exactly what running `node server.js` directly already achieves |

### 8.3.3 Requirements That Would Apply If Containerization Were Adopted

The following is documented **only** as the requirement set a future adopter would face. **None of it exists in the repository today**, and adopting any of it would require adding tracked files, which **C-001** forbids.

| Prompt-required area | What the repository's facts imply | Why it is unusual here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container platform selection | Any OCI-compatible runtime would suffice; nothing in the repository constrains the choice | There is no platform-specific construct (no compose service definition, no runtime flag, no volume, no health-check directive) to be compatible with |
| Base image strategy | A base image would have to supply the Node.js runtime, because the repository ships no runtime and pins no version | `package.json` declares no `engines` field (**D-005**), so **no base image tag can be derived from the repository** — the adopter, not the repository, would be choosing the runtime version and thereby the default behaviours recorded in **C-004** |
| Image versioning approach | The only version signal available is `version: "1.0.0"` in `package.json` and the commit hash `1a0874d` | The git history has **no tags at all**, so a tag-driven image versioning scheme has no input; the manifest version has never been incremented (single-commit history) |
| Build optimization techniques | Layer caching, multi-stage builds, and dependency pre-fetch layers would all be no-ops | There is no build step, no transpilation, and no dependency layer to cache: `npm ci` exits 0 and creates no `node_modules`. The build context is 913 bytes of source; because **no `.dockerignore` exists**, a naive `COPY . .` would additionally copy the `.git` directory (31,055 bytes of content, 188 KB of disk blocks) into the image |
| Security scanning requirements | Application-layer scanning would find nothing to report | The dependency graph is one node with zero edges (§3.3) and `npm audit` returns `vulnerabilities: {}` with `dependencies.total = 0`, so an SCA gate can never fire. **All** image CVE findings would therefore originate from the chosen base image, i.e. from the adopter's decision rather than from this repository's content |
| Runtime hardening | Nothing in the repository requires elevated privilege | No filesystem write, no privileged port (3000 is unprivileged), no credential material; the process needs only read access to four files (§3.6.7) |

### 8.3.4 Containerization Determination Summary

| Prompt-required area | Determination | Primary evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container platform selection | None selected; none present | No Dockerfile, Containerfile, compose file, or any YAML in the tree |
| Base image strategy | Not applicable; no image is built | No base-image reference in any tracked file; no runtime pin to derive one from (**D-005**) |
| Image versioning approach | Not applicable; no image and no tags | `git tag -l` empty; single commit `1a0874d`; manifest version fixed at `1.0.0` |
| Build optimization techniques | Not applicable; there is no build | §3.6.2 — "the tracked tree *is* the artefact"; `npm ci` is a no-op |
| Security scanning requirements | Not applicable at the application layer | `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities across one audited package; zero dependencies (§3.3) |
| Practical value of containerizing as-is | Negative | An unmodified image cannot publish the loopback listener (§3.6.4, **C-002**), and modifying the bind is forbidden (**C-001**) |


## 8.4 Orchestration

**The system does not require orchestration, and no orchestration platform could manage it usefully in its present form.** Orchestration exists to schedule replicas, route traffic to them, probe their health, and scale them. This system supports exactly one replica per host, admits no routed traffic, and exposes no distinguishable health signal — so all four orchestration functions are inapplicable.

### 8.4.1 Orchestration Applicability Determination

| Artefact probed | Result | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kubernetes manifests (`k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `manifests/`, any Deployment/Service/Ingress YAML) | Absent | Filename audit across the whole tree; the repository contains **no YAML file at all** and **no subdirectories at all** |
| Helm chart (`Chart.yaml`, `values*.yaml`, `helm/`) or Kustomize overlay (`kustomization*`) | Absent | Same audit |
| Nomad job (`*.nomad`), Docker Swarm stack, ECS task definition (`*task-definition*`) | Absent | Same audit |
| Process supervisors (`ecosystem.config*` for PM2, `*.service` for systemd, `Procfile*`) | Absent | Same audit |
| Scheduling or replica vocabulary in tracked content | Absent | §4 records zero matches for `cluster`, `worker`, `queue`, `scheduler`, `cron`, `batch`, `job` across all four files |
| Orchestration CLIs in the verification environment | Absent | `command -v kubectl` and `command -v helm` report nothing on the verification host (an environment observation, not a repository fact) |

### 8.4.2 Why Orchestration Cannot Apply

Three independent structural blockers exist; any one of them alone would be sufficient.

| Blocker | Mechanism | Consequence for an orchestrator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-instance port exclusivity | A second `node server.js` on the same host raises an unhandled `'error'` event — `Error: listen EADDRINUSE`, `errno -98`, `syscall 'listen'`, address `127.0.0.1`, port `3000` — and the process exits with code 1 (**F-001-RQ-004**, assumption **A-002**) | `replicas: 2` on a single node fails immediately; §3.6.3 states that consuming automation "must serialise its use of port 3000" |
| Loopback-only bind | `server.js` line 3 binds `127.0.0.1`; a probe to the host's routable address on port 3000 is refused (`curl` exit 7, code `000`) — **C-002**, **F-001-RQ-002** | A Kubernetes `Service`, an ingress controller, a Swarm routing mesh, or a Nomad `service` block cannot reach the container's port; §3.6.4 records the same conclusion for the container case |
| No distinguishable health signal | Every conventional probe path (`/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/metrics`, …) returns the identical `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte body, and §6.5 records that all 17 probed paths collapse to one signature with "no negative case to assert against — a 404 is unreachable" | Liveness and readiness probes cannot fail for an application reason; they would report healthy for any request that a bound socket answers, so probe-driven restart and traffic-gating semantics carry no information |

A fourth, governing consideration: adding a manifest, chart, or supervisor file to the repository would itself violate the content freeze recorded in **C-001** and invalidate **F-006-RQ-003**.

### 8.4.3 Prompt-Area Determinations

| Prompt-required area | Determination | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Orchestration platform selection | None selected, none present, none required | No manifest, chart, job file, or supervisor config exists anywhere in the four tracked files |
| Cluster architecture | Not applicable — the deployment unit is one OS process on one host | §2.4.3 records a single process, a single port, and a single host, with no `cluster` or `worker_threads` usage |
| Service deployment strategy | Direct process invocation: `node server.js` (or `npm start`, which resolves only through npm's implicit default — **D-004**) | Verified; readiness is signalled by the single stdout line from `server.js` line 13 (**F-003-RQ-001**) |
| Auto-scaling configuration | Not applicable and structurally excluded | Horizontal scaling is impossible (port exclusivity + loopback bind); vertical scaling changes nothing because JavaScript execution is single-threaded — measured throughput was ~12,300–12,761 requests/second on one core (§6.5.3.2) |
| Resource allocation policies | None declared by the repository | `package.json` declares no `engines`, no resource hint, and no limit of any kind; there is no manifest in which requests/limits could be expressed |

If an operator nonetheless wrapped the process in a scheduler of their own, the following allocations follow from the measurements in 8.1.1.4 and §6.5.3.5. **These are derived operator guidance, not repository declarations** — the repository states no resource requirement anywhere.

| Allocation dimension | Derived value | Measurement it derives from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU request / limit | 100m request; 1 core is more than sufficient as a limit | ~0.18 s of CPU consumed serving ~1,300 requests; single JS thread |
| Memory request / limit | 128 MB request, 256 MB limit | Idle RSS ≈ 46.9 MB; VmRSS ceiling 61.9 MB after 25,000 requests (+268 kB across the final 20,000) |
| Ephemeral storage | 100 MB is generous; the workload itself writes nothing | 913 bytes of source, no `node_modules`, zero log or data growth under load |
| Replica count | Exactly 1 per network namespace | `EADDRINUSE` on the second bind (**A-002**) |
| File-descriptor and thread ceilings | Well under any default (22 fds, 7 threads, both constant) | §6.5.3.5 |

### 8.4.4 Process Lifecycle Management in Place of Orchestration

What actually manages the process is an operator or a harness. The repository provides no supervision, and the process's response to signals is entirely the Node.js runtime default.

| Lifecycle concern | Actual behaviour | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Manual or harness invocation of `node server.js`; readiness is the single 41-byte stdout line | `server.js` lines 12–14; measured 26.9–34 ms to readiness (§6.5) |
| Restart on failure | None. There is no supervisor, no restart policy, and no `'error'` listener, so a bind conflict is terminal (exit code 1) | Verified `EADDRINUSE` probe; §6.5 runbooks RB-01…RB-04 assign recovery to the operator |
| Graceful shutdown / draining | None. No `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` handler is registered, so termination is immediate and silent, releasing the port at once | §6.5 records the exit-code census 143 (SIGTERM), 130 (SIGINT), 129 (SIGHUP), 131 (SIGQUIT), 137 (SIGKILL) — each exactly `128 + signum`, which proves no handler ran |
| Rolling update / zero-downtime replacement | Not achievable. The old process must release port 3000 before the new one can bind it | Port exclusivity (**A-002**); measured restart ≈23 ms, so the outage window is short but real |
| Concurrency safety within the single instance | Safe. The handler holds no state and never reads the request | §2.4.3 records the stateless handler; §6.5 measured 100 requests at parallelism 50 with zero non-200 responses |
| Operator obligation | Serialise all use of port 3000 on the host, and stop the process when it is not in use | §3.6.3; there is no idle timeout or self-termination in the code |


## 8.5 CI/CD Pipeline

**No CI/CD pipeline exists in this repository.** The engineering content of this sub-section is therefore twofold: the evidence that no pipeline is defined, and — because the repository is consumed by an external harness — a precise account of what a *consuming* pipeline actually encounters at every stage, including the two stages that fail or gate on nothing.

### 8.5.1 CI/CD Applicability Determination

| Pipeline artefact probed | Result | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.github/` and any workflow file | Absent | Filename audit of the whole tree; corroborated by §3.6.5 |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.travis.yml`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `.drone*`, `.buildkite`, `*.tekton` | Absent | Same audit — the repository contains **no YAML file of any kind** |
| Build drivers (`Makefile*`, `*.sh`, `*.bat`, `*.ps1`) and PaaS descriptors (`Procfile*`, `app.yaml`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `fly.toml`, `render.yaml`, `serverless*`) | Absent | Same audit |
| Active Git hooks | None | `.git/hooks` contains 14 entries and **all 14 are `.sample` templates**, so `ls .git/hooks \| grep -vc '\.sample$'` yields 0 |
| `CODEOWNERS`, review policy, or release configuration (`.releaserc`, changelog) | Absent | §3.6.5 records the absent `CODEOWNERS`; no changelog or release config exists among the four tracked files |
| Semantic index corroboration | Empty result set | Semantic searches for CI/deployment definitions and for build-automation/release-pipeline folders both returned no results |

Two consequences follow. First, nothing inside the repository enforces the content freeze of **C-001** — §3.6.5 records that enforcement is by convention only. Second, §1.3.2.4 explicitly records use of this repository as a CI quality gate as an **unsupported use case**, because the declared test command fails by design (**D-003**).

### 8.5.2 Build Pipeline

#### 8.5.2.1 Source Control Triggers

No trigger is defined, and no trigger mechanism is present to define one with.

| Trigger dimension | Observed state | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branches | One branch, `main`, tracking `origin/main` | There is no branch pattern (`develop`, `release/*`, `feature/*`) on which a workflow could be filtered |
| Commits | Exactly one commit, `1a0874d26682e67dac744b29b198b666cf39c126`, message "Add files via upload" | The message pattern indicates a web-UI bulk upload rather than an engineered commit flow; there is no commit-message convention for a pipeline to parse |
| Tags and releases | None (`git tag -l` is empty) | Tag-triggered release pipelines have no input |
| Repository-side automation | None: no workflow file, no active hook, no `CODEOWNERS` | Push, pull-request, schedule, and manual-dispatch triggers are all undefined. Server-side settings such as branch protection are not observable from a checkout and are therefore not asserted here either way |
| Remote | A single `origin` HTTPS remote for the GitHub repository `Sandeep01Kumar/28-july-existing-projects-qa-test-01`; the URL carries an ephemeral checkout credential supplied by the environment and stored in no tracked file | Hosting on GitHub does not imply automation: §3.6.5 records that GitHub Actions is **not present** despite GitHub hosting |
| What a consuming pipeline can trigger on | A change to the four tracked files, detected externally | The only meaningful trigger semantics are *"has the frozen baseline moved?"* (**F-006-RQ-003**) |

#### 8.5.2.2 Build Environment Requirements

| Requirement | Specification | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime | A Node.js build providing CommonJS `require`, the core `http` module, and ES2015 syntax (**A-001**) | No version is pinned — `package.json` declares no `engines` field (**D-005**). All measurements in this section used Node.js v22.23.1 |
| Package manager | npm, only if manifest-driven steps are run; must understand `lockfileVersion: 3` (**A-005**) | Measured with npm 11.18.0; §3.3 records the format as npm v9+, backwards compatible to npm v7 |
| Version control | Git, to obtain the tree and assert the baseline | Measured with git 2.43.0; a local clone completed in 7 ms |
| Network access | **None required.** `npm ci --offline` exits 0 | The npm registry is a latent default that is never contacted (§3.3) |
| Credentials | **None required** at any stage | No `.npmrc`, token, key, or certificate exists in the tree (§2.4.4) |
| Compute and disk for the build | 1 vCPU; ~120 MB of disk, dominated entirely by the Node.js binary | The repository contributes 913 bytes of source; no build output is produced |
| Host resource claimed only for verification | TCP port 3000 free on the loopback interface | Needed only if the pipeline smoke-tests the listener; **A-002** applies and use must be serialised |
| Toolchain that is *not* required | Container runtime, IaC CLI, `make`, linter, formatter, type checker, test runner | §3.6.1/§3.6.2 record all of these as absent; none is installed on the verification host either |

#### 8.5.2.3 Dependency Management

Dependency management is fully determinate and completely inert.

| Aspect | Measured behaviour | Consequence for a pipeline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declared dependencies | Zero across every dependency-bearing manifest field (§3.3) | Nothing to resolve, cache, or pin beyond what is already committed |
| Lockfile | `package-lock.json`, 247 bytes, `lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`, a single `""` root entry naming `hello_world@1.0.0` with licence MIT (**F-005-RQ-001**, **F-005-RQ-003**) | Lockfile integrity checks pass trivially; there is no transitive graph to audit |
| `npm ci` | Exit 0; "up to date", "audited 1 package", "found 0 vulnerabilities"; measured 188 / 181 / 179 ms across three consecutive runs on the verification host | Install is a sub-second no-op; §3.6.2 measured roughly 120 ms on its host, the same order of magnitude |
| `node_modules` | **Never created** | Assumption **A-004**: automation must not assert that `node_modules` exists, and dependency-cache steps have nothing to cache |
| Offline capability | `npm ci --offline` exits 0 with the same output | Registry outages and air-gapped runners are non-issues |
| Manifest consistency obligation | The identity fields of `package.json` and the `package-lock.json` root record must continue to agree (`hello_world`, `1.0.0`, MIT) | §2.4.5 records this as the only synchronisation duty in the repository |

#### 8.5.2.4 Artifact Generation and Storage

§3.6.2 states the position exactly: **the tracked tree *is* the artefact.** No pipeline stage produces a new artefact, and no artefact repository is involved.

| Artefact concern | Observed state | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build output | None. No transpilation, bundling, minification, or native compilation occurs | No bundler, compiler, or build script exists; the only npm script is `test` |
| The artefact itself | The four tracked files, 913 bytes in total: `README.md` 73 B, `package-lock.json` 247 B, `package.json` 251 B, `server.js` 342 B | Byte counts measured on the checkout |
| Artefact store | The git object store only — 31,055 bytes of content occupying 188 KB of disk blocks, mirrored by the GitHub `origin` remote | `du` on `.git`; `git remote -v` |
| Package publication | Not possible as configured. `package.json` declares no `files`, `publishConfig`, `repository`, `bin`, or `private` field, and `main: "index.js"` points at a file that does not exist, so `require('hello_world')` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (**D-001**, **C-005**) | §3.6.2/§3.6.3 |
| Container image or registry | None (see 8.3) | No image is built, tagged, or pushed |
| Artefact versioning | Static `version: "1.0.0"` in both manifests; no tags and a single commit, so the commit hash `1a0874d` is the only unique artefact identifier available | `git tag -l` empty; §2.5.5 treats the commit as the requirement baseline |
| Retention and promotion of artefacts | Not applicable — the same immutable commit is used everywhere | See 8.1.2.3 |

#### 8.5.2.5 Quality Gates

This is the most consequential part of the pipeline analysis: **every conventional quality gate is either impossible to fail or guaranteed to fail, and neither outcome carries information about the software.**

| Gate | Behaviour against this repository | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit / integration tests | `npm test` runs `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1` and terminates with exit code **1** | **Fails by design.** Deviation **D-003**, requirement **F-007-RQ-001**; §3.6.5 requires the consuming pipeline to skip the stage or explicitly tolerate exit 1 |
| Dependency vulnerability scan | `npm audit --json` returns `vulnerabilities: {}` with every severity total at 0, `dependencies.prod = 1`, `dependencies.total = 0`; exit 0 | **Can never fire.** Safe to run, but it gates on an empty graph |
| Lint / format / type check | No configuration exists for any tool, and none is installed (§3.6.1) | **Nothing to run.** A gate would have to be added as a new tracked file, which **C-001** forbids |
| Code coverage threshold | Not measurable with built-in tooling: §6.6 records that V8 coverage profiles are never flushed because the process registers no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler and never exits cleanly | **Not applicable.** §6.6 expresses coverage behaviourally instead of by line |
| Build success | No build stage exists | **Vacuously green** |
| Container image scan | No image is produced (8.3) | **Not applicable** |
| Licence compliance scan | Zero dependencies; MIT declared as a string in both manifests, with no `LICENSE` file present | **Vacuously green**, though the missing `LICENSE` file is worth noting for any downstream compliance tooling |
| **Content-integrity assertion** | `git status --porcelain` must be empty and `HEAD` must remain `1a0874d` | **The only gate that carries information.** §2.5.5 records that any change to a tracked file simultaneously establishes a new requirement baseline and violates **F-006-RQ-003** |

### 8.5.3 Deployment Pipeline

#### 8.5.3.1 Deployment Strategy

None of the strategies named in the section prompt is achievable, for a single mechanical reason: two instances cannot coexist on one host.

| Strategy | Achievable? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blue-green | No | Both colours would need to bind `127.0.0.1:3000` simultaneously; the second bind raises unhandled `EADDRINUSE` and exits 1 (**A-002**, **F-001-RQ-004**). There is also no router to switch traffic between them (**C-002**) |
| Canary | No | Requires traffic splitting across two versions — impossible without a proxy that can reach a loopback listener, and impossible to run two instances in the first place |
| Rolling update | No | A rolling update presumes N > 1 replicas; the maximum is 1 per host (§3.6.3) |
| Recreate (stop-then-start) | **Yes — this is the actual strategy** | The old process must exit and release port 3000, then `node server.js` is invoked again. §6.5 measured a ~23 ms restart and 26.9–34 ms to readiness, so the outage window is short but non-zero |
| In-place hot reload | No | No watcher, no supervisor, no `SIGHUP` handler; SIGHUP terminates the process with exit code 129 (§6.5) |

#### 8.5.3.2 Environment Promotion Workflow

There is no promotion workflow because there is only one environment; the full evidence and the promotion diagram are in 8.1.2.3 (Diagram **8.1.2-A**) and are not duplicated here. In summary: the single commit on `main` is cloned directly onto whichever host will run it, no environment-specific configuration exists to substitute (**C-003**), and no approval gate, change record, or promotion tool is present in the repository.

#### 8.5.3.3 Rollback Procedures

| Rollback aspect | Procedure | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rollback target | Commit `1a0874d` — the only commit, and therefore the only possible target | `git log` shows a single commit; no tags exist |
| Mechanism | Stop the process, `git checkout` the baseline commit (or re-clone), relaunch `node server.js` | Measured: 7 ms local clone, ~23 ms process restart, 26.9–34 ms to readiness (§6.5) |
| Data restoration | None required | Nothing is persisted; §6.5 records zero storage growth even after 25,000 requests |
| Recovery point objective | Zero data loss, by construction | The system holds no mutable state at all |
| Artefact rollback | Not applicable | There is no registry, image, or published package to revert (8.5.2.4) |
| Failed-rollback risk | Port 3000 still held by the previous process | Terminal `EADDRINUSE` with no retry; §6.5 runbooks RB-01…RB-04 cover operator recovery |
| Automated rollback | None | No pipeline, supervisor, or orchestrator exists to trigger one (8.4.4) |

#### 8.5.3.4 Post-Deployment Validation

Validation is entirely manual, and the complete assertable surface is small enough to enumerate. Each expected result below was measured against a disposable copy of the repository.

| Check | Command | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | Observe stdout after launch | Exactly one line: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` — 41 bytes including the newline (**F-003-RQ-001**) |
| Response contract | `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, body `Hello, World!` — `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` are Node defaults, not repository configuration (**C-004**) |
| Route and method invariance | Request any other path or method, e.g. `curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/does/not/exist` | Identical `200` and 14-byte body — no routing and no method discrimination (**F-002-RQ-001**, **F-002-RQ-005**) |
| Confinement | Probe the host's routable address on port 3000 | Connection refused: `curl` exit 7, HTTP code `000` — confirms **C-002**. §6.5 warns this signature is ambiguous, so a liveness probe must pin `127.0.0.1` |
| Telemetry quiescence | Re-inspect stdout after traffic | Still exactly one line — there is no per-request logging (§6.5 verified this at 25,000 requests) |
| Instance uniqueness | Attempt a second `node server.js` | Fails with `Error: listen EADDRINUSE`, exit code 1 — confirms exclusivity rather than indicating a defect |
| Baseline integrity | `git status --porcelain` and `git rev-parse HEAD` | Empty output and `1a0874d…` — the content-integrity gate of 8.5.2.5 (**F-006-RQ-003**) |

#### 8.5.3.5 Release Management Process

There is no release management process, and the repository carries no evidence of one ever having been exercised.

| Release management element | Observed state |
| --- | --- |
| Versioning scheme | `version: "1.0.0"` declared in `package.json` and mirrored in the `package-lock.json` root record; never incremented, because the history contains one commit |
| Tags, releases, or release notes | None — `git tag -l` is empty and no changelog, release configuration, or notes file exists among the four tracked files |
| Change approval and review | No `CODEOWNERS`, no review configuration, and no active hooks (§3.6.5); the governing control is the prose directive in `README.md` line 2 (**C-001**) |
| Release cadence | Not applicable. §2.4.5 records that "the correct maintenance action for this repository is **no action**" |
| Release artefact | The commit itself; §2.5.5 defines the requirement baseline as the repository state at commit `1a0874d` |
| Deprecation or sunset process | None declared; §1.3.2.5 records no future phases, roadmap, backlog, or changelog |
| Auditability of releases | The single-commit git history is the complete audit record: author, timestamp, and message, with a clean working tree confirming no post-upload modification (**F-006-RQ-003**) |


## 8.6 Infrastructure Monitoring

**No monitoring infrastructure exists in this repository, and none can be added to it without violating the content freeze (C-001).** §6.5 has already established the application-observability position in depth, recording that "Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system", that 66 conventional monitoring artefact paths were probed and none is present, and that the entire telemetry output is one 41-byte readiness line emitted from `server.js` line 13.

### 8.6.1 Scope and Division of Responsibility with Section 6.5

To avoid duplication, this sub-section is confined to the **infrastructure** dimension of monitoring — the host, its resources, its cost, its security posture, and the auditable facts about the artefact — and cross-references §6.5 for everything application-level.

| Monitoring dimension | Documented in | Position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application telemetry, health probes, alert conditions AL-01…AL-10, runbooks RB-01…RB-04, diagnostic channels | §6.5 | Not repeated here |
| Host resource monitoring, capacity envelope in infrastructure terms | 8.6.2 | Externally observed from the OS; nothing in-process |
| Performance metrics collection and reference baselines | 8.6.3 | No instrumentation exists; measured values are reference points, not targets |
| Cost monitoring and optimisation | 8.6.4 | No metered resource exists to monitor |
| Security monitoring | 8.6.5 | No access log, no audit trail, no agent |
| Compliance auditing | 8.6.6 | Nothing regulated; artefact integrity is the only auditable property |
| Maintenance procedures | 8.6.7 | The correct routine action is no action (§2.4.5) |

### 8.6.2 Resource Monitoring Approach

There is no agent, exporter, sidecar, or scrape configuration in the repository, and the process publishes no metric of its own. Consequently **all resource monitoring must be external and OS-level**, using tools the operator already has. The signals below are those that were actually read during verification.

| Observable signal | Source on the host | Observed value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resident memory | `process.memoryUsage()` / `/proc/<pid>/status` `VmRSS` | RSS ≈ 46.9 MB idle; §6.5.3.5 records 48.2 MB at start rising to 61.9 MB after 25,000 requests, with only +268 kB across the final 20,000 |
| Virtual memory and JS heap | `/proc/<pid>/status` `VmSize`; `process.memoryUsage()` | heapTotal ≈ 5.6 MB, heapUsed ≈ 4.7 MB, external ≈ 1.7 MB; §6.5 records `VmSize` at 1,014,076 kB, which is address space rather than consumption |
| CPU consumption | `/proc/<pid>/stat` user/system ticks | §6.5 measured ~0.18 s of CPU for ~1,300 requests on a 16-CPU host; the process is idle between requests |
| Thread and descriptor counts | `/proc/<pid>/status` `Threads`; `/proc/<pid>/fd` | Constant 7 threads and 22 file descriptors under sustained load (§6.5.3.5) — a flat line is the expected signature, so any drift is itself the signal |
| Listener presence | `ss -ltn` / `netstat -ltn`, or `/proc/net/tcp` | One listening socket on `127.0.0.1:3000`; §6.5 records the TCP-table key `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A` |
| Process liveness | `ps -p <pid>` and the loopback probe | Both are required: §6.5 warns that `curl` exit 7 / code `000` is ambiguous between "nothing is listening" and "probing a non-loopback interface", so a probe must pin `127.0.0.1` |
| Disk consumption | `du` on the checkout | Static: 913 bytes of source, no `node_modules`, and **zero** log or data growth — §6.5 confirms no storage growth under load |
| Cadence guidance | Operator choice; nothing in the repository schedules anything | No cron, timer, `setInterval`, or scheduled task exists anywhere in the tree |

### 8.6.3 Performance Metrics Collection

No performance metric is collected, exported, or exposed. There is no `/metrics` endpoint — and, importantly, one cannot be simulated: §6.5 records that all 17 conventional probe paths (`/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/metrics`, `/debug/vars`, and others) return the identical `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte body, so a scraper would receive the greeting rather than metrics.

The repository declares **no SLA, SLO, KPI, latency target, throughput target, rate limit, or timeout of its own**; §1.2 records that no KPIs are declared, and §2.2 records that no threshold exists from which a monitoring alarm could be derived. The values below are therefore **reference baselines for comparison**, not commitments.

| Reference baseline | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency, new connection per request | p50 0.138 ms, p90 0.197 ms, p95 0.237 ms, p99 0.346 ms, max 0.876 ms | §6.5.3.2 (n = 200) |
| Latency, reused keep-alive connection | p50 0.064 ms, p99 0.184 ms | §6.5.3.2 |
| Sequential throughput | ~12,300 requests/second (1,000 requests in 81 ms) and ~12,761 requests/second (2,000 in 156.7 ms) | §6.5.3.2 |
| Concurrency behaviour | 100 requests at parallelism 50 completed in 45 ms with zero non-200 responses | §6.5.3.2 |
| Time to readiness | 26.9–34 ms; a no-op `node -e "1"` start costs ~18 ms on the same host, so most of it is runtime bootstrap | §6.5.3.2 and this section's measurement |
| Inherited runtime timeouts that shape observed behaviour | `keepAliveTimeout` 5,000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60,000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300,000 ms, `timeout` 0, accept backlog 511 | Node.js defaults, not repository settings — **C-004**, and unversioned because of **D-005** |

### 8.6.4 Cost Monitoring and Optimization

There is no cost surface to monitor. No billing account, resource tag, cost-allocation label, budget, or metered resource is referenced anywhere in the four tracked files, and 8.2.5 records every cost line as structurally zero.

| Cost monitoring concern | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Billing telemetry or budget alerts | Not applicable — no cloud account or subscription exists to bill (8.2) |
| Resource tagging / cost allocation | Not applicable — no resource is created, so there is nothing to tag |
| The only real cost driver | Wall-clock time the process occupies capacity on an existing host: one core mostly idle and ~47–62 MB of RAM |
| Practical optimisation lever | Stop the process when the fixture is not being exercised; there is no idle timeout or self-termination in the code, so it will hold port 3000 indefinitely |
| Storage cost trend | Flat by construction — no logs, no data, no artefacts; 913 bytes of source and a 188 KB git object store |
| Data-transfer cost trend | Zero — all traffic is loopback and there is no egress socket (§3.4) |

### 8.6.5 Security Monitoring

Security monitoring is limited to what the host provides, because the application records nothing about its callers.

| Security monitoring capability | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access / request logging | **None.** stdout remains exactly one line and stderr zero bytes even after 25,000 requests | §6.5.2.2; the request object is never dereferenced (**F-002-RQ-004**), so no client identity, IP, path, or header is ever captured |
| Audit trail of requests or administrative actions | **None** — there is nothing to retain and no retention obligation (8.1.1.6) | §6.5 records no log growth |
| Authentication / authorisation failure monitoring | Not applicable — every caller receives `200`; there is no 401 or 403 path to alert on (§6.4) | §3.4 records that "all callers are anonymous and indistinguishable" (**F-002-RQ-001**) |
| Network-level detection (IDS, WAF, flow logs) | **None, and largely moot** — the kernel refuses every non-loopback connection to port 3000, so no off-host traffic ever reaches the process (**C-002**) | Verified refusal probe: `curl` exit 7, code `000` |
| Malformed-traffic visibility | Runtime-only, with no application record. An oversized header block returns `431` and stdout stays at 41 bytes, proving the handler was never invoked | Measured during verification; §6.5 records the equivalent `400`/`431`/`408` runtime paths as conditions AL-02 |
| Supply-chain / vulnerability monitoring | The only automatable check is `npm audit`, which reports `vulnerabilities: {}` with `dependencies.total = 0` | It is a valid recurring check, but it can never fire — the dependency graph is one node with zero edges (§3.3) |
| Information disclosure on failure | Bounded and small: the `EADDRINUSE` stack trace discloses only the address, port, syscall, and Node internal frames | §2.4.4 reaches the same conclusion; nothing about request content is ever printed |
| Integrity monitoring of the artefact | **The one security check that carries information** — assert `git status --porcelain` is empty and `HEAD` is `1a0874d` | **F-006-RQ-003**; §6.5 records unexpected baseline drift as an alert condition |

### 8.6.6 Compliance Auditing

There is nothing to audit for regulatory compliance — 8.1.1.6 and §2.4.4 both record that no compliance requirement is expressed or implicated. What *can* be audited is the integrity and provenance of the artefact itself, and that audit is fully mechanised by git.

| Auditable property | Evidence source | Expected finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Content immutability | `git status --porcelain`; `git rev-parse HEAD` | Empty output; `1a0874d26682e67dac744b29b198b666cf39c126` (**F-006-RQ-003**) |
| File inventory | `git ls-files` | Exactly four files, no subdirectories |
| Byte-level integrity | `wc -c` per file | `README.md` 73 B, `package-lock.json` 247 B, `package.json` 251 B, `server.js` 342 B — 913 B total |
| Provenance | `git log` | One commit, one author, one timestamp, message "Add files via upload"; §2.5.5 defines this commit as the requirement baseline |
| Dependency provenance | `package-lock.json`; `npm audit` | `lockfileVersion: 3` with a single root entry; zero vulnerabilities across one audited package |
| Licence declaration | `package.json` and the `package-lock.json` root record | MIT declared as a string; **no `LICENSE` file exists**, which downstream compliance tooling should expect |
| Data-handling audit | Not applicable | No personal, financial, or health data is processed; the entire payload is a static 14-byte literal |

### 8.6.7 Maintenance Procedures

§2.4.5 states the routine position directly: **the correct maintenance action for this repository is no action.** The procedures below are therefore verification and hygiene tasks rather than change activities.

| Procedure | Action | Trigger or cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline verification | Confirm the working tree is clean and `HEAD` is `1a0874d`; confirm the four byte counts | Before and after any use of the fixture (8.6.6) |
| Functional verification | Launch, confirm the exact readiness line, then assert `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes on `127.0.0.1:3000` | After every launch (the checklist in 8.5.3.4) |
| Port hygiene | Ensure port 3000 is free before launching, and stop the process when finished | Every launch; a second instance is terminal (**A-002**) |
| Manifest consistency | Confirm `package.json` and the `package-lock.json` root record still agree on `hello_world` / `1.0.0` / MIT | Only if either manifest is ever touched — which **C-001** forbids |
| Dependency hygiene | Run `npm audit`; expect zero findings, permanently | Optional; it can never fire (§3.3) |
| Runtime-drift watch | Re-run the verification checklist after a host Node.js upgrade | The material external risk: **D-005** means the runtime is unpinned, and §2.4.5 notes that a runtime change could alter the default framing headers of **C-004** without any code change |
| Deep diagnosis without code change | `NODE_DEBUG=http` (~5 stderr lines per request), `SIGUSR1` to open the inspector on `127.0.0.1:9229`, or `--report-on-signal` plus `SIGUSR2` for an 11-section JSON report | Incident only. **Hazard:** without the `--report-on-signal` flag, `SIGUSR2` **terminates** the process (exit 140) — see §6.5 |
| Recovery from failure | Stop any conflicting listener, then relaunch; re-clone if the tree has drifted | ~23 ms restart, 26.9–34 ms to readiness, 7 ms local clone; §6.5 runbooks RB-01…RB-04 |
| What must **not** be done | Do not add monitoring agents, exporters, health endpoints, dashboards, or configuration files to the repository | `README.md` line 2 (**C-001**); any such addition invalidates **F-006-RQ-003** |


## 8.7 References

### 8.7.1 Repository Files and Folders Examined

Every file tracked by the repository was read in full; there are only four, and all four are cited above.

- `server.js` — the sole executable artefact. Established the loopback bind (`const hostname = '127.0.0.1'`, line 3), the fixed port (`const port = 3000`, line 4), the invariant handler that never dereferences the request (lines 6–10), the `server.listen(port, hostname, …)` call and the single readiness `console.log` (lines 12–14), and — by omission — the absence of any `process.env`, `process.argv`, `'error'` listener, signal handler, `fs` call, `cluster`/`worker_threads` usage, or egress client.
- `package.json` — established `name: hello_world`, `version: 1.0.0`, `main: index.js` (a file that does not exist, **D-001**/**C-005**), the single `test` script that exits 1 (**D-003**/**F-007-RQ-001**), `author: hxu`, `license: MIT`, and the absence of `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `engines` (**D-005**), `files`, `publishConfig`, `repository`, `bin`, `private`, and any `start`/`build`/`lint` script (**D-004**). Size 251 bytes.
- `package-lock.json` — established `lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`, and a single `""` root entry naming `hello_world@1.0.0` with licence MIT (**F-005-RQ-001**, **F-005-RQ-003**), hence a zero-package install graph and assumption **A-005**. Size 247 bytes.
- `README.md` — established the declared purpose (a test project for a *backprop* integration) and the "Do not touch!" content freeze that governs the whole section as constraint **C-001**. Size 73 bytes.
- Repository root folder (`/`, the checkout top level) — established the complete inventory: four files and **no subdirectories at all**, which is the structural basis for every not-applicable determination in 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. Working tree 913 bytes.
- `.git/hooks/` — established that all 14 entries are `.sample` templates and **zero hooks are active**, so nothing inside the repository automates or enforces anything (cited in 8.5.1).
- `.git/` object store — established the artefact-storage position: 31,055 bytes of content occupying 188 KB of disk blocks; the only artefact repository the system has (8.5.2.4).

### 8.7.3 Verification Activities Performed for This Section

- **Exhaustive filename audits** across the whole tree (excluding `.git`) for six artefact classes — containers, CI/CD, IaC, orchestration, PaaS/serverless/process-supervision, and monitoring/environment/build tooling — returning **zero hits in every class**; the root listing contains only `.git`, `README.md`, `package-lock.json`, `package.json`, and `server.js`.
- **Two semantic index searches** — one for deployment/Dockerfile/CI/IaC definitions and one for build-automation, release-pipeline, orchestration-manifest, and provisioning folders — both returning empty result sets.
- **Content greps** across all four tracked files for infrastructure, cloud, observability, TLS, and configuration vocabulary (including `process.env`, `docker`, `kubernet`, `terraform`, `aws`, `azure`, `gcp`, `prometheus`, `https`, `tls`, `cluster`, `0.0.0.0`) — the only matches were the local `port` variable; and a container/registry census (`image`, `registry`, `tag`, `latest`, `alpine`, `distroless`, `slim`, `buildkit`, `layer`) returning **no matches**.
- **Executed-command evidence** against a disposable copy: `npm test` (exit 1), `npm start` (npm's implicit default), `npm ci` (exit 0, 188/181/179 ms, no `node_modules`), `npm ci --offline` (exit 0), and `npm audit --json` (`vulnerabilities: {}`, all severity totals 0, `dependencies.prod = 1`, `dependencies.total = 0`).
- **Runtime probes**: loopback `GET` returning `200` / `text/plain` / `Content-Length: 14`; `POST /does/not/exist` returning the same `200`/14 bytes; an off-host probe to the host's routable address returning `curl` exit 7 / code `000`; a duplicate launch producing unhandled `EADDRINUSE` (`errno -98`, `syscall 'listen'`) with exit code 1; and `process.memoryUsage()` giving RSS ≈ 46.9 MB, heapTotal ≈ 5.6 MB, heapUsed ≈ 4.7 MB, external ≈ 1.7 MB.
- **Size and timing measurements**: per-file byte counts summing to 913 bytes; `.git` at 31,055 bytes of content / 188 KB of disk blocks; a 7 ms local clone; and an ~18 ms no-op `node -e "1"` start.
- **Git facts**: single commit `1a0874d26682e67dac744b29b198b666cf39c126` on branch `main` with message "Add files via upload"; no tags; clean working tree; a single HTTPS `origin` remote for the GitHub repository `Sandeep01Kumar/28-july-existing-projects-qa-test-01` — the remote URL carries an ephemeral checkout credential supplied by the environment, which is stored in no tracked file and is deliberately not reproduced anywhere in this specification.
- **Diagram validation**: all four Mermaid diagrams in this section — **8.1.1-A** infrastructure architecture, **8.1.1-B** network architecture, **8.1.2-A** environment promotion flow, and **8.5-A** deployment workflow — were rendered to SVG with the local mermaid-cli before publication (all exits 0) and audited for balanced `subgraph`/`end` pairs, unique node identifiers, and the absence of any edge originating from or terminating on a subgraph identifier.
- **Repository integrity**: `git status --porcelain` was empty and `HEAD` remained `1a0874d…` after every activity; all verification ran against copies outside the checkout, honouring **C-001**, and no probe process was left running.

### 8.7.4 External Sources

**None were required or used.** Every figure in this section is either a repository fact from a tracked file, a measurement executed during verification, or an attributed cross-reference to another specification section. Two external lookups were attempted — the current Node.js release lines and the npm release that introduced `lockfileVersion: 3` — and neither returned a result, so **no external claim is asserted**: the runtime is documented as unpinned (**D-005**), and the lockfile-format statement is carried as an attributed cross-reference to §3.3 rather than as an independent assertion.

Host-level figures used for sizing guidance — Node.js v22.23.1, npm 11.18.0, git 2.43.0, 16 logical CPUs, ~127.8 GB RAM, a ~119 MiB `node` binary, and the absence of `docker`, `terraform`, `kubectl`, `helm`, and `make` — are **verification-environment observations**, not repository declarations, and are labelled as such at every point of use.


# 9. Appendices

## 9.1 Additional Technical Information

This appendix records residual technical detail that was verified directly in the repository but is not carried by Sections 1 through 8. It covers the line-addressable source index, the cryptographic and version-control integrity baseline of the four tracked files, the provenance of the single commit, the response envelopes produced under different HTTP protocol variants, the command reference with observed exit codes, the identifier conventions used across this specification, and the external standards that define the mechanisms the implementation depends upon.

All measurements reported here were taken non-destructively against the checked-out working tree at commit `1a0874d26682e67dac744b29b198b666cf39c126`. After every probe, `git status --porcelain` produced empty output and the digest of `server.js` was unchanged, so the "Do not touch" directive in `README.md` (recorded as constraint C-001 in Section 2.4.6) was preserved throughout.

### 9.1.1 Source Artifact Index and Line Accounting

The repository contains exactly four tracked files and no subdirectories other than `.git`. All four files carry POSIX mode `644` (`rw-r--r--`); none carries the executable bit, and `server.js` contains no shebang line. Consequently the program cannot be invoked as `./server.js` — the interpreter must be named explicitly (`node server.js`), which is the form used by every measurement in this specification.

| File | Octets | Lines (`wc -l` / git) | Final byte |
|---|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | 73 | 2 / 2 | `0x0a` (LF) |
| `package.json` | 251 | 10 / 11 | `0x7d` (`}`, no LF) |
| `package-lock.json` | 247 | 13 / 13 | `0x0a` (LF) |
| `server.js` | 342 | 14 / 14 | `0x0a` (LF) |
| **Total** | **913** | **39 / 40** | — |

Two different line totals are in circulation and both are correct under their own convention. The figure of 39 lines quoted in Sections 1.2 and 3.1 is the count of newline characters, as reported by `wc -l`. Git's `numstat` reports 40 insertions for the same content because it counts the unterminated final line of `package.json` as a line. The one-line discrepancy is therefore fully attributable to `package.json` ending at its closing brace without a terminating newline; no other file is affected.

`server.js` is line-addressable as follows. Lines 2, 5 and 11 are blank, leaving 11 non-blank lines. The file contains exactly one `require()` call, two arrow-function expressions, one template literal, no `"use strict"` directive and no `TODO`, `FIXME` or `HACK` marker.

| Lines | Role | Verified literals |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Imports the built-in `http` module under CommonJS | `require('http')` |
| 3–4 | Binds the two configuration constants | `'127.0.0.1'`, `3000` |
| 6–10 | Registers the invariant request handler on a new server instance | `200`, `'text/plain'`, `'Hello, World!\n'` |
| 12–14 | Activates the listener and emits the readiness line | template literal over the two constants |

The handler body is the entire request-processing logic of the system:

```javascript
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
res.end('Hello, World!\n');
```

The response body was confirmed octet-by-octet as `H e l l o ,` SPACE `W o r l d !` LF — 14 octets. The readiness line written to standard output is exactly 41 octets, matching the figure used in Section 6.5.

All four files are pure US-ASCII: a scan for octets outside the printable ASCII range plus tab returned zero matches in every file. No file contains a carriage-return octet, so every line ending is a bare LF. `server.js` uses two-space indentation while both JSON manifests use four-space indentation.

### 9.1.3 Repository Provenance and Identifier Divergence

The commit object carries four header fields and no parent, making it a root commit. Its unusually large size for a four-file change is explained by an embedded PGP signature block; the signature payload is intentionally not reproduced in this specification.

| Commit header field | Observed value | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| `tree` | `a650329703778bd216de08fdce13e4531003127c` | binds the four blobs listed in Section 9.1.2 |
| `author` | `Sandeep01Kumar <sandeep@blitzy.com>`, epoch `1785225641 +0530` | authored `2026-07-28T08:00:41Z` (13:30:41 at UTC+05:30) |
| `committer` | `GitHub <noreply@github.com>`, same timestamp | committer identity differs from the author identity |
| `gpgsig` | PGP signature block present | commit was signed server-side, not by a local developer key |

Taken together, the commit subject "Add files via upload", the `GitHub` committer identity and the server-side signature indicate that all four files were introduced through a web-based upload in a single operation rather than through a local development and commit sequence. This corroborates the absence of any local engineering residue: no `.gitignore`, no `.gitattributes`, no editor or linter configuration, and — as detailed in Section 9.1.8 — no active git hooks.

Five distinct names refer to this one artifact. The divergence is benign for a fixture but is a genuine navigation hazard for anyone searching for the project by name, and it is the reason this specification consistently anchors on file paths rather than on project names.

Branch topology is minimal: a local `main` branch, a remote-tracking `origin/main`, and `origin/HEAD` resolving to `origin/main`. There are no tags, no stashes and no additional refs. The configured `origin` remote is an HTTPS URL that embeds a short-lived access credential; that URL is treated as sensitive and is deliberately excluded from this document. Any reproduction of the clone command must supply credentials out of band.

### 9.1.4 Protocol-Variant Response Envelope Reference

Sections 1.2 and 6.5 describe the response as a status line plus header fields sourced from Node.js defaults. The table below completes that picture by recording how the envelope actually varies with the request's protocol version and method. The application code sets only `res.statusCode` and `Content-Type`; every other field, and the decision whether to frame the body with `Content-Length` at all, is made by the Node.js HTTP layer.

| Request variant | Header fields | `Content-Length` | Octets (header + body) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET`, HTTP/1.1 default | 5: `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, `Content-Length` | present, `14` | 149 + 14 |
| `GET`, HTTP/1.1 with request `Connection: close` | 4: `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection: close`, `Content-Length` | present, `14` | 121 + 14 |
| `GET`, HTTP/1.0 | 3: `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection: close` | absent | 101 + 14 |
| `HEAD`, HTTP/1.1 | 4: `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` | absent | 129 + 0 |

Three consequences follow, all of which matter to anyone writing an automated check against this fixture:

- The status line is always `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, even in response to an HTTP/1.0 request. A client that matches on the literal string `HTTP/1.0` in the response will never match.
- Under HTTP/1.0 the response carries neither `Content-Length` nor `Transfer-Encoding`, so the body is delimited solely by connection closure. An HTTP/1.0 client must read to end-of-stream to obtain the 14 octets.
- A `HEAD` probe receives no `Content-Length` and no body. A health check that asserts `Content-Length: 14` therefore succeeds over `GET` and fails over `HEAD`, even though the server is perfectly healthy. Probes should assert on the status code, or use `GET`, as the probe guidance in Section 6.5 does.

The raw HTTP/1.0 header block, exactly as written to the wire, opens and closes with:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Connection: close
```

Eleven response header fields that consumers commonly expect were probed on an HTTP/1.1 `GET` and none is emitted. This confirms at the wire level that the fixture performs no cache validation, no server-identity advertisement, no browser-security signalling and no session state — consistent with the security and interface determinations in Sections 6.4 and 7.1.

| Concern | Header fields probed (all absent) |
|---|---|
| Server identification | `Server`, `X-Powered-By` |
| Caching and validation | `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Cache-Control`, `Vary` |
| Browser security | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy` |
| State and alternate framing | `Set-Cookie`, `Transfer-Encoding` |
