### 9.1.7 Normative External Standards Catalogue

No file in the repository cites any external specification, and Section 1.4.4 records that the preceding sections were written without external sources. The behaviour observed empirically is nevertheless governed by well-established public standards, catalogued here so that reviewers can distinguish what the 14 lines of application code decide from what the surrounding standards and runtime decide.

| Standard | Designation | Mechanism it defines | Observed manifestation |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 9110 | HTTP Semantics | status codes, request methods, `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` semantics | `200` for every request; `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST` and `DELETE` handled identically |
| RFC 9112 | HTTP/1.1 message syntax and routing | message framing, `Connection` option, persistent connections | the four envelopes tabulated in Section 9.1.4 |
| RFC 2046 | MIME Part Two: Media Types | the `text/plain` media type | `Content-Type: text/plain` set on line 8 |
| RFC 1122 and RFC 6890 | Host requirements; special-purpose address registry | `127.0.0.0/8` loopback semantics | bind to `127.0.0.1`; connections to the container address are refused |
| RFC 8259 and ECMA-404 | JSON data interchange format | manifest and lockfile syntax | both JSON files parse without error |
| ECMA-262 6th edition (ES2015) | ECMAScript language specification | `const` bindings, arrow functions, template literals | the construct census in Section 3.1.2 |
| RFC 20 | ASCII format for network interchange | 7-bit character repertoire | zero non-ASCII octets across all four files |
| Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 | version-string grammar | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` ordering | `"version": "1.0.0"` in both manifests |
| SPDX License List | license identifier registry | short-form license identifiers | `"license": "MIT"` with no license text file |
| CommonMark | Markdown specification | ATX heading and paragraph syntax | the two-line `README.md` |
| IANA port number registry | service name and port assignments | the user-port range 1024–49151 | port `3000`, a development convention rather than an HTTP assignment |
| POSIX.1 (IEEE Std 1003.1) | shell, utilities and signals | `echo` and `exit` semantics; signal numbering | placeholder test script exiting `1`; the `128 + signum` exit codes in Section 6.5 |

One external lookup was attempted during the preparation of this appendix, seeking the published support window for the Node.js 22 release line that the verification environment uses. It returned no usable result, repeating the outcome recorded in Section 1.4.4. No claim about Node.js release support dates is therefore made anywhere in this specification, and the practical impact of the missing `engines` declaration (deviation D-005) remains qualitative rather than dated.

### 9.1.8 Inert and Absent Infrastructure Residue

The `.git` directory contains a `hooks` subdirectory with 14 files, every one of which carries the `.sample` suffix. These are the templates git installs at initialisation; because none has been renamed to an active hook name, **zero** git hooks execute on any operation. No commit-time formatting, linting, testing or signing is enforced locally.

Probing for conventional engineering artifacts found none of the 35 paths tested. The absences themselves are interpreted in Sections 1.3, 3.6 and 8.x; the ledger below is recorded here only so that the breadth of the probe is auditable.

| Category probed | Representative paths, all absent |
|---|---|
| Version-control configuration | `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes` |
| Licensing and project docs | `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` |
| Runtime and package pinning | `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.npmrc`, `engines` field |
| Code style and typing | `.editorconfig`, four ESLint variants, two Prettier variants, `tsconfig.json` |
| Environment and secrets | `.env`, `.env.example` |
| Containers and build | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore`, `Makefile`, `Procfile` |
| Automation and testing | `.github/`, `.travis.yml`, `jest.config.js`, `test/`, `tests/`, `__tests__/` |
| Source and artifact layout | `src/`, `dist/`, `index.js`, `node_modules/`, `.vscode/` |

Two consequences of the version-control absences are specific to this appendix. Because there is no `.gitattributes`, no end-of-line normalisation or content filter is configured — the LF-only line endings recorded in Section 9.1.1 are the literal committed bytes, not the product of a checkout transformation. Because there is no `.gitignore`, any file created inside the working tree becomes immediately visible to `git status`, which is precisely what makes the empty `git status --porcelain` output a reliable proof that the verification programme in this specification left no residue.


## 9.2 Glossary

The terms below are used in this specification with the specific meanings given here. Definitions are anchored to what was observed in this repository rather than to general industry usage, so that a reader can map each term onto concrete evidence. Where a term denotes something the repository deliberately does *not* contain, that is stated explicitly.

### 9.2.1 Fixture, Governance and Scope Terms

| Term | Definition | Basis in this system |
|---|---|---|
| Fixture | A deliberately unchanging artifact used as known-good input when verifying some other system | `README.md` designates the repository a test project; every section treats it as an input to another process rather than as a product |
| Backprop integration test project | The self-declared purpose of the repository: a target against which an integration named "backprop" is exercised | `README.md` line 2 |
| Change freeze | The prohibition on modifying repository content, which converts ordinary maintenance activities into out-of-scope work | The "Do not touch!" directive in `README.md`, formalised as constraint C-001 in Section 2.4.6 |
| Hello-world program | The canonical minimal program shape whose only purpose is to prove that a runtime and transport work end to end | `package.json` describes the project as "Hello world in Node.js"; the response body is `Hello, World!` |
| Verified absence | A documented negative finding established by probing for an artifact and not finding it, as distinct from an unexamined gap | Used throughout for monitoring (Section 6.5), user interfaces (Section 7.1) and dependencies (Section 3.3) |
| Deviation | A mismatch between what a manifest declares and what the repository actually contains | The `main` field naming `index.js`, which does not exist (D-005 family in Section 2.4.6) |
| Identifier divergence | The condition in which several different names refer to the same artifact, none of them authoritative | Five distinct names are catalogued in Section 9.1.3 |
| Ecosystem-level integration | Reliance on a runtime's built-in modules and its package manager's conventions instead of on third-party packages or external services | The only import is the built-in `http` module; the dependency set is empty |

### 9.2.2 Runtime, Process and Protocol Terms

| Term | Definition | Basis in this system |
|---|---|---|
| Loopback interface | The host-local network interface addressed by `127.0.0.0/8`, reachable only from the machine itself | `server.js` binds the literal `'127.0.0.1'` |
| Loopback confinement | The property that a listening socket cannot be reached from outside its host, making the service unreachable by design rather than by firewall policy | A request to the container's routable address is refused while the loopback request succeeds |
| Listener | The bound server socket that accepts incoming connections | Created by the `listen` call on line 12 of `server.js` |
| Bind contention | Failure to acquire an address and port because another process already holds it | A second instance exits with `EADDRINUSE`, `errno -98`, `syscall 'listen'` |
| Foreground process | A process that occupies its terminal and terminates only on signal or fatal error, with no daemonisation or supervisor | `node server.js` runs until signalled; no service manager, container or process supervisor is configured |
| Graceful shutdown | Orderly refusal of new connections and draining of in-flight ones before exit — a behaviour this system does not implement | No signal handler or `server.close()` call exists in `server.js` |
| Event loop | The runtime scheduling mechanism that keeps the process alive while a server handle remains open and dispatches each request callback | Implicit in Node.js; the open listener is what prevents the process from exiting after line 14 |
| Invariant response handler | A request callback whose output does not vary with method, path, query string, headers or body | Lines 6–10 of `server.js`; verified identical for `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST` and `DELETE` and for arbitrary paths |
| Response envelope | The status line plus header block that frames a response body | Enumerated per protocol variant in Section 9.1.4 |
| Status line | The first line of an HTTP response, carrying protocol version, status code and reason phrase | Always `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, including in replies to HTTP/1.0 requests |
| Persistent connection (keep-alive) | HTTP/1.1 connection reuse across requests, advertised by `Connection: keep-alive` | Emitted by default with `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; both fields come from Node.js, not application code |
| Close-delimited body | A body whose end is signalled only by connection closure, because no `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` framing is present | The HTTP/1.0 response variant in Section 9.1.4 |
| Media type | The `type/subtype` label declaring how a body should be interpreted | `Content-Type: text/plain`, the only header the application sets explicitly |
| Readiness announcer | The startup log statement that reports the bound address once the listener is active | The `console.log` in the `listen` callback, emitting exactly 41 octets to standard output |
| De-facto liveness probe | Use of an ordinary application request as a health check because no dedicated health endpoint exists | Section 6.5 establishes that any path returns `200`, so any request doubles as a probe |
| Signal boundary | The perimeter across which the process emits externally observable output, and therefore the limit of what can be monitored without changing code | Section 6.5 identifies exactly two crossings: the stdout readiness line and the HTTP response |

### 9.2.3 JavaScript Language and Packaging Terms

| Term | Definition | Basis in this system |
|---|---|---|
| CommonJS | Node.js's original module system, characterised by synchronous `require()` resolution and `module.exports` | `require('http')` on line 1, with no `"type": "module"` declaration to override the default |
| ECMAScript module (ESM) | The standardised `import`/`export` module system — not used here | No `import`/`export` statements and no `.mjs` file exist |
| Sloppy mode | Default, non-strict JavaScript execution semantics | No `"use strict"` directive is present, and CommonJS files are not implicitly strict |
| Built-in module | A module compiled into the runtime, requiring no installation step | `http` is the only module imported |
| `const` binding | A block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned | All four top-level bindings in `server.js` use `const` |
| Arrow function | A concise function expression form introduced in ES2015 | Two occurrences: the request handler and the `listen` callback |
| Template literal | A backtick-delimited string supporting interpolation | One occurrence, composing the readiness line from the host and port constants |
| Manifest | `package.json`, the file declaring package identity, entry point, scripts and dependencies | Declares seven top-level keys; `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `engines`, `type` and `private` are all absent |
| Lockfile | `package-lock.json`, which pins the exact resolved dependency tree for reproducible installs | Present with `lockfileVersion: 3` and a single root package record, pinning nothing because nothing is depended upon |
| Empty install graph | A dependency tree containing only the root package | `npm ls --all` reports `hello_world@1.0.0` followed by `(empty)`; no `node_modules` directory exists |
| Placeholder test script | A `test` script that emits a message and fails deliberately, standing in for absent tests | The `test` script prints "Error: no test specified" and exits `1` |
| Semantic version | A `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` version string ordered by precedence rules | `"version": "1.0.0"` in both the manifest and the lockfile |
| SPDX license identifier | A short registry token naming a license without embedding its text | `"license": "MIT"`, declared in both files with no license text file present |
| Registry | The package host from which npm resolves dependencies | The public default registry is configured implicitly and is never contacted, since nothing needs resolving (Section 3.3.3) |

### 9.2.4 Version Control and Integrity Terms

| Term | Definition | Basis in this system |
|---|---|---|
| Root commit | A commit with no parent, and therefore the beginning of history | The repository's single commit has zero parents |
| Blob | The git object holding a file's content, addressed by the hash of that content | Four blobs, one per tracked file (Section 9.1.2) |
| Tree | The git object recording file names, modes and the blob each name points to | One tree of 159 octets listing four `100644 blob` entries |
| Commit object | The git object binding a tree to author, committer, message and optional signature | One commit of 1007 octets, whose size is inflated by an embedded signature |
| Packed object store | Git's compressed container holding many objects in a single file | All six objects reside in one pack of 2.74 KiB, with zero loose objects |
| Web-flow commit | A commit created by a hosting provider's web interface rather than by a local client, identifiable by the provider's committer identity and server-side signature | Committer `GitHub <noreply@github.com>` with a `gpgsig` header and the subject "Add files via upload" |
| Working tree | The checked-out files on disk, as distinct from the object store | Verified clean by empty `git status --porcelain` output after all measurements |
| File mode `100644` | Git's mode for a regular, non-executable file | Recorded for all four entries in the tree; no file carries the executable bit |
| Shebang | A leading `#!` line that lets an operating system select an interpreter for a script | Absent from `server.js`, so `./server.js` cannot be executed directly |
| Incomplete final line | A file's last line that is not terminated by a newline character | `package.json` ends at `}` with no trailing LF, which is why line totals of 39 and 40 both appear (Section 9.1.1) |
| Content digest | A cryptographic hash used to assert byte-for-byte equality of a file | The SHA-256 baseline in Section 9.1.2 |
| Integrity baseline | The published set of digests against which a later copy of the fixture can be compared to detect drift | Section 9.1.2, which also enables verification without contacting the origin |
| Hook sample | An inert `.sample` template that git installs at initialisation and that never executes | 14 `.sample` files with zero active hooks, so no local automation runs on commit or push |

### 9.2.5 Operations, Observability and Verification Terms

| Term | Definition | Basis in this system |
|---|---|---|
| Non-destructive verification | Inspection that leaves file digests and version-control status unchanged, and therefore respects a change freeze | All measurements in Sections 3.3, 6.5 and 9.1 were re-checked against the digest and status baselines |
| Octet | An eight-bit byte, used when counting exact wire and file sizes | Response bodies are 14 octets; the readiness line is 41 octets |
| Health probe | A request whose response is interpreted as evidence that a process is alive or ready to serve | Section 6.5 documents the probe matrix; Section 9.1.4 records why a `HEAD` probe must not assert `Content-Length` |
| Alert condition (`AL-nn`) | A named trigger describing an observable state that would warrant operator attention | Defined in Section 6.5 for a system that emits no metrics |
| Runbook (`RB-nn`) | A documented operator procedure for responding to a specific condition | Defined in Section 6.5 |
| Component identifier (`CMP-nn`) | A stable label for an architectural element, used to cross-reference it between sections | Introduced in Sections 5.2 and 6.5 |
| procfs | The `/proc` pseudo-filesystem through which an operating system exposes per-process statistics | The external metric source used in Section 6.5, since the process itself emits no telemetry |
| Resident set size | The physical memory a process currently occupies, as reported by the operating system | Reported in Section 6.5 from procfs |
| Exit status convention | The shell convention of reporting a signal-terminated process as `128 + signum` | The signal exit codes catalogued in Section 6.5 |
| User port range | The `1024`–`49151` port band that requires no elevated privileges to bind and is not reserved for well-known services | Port `3000` sits in this band, which is why the server runs without privilege escalation |
| Baseline drift | Any measured divergence from a previously recorded value, treated as the signal that something changed | Digests, `npm ls` output and response sizes all serve as drift detectors for this fixture |


## 9.3 Acronyms

Acronyms and initialisms appearing in this specification are expanded below and grouped by subject. The third column states the acronym's relevance to this particular system. Because much of this specification consists of negative determinations, several entries name technologies or practices whose referents were verified to be **absent** from the repository; those entries are marked accordingly so that the expansion list cannot be mistaken for an inventory of what is present.

### 9.3.1 Protocol, Network and Web

| Acronym | Expanded form | Relevance in this specification |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | Hypertext Transfer Protocol | The only application protocol implemented; served by the built-in `http` module |
| HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 | Hypertext Transfer Protocol version tokens | Both request versions were exercised; the reply always carries the `HTTP/1.1` token (Section 9.1.4) |
| HTTPS | HTTP Secure (HTTP over TLS) | Absent — no certificate, key or `https` module usage exists |
| TCP | Transmission Control Protocol | Transport beneath the listening socket bound on port 3000 |
| IP | Internet Protocol | Addressing layer; the bound address is the IPv4 literal `127.0.0.1` |
| IPv4 | Internet Protocol version 4 | The address family of the bind literal; no IPv6 address is configured |
| URL | Uniform Resource Locator | The readiness line emits the server URL; request URLs are accepted but never inspected |
| URI | Uniform Resource Identifier | The general form of which request URLs are an instance; no routing on URI is performed |
| DNS | Domain Name System | Not used — the bind target is a numeric literal, so no name resolution occurs |
| TLS | Transport Layer Security | Absent — all traffic is cleartext over loopback |
| MIME | Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions | Origin of the media-type system from which `text/plain` is drawn |
| CORS | Cross-Origin Resource Sharing | Absent — no `Access-Control-*` header is emitted (Sections 7.1 and 9.1.4) |
| CSP | Content Security Policy | Absent — no `Content-Security-Policy` header is emitted |
| HSTS | HTTP Strict Transport Security | Absent — no `Strict-Transport-Security` header is emitted |
| WS | WebSocket (URI scheme `ws`) | No upgrade is honoured; an `Upgrade: websocket` request receives an ordinary `200` (Section 7.1) |
| h2c | HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP | Not supported; an `h2c` upgrade request also receives an ordinary `200` |
| REST | Representational State Transfer | Not implemented — there are no resources, methods or status codes beyond the single fixed reply |
| RPC | Remote Procedure Call | No RPC framework or interface definition exists in the repository |
| CDN | Content Delivery Network | Absent — no static assets and no edge distribution |

### 9.3.2 Language, Runtime and Data Formats

| Acronym | Expanded form | Relevance in this specification |
|---|---|---|
| JS | JavaScript | The sole implementation language; one `.js` file of 342 octets |
| ES | ECMAScript | The standardised language of which JavaScript is the implementation |
| ES2015 / ES6 | ECMAScript 2015, the sixth edition | The highest language edition required by the observed constructs (Section 3.1.2) |
| ECMA | European Computer Manufacturers Association | Publisher of the ECMAScript specification, now trading as Ecma International |
| CJS | CommonJS | The module system in force, evidenced by `require()` and the absent `type` field |
| ESM | ECMAScript Modules | Absent — no `import`/`export` syntax and no `.mjs` file |
| ABI | Application Binary Interface | The native module ABI version reported by the runtime in Section 3.1.3; no native addon is used |
| LTS | Long-Term Support | Release-line classification of the verification runtime; the repository itself pins no version |
| API | Application Programming Interface | Used to denote the Node.js interfaces consumed and the absence of any published interface of the system's own |
| CLI | Command-Line Interface | The only way to start and verify the system; commands are catalogued in Section 9.1.5 |
| JSON | JavaScript Object Notation | Format of both manifests; the response body is plain text, never JSON |
| YAML | YAML Ain't Markup Language | Absent — the repository contains no YAML file of any kind |
| TS / TSX | TypeScript / TypeScript with JSX | Absent — probed for and not found (Section 3.1.5) |
| JSX | JavaScript XML syntax extension | Absent — no component syntax or build step exists |
| I/O | Input/Output | Used when discussing the process's read and write counters in Section 6.5 |

| Acronym | Expanded form | Relevance in this specification |

| npm | Node Package Manager (the registry and CLI) | Manages the manifest, lockfile and the single placeholder script; installs nothing |
| MIT | Massachusetts Institute of Technology | The institution whose name the declared permissive license carries |

### 9.3.6 Encoding, Units, Time and Error Codes

| Acronym | Expanded form | Relevance in this specification |
|---|---|---|
| ASCII | American Standard Code for Information Interchange | All four files are pure 7-bit ASCII (Section 9.1.1) |
| UTF-8 | Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit | The default encoding assumption; indistinguishable from ASCII here because no byte exceeds `0x7f` |
| LF | Line Feed (`0x0a`) | The only line terminator used in the repository |
| CR | Carriage Return (`0x0d`) | Verified absent from all four files |
| CRLF | Carriage Return plus Line Feed | The HTTP header line terminator on the wire; not used in any repository file |
| EOL | End of Line | Used when discussing line terminators and the unterminated final line of `package.json` |
| EOF | End of File / End of Stream | How an HTTP/1.0 client must detect the end of the close-delimited body (Section 9.1.4) |
| B / KiB / MB | Byte / Kibibyte (1024 B) / Megabyte | Units for file sizes, pack size and memory figures |
| GMT | Greenwich Mean Time | The zone label Node.js writes into the `Date` response header |
| UTC | Coordinated Universal Time | Reference zone used to normalise the commit timestamp in Section 9.1.3 |
| IST | India Standard Time (UTC+05:30) | The offset recorded in the commit's author and committer timestamps |
| EADDRINUSE | "Address already in use" — a symbolic error constant, not an acronym | Raised when a second instance attempts the same host and port; accompanied by `errno -98` |
| errno | Error number | The numeric error code reported alongside the symbolic constant |
| CLK_TCK | Clock ticks per second | The scaling constant used to convert procfs CPU counters in Section 6.5 |

## 9.4 References

Every factual claim in Section 9 derives from one of the sources listed below: a file or directory in the repository, a verification command executed against the checked-out working tree, or an already-written section of this specification. No claim in this appendix rests on inference about unobserved behaviour.

### 9.4.1 Repository Files Examined

- `server.js` — established the complete application logic cited in Section 9.1.1: the single `require('http')` import, the `'127.0.0.1'` and `3000` constants, the invariant handler setting status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain` and the 14-octet body, and the `listen` callback that emits the 41-octet readiness line. Also established the blank-line positions (2, 5, 11), two-space indentation, absence of `"use strict"`, absence of a shebang and absence of `TODO`/`FIXME`/`HACK` markers.
- `package.json` — established the seven declared keys, the `hello_world` name, `1.0.0` version, the `index.js` value of `main` that has no corresponding file, the `hxu` author, the `MIT` license token, the placeholder `test` script, the absence of `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `engines`, `type` and `private`, four-space indentation, and the unterminated final line that reconciles the 39-versus-40 line totals.
- `package-lock.json` — established `lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`, the single root package record with matching name, version and license, and the empty locked dependency set.
- `README.md` — established the `hao-backprop-test` documentation title, the declaration that the project exists for backprop integration testing, and the "Do not touch!" directive underpinning the change freeze.
- `.git/` — established branch topology (`main`, `origin/main`, `origin/HEAD`), the absence of tags and additional refs, the clean working-tree status used as the non-destructiveness proof, the six-object store in a single 2.74 KiB pack, and the existence of a credential-bearing `origin` URL that is deliberately not reproduced.
- `.git/hooks/` — established the 14 `.sample` template files and the resulting total absence of active git hooks reported in Section 9.1.8.
- Repository root — established the complete four-file inventory, the absence of any subdirectory other than `.git`, and the 913-octet total.

### 9.4.2 Verification Activities Unique to This Appendix

| Activity | Method | What it established |
|---|---|---|
| Content digest baseline | `sha256sum`, `md5sum` over all four files | The integrity baseline published in Section 9.1.2 |
| Object store inspection | `git ls-files -s`, `git cat-file --batch-check`, `git cat-file -p`, `git count-objects -vH` | Blob, tree and commit ids with sizes; `100644` modes; pack statistics |
| Commit provenance inspection | `git cat-file -p HEAD`, `git rev-list --parents` | Root-commit status; `tree`, `author`, `committer` and `gpgsig` headers; the divergent author and committer identities |
| File mode and shebang check | `stat -c '%a %n'`, inspection of the first two octets of `server.js` | Mode `644` on all files and the absence of a shebang |
| Line and byte accounting | `wc -l`/`wc -c`, `git show --numstat`, last-byte inspection with `od` | The 39-versus-40 reconciliation and per-file final-byte values |
| Character and line-ending census | Byte-class scans for non-ASCII octets and carriage returns | Pure ASCII content with LF-only line endings |
| Protocol-variant response probes | `curl` with default HTTP/1.1, `--http1.0`, `-I`, and `Connection: close`; raw request writes over a shell TCP redirection | The four-variant envelope matrix, header-field counts, `Content-Length` presence and octet sizes in Section 9.1.4 |
| Absent response header census | Header-block inspection of an HTTP/1.1 `GET` for eleven named fields | Confirmed absence of all eleven fields |
| Command and exit-code capture | Execution of each command in Section 9.1.5 with status capture | Observed outputs and exit codes, including `npm test` exiting `1` and the second instance failing with `EADDRINUSE` |
| Non-destructiveness confirmation | `git status --porcelain` and digest re-verification after all probes | Empty status and unchanged `server.js` digest, upholding constraint C-001 |

### 9.4.4 External Sources

One external lookup was attempted while preparing this appendix, seeking the published support window for the Node.js 22 release line used in the verification environment. It returned no usable result, matching the outcome already recorded in Section 1.4.4. Consequently no external source is cited as evidence for any claim in this specification.

The standards catalogued in Section 9.1.7 — the RFC series entries, ECMA-262, ECMA-404, the SPDX License List, Semantic Versioning, CommonMark, the IANA port registry and POSIX.1 — are listed there as the normative context that defines the mechanisms observed empirically. They are not repository citations: no file in the repository references any of them, and each row in that table is anchored to a behaviour or literal that was measured directly.
